title: Kubernetes OIDC requires authentication for well-known and JWKS endpoints, contrary to OIDC Specification
body:
### What happened?

Kubernetes' OIDC authentication mechanism enforces authentication when querying the OIDC provider’s /.well-known/openid-configuration and JWKS (/keys) endpoints. This behavior contradicts the OIDC specification, which states that these endpoints must be publicly accessible.

The primary issue is that many services supporting resource server authentication (such as RabbitMQ and OpenSearch) rely on OIDC token validation but fail to work with Kubernetes OIDC due to the enforced authentication on these endpoints. These services expect to fetch the discovery and public keys without authentication, as per the OIDC spec, but Kubernetes' behavior prevents this, breaking compatibility with standard OIDC validation flows.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes should allow unauthenticated access to these endpoints, as OIDC-compliant providers may not require authentication for retrieving discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and signing keys (/keys).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. GET https://api.k8s,example:6443/.well-known/openid-configuration
E.R. get well-known without authentication

title: DRA: the capacityPools referred under ResourceSliceSpec should be unique across the resource pool rather than within the resource slice
body:
### What would you like to be added?

From @johnbelamaric https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130764/#discussion_r1993803425
```
For 1.34+: Theoretically, ResourceSlices are just, well, slices of a larger resource pool. Thus, the CapacityPools (and later the Mixins), could be considered unique across the resource pool rather than within the resource slice. If that's true, we could move to a place where we define capacitypools and mixins in one slice, and the devices in different slices. This would allow very large devices partitionable devices that share capacity pools and mixins (think: very large multi-host partitionable devices). Now, we don't do that today because this makes validation hard (impossible?) at admission time. But I want to at least introduce the idea that we might want to do it at some point. Likely we would need a controller to validate across slices and all slices in a pool generation would need to have something set in their status to say they are valid.
```

### Why is this needed?

Further validate the incoming resources.

title: CVE-2025-1767: GitRepo Volume Inadvertent Local Repository Access
body:
**Issue Details**
A security vulnerability was discovered in Kubernetes that could allow a user with create pod permission to exploit gitRepo volumes to access local git repositories belonging to other pods on the same node.
This issue has been rated Medium ([CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N)) (score: 6.5), and assigned CVE-2025-1767.

**Am I vulnerable?**

This CVE only affects Kubernetes clusters that utilize the in-tree gitRepo volume to clone git repositories from other pods within the same node. Since the in-tree gitRepo volume feature has been deprecated and will not receive security updates upstream, any cluster still using this feature remains vulnerable. 
Affected Components
kubelet

**Affected Versions**
All versions of Kubernetes

**How do I mitigate this vulnerability?**

To mitigate this vulnerability, you must use an init container to perform git clone operation and then mount the directory into the Pod's container. An example of this approach is provided [here](https://gist.github.com/tallclair/849601a16cebeee581ef2be50c351841).

Note: You can also restrict the use of gitRepo volumes in your cluster using policies such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or through Restricted pod security standard policy. You can use the following Common Expression Language (CEL) expression as part of a policy to reject use of gitRepo volumes: `has(object.spec.volumes) || !object.spec.volumes.exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))`

**Detection**

To detect whether this vulnerability has been exploited, you can use the following command to list all pods that use the in-tree gitRepo volume and clones to a .git subdirectory. 
`kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[].gitRepo.repository | test("^/")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, repository: (.spec.volumes[] | select(.gitRepo) | .gitRepo.repository)}'`

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](mailto:security@kubernetes.io) 

**Acknowledgements**
This vulnerability was reported by Christophe Hauquiert.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128152 is introducing a new feature that secures access to kubelet-pulled images. At the point of originally writing the feature, there were only 2 kinds of credentials one can use to pull images for their workload:

Restricted access to images pulled with a particular secret should be opaque to the user, and should behave the same for all kinds of secrets.

title: Explicitly prohibit Alpha + Enabled-By-Default feature gates
body:
It seems we don't mechanically enforce this currently with any tooling, but after asking around a bit nobody (so far...) seems to think this is something we'd want to allow.

It's confusing to users if we wind up saying "this is an alpha level feature, but also it is turned on by default", that just sounds like a beta or GA feature.

We should probably enforce this, possibly in `test/compatibility_lifecycle`.

I raise this now because SIG Testing is looking at revamping how we get coverage for alpha/beta features that don't have special requirements beyond feature gate enablement, and while designing this I made the assumption that "alpha+default-enabled" is not a featuregate state we want to support.

It seems like it would be best to actually prevent this.

/sig api-machinery
/sig architecture
/sig testing

title: allow log files to stick around after a pod is deleted for a configurable amount of time
body:
### What would you like to be added?

propagated from https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/10692

@ningmingxiao mentioned that containerd creates the logs but doesn't handle deleting them, that's done by kubelet if using K8s

-----------------

**What is the problem you're trying to solve**

We use daemons (fluent-bit, vector, etc) to suck up all of the logs for all pods that run on K8S nodes and send them to an aggregator (cloudwatch).

For short-lived pods that start and exit very quickly it turns out that the log files are deleted from disk before the daemon has a chance to read the log file.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A configuration parameter in containerd to keep the log files around for an amount of time like 60s before they are deleted. This would allow me to configure the daemon to ensure it can find the files and read them before they are deleted.

**Additional context**

I'm generally running on AWS EKS, so I'd be looking at configuring containerd via cloud-init but that is already supported.

https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/issues/20541

Is there a better way to do this than what I'm proposing? I believe containerd is managing the lifecycle of those logfiles, but maybe that isn't correct? If not, I'd appreciate being pointed in the right direction!

-------------------

if I'm correct, this would be done in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go potentially...? 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go#L202-L226 looks to handle cleaning up logs today, we'd just need a configurable delay mechanism in there?

_Note: ideally we wouldn't set this to a high value, to avoid consuming disk space for unnecessary amounts of time. if a hardcoded maximum value was to be configured for node resiliency reasons, that would be wise. maybe 90 seconds?_

### Why is this needed?

to avoid logs from short lived containers not being shipped off to centralised logging systems, due to the file being deleted before it can be read by the log shipping daemon

title: Cronjob may run at unexpected time in certain conditions
body:
### What happened?

We had a job scheduled to run every day at 11pm.
We updated it to run every day at 5am and we applied the change between 5am and 11pm.
The job unexpectedly run at 11pm the same day and now run every day at 5am as expected.

### What did you expect to happen?

The job should have run the next day a 5am.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a cronjob and schedule it to run at a past date
- Patch its status as if it already ran in the past
- Patch it to run in the next minute
- Patch it to run in the next two minutes

Wait a minute and see that a job has unexpectedly run.
Wait another minute to see that the job runs at the expected time.

Example:
```bash
# Create a cronjob scheduled to in the past
kubectl apply -f- <<EOF
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  schedule: "$(date -u -d "1 day ago" +"%M %H %d %m *")"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: hello
            image: busybox:1.28
            imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - date; echo Hello from the Kubernetes cluster
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
EOF

# Patch its status as if it already ran in the past
yersterday=$(date -u -d "1 day ago" +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:00Z")
kubectl patch cronjob hello --subresource=status -p '{"status":{"lastScheduleTime":"'"${yersterday}"'","lastSuccessfulTime":"'"${yersterday}"'"}}'
echo -e "$(kubectl get cronjob hello -o jsonpath='schedule: {.spec.schedule}\nlastScheduleTime: {.status.lastScheduleTime}')"

# Patch it to run in one minute
kubectl patch cronjob hello -p '{"spec":{"schedule":"'"$(date -u -d "1 minute" +"%M %H * * *")"'"}}'
echo "New schedule: $(kubectl get cronjob hello -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedule}')"

# Patch it to run in two minute
kubectl patch cronjob hello -p '{"spec":{"schedule":"'"$(date -u -d "2 minute" +"%M %H * * *")"'"}}'
echo "New schedule: $(kubectl get cronjob hello -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedule}')"

```

title: How To Test Code That Calls leaderelection.RunOrDie
body:
I have an application that uses K8s leader election via leaderelection.RunOrDie().  Unfoertunately I've have greate difficulty writing a unit test for my code becuase of the way that leaderelection.RunOrDie() works.  Specifically:

- I can inject a `coordinationv1client.LeasesGetter` via the lock in the Config I pass to RunOrDie().  This allows me to control the leader election results.
- Unfortunately this only solves part of the problem becuase leaderelection.RunOrDie is controlled via an internal clock.  Without being able to control this clock it is almost impossible to control the behaviour of the function in the unit test.  I think this was realised because this clock has been made configurable for test purposes, but because the clock is packag-private this approach isn't available outside of client-go.

It's therefore not clear to me how I can test my code.  Options I have considered are:
- Changing my code so that instead of calling `leaderelection.RunOrDie()` I just call a generic `func(ctx context.Context, lec LeaderElectionConfig)` which I inject at runtime.  I dislike this becuase the config you pass in to leaderelection.RunOrDie() is relatively complex and this would give me no real verfication that I'm passing in arguments that make sense.
- Accepting that I can't unit test this code and try to deal with this via integration tests.  This again isn't an attractive option as the integration tests would be relatively complex to set up and race conditions (which are inherant in leder election scenarios) are extremely hard to test in this way.

I think the most practical solution here would be if you made the clock settable outside the packge.  Alternatively I wonder if it would be possible to write some simplified facade ovet the leader election client such that it would be so easy to reason about what was going to happen that users would be happy to simply abstract this into an interface and not worry about needing to test integration.

title: DRA helper: report dropped fields
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When a DRA driver asks to publish ResourceSlices, the ResourceSlice controller creates or updates existing slices. If the DRA driver is asking to publish slices that the cluster doesn't support (for example, need the partitionable devices feature and that feature is turned off), the unknown or unsupported fields get dropped.

A DRA driver might want to be notified when this happens.

/wg device-management
/sig node


### Why is this needed?

Normally, the admin should avoid that by configuring the driver appropriately *before* disabling a feature.
But as a second line of defense, perhaps the DRA driver can switch to a simpler mode of operation instead of publishing incomplete ResourceSlices.

title: introduce topology.kubernetes.io/rack label
body:
I propose introducing `topology.kubernetes.io/rack` as a standardized label key in Kubernetes. This label would complement the existing well-known topology labels (`topology.kubernetes.io/region`, `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) by enabling rack-level topology awareness.

**Why is this needed:**

**1. Rack-Level Collocation**
Some workloads—such as those with low-latency or high-throughput requirements—benefit from being placed on the same or nearby racks. Currently, there is no established “rack” key in the well-known topology labels, making it difficult to consistently label and schedule workloads by rack boundaries.

**2. Granularity Between Zone and Node**
While `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` offers a broader grouping of resources and `kubernetes.io/hostname` identifies individual nodes, there is a gap in the middle. Many data centers manage hardware and networking at the rack level; a standard label would help reflect that common topology layer.

**3. Consistency with Existing Label Patterns**
Kubernetes already uses the `topology.kubernetes.io/*` pattern for recognized topology labels (region, zone). Following the same pattern for rack labeling would align with best practices and reduce confusion.

**4. Enhanced Scheduling Strategies**
With a well-known rack label, advanced scheduling plugins or custom schedulers can use rack information for optimized workload distribution, fault tolerance, or data locality in distributed applications (e.g., databases, analytics, or HPC workloads).

title: Specify hostname as FieldRef (in PodSpec of Deployment)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

There is a very useful feature for headless service, which create an A-record for each pod when the subnet of the pod matches the name of a headless service. However this feature requires that the hostname of the pod is explicitely set with spec.hostname.

I verified this with an Deployment (replica 1) setting the hostname to a fixed string works, and also shows up as expected as a single-a record (in addition to the headless collection):

subdomain.namespace.svc.cluster.local A 10.40.x.x
fixedhost.subdomain.namespace.svc.cluster.local A 10.40.x.x


`subdomain` in this case is the name of the headless service and the subdomain of the pod, and `fixedhost` the spec.hostname parameter.

However this does not work if I increase the replica count, since the hostname is fixed. So I either need to specify a flag which turns on those A records without explicitly setting a hostname (i.e. using the implicite hostname) or a way to specify hostname as a field ref (metadata.name for example).




### Why is this needed?

This shortcoming forces me to use stateful sets instead of deployments, it would therefore be good if it can be changed. I use this since my pods have the need to address specific instances with a name. In simple scenarios I can use the podID for it, but when Istio is used, a service dns is required for this.

title: API server reflector may lose events if TransformFromStorage fails
body:
### What happened?

Hi 👋 ,

I'm investigating an issue where create or update operations on `Secrets` are _randomly_ not reflected in the controller runtime client cache. We have observed this behaviour multiple times, in at least 3 different operators, all relying on the controller-runtime client, and one of them being the External Secrets Operator. As a result the controllers indefinitely attempt to reconcile the missed `Secrets` from their stale cache, perpetually getting `409` errors until they are manually restarted. These Secrets seem to be lost by the `Watch` mechanism, while they are successfully created (as confirmed by audit logs), and eventually available in a `List` result.

After some investigations I realized that when this problem occur we also have transient errors related to Secret decryption, for example:

```
watcher.go:471] failed to prepare current and previous objects: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
reflector.go:467] storage/cacher.go:/secrets: retrying watch of *core.Secret internal error: Internal error occurred: failed to decrypt DEK, error: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = grpc: the client connection is closing
```

I have tried to understand how events are processed in `storage/etcd3/watcher.go`, more specifically here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L427-L437

IIUC when an error occurs, an "error event" is sent back to the reflector through a channel:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go#L469-L474


But IIUC we keep processing other incoming events? This leads me to wonder if there is not a situation where:

1. etcd watcher temporary fails to decrypt a Secret with `resourceVersion=V`, the error is sent to the reflector:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L737-L743

2. Assuming that `case apierrors.IsInternalError(err) && retry.ShouldRetry()` is true the reflector is going to run the `watchHandler` again:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L466-L468

3. Meanwhile, let's suppose that the etcd watcher managed to decrypt another `Secret`, with a different name and with `resourceVersion=V+1`, the result is sent to the watcher which calls `setLastSyncResourceVersion` with `V+1` as a value here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/6a074997c960757de911780f250ecd9931917366/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L791

Which feels wrong since `Secret` with `resourceVersion` `V` has not been observed yet?

I would like to know if this sounds like a possible scenario that may explain what we are observing. If not please let me know if you have any ideas that might explain it. Thanks!

We have observed this issue on K8s 1.30 (v1.30.10-eks-bc803b4) with the following libraries:
* k8s.io/api v0.32.2
* k8s.io/apimachinery v0.32.2
* k8s.io/client-go v0.32.2
* sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime v0.20.2

### What did you expect to happen?

I think I would expect the Secrets which suffered what could be a temporary decryption failure to be eventually reflected in the cache.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unfortunately, this happens randomly in our case 😕 That being said if I run the API Server in a dev environment and _temporarily_ return an error in the `TransformFromStorage` function for a specific `Secret`, I can observe that this `Secret` is never going to be sent to a client while other `Secrets` created at the same time are correctly reflected in the controller-runtime client.

### Anything else we need to know?

This part of the code is (really) new to me but I'm happy to help, so please let me know if there is anything else I should investigate!

```console
$ kubectl version
```

title: Performance with Large-Scale list-watch in Serverless Scenarios
body:
hi,

I have encounter a performance issue related to a Serverless scenario in Kubernetes.

In my use case, I have N Pods (where N could be very large). Each Pod runs a component similar to kube-proxy and is responsible for performing a list-watch on Services and Endpoints. Importantly, these Pods do not include any specific Selector, which might sound unusual, but this setup is necessary for our use case.

The problem arises in the following scenarios:
- **Pod Restarts**: When these Pods restart, there could potentially be N simultaneous list-watch requests, which may overwhelm the APIServer and cause it to become unresponsive.
- **Rolling Updates**: During a rolling update of the Pods in the cluster, M events could be generated, and the APIServer would need to send M events to N active watchers. This can lead to event delays and an excessive amount of data being pushed to the watchers, causing performance degradation.

Currently, my proposed solution is to introduce a Proxy in front of the APIServer. All Pods would list-watch this Proxy, and the Proxy would then handle the list-watch requests to the APIServer. This way, the APIServer would only need to handle a few list-watch requests from the Proxy. However, I understand that this only shifts the load to the Proxy and doesn’t truly solve the underlying problem.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/96c3d641-5030-4672-a281-abe560a003c6)

I wander if there are any better approaches or solutions for handling this kind of problem at scale.

thanks

title: Prevent Pod Rescheduling When Other Replica is Healthy
body:
### What would you like to be added?

#### Problem Statement
Currently, when a node fails, Kubernetes reschedules pods onto other nodes even if another healthy replica exists on a different node. This behavior can lead to unnecessary resource usage, overloading of remaining nodes, and increased costs in environments where resource optimization is critical.

#### Proposed Solution
Introduce a new field in the Deployment or Pod spec, such as `preventRescheduleIfHealthy: true` or `maxUnavailable: 1`. When this field is set, the Kubernetes scheduler would check if another healthy replica of the same application is running on a different node. If a healthy replica exists, the scheduler would skip rescheduling the failed pod until the healthy replica becomes unhealthy or the node is restored.

#### Alternatives Considered
I explored using Pod Anti-Affinity to ensure replicas are not co-located on the same node, but this does not prevent rescheduling when a node fails. I also considered writing a custom controller to enforce this behavior, but this approach is complex, error-prone, and not scalable. A native Kubernetes feature would provide a more robust and maintainable solution.

#### Example Implementation 1
Here’s an example of how the new field could be added to a Deployment spec: The `preventRescheduleIfHealthy`  specifies to prevent reschedule if any other pod is already healthy.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      preventRescheduleIfHealthy: true
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-image
```

#### Example Implementation 2
Here’s an example of how the new field could be added to a Deployment spec: The `maxUnavailable` specifies that at most one replica can be unavailable at any time.
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-app
    spec:
      disruptionBudget:
        maxUnavailable: 1
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: my-image
```

### Why is this needed?

#### Use Case
In my deployment, I have a stateful application that runs two replicas for high availability. When a node fails, Kubernetes reschedules the failed pod onto another node, even though the second replica is already healthy and running on a different node. This results in unnecessary resource consumption and potential performance degradation. I want to ensure that the second replica is not rescheduled unless the first replica is unhealthy, to optimize resource usage and reduce costs.

#### Impact
This feature would help users optimize resource usage, reduce unnecessary pod rescheduling, and lower costs in environments where resource efficiency is critical. It would also simplify the management of stateful applications and improve the overall stability of deployments.

#### References
- [Pod Topology Spread Constraints Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints/)

title: Removing dependence on PrevKV when watch cache is enabled
body:
### What would you like to be added?

When watching from etcd, apiserver sets `WithPrevKV` flag so the  returned watch events include information about previous version. This is used by apiserver to handle watch with selector, where it needs to be aware of  what were fields/labels of previous object to notice changes. This is always done on etcd3 layer.

When watch cache is enabled, the watches to etcd3 never include those selectors as they are handled by cache and prevKV is replaced with value from cache. This allows us to deallocate the object, but only after it was decoded on etcd3 layer.

I would propose to stop setting PrevKV when watch cache is enabled.

Pros:
* Reduces lock contention in etcd MVCC by reducing number of reads by 50% and increases write throughput by 20% (from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131862)
* Watch no longer will break when there is a missing PrevKV field. Etcd doesn't guarantee PrevKV as the field is filled just before sending event and can race with compaction.
* Doubles capacity of watch stream, which was proved that can be overloaded with bad consequences. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123448
* Halfs allocations needed to handle watch events.

Cons:
* Complicates watch code as it creates special cache for watch cache

/cc @wojtek-t @deads2k


### Why is this needed?

Presented benefits are nice, so I think we might want to consider it, however I don't think there is a strong "need". Would need to measure the direct impact of reducing watch reintializations due to PrevKV, reducing allocations and watch capacity problem.

title: [Windows] HNS endpoints creation fails after remote HNS endpoints with same IP address were created
body:
### What happened?

When deploying Windows containers on Windows Nodes, some Windows containers fails to have network configuration inside like this:
```
S C:\> ipconfig /all

Windows IP Configuration

   Host Name . . . . . . . . . . . . : windows-server-iis-ltsc2022-58467d4759-vgzjr
   Primary Dns Suffix  . . . . . . . : 
   Node Type . . . . . . . . . . . . : Hybrid
   IP Routing Enabled. . . . . . . . : No
   WINS Proxy Enabled. . . . . . . . : No
```

This issue happens for Windows containers that got assigned the same IP address that was previously assigned to pods on Linux but were deleted later.

When we create a Pod on Linux and a `LoadBalancer` service type that refers to Linux pod, `kube-proxy` on Windows create HNS endpoints of Remote type. If we delete these Linux pods, IP addresses assigned to these pods are released and Remote HNS endpoints are deleted from Windows nodes.

When I deploy Windows pod, and if this Windows pod gets assigned the same IP as Linux pod, HNS endpoint for these Windows containers fails to be created causing networking issues inside Windows container.

This issue is a likely regression due to #124092

### What did you expect to happen?

All Windows containers should successfully create HNS endpoint and networking should work inside Windows containers.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy kubernetes cluster with limited available IPs for pods on both Linux and Windows node.
2. Deploy Linux pods that consume almost all IPs.
3. Deploy service type LoadBalancer that refer to Linux pods, This will trigger `kube-proxy` to create Remote HNS endpoint on Windows. This Remote HNS endpoint will have Linux pod IP.
4. Scale down the Linux pods to 1.
5. Deploy Windows pods so that same IP address from Linux pod can be reassigned to Windows Pods.
6. HNS endpoints for Windows pods with same address will not be created.
7. Internet connectivity inside these Windows pod will fail.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Scheduling queue cleanup ideas
body:
While adding PopFromBackoffQ feature I found some areas of improvements in the scheduling queue code:

- [ ] Add comments to `activeQueuer` and `SchedulingQueue` interfaces.
- [ ] Move `unschedulablePods` struct and its methods to a separate file. We have already moved activeQ and backoffQ. (@onasser1)
- [ ] Make the interfaces of  `activeQueue`, `backoffQueue` and `unschedulablePods` consistent to improve readability. Especially, add `has` method to the `unschedulablePods`, split its `addOrUpdate` to `add` and `update`, make `get` returning `ok` parameter.
- [ ] Unify logging "Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue". Sometimes it's logged two times. Probably, it would be the best to log it in queues' add methods where we already increment `scheduler_queue_incoming_pods_total` metric.

title: Inconsistent cgroup placement and naming between containerd and CRI-O with user namespaces
body:
### What happened?

When running Kubernetes with user namespaces enabled, there is an inconsistency in cgroup hierarchy and naming convention between containerd and CRI-O.

## Containerd behavior (using user namespace)
 * **Sandbox cgroup** is created inside `kubepods.slice`
 * **Container cgroup** is placed under `system.slice` instead of `kubepods.slice`, using a non-standard format that includes `slice:cri-containerd:<container_id>`
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   └── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice 
│   │       └── cri-containerd-<sandbox_id>.scope
│   ...
├── system.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice:cri-containerd:<continer_id>
```

## Containerd behavior (without user namespace)
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   └── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice 
│   │       ├── cri-containerd-<sandbox_id>.scope
│   │       └── cri-containerd-<continer_id>.scope
```

It looks inconsistent because:
 * Cgroup of container that use user namespaces should be inside `kubepods.slice` just like the sandbox.
 * Naming convention is different depending on the use of userns.

## CRI-O behavior (with and without user namespaces)
 * Container and sandbox cgroups are always placed in the same location and follow a consistent naming format, whether user namespaces are enabled or not.
```bash
/sys/fs/cgroup/
├── kubepods.slice
│   ├── kubepods-besteffort.slice
│   │   ├── kubepods-besteffort-pod<pod_id>.slice
│   │   │   ├── crio-<sandbox_id>
│   │   │   └── crio-<container_id>.scope
│   │   │       └── container
├── system.slice
│   ├── crio-conmon-<container_id>.scope
```









### What did you expect to happen?

Both container runtimes should follow **consistent cgroup hierarchy and naming rules:**

 * Container cgroups should be placed inside `kubepods.slice`, not `system.slice` (as containerd currently does).

 * **Naming should follow a predictable format**, rather than using `slice:cri-containerd:<container_id>`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable user namespaces [Use a User Namespace With a Pod](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/user-namespaces/).
2. Deploy a pod on both container runtimes (containerd and CRI-O).
3. Compare the resulting cgroup hierarchy under: `/sys/fs/cgroup/`

title: CVE-2025-24513: ingress-nginx controller auth secret file path traversal vulnerability
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:L](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:L)) (Score: 4.8, Medium)

A security issue was discovered in [ingress-nginx](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx) where attacker-provided data are included in a filename by the ingress-nginx Admission Controller feature, resulting in directory traversal within the container. This could result in denial of service, or when combined with other vulnerabilities, limited disclosure of Secret objects from the cluster. 

### Am I vulnerable?

This issue affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running \`kubectl get pods \--all-namespaces \--selector app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx\`.

#### Affected Versions

- < v1.11.0
- v1.11.0 \- 1.11.4  
- v1.12.0

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

**ACTION REQUIRED:** The following steps must be taken to mitigate this vulnerability: Upgrade ingress-nginx to v1.11.5, v1.12.1, or any later version.

Before applying the patch, this issue can be mitigated by disabling the Validating Admission Controller functionality of ingress-nginx.  

#### Fixed Versions

- ingress-nginx [main@cbc1590](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/pull/13068/commits/cbc159094f6d1b1bf8cf1761eb119138d1f95df1)

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: [Upgrading Ingress-nginx](https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/deploy/upgrade/)

### Detection

There are no known indicators of compromise that prove this vulnerability has been exploited.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Nir Ohfeld and Ronen Shustin from Wiz

The issue was fixed and coordinated by Marco Ebert, James Strong, Tabitha Sable, and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

title: CVE-2025-24514: ingress-nginx controller configuration injection via unsanitized auth-url annotation
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) (Score: 8.8, High)

A security issue was discovered in [ingress-nginx](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx) where the \`auth-url\` Ingress annotation can be used to inject configuration into nginx. This can lead to arbitrary code execution in the context of the ingress-nginx controller, and disclosure of Secrets accessible to the controller. (Note that in the default installation, the controller can access all Secrets cluster-wide.)

### Am I vulnerable?

This issue affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running \`kubectl get pods \--all-namespaces \--selector app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx\`.

This issue does not affect you if you have the \`enable-annotation-validation\` CLI argument enabled. (This option is enabled by default starting from ingress-nginx v1.12.0.)

#### Affected Versions

- < v1.11.0
- v1.11.0 \- 1.11.4  
- v1.12.0

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

**ACTION REQUIRED:** The following steps must be taken to mitigate this vulnerability: Upgrade ingress-nginx to v1.11.5, v1.12.1, or any later version.

Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by setting the \`enable-annotation-validation\` CLI argument to “true”.

#### Fixed Versions

- ingress-nginx [main@ab470eb](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/pull/13068/commits/ab470eb920924d62a197ebddd8a4cc3031a77ddf)

To upgrade, refer to the documentation: [Upgrading Ingress-nginx](https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx/deploy/upgrade/)

### Detection

Suspicious data within the \`auth-url\` annotation of an Ingress resource could indicate an attempt to exploit this vulnerability.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Nir Ohfeld, Ronen Shustin and Sagi Tzadik from Wiz

The issue was fixed and coordinated by Marco Ebert, James Strong, Tabitha Sable, and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

title: Test tooling: agnhost pause command may exit with 0 occasionally
body:
### What happened?

The agnhost command may occasionally exit with 0 which is not the intention: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/78e9ba9d9ac70ceeadd90e95af553add0e2ed36e/test/images/agnhost/pause/pause.go#L37-L56

### What did you expect to happen?

Only exit with failure, 1 (sigint), 2 sigterm, if the traps are registered.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Compile the agnost image with the following changes to make it more likely to happen:
```
func pause(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
        fmt.Println("Paused")
        sigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
        done := make(chan int, 1)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGTERM)
        fmt.Println("Signals registered")
        go func() {
                sig := <-sigCh
                switch sig {
                case syscall.SIGINT:
                        fmt.Println("received SIGINT")
                        done <- 1
                        time.Sleep(time.Minute)
                        os.Exit(1)
                case syscall.SIGTERM:
                        fmt.Println("received SIGTERM")
                        done <- 2
                        time.Sleep(time.Minute)
                        os.Exit(2)
                }
        }()
        result := <-done
        fmt.Printf("exiting %d\n", result)
}
```
Such an image is here: https://hub.docker.com/repository/docker/mszadkow256/moje/tags/2.53-sleep-pause/sha2[…]de7b47e396a90e6ed9eaf66b0e3a66d6378211327fd18cbfd9deb090db06a

2. Run it `docker run --rm mszadkow256/moje:2.53-sleep-pause pause`
3. In another console send SIGTERM: `docker exec 60a273597124 kill 1` 
Issue: The pause command exists with 0 (check with `echo $?`



### Anything else we need to know?

This caused flakes in Kueue tests which was assuming the exit code is always a failure: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kueue/issues/4733

I think the intention of the code is 

```golang
func pause(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {
        fmt.Println("Paused")
        sigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
        done := make(chan int, 1)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT)
        signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGTERM)
        fmt.Println("Signals registered")
        go func() {
                sig := <-sigCh
                switch sig {
                case syscall.SIGINT:
                        done <- 1
                case syscall.SIGTERM:
                        done <- 2
                }
        }()
        result := <-done
        fmt.Printf("exiting %d\n", result)
        os.Exit(result)
}
```

title: Get with resourceVersion on old CustomResource APIVersion shows deleted object.
body:
### What happened?

kube-apiserver still shows an CustomResource object which already got deleted.
But only if using the `resourceVersion` parameter and an old apiVersion of the Custom Resource.

Example `kubectl get` in the old and new api version does not show anything:
```sh
❯ kubectl get virtualmachines.v1alpha2.vmoperator.vmware.com -A
No resources found
❯ kubectl get virtualmachines.v1alpha4.vmoperator.vmware.com -A
No resources found
```

Emulating what a controller does (List and Watch with resourceVersion) for the current api version (v1alpha4) behaves as expected:

```sh
❯ kubectl get --raw '/apis/vmoperator.vmware.com/v1alpha4/virtualmachines'
```

title: Liveness probes failure does not log event
body:
### What happened?

It has been observed that liveness probe is not logging event every time in all scenario. We have executed below steps:


1. Created nginx pod with below readiness and liveness probes parameter values. Keep touch /var/opt/podinstalled and /var/opt/liveness file.

```
readinessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["ls", "/var/opt/podinstalled" ]
  initialDelaySeconds: 60
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
  successThreshold: 1
livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["ls", "/var/opt/liveness" ]
  initialDelaySeconds: 120
  timeoutSeconds: 20
  periodSeconds: 30
  failureThreshold: 4
  successThreshold: 1
```



2. Verify pod describe logs after deleting liveness file. 

```
root@web-0:/# rm -rf /var/opt/liveness
root@web-0:/#
```

Liveness probe failed and container restarted 

```
  Normal   Pulled          13m               kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.14.2" already present on machine
  Normal   Created         13m               kubelet            Created container web
  Normal   Started         13m               kubelet            Started container web
  Warning  Unhealthy       1s (x4 over 91s)  kubelet            Liveness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/liveness': No such file or directory
  Normal   Killing         1s                kubelet            Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted
```


3. After touching both files and waited for few mins after container restart


```
$ kubectl get pods | grep -i web
web-0                                                             1/1     Running                 1 (8m39s ago)    21m
$
```

There is no further readiness and liveness probe failure observed

  ```
Warning  Unhealthy       9m1s (x4 over 10m)     kubelet            Liveness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/liveness': No such file or directory
  Normal   Killing         9m1s                   kubelet            Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted
  Normal   Pulled          8m58s (x2 over 22m)    kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.14.2" already present on machine
  Normal   Created         8m58s (x2 over 22m)    kubelet            Created container web
  Normal   Started         8m57s (x2 over 22m)    kubelet            Started container web
  Warning  Unhealthy       7m1s (x13 over 7m56s)  kubelet            Readiness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/podinstalled': No such file or directory
```

4. Now delete liveness file again

`root@web-0:/# rm -rf /var/opt/liveness`

Container will be restarted again.

```
  Normal   Pulled          12m (x2 over 25m)   kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.14.2" already present on machine
  Normal   Created         12m (x2 over 25m)   kubelet            Created container web
  Normal   Started         12m (x2 over 25m)   kubelet            Started container web
  Warning  Unhealthy       10m (x13 over 10m)  kubelet            Readiness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/podinstalled': No such file or directory
  Warning  Unhealthy       64s (x8 over 13m)   kubelet            Liveness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/liveness': No such file or directory
  Normal   Killing         64s (x2 over 12m)   kubelet            Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted
```


5. Now wait for few seconds after container to be up again and this time do not touch any file related to readiness and liveness probes.
Now real problem beigns.


```
$ kubectl get pods | grep -i web
web-0                                                             0/1     Running                 2 (97s ago)      25m
$
```

Readiness probe event generated

```
  Normal   Pulled          15m (x2 over 28m)     kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.14.2" already present on machine
  Normal   Created         15m (x2 over 28m)     kubelet            Created container web
  Normal   Started         15m (x2 over 28m)     kubelet            Started container web
  Warning  Unhealthy       4m18s (x8 over 16m)   kubelet            Liveness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/liveness': No such file or directory
  Normal   Killing         4m18s (x2 over 15m)   kubelet            Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted
  Warning  Unhealthy       3m13s (x14 over 14m)  kubelet            Readiness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/podinstalled': No such file or directory
```

However no new event related to liveness failure generated and container restarted without any information this time.

```
$ kubectl get pods -w| grep -i web
web-0                                                             0/1     Running                 2 (2m36s ago)    26m

web-0                                                             0/1     Running                 3 (1s ago)       28m

```

6. Now this time touch readiness file and do not touch liveness file. Event for liveness generated this time.

```
  Normal   Pulled          22m (x2 over 35m)     kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.14.2" already present on machine
  Normal   Created         22m (x2 over 35m)     kubelet            Created container web
  Normal   Started         22m (x2 over 35m)     kubelet            Started container web
  Normal   Killing         11m (x2 over 22m)     kubelet            Container web failed liveness probe, will be restarted
  Warning  Unhealthy       5m33s (x66 over 21m)  kubelet            Readiness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/podinstalled': No such file or directory
  Warning  Unhealthy       8s (x19 over 24m)     kubelet            Liveness probe failed: ls: cannot access '/var/opt/liveness': No such file or directory
```
  

Container also restarted.
```
$ kubectl get pods -w| grep -i web
web-0                                                             1/1     Running                 4 (115s ago)       33m

web-0                                                             0/1     Running                 5 (1s ago)         36m

```


**Query:** Is there any event logging problem related to liveness if readiness is already failed? Is it some known behavior or some kind of bug in event logging?






### What did you expect to happen?

**Expected Behavior** - Liveness probe should log event every time so that container restart reason can be identified.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**Repoduction:** Every time with same steps as shared in problem section.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: cleanup CI hardcoded ssh skips
body:
Currently we have manual skip regexes on kind jobs (and probably others) that look for "SSH|ssh", as we move to label filter we'll need a better way to handle this. 

cluster e2e (not node e2e) tests that depend on SSH access are highly suspect and cannot be conformance, and limit our options for cluster deployment tools

I think we should probably have `features.SSH`, but I'm a little concerned about how we might drop coverage in the jobs that _do_ support SSH (and downstreams).

cc @pohly @aojea 

Place holder from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130990#issuecomment-2745307148, we don't have to solve this right now but I think we need a better answer.

Also we might need to make sure some of the label filter jobs still skip these in the meantime.

title: Support unix domain sockets for `cluster.server` in kubeconfig
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to be able be able to specify unix domain socket paths in my kubeconfig, e.g.:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- cluster:
    server: unix:/run/user/1000/ops-staging.sock
  name: proxy-ops-staging
```

(bonus points if it's possible to use something like `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or the systemd `%t` placeholder for `/run/user/1000`, but that would introduce templating into the kubeconfig and is *far* out of scope for this request)

### Why is this needed?

#64783 was closed with the [justification](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/1749#issuecomment-755738311) that users who require alternative authentication mechanisms should use a proxy server. The comment even touched upon maybe enhancing kubectl with unix domain socket support.  
Right now [my proxy](https://github.com/orbit-online/step-plugin-kmsproxy) binds to a port on `127.0.0.1`. This works, but is not ideal from a security standpoint: Any user with network access on the current machine is able to authenticate towards the cluster.  
Unix domain sockets reduce the attack surface by allowing users to restrict read/write access to a socket through filesystem permissions.

title: [Coordinated Leader Election] Version introduction of various Strategies
body:
CEL and Declarative Validation follow a really nice pattern of recording when new features are introduced, and then based on the compatibility version of the cluster toggle the feature on or off.

Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/41469004282b2ad9034993427ce4ec9d1c7f88bb/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/environment/base.go#L180-L185

The benefit is that the entire feature is downgrade safe, and features are only enabled 1 release after introduction. 

I think it would be great if coordinated leader election could also adopt for `Strategy` in the future. I don't want over-optimize if we only have one strategy (OldestEmulationVersion), but I can see us expanding the `Strategy` list and having this would make introducing new strategies much safer.

/cc @jpbetz @Henrywu573 
/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted

title: Migrate deprecated syscall functions in pkg/kubelet/winstats
body:
It seems the `pkg/kubelet/winstats` package contains multiple deprecated `syscall` functions. We probably need to migrate them. If it's the case, I could open a PR to fix it.


#### Files Affected
1. **`pkg/kubelet/winstats/winstats.go`**
   - Impacted functions: 
       - `syscall.Syscall6` -> `syscall.SyscallN`
       - `syscall.StringToUTF16Ptr` -> `syscall.UTF16PtrFromString`
   - Example usage:
     ```go
     ret, _, err := syscall.Syscall6(
         procGetDiskFreeSpaceEx.Addr(),
         4,
         uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(syscall.StringToUTF16Ptr(path))),
         uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&freeBytesAvailable)),
         uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&totalNumberOfBytes)),
         uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&totalNumberOfFreeBytes)),
         0,
         0,
     )
     ```

2. **`pkg/kubelet/winstats/perfcounter_nodestats_windows.go`**
   - Impacted function: 
       - `syscall.Syscall` -> `syscall.SyscallN`
   - Example usage:
     ```go
     r0, _, _ := syscall.Syscall(procGetActiveProcessorCount.Addr(), 1, uintptr(groupNumber), 0, 0)
     ```

#### References
From `syscall\dll_windows.go`
```go
// Deprecated: Use [SyscallN] instead.
func Syscall(trap, nargs, a1, a2, a3 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno)

// Deprecated: Use [SyscallN] instead.
func Syscall6(trap, nargs, a1, a2, a3, a4, a5, a6 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno)
```

From `syscall\syscall_windows.go`
```go
// StringToUTF16Ptr returns pointer to the UTF-16 encoding of
// the UTF-8 string s, with a terminating NUL added. If s
// contains a NUL byte this function panics instead of
// returning an error.
//
// Deprecated: Use [UTF16PtrFromString] instead.
func StringToUTF16Ptr(s string) *uint16 { return &StringToUTF16(s)[0] }
```

title: [release-1.33] Land etcd v3.5.21 in K8s 1.33.0
body:
As mentioned in https://etcd.io/blog/2025/upgrade_from_3.5_to_3.6_issue/, we fixed an upgrade issue (3.5 -> 3.6) in 3.5.20, and the root cause is the membership data may become inconsistent between v2store (deprecated, but remain source of truth for membership data in 3.5) and v3store (source of truth in 3.6).

Without it, the K8s 1.33.0 → 1.34 upgrades may fail due to https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/19557.

So we should land etcd v3.5.20+ (latest 3.5.21) in k8s 1.33.0 instead of 1.33.1

title: Allow users to modify the nodeAffinity field inside a persistentVolume.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I hope to make nodeAffinity field in persistentvolume editable

### Why is this needed?

We（AlibabaCloud）has recently introduced [Regional EBS](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/ecs/user-guide/regional-essd-disks?spm=a2c63.p38356.0.i1). a new type of EBS that enables pod(app) to utilize it across all zones within a specific region, thereby achieving higher availablity. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a42d92b1-2393-42c6-9b05-ff39f4a54792)

Meanwhile, users can modify their existing EBS to a regional EBS by openapi to use the EBS in the other zone. However, after changing the EBS type, we cannot modify the current PV's nodeAffinity to enable the new feature, as it remains limited to its original zone.

current state
```
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          operator: In
          values:
          - cn-hangzhou-i
```

desired state
```
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: "topology.kubernetes.io/region"
          operator: In
          values:
          - cn-hangzhou
```

therefore, we want to make nodeAffinity editable to transition PVs from their current state to the desired state. 

We also note that [Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/disks/hyperdisks) in GCP has a similar definition, may suggesting similar requirements. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0e5a1c4f-b573-4195-9b12-988256fc4b12)

title: Support perferred field in VolumeNodeAffinity of persistentVolume
Add Container Event Notification for CRI's Update*Resources Interface to Support In-Place Pod Resizing
body:
The current evented PLEG implementation in CRI generates container events (create/start/stop/delete) to trigger `syncPod`, but it fails to accommodate the in-place pod resizing feature. During in-place pod resizing, after completing container resource updates via `UpdateContainerResources/UpdatePodSandboxResources`, we need to re-trigger `syncPod` to update the container status.

In the generic PLEG implementation, this is achieved by forcing a synthetic container event during the next PLEG relist after doPodResizeAction, which triggers `syncPod`. However, for evented PLEG (where events originate directly from the container runtime via CRI), there is no native event generated when resource updates occur. Currently, In PR #131024, I implemented a temporary workaround by simulating container runtime-generated events to achieve this behavior. While this approach unblocks testing, it remains a short-term fix.

To fully align with evented PLEG's design, we need container runtimes to emit a dedicated "Update" event when their `UpdateContainerResources` or `UpdatePodSandboxResources` CRI interfaces are invoked. This event should notify the Kubelet to trigger syncPod, ensuring consistent behavior between generic and evented PLEG implementations.

/sig node
/kind feature

body:

Hi, we found a situation similar to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115325, while caused by etcd being restored to a previous snapshot, which "erased" a created pod.

Kubelet complains resource problem and fails newly scheduled pods, as if the original pod is still there (well, it is).

4. restart etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler, notice kubelet isn't restarted.

title: Is it necessary to keep the Duration at the Cap value
body:
### What happened?

I'm encountering a scenario where a check operation needs to be executed at intervals of `1s, 2s, 4s... (doubling each time) up to a cap of 1 minute`. After reaching the 1-minute cap, the check operation should persistently run every 1 minute. So I try to implement it with following code
```go
backoff: &Backoff{
		Duration: time.Second,
		Factor:   2,
		Steps: math.MaxInt32,
		Cap:   time.Minute,
	}
```
But the current `wait.BackOff` implementation fails to achieve this behavior because once the `Cap` is reached, it immediately sets the `Step` field value to zero, thereby terminating the looped check operation. Therefore, is it necessary to add an option to ensure the `Duration` remains at the `Cap` value after reaching it?

/sig api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

check operation needs to be executed at intervals of `1s, 2s, 4s... (doubling each time) up to a cap of 1 minute`. After reaching the 1-minute cap, the check operation should persistently run every 1 minute

title: Potential incorrect RealServer weight update logic in IPVS proxier initial sync
body:
### What happened?

In the `syncProxyRules` logic of kube-proxy's IPVS mode, during the initial sync phase, the weight of each RealServer is updated if **any** of the existing destinations (`curDests`) has a different weight from the newly created `newDest`. This logic may lead to unnecessary or even incorrect updates.

#### Where the code is:
File: `pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go`  
Function: `syncProxyRules`  
Related snippet:
```go
for _, dest := range curDests {
    if dest.Weight != newDest.Weight {
        err = proxier.ipvs.UpdateRealServer(appliedVirtualServer, newDest)
    }
}
```

#### Why it's problematic:
The current code updates `newDest` without checking if the existing `dest` in `curDests` actually matches the IP and port of `newDest`. This can result in:
- Unnecessary repeated updates to the same RealServer.
- Updates triggered by unrelated `dest` entries.
- Inefficient syncing behavior during startup.



### What did you expect to happen?

The logic should compare the `Address` and `Port` of `dest` and `newDest`, and only perform an update if:
```go
dest.Address.Equal(newDest.Address) && dest.Port == newDest.Port && dest.Weight != newDest.Weight
```

This ensures only the correct RealServer is updated when needed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This logic runs during the initial sync phase. In environments with multiple RealServers with varying weights, the current code may repeatedly trigger `UpdateRealServer` on unrelated destinations.

### Anything else we need to know?

The logic should compare the `Address` and `Port` of `dest` and `newDest`, and only perform an update if:
```go
dest.Address.Equal(newDest.Address) && dest.Port == newDest.Port && dest.Weight != newDest.Weight
```

This ensures only the correct RealServer is updated when needed.

title: TopologySpreadConstraints to specify "max number or % of replicas"
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I didn't find any open or closed issue regarding this topic, so I thought to ask here for feedback.

Today, TopologySpreadConstraints allow us to express distribution conditions focused on how many domains or topologies are created when scheduling a particular workload.

We're managing large multi-tenant clusters and often feel the need to express a "limit" in the topology, such as "I want this workload to be distributed as per maxSkew, but not more than X replicas per node or no more than 10% of the replicas per node."

I'm not an expert in scheduling terminology, but I think adding something like "maxReplicas" (which could be an integer or a percentage) would help with this scenario, expressing the additional conditions mentioned above.

### Why is this needed?

In large multi-tenant clusters, where different applications are expected to run on shared nodes, it's useful to specify a further degree of distribution (not more than X replicas per node or not more than Y% per node). This ensures that, in case of node loss, we can control how many replicas per application we can afford to lose. This is particularly important with spot offerings (nodes that can be reclaimed at short notice by the cloud provider).

title: Same RWO PVC ends up on different nodes
body:
### What happened?

I applied the following configuration that has two pods using the same RWO PVC.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: vol1
  labels:
    type: local
spec:
  storageClassName: manual
  capacity:
    storage: 10Mi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: "/mnt/data"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: claim1
spec:
  storageClassName: manual
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod1
spec:
  containers:
    - name: myfrontend
      image: nginx
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: "/var/www/html"
        name: data
      resources:
        limits:
          cpu: "1"
          memory: "200Mi"
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: claim1
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod2
spec:
  containers:
    - name: myfrontend
      image: nginx
      volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: "/var/www/html"
        name: data
      resources:
        limits:
          cpu: "1"
          memory: "200Mi"
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: claim1

```

According to #103305 and #26567, pods could be scheduled on different nodes, and actually were. But, contrary to these issues, both pods were able to attach to the volume (s?) and run just fine.

It really seems that the PVC "used" both nodes because data written by both pods were present on each corresponding node, and this happened **without any notice**.

Is this expected behavior?



### What did you expect to happen?

Volume attachment should fail for at least one of the two pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

By applying the provided configuration.

title: DaemonSets should be scheduled before Deployments on new Nodes
body:
### What happened?

We're trying to reduce AWS EC2 costs by reducing the number of nodes to 0 automatically during times the enter cluster is not needed using an autoscaling_schedule (see e.g. https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/autoscaling_schedule). We have observed that, when a single node is started after no nodes at all have been available, the kube-scheduler may start a large number of Deployments on that node, leaving insufficient resources (in our case memory) for the pods of all DaemonSets to be started on that node. That situation was not rectified automatically after adding more nodes to the cluster, instead, I had to cordon the server and terminate some pods on the first node for them to be moved to another node.

It would be preferable if resources for DaemonSets were reserved before Workloads that are not tied to nodes (Deployments, ReplicaSets, ...) are scheduled.



### What did you expect to happen?

Resources for DaemonSets were reserved before Workloads that are not tied to nodes (Deployments, ReplicaSets, ...) are scheduled.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. configure a cluster with 0 worker nodes
2. create daemonset that use a significant amount of resources
3. create Deployments and Replicasets to use all the resources (of at least one type) of one of the worker nodes to be added to the cluster
4. add one worker node
5. sometimes, Deployments and Replicasets are scheduled on the single worker node, leaving too few or no resources for Daemonsets
6. if all Daemonsets were scheduled, remove the worker node and re-add it
7. add more nodes

title: Kube-Controller-Manager add flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate
body:
### What would you like to be added?

We want to add flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate. This is used to limit number of nodes per second on which pods are deleted in case of node failure when some zone is disruption.



### Why is this needed?

Currently the node-lifecycle-controller has three types of state categories corresponding to different eviction QPS.


| state| condition| QPS|
|  ----  | ----  | ---- |
|Normal| NotReady nodes accounts for less than 55%| depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|PartialDisruption|NotReady nodes accounts for large than 55% |depends on secondary-node-eviction-rate,  Default: 0.01|
|FullDisruption|All nodes are not ready|depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|AllZoneFullDisruption|All zones are `FullDisruption`| The eviction QPS is 0|




With the flag zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate, we can control `FullDisruption` states：

| state| condition| QPS|
|  ----  | ----  | ---- |
|Normal| NotReady nodes accounts for less than 55%| depends on node-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|PartialDisruption|NotReady nodes accounts for large than 55% |depends on secondary-node-eviction-rate,  Default: 0.01|
|FullDisruption|All nodes are not ready|depends on zone-full-disruption-eviction-rate, Default: 0.1|
|AllZoneFullDisruption|All zones are `FullDisruption`|0|


Some systems already have similar capabilities:
1. The control plane does not apply the node.kubernetes.io/unreachable=NoExecute taint to the nodes if the zone is fully disrupted.  https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/openshift-edge-disruption-mitigation
2. If all nodes in a zone are unreachable, Kubernetes cancels pod evictions for the nodes in that zone. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/hybrid-nodes-network-disconnection-best-practices.html

Preview disscussion: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110114

Please take a look. Will this be accepted?

title: Severe file copy slowdown in pod using Local PV after node reboot (resolved by pod recreation)
body:
### What happened?

We are using Local PersistentVolume (local PV) to mount a local directory to a pod. After a node reboot, the pod is still running, but performing file copy operations inside the pod (e.g., using `cp`) becomes very slow.

Using `strace -f -tt -T -p <PID>` to trace the cp process shows that `sendfile()` system calls are taking 0.7+ seconds per 16MB chunk:
```
15:02:53.949729 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.715818>
15:02:54.665935 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.731067>
15:02:55.397318 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.737302>
...

```

However, if we delete the pod and let it be recreated, the file copy speed returns to normal. sendfile() calls then complete in ~0.015 seconds:
```
15:04:38.006504 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.015368>
15:04:38.022146 sendfile(4, 3, NULL, 16777216) = 16777216 <0.015512>
...
```



### What did you expect to happen?

After node reboot, the pod using local PV should continue to perform file copy operations at normal speed without requiring a pod delete and recreate.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Create a pod that mounts a local directory using local PersistentVolume.
2.Perform a file copy operation inside the pod (e.g., cp largefile /tmp/), observe performance is good.
3.Reboot the node where the pod is scheduled.
4.After the node is back and the pod is still running, repeat the file copy operation.
5.Observe that file copy is very slow.
6.Delete the pod, let it be recreated (same node), and copy files again — performance is back to normal.

title: kubectl does not honor  "insecure-skip-tls-verify" flag in in-cluster mode

### What happened?

I am trying to execute a kubectl command within a pod. The pod does not have a kube-config file; but it has a service account token and ca-cert.
I think running kubectl this way (within the pod) runs it in "in-cluster" mode.
I see certificate validation errors even when "insecure-skip-tls-verify" flag is specified. Please see **Case1** output below.
However the same command works when a kubeconfig file is loaded within the pod and specified in the kubectl command. Please see **Case2** output below

The server-certificate presented by my apiserver does not contain the IP address 192.168.0.1 (kubernetes clusterIP service) in the SAN. This is the reason for specifying `--insecure-skip-tls-verify=true`

The kubeconfig file used in Case2 below uses 192.168.0.1  (kubernetes clusterIP service) as the "server" (apiserver) to connect to. It should thus have the same certificate validation issue ... but it works !

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
```

title: Extensible Node Readiness/Schedulability Conditions
body:
**[Update] This is being tracked as a KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5233.
 Proposal doc** here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/11i2_rewvcbQkFFq1BIwHa7lgIefgZ8Mak-QMZjP7fFs/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.jtg1hwbt8shd


**Labels**: sig-node, kind/feature, wg-node-lifecycle

### Summary / Motivation:
This proposal suggests introducing a mechanism to define custom, extensible readiness conditions for Kubernetes Nodes. The goal is to allow nodes to signal true readiness for application workloads only after essential node-level components (like monitoring agents, security scanners, CNI plugins, runtime patchers) are confirmed operational, improving upon the current workarounds using taints.

### Problem:

Currently, a Node transitions to the Ready state primarily based on Kubelet's health, network availability (via CNI), and its ability to run a basic pod sandbox. However, many clusters rely on critical DaemonSets or agents (e.g., for monitoring, logging, security, storage, or applying runtime configurations) that need to be fully functional on a node before general application pods are scheduled onto it.

Scheduling application pods onto a node where these critical components are not yet ready can lead to:
- Missing observability data during pod startup.
- Pods running in an insecure or non-compliant state.
- Pods failing if they depend on runtime patches or configurations applied by a DaemonSet that hasn't finished yet.

### Use Cases:

**Observability Agent Readiness:** A user running Datadog or Prometheus Node Exporter, etc. deployed as a DaemonSet wants to ensure the agent on a specific node is running and has successfully registered/checked-in before business application pods, which rely on this agent for metrics/logs/traces, are scheduled onto that node.

**Runtime Patching/Configuration:** A user deploys a DaemonSet to apply necessary runtime configurations or security patches (e.g., sysctl settings, runtime config patch, eBPF program loading) upon node startup. Application pods should only be scheduled after this DaemonSet has successfully completed its task on the node.

### Current Workarounds & Limitations:

The common workaround involves:

1. Applying a `NoSchedule` taint (e.g., `node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable`) to new nodes.
2. Configuring critical DaemonSets/workloads to tolerate this taint.
3. Implementing an external controller (or a daemonset / process) that monitors the status of these critical workloads on each node.
4. Once the critical workloads are deemed ready, this controller removes the taint from the node, allowing general pods to be scheduled.

This approach has several drawbacks:

- **Complexity**: Requires building and maintaining custom controllers and managing taint/toleration logic.
- **Friction**: Adds latency and potential points of failure to the node provisioning process.
- **High Privileges**: The controller removing the taint typically requires nodes/patch RBAC permission, which is highly privileged and undesirable for cluster automation components.
- **Potential Race Conditions:** Timing issues can occur between taint removal and scheduler decisions.

### Proposal / Feature Description:
We propose investigating and developing a Kubernetes-native mechanism to make node readiness/schedulability dependent on custom criteria defined by the cluster administrator or specific workloads. This would allow critical components to directly influence when a node is considered fully prepared for general pod scheduling.

One possible approach could be -

**Node Readiness Gates**

**Overview:**
The core idea is to introduce a mechanism where the node's transition to a fully schedulable state depends not only on the Kubelet's default Ready condition but also on the successful status of custom conditions defined in the Node's spec. This should look similar to [Pod Readiness Gates](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-readiness-gate) that the node must satisfy. The readiness will be signaled via `NodeStatus.Conditions` updates by external controllers or agents before the node is considered fully schedulable.

**Proposed API Changes:**

- `NodeSpec.ReadinessGates` (New Field):

Similar to `PodSpec.ReadinessGates`, this would be an array within the `NodeSpec`.
Each entry in the array would define a `conditionType` that must be met. These `conditionType` names should follow the standard Kubernetes convention (e.g., domain.com/MyConditionName).

- `NodeStatus.Conditions` (Existing Field):

This existing array would be used by external controllers to report the status of the conditions listed in `spec.readinessGates`. The external controller would add or update entries in this array, setting the type to match the gate's conditionType, and setting the status field to "True", "False", or "Unknown", along with reason and message fields for details.

**Evaluation Logic:**
A Node would be considered fully ready for scheduling general workloads only if:

The standard Ready condition in `NodeStatus.Conditions` has `status: "True"`.
**AND** for _every_ `conditionType` listed in `NodeSpec.ReadinessGates`, there is a corresponding entry in `NodeStatus.Conditions` with the matching type and `status: "True"`.

**Example**:
Let's consider a scenario where a node needs the Datadog agent to be healthy and a custom runtime patch applied before being used for business pods.

**Use-case 1:**
kubernetes user is running Datadog and doesn't want the node to be marked ready until verification from Datadog that the observability pieces are up and running.

**Use-case 2:**
kubernetes user wants to patch some runtime configuration in the node using a daemonset before running a business pod. Since this is a runtime patch, this needs to happen before other pods.

**Walkthrough:**
1. Node is created with configuration:

Kubelet Configuration:
Kubelet upon self-registration will add the nodeReadinessGates to the node-spec. Kubelet itself will not evaluate these conditions, it will only populate this in node-spec for external controllers / agents to consume.

```
# -- Proposed Configuration --
# nodeReadinessGates specifies the conditions that will be added by kubelet to nodespec after self-registration. 
# alternatively, kubelet could be started with flags like "--node-readiness-gates=..."
nodeReadinessGates:
-  "datadog.com/AgentReady"
-  "ai-corp.com/RuntimePatchApplied"
-  "storage.corp.com/DriverInstalled"

```

Node spec:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  name: node-123
spec:
  readinessGates:
    - conditionType: "datadog.com/AgentReady"
    - conditionType: "ai-corp.com/RuntimePatchApplied"
  taints:
    - key: "node.kubernetes.ioio/initializing"
      effect: "NoSchedule"
```
2. Kubelet starts and registers node
```
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "False"
      reason: KubeletStarting
      message: Kubelet is starting.
```
Node is not schedulable because Ready is not True and the conditions defined in readinessGates are missing from the status.

3. Kubelet becomes ready
```
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: KubeletReady
      message: Kubelet is ready.
```
The node is still not considered fully schedulable because the readinessGates conditions are not yet met
4. External Controller (eg: Daemonset): Datadog agent is ready
- Datadog agent (daemonset) starts on node-123
- Agent / operator monitors status of the agent health
- Operator uses kubernetes api to update node /status  

```
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      # ...
    - type: "datadog.com/AgentReady" # Added/Updated
      status: "True"
      reason: AgentHealthy
      message: "Datadog agent started successfully."
```
5. External Controller: Runtime is patched / ready
```
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      # ...
    - type: "datadog.com/AgentReady"
      status: "True"
      # ...
    - type: "ai-corp.com/RuntimePatchApplied" # Added/Updated
      status: "True"
      reason: PatchSucceeded
      message: "Runtime patch v1.2 applied successfully."
```
6. Node becomes ready / schedulable

**Benefits:**

Reduces the need for complex, custom taint-management controllers.
Ensures application pods are only scheduled on nodes where prerequisite services are confirmed ready.
Decreases the need for cluster components to hold broad nodes/patch permissions.
Provides a standardized, built-in way to handle kubetnetes node initialization dependencies.
