title: Lack of Graceful Rolling Eviction When Using PriorityClass Can Cause Downtime
body:
I'm trying to understand the eviction behavior in Kubernetes when using `PriorityClass` for preemption, and I believe there's a gap in how gracefully the system handles eviction of lower-priority pods.

Let's say I have the following setup:

- A critical DaemonSet using a high PriorityClass
- That DaemonSet needs to schedule a pod on a specific node
- The node already hosts a lower-priority Deployment with two pods running
- The Deployment is configured with a rolling update strategy, e.g.:

```yaml
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0
    maxSurge: 1
```

My expectation was that Kubernetes would attempt to evict one pod at a time from the lower-priority Deployment in a rolling fashion, honoring the update strategy and avoiding disruption.

However, from what I understand, Kubernetes may evict both pods immediately to make room for the higher-priority DaemonSet pod — potentially causing application downtime, even though the Deployment's maxUnavailable is 0.

What I’d Expect:

Some sort of graceful eviction mechanism that:

- Evicts pods one at a time if possible
- Honors maxUnavailable or respects PodDisruptionBudget
- Provides better coordination between PriorityClass-based preemption and Deployment rolling update behavior

Questions / Discussion Points:
- Is this the intended behavior, or is it a known limitation?
- re there any plans or proposals to make preemption more graceful - for example, by allowing a custom `.sh` script to handle restarts as a plugin for more complex resources like StatefulSets?
- Would this be a fit for future enhancement (e.g., opt-in rolling eviction mode)?
- Should the scheduler consider Deployment strategies or disruption budgets during preemption?

This behavior can lead to unintended outages when using `PriorityClass` to protect critical workloads (e.g., system agents, DaemonSets, StatefulSets), especially when the cluster is under pressure. Graceful degradation is often essential in production-grade systems.

P.S: As I understand PDB **will not be able to help as well** as the eviction strategy is not taking it into consideration, either way since we have hundreds of microservices in our system, it'll not be possible to create a PDB, for each one of our services (Even if PDB helped)

Your thoughts? I think it's a much needed feature...

title: CVE-2025-7342: VM images built with Kubernetes Image Builder Nutanix or OVA providers use default credentials for Windows images if user did not override
body:
CVSS Rating High 7.5: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H)

A security issue was discovered in the Kubernetes Image Builder where default credentials are enabled during the Windows image build process when using the Nutanix or VMware OVA providers. These credentials, which allow root access, are disabled at the conclusion of the build. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if their nodes use VM images created via the Image Builder project and the vulnerability was exploited during the build process, which requires an attacker to access the build VM and modify the image while the build is in progress.

### Am I vulnerable?

Clusters using virtual machine Windows images built with Kubernetes Image Builder (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/image-builder) version v0.1.44 or earlier are affected if built with the Nutanix or OVA provider.

VMs using images built with all other providers are not affected by this issue.

To determine the version of Image Builder you are using, use one of the following methods:
- For git clones of the image builder repository:
```
    cd <local path to image builder repo>
    make version
```
- For installations using a tarball download:
```
    cd <local path to install location>
    grep -o v0\\.[0-9.]* RELEASE.md | head -1
```
- For a container image release:
    `docker run --rm <image pull spec> version`
  or
    `podman run --rm <image pull spec> version`
  or look at the image tag specified, in the case of an official image such as `registry.k8s.io/scl-image-builder/cluster-node-image-builder-amd64:v0.1.44`


#### Affected Versions

- Kubernetes Image Builder versions <= v0.1.44

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
Rebuild any affected images using a fixed version of Image Builder. Fixed in Kubernetes Image Builder release v0.1.45
Re-deploy the fixed images to any affected VMs or use image-builder v0.1.41 (February 2025) or later, and set the `admin_password` JSON variable.
Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by changing the password of the Administrator account on affected VMs:
`net user Administrator <new-password>`

#### Fixed Versions

Fixed in Kubernetes Image Builder release v0.1.45 https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/image-builder/pull/1800


### Detection

`Get-LocalUser -Name Administrator | Select-Object Name,Enabled,SID,Lastlogon | Format-List`

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

## Additional Details

The fixed version requires users to specify a password in the WINDOWS_ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable or in the `admin_password` JSON variable. If both are empty, then the image builder would not build the image and return an error.

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Abdel Adim Oisfi, Davide Silvetti, Nicolò Daprelà, Paolo Cavaglià, Pietro Tirenna from Shielder.

The issue was fixed and coordinated by Matt Boersma of the Image Builder project.

title: [KEP-4680] DRA: Make device health check timeout configurable
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The timeout for marking a DRA device's health as "Unknown" is currently hardcoded to 30 seconds. This should be made configurable.

This is an update/enhancement for the new DRA Device Health feature being introduced by KEP-4680.

### Why is this needed?

As discussed in the review for PR #130606 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130606/files#r2221829511), a single hardcoded timeout is not ideal for all types of hardware. Different devices (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs, TPUs, storage) may have very different health-reporting characteristics and require different timeout values.

The most robust long-term solution would be to make this a per-plugin setting, allowing each vendor to specify an appropriate timeout for their hardware. This issue tracks the work to add this configurability, which should be a prerequisite for graduating the feature to Beta.

/sig node
/assign @jpsassine
/priority important-longterm

title: Kubelet shutdown manager not properly initialized due to race condition in systemd-logind configuration reloading
body:
### What happened?

Observed error log 
`
kubelet.go:1667] "Failed to start node shutdown manager" err="node shutdown manager was unable to update logind InhibitDelayMaxSec to 30s (ShutdownGracePeriod), current value of InhibitDelayMaxSec (5s) is less than requested ShutdownGracePeriod"
`

And the shutdown inhibitor is not registered to the system so shutdown manager would not be in effect.

The bug seems to be a race condition between systemd-logind config reloading and getting the updated `InhibitDelayMaxSec`. The root cause is the reload command is signaled to systemd-logind with no waiting until the reload is complete.

I am thinking a low cost fix,  rather than properly implementing something to get the reload completion signal, is to just backoff wait up to 5 retries to get the new `InhibitDelayUSec` value


### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet shutdown manager should work properly

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Wrote a program trying to reproduce it

```go
package main

import (
        "fmt"
        "math/rand"
        "os"

        "github.com/godbus/dbus/v5"
)

const (
        logindConfDir = "/etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/"
        tempConfFile  = logindConfDir + "99-test-inhibit-delay.conf"
        logindService = "org.freedesktop.login1"
        logindObject  = dbus.ObjectPath("/org/freedesktop/login1")
)

func main() {
        // This program must be run as root to modify systemd config and call D-Bus methods.
        if os.Geteuid() != 0 {
                fmt.Println("This program must be run as root (sudo).")
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        neg, total := 0, 100000
        for i := 0; i < total; i++ {
                if test() {
                        neg++
                }
                if i%500 == 0 {
                        fmt.Printf("Tested %d times, reproduced the bug %d times\n", i, neg)
                }
        }
        fmt.Printf("Tested %d times, reproduced the bug %d times", total, neg)
}

func test() bool {
        newInhibitDelaySec := rand.Intn(100) + 15
        conn, err := dbus.SystemBus()
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to connect to system D-Bus: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        defer conn.Close()

        if err := os.MkdirAll(logindConfDir, 0755); err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to create logind.conf.d directory: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        confContent := fmt.Sprintf("[Login]\nInhibitDelayMaxSec=%ds\n", newInhibitDelaySec)
        err = os.WriteFile(tempConfFile, []byte(confContent), 0644)
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to write temporary config file: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        defer os.Remove(tempConfFile)

        obj0 := conn.Object("org.freedesktop.systemd1", dbus.ObjectPath("/org/freedesktop/systemd1"))
        obj1 := conn.Object(logindService, logindObject)

        call := obj0.Call("org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager.KillUnit", 0, "systemd-logind.service", "all", 1)
        if call.Err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Reload call failed: %v\n", call.Err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }
        variant, err := obj1.GetProperty("org.freedesktop.login1.Manager.InhibitDelayMaxUSec")
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("Failed to get property: %v\n", err)
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        updatedInhibitDelayUSec, ok := variant.Value().(uint64)
        if !ok {
                fmt.Println("Failed to assert property type to uint64.")
                os.Exit(1)
        }

        expectedUSec := uint64(newInhibitDelaySec * 1_000_000)

        return expectedUSec != updatedInhibitDelayUSec
}
```

, which had pretty low reproduction rate (`Tested 80500 times, reproduced the bug 1 times/Tested 257500 times, reproduced the bug 4 times`) but on real cases, it should significantly higher because the kubelet is started during OS boot period and a lot of churns on systemd so the logind reload takes more time to take effect.

title: Add stateful workload to support testing
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I wonder if we can make a toy database-like workload that is deliberately intolerant of various snags 

eg:
* workload runners must be upgraded in index order
* if there is at any point no running replica during an upgrade, the upgrade is considered failed
* if there is at any point no quorum during an upgrade, the upgrade is considered failed
* the readiness check takes 30 seconds* 
* the workload balks at being co-hosted (same node) as another replica
* the workload checks that there are at least n÷2 other replicas with storage mounted and (indirectly) writable
* something relating to the workload runs a Job for an upgrade, and the Job that can only succeed if scheduled to a node where the workload is running
* the workload resolves its peers via DNS and is only ready if 100% of replicas are resolvable and reachable
* the workload fails if any replica has index 0
* the workload relies on a mechanism (eg init container) to translate Pod indices into letters / Roman numerals / whatever
* the workload requires a healthy sidecar container

### Why is this needed?

Inspired by #133054

Backlog priority or lower

title: Deprecated Usage of `strings.Title` in `ServiceCheck.Name()`
body:
## Problem

The following method uses the deprecated `strings.Title` function:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/041974709cd8d259aec104f3f3a53d5df43d0268/cmd/kubeadm/app/preflight/checks.go#L107

```

As per the Go documentation:

> `strings.Title` is **deprecated** because it does not correctly handle Unicode punctuation and casing rules.  
> **Recommendation:** Use `golang.org/x/text/cases` instead, which is locale-aware and Unicode-correct.

---

## Suggested Fix

Replace `strings.Title` with `cases.Title` from the `golang.org/x/text/cases` package:

```go
import (
	"fmt"
	"golang.org/x/text/cases"
	"golang.org/x/text/language"
)

func (sc ServiceCheck) Name() string {
	if sc.Label != "" {
		return sc.Label
	}
	titleCaser := cases.Title(language.English)
	return fmt.Sprintf("Service-%s", titleCaser.String(sc.Service))
}
```

This ensures correct title casing for Unicode and localized text input.

---

## Performance Consideration

A microbenchmark was conducted to compare the performance and memory usage between `strings.Title` and `cases.Title`. Results are as follows:


### Benchmark Results

```
goos: linux
goarch: amd64

BenchmarkStringsTitle-20        10613290	       115.2 ns/op	      24 B/op	       1 allocs/op
BenchmarkCasesTitle-20           3073608	       386.6 ns/op	     280 B/op	       2 allocs/op
```

| Function        | ns/op  | B/op | Allocs/op | Unicode Support | Locale-Aware | Status     |
|----------------|--------|------|-----------|------------------|---------------|-------------|
| `strings.Title` | 115.2  | 24   | 1         | Poor             | No            | Deprecated  |
| `cases.Title`   | 386.6  | 280  | 2         | Correct          | Yes           | Recommended |

While `cases.Title` is slower and allocates more, it is the correct and future-proof choice unless this is in a hot path.

---

## Proposed Actions

- [ ] Replace deprecated `strings.Title` with `cases.Title`.
- [ ] Audit the codebase for similar usages of deprecated string functions.
- [ ] Add test coverage for Unicode input (if not already present).
- [ ] Evaluate performance implications if the usage occurs in high-throughput paths.

---

title: Support scheduling hint in Pod.Spec to have sticky scheduling
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Provide a mechanism to hint the scheduler to schedule a pod, which is to be created, to a node where the pod's owner controller believe it's optimal to schedule that specific pod to that node.

### Why is this needed?

Some batch workloads have checkpoints saved in local storage, although they can restore checkpoints from previous node's storage via network, the network overhead is non-trivial. This is common in using IndexedJob or JobSet. When there is a disruption, Pods are recreated and users have to implement mechanisms outside k8s to workaround this problem or have suboptimal performance.

Currently, `pod.status.nominatedNodeName` achieves similar logic with one drawback: the `pod.status` field can't be initialized at pod creation so pod controllers can't really rely on it otherwise race conditions may happen.

title: Connection leak in cri-client
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9eb462ef4a86cc68c545a88392e8b78ddfefec84/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go#L83 creates a connection to the specified endpoint, howewer, it is not possible for the caller to later close it. CRI-O uses this method for its internal [health check](https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/cb591e06e245d0e2409ed263b1b70f3ab3cf5f8a/server/health.go#L21). As client connections dont get closed, nor do server ones, and then they'll eat up resources.

No memory/connection leaks in client libraries too.

title: PodLevelResources + DRA discovery
body:
As the [KEP for PodLevelResources](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837) evolved, it included accomodation for how its forward-looking API and behaviors will integrate with the existing container-specific resources APIs and behaviors (e.g., determining that pod-level resources take precedence; ref: https://github.com/ndixita/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2837-pod-level-resource-spec/README.md#podspec-validation-rules).

Now that DRA is GA, and PodLevelResources are slated for beta in 1.34, we should fully flesh out the cooperative story here between the two. We can start with simply "what do we do when a pod spec includes both a pod-level resource configuration, and includes resource claims for one or more of its containers?".

It will probably make sense to update https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2837 with our conclusions, and prioritize any needed implementation work, to optimize for a smooth graduation of PodLevelResources to GA.

title: When there are two resource quotas under the same namespace, the used resource values of the two resource quotas are inconsistent.
body:
### What happened?

Under the same namespace, there are two resource quotas. I set the deployment hard values for both quotas to 3000, and then created deployments one by one. During the creation process, the quota might fail to update due to the error "**Operation cannot be fulfilled on resourcequotas 'aaa-rq': the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again**" leading to the failure of the deployment creation. The last one quota reached its limit, but the other quota did not reach its limit.

### What did you expect to happen?

These two quotas should have the same usage value.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a namespace
2. crate two resourcequota under the namespace, and the two quota have the same hard value, may be 3000 deployments
3. quickly,create deployments one by one
4. the problem is present that the actual deployments have not reached 3000, but the usage of one quota has already hit 3000. Any further creation attempts will be rejected.

### Anything else we need to know?

I believe the issue is related to this piece of code.
```
func (e *quotaEvaluator) checkQuotas(quotas []corev1.ResourceQuota, admissionAttributes []*admissionWaiter, remainingRetries int) {
...
		if err := e.quotaAccessor.UpdateQuotaStatus(&newQuota); err != nil {
			updatedFailedQuotas = append(updatedFailedQuotas, newQuota)
			lastErr = err
		}
...
	quotasToCheck := []corev1.ResourceQuota{}
	for _, newQuota := range newQuotas {
		for _, oldQuota := range updatedFailedQuotas {
			if newQuota.Name == oldQuota.Name {
				quotasToCheck = append(quotasToCheck, newQuota)
				break
			}
		}
	}
	e.checkQuotas(quotasToCheck, admissionAttributes, remainingRetries-1)
```

quota A and quota B, A was successfully updated, but B never managed to update successfully, ultimately causing the deployments to be forbidden. However, in reality, A had already been updated, while B had not yet been updated. This eventually led to A quickly reaching its limit.

title: default_servicecidr_controller logs that it's shutting down at startup
body:
It does a `defer klog.Infof("Shutting down %s", controllerName)`, but then at the end it spawns a goroutine and then `Start()` returns, so it ends up logging that at startup rather than at shutdown.

A bigger problem is that it also does `defer c.eventBroadcaster.Shutdown()`, so presumably none of the event broadcasting actually works?

/assign @aojea

title: pod name and host name differ in indexed completion mode
body:
In case[ .spec.completionMode = Indexed](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/#completion-mode) in our Kubernetes job yaml,
The host name will look like (in /etc/hostname in a pod container) looks like:
'xxxxxxxxx-0'
'xxxxxxxxx-1'
'xxxxxxxxx-2'
etc.

However,
The pod name will be:
'xxxxxxxxx-0-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-1-{randomid}'
'xxxxxxxxx-2-{randomid}'
etc.

Why is the pod name not set identical to the host name? 
In case of  .spec.completionMode=NonIndexed mode pod name and hostname are identical.  
So this is an unexpected inconsistency.
The random id can be left out:  xxxxxxxxx-{IndexNr}  is already an unique id.


It is important, because we let our containers write their hostname in our log messages.
However, we cannot directly derive the pod name from the host name, which is needed to find back the pod logs written to persistent storage later on.
Of course we can work around this, by adding the pod name to the env variables of the container and log that additionally, but that should not be necessary in my opinion. It is very confusing that pod name and host name differ in indexed mode.

### What happened?

I would expect CLI option --grace-period should override configured or default gracePeriod.

kubectl delete pod/test2 --force=true --grace-period=0

title: Scheduler: nil pointer dereference when RequestedToCapacityRatio field is missing in NodeResourcesFitArgs
body:
### What happened?

When configuring the scheduler's NodeResourcesFitArgs with `RequestedToCapacityRatio` scoring strategy, if the `RequestedToCapacityRatio` field is not specified in the configuration, the scheduler will encounter a nil pointer dereference error during validation.

Logs like this:
```shell
I0801 10:12:35.433071   19683 serving.go:386] Generated self-signed cert in-memory
W0801 10:12:35.579568   19683 authentication.go:368] No authentication-kubeconfig provided in order to lookup client-ca-file in configmap/extension-apiserver-authentication in kube-system, so client certificate authentication won't work.
W0801 10:12:35.579579   19683 authentication.go:392] No authentication-kubeconfig provided in order to lookup requestheader-client-ca-file in configmap/extension-apiserver-authentication in kube-system, so request-header client certificate authentication won't work.
W0801 10:12:35.579587   19683 authorization.go:193] No authorization-kubeconfig provided, so SubjectAccessReview of authorization tokens won't work.
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x2 addr=0x0 pc=0x103fac068]
````

### What did you expect to happen?

If the `RequestedToCapacityRatio` field is missing, the scheduler should return a descriptive error message.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a scheduler configuration with NodeResourcesFitArgs
2. Set the scoring strategy type to `RequestedToCapacityRatio`
3. Omit the `RequestedToCapacityRatio` field in the configuration
4. Start the scheduler

Example configuration that triggers the issue:

```yaml
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
clientConnection:
  kubeconfig: "/Users/bin/.kube/config"
profiles:
- schedulerName: default-scheduler
  plugins:
    score:
      enabled:
      - name: "NodeResourcesFit"
        weight: 100
      disabled:
      - name: "*"
  pluginConfig:
  - name: "NodeResourcesFit"
    args:
      scoringStrategy:
        resources:
        - name: "nvidia.com/gpu"
          weight: 1
        type: RequestedToCapacityRatio

title: Slow Binding During Burst Creation of Static PVs/PVCs
body:
### What happened?

The latency of binding a large number of PVs/PVCs created in a short time is high. For example, when creating 1,000 PVs/PVCs at 100 QPS, we observed the elapsed time from PVC creation to binding as follows::
```json
{
  "data": {
    "Max": 65.25025412,
    "Perc50": 37.856062129,
    "Perc90": 51.360338175,
    "Perc99": 59.350783709
  },
  "unit": "s",
  "labels": {
    "Metric": "pvc_startup"
  }
}
```
If we increase the number of PVs/PVCs to 10,000, the situation gets even worse.:
```json
{
  "data": {
    "Max": 494.581873344,
    "Perc50": 453.175475447,
    "Perc90": 485.963995641,
    "Perc99": 493.624297649
  },
  "unit": "s",
  "labels": {
    "Metric": "pvc_startup"
  }
}
```

For each client thread, create a PV first, then create the corresponding PVC.
PV:
```yaml
{{$index := .Index}}
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-{{$index}}
  labels:
    app: pvc-test
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteMany
  capacity:
    storage: 20Gi
  claimRef:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
    name: pvc-{{$index}}
    namespace: perf
  csi:
    driver: xxx
    volumeAttributes:
      key: xxx
    volumeHandle: pv-{{$index}}
```

PVC
```yaml
{{$index := .Index}}
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-{{$index}}
  namespace: perf
  labels:
    app: pvc-test
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  volumeName: pv-{{$index}}

```

### What did you expect to happen?

Since there is no need to call other components and only the PV/PVC resources are modified to achieve binding, this process should be very fast.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create file pv.yaml
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: test-pv
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteMany
  capacity:
    storage: 20Gi
  csi:
    driver: test
    volumeAttributes:
      test: "true"
    volumeHandle: test-pv
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  volumeMode: Filesystem
```
2. Create file pvc.yaml
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: test-pvc
  namespace: default
  labels:
    test: "true"
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  volumeName: test-pv
```
3. Create file test.sh
```shell
#!/bin/bash

total=1000

mkdir -p pvs
mkdir -p pvcs
mkdir -p outputs

function init() {
    for i in $(seq $total); do
        sed "s/  name: test-pv.*/  name: test-pv-$i/g" pv.yaml >pvs/$i.yaml
        sed -i "s/    volumeHandle: test-pv.*/    volumeHandle: test-pv-$i/g" pvs/$i.yaml
        
        sed "s/  name: test-pvc.*/  name: test-pvc-$i/g" pvc.yaml >pvcs/$i.yaml
        sed -i "s/  volumeName: test-pv.*/  volumeName: test-pv-$i/g" pvcs/$i.yaml
    done
}

function handle_start() {
    i=$1
    kubectl create -f pvs/$i.yaml
    kubectl create -f pvcs/$i.yaml
}

function start() {
    for i in $(seq $total); do
        handle_start $i > outputs/$i.log 2>&1 &
    done
}

function handle_stop() {
    i=$1
    kubectl delete -f pvcs/$i.yaml
    kubectl delete -f pvs/$i.yaml
    
}

function stop() {
    for i in $(seq $total); do
        handle_stop $i > outputs/$i.log 2>&1 &
    done
}

function show_bind_latency() {
    kubectl get pvc -l test=true | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | while read name; do
        kubectl get pvc "$name" --show-managed-fields=true -o json | jq -r '
        "\(.metadata.creationTimestamp) \(
        (.metadata.managedFields // [])
        | map(select(
            .manager == "kube-controller-manager"
            and (.fieldsV1."f:metadata"."f:annotations"."f:pv.kubernetes.io/bind-completed"?)
            ))
        | .[0].time // "N/A"
        ) \(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
        done | while read created bound full_name; do
        if [[ "$bound" != "N/A" ]]; then
            created_ts=$(date -d "$created" +%s)
            bound_ts=$(date -d "$bound" +%s)
            diff=$((bound_ts - created_ts))
            echo "$full_name: $created -> $bound = ${diff}s"
        else
            echo "$full_name: $created -> N/A = N/A"
        fi
    done
}


# Check if a subcommand is provided
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <init|start|stop>"
    exit 1
fi

case "$1" in
    init)
        init
    ;;
    start)
        start
    ;;
    stop)
        stop
    ;;
    show)
        show_bind_latency
    ;;
    *)
        echo "Invalid subcommand. Usage: $0 <init|start|stop|show>"
        exit 1
    ;;
esac
```
4. Prepare your kubeconfig file
5. Run the following command:
```shell
./test.sh init && ./test.sh start
```
6. Wait PVCs bind to PVs
7. Run the following command to get binding elapsed time:
```shell
./test.sh show
```

You will see an output similar to this:
```
default/test-pvc-63: 2025-08-01T06:57:36Z -> 2025-08-01T06:58:04Z = 28s
default/test-pvc-630: 2025-08-01T06:57:38Z -> 2025-08-01T06:58:02Z = 24s

default/test-pvc-636: 2025-08-01T06:57:39Z -> 2025-08-01T06:57:59Z = 20s

title: Shared Counter attributes in DRA
body:
### What would you like to be added?

DRA Shared Counter attributes, like the existing device attributes.

### Why is this needed?

Cluster autoscaler is currently in the process of adding cluster limits on dynamic resources, to avoid over-scaling. With the current implementation of partitionable devices, it is difficult for controllers to discern between a device and its partitions, if a counter can be attributed as a counter for a specific device, this would solve that problem.

title: HPA - optimize calculatePodRequestsFromContainers func specific container lookups
body:
The `calculatePodRequestsFromContainers` function currently iterates through all containers in a pod, even when a specific container name is provided. This is inefficient. When the container parameter is not an empty string, the function should locate the specified container and return its resource request without iterating through the entire list. We should exit the loop early once the matching container is found.

ref: [comment](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132430/files#r2217338178)

/triage accepted
/assign @laoj2 
/sig autoscaling

title: Support both maxSurge and maxUnavailable Option in RollingUpdate for Daemonset
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The doc for [Daemonset](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-daemon/update-daemon-set/) only mentioned that maxSurge and maxAvailable cannot be both 0. maxSurge and maxUnavailable is supported for [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#max-surge), and there is no obvious reason why this option cannot be supported. 

### Why is this needed?

We want the same granular control of Daemonset like Deployment.

title: Deprecated field serviceAccount still influences serviceAccountName, preventing null updates
body:
### What happened?

When trying to explicitly set `.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName` to `null` in a Deployment (or PodSpec),  
the update is ignored unless `.spec.template.spec.serviceAccount` is also set to `null` in the same request.

This is surprising because `serviceAccount` is a deprecated alias for `serviceAccountName` and is not part of the public OpenAPI schema anymore.

It effectively prevents clearing `serviceAccountName` via Server-Side Apply or Merge Patch if the deprecated `serviceAccount` field still has a value internally.

Changing the service account work well, the problem occurs only when trying to suppress service account

### What did you expect to happen?

- The deprecated `serviceAccount` field should no longer affect the behavior of `serviceAccountName`.
- Setting `serviceAccountName: null` should be enough to remove the custom ServiceAccount and fall back to `"default"`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Apply a Deployment with a custom ServiceAccount:
```yaml
 apiVersion: apps/v1
 kind: Deployment
 metadata:
   name: dummy
 spec:
   selector:
     matchLabels:
       app: dummy
   template:
     metadata:
       labels:
         app: dummy
     spec:
       serviceAccountName: dummy
       containers:
       - name: dummy
         image: nginx
```

Apply the same manifest but set serviceAccountName: null:
 ```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dummy
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dummy
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dummy
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: null
      containers:
      - name: dummy
        image: nginx
```
(Same result by removing the serviceAccountName)

### Anything else we need to know?

This happens with both Server-Side Apply and Merge Patch.

Looking at the apiserver code, serviceAccount and serviceAccountName still point to the same internal variable in the PodSpec, and the defaulting code copies values between them. This happens before SSA field ownership resolution.

title: An object created through SSA with a non-nil deletion timestamp will not get deleted
body:
### What happened?

```
$ cat cm.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:42:06Z"
  deletionTimestamp: 2025-08-05T16:42:06Z
  name: test
  namespace: kubevirt-vm

$ k apply --server-side -f cm.yaml
Warning: Detected changes to resource test which is currently being deleted.
configmap/test serverside-applied

$ k get cm test  -oyaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:45:59Z"
  deletionTimestamp: "2025-08-05T16:42:06Z"
  name: test
  namespace: kubevirt-vm
  resourceVersion: "257079249"
  uid: caa288c7-9b51-4365-a062-a4020d4bef93
```

Then deleting it causes it to go, so I am guessing this is rooted in insufficient event handling in the GC controller, since only SSA allows to create objects with a non-nil deletion timestamp:
```
$ k delete    -f cm.yaml
configmap "test" deleted

$ k get cm test  -oyaml
Error from server (NotFound): configmaps "test" not found

The CM to immediately be gone

title: Update json-patch to v5.9.10 / v4.0.13 or later, in-order to remove pkg/errors as an indirect dependency
body:
Hi,

Currently `github.com/pkg/errors` is an indirect dependency used by `gopkg.in/evanphx/json-patch.v4`.
However `github.com/pkg/errors` repository has already been archived for over a year, due to which `json-patch` has replaced it with the standard `errors` package in their latest `v5` release.

Requesting to kindly update json-patch to v5 (v5.9.10 or later)

Additional Links:
- [Issue in json-patch to replace pkg/errors](https://github.com/evanphx/json-patch/issues/205)
- [PR where json-patch removed pkg/errors](https://github.com/evanphx/json-patch/pull/206)

title: Segfault on e2e tests after 1.34 RC
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

All kind tests are failing due to a segfault in the apiserver with the 1.34 rc

### Which tests are failing?

Many e2e tests running on the newest RC

### Since when has it been failing?

Since the release was cut and we bump the tag to 1.34

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-release-master-blocking#kind-master

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Not fully sure but it seems due to these two commits conflicting with each other.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131902/files

and 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132965/files

One uses a metric that is deprecated in 1.34 and is causing a nil pointer exception, seems like that causes that metric to be set to nil but seems likely to be the case from the logs.

An easy fix might be to use the new metric defined by @serathius in the second PR. 

CC @liuxu623 who made the first change.

Seems likely to be a release blocker.

### Anything else we need to know?

Logs of apiserver

title: SELinux warning controller does not report conflicts with ""
body:
### What happened?

A pod with label `:::s0:c0,c2` should conflicts with a pod with label `:::` (or `""`).

Kubelet defaults the first three components of the label to `system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2` / `system_u:object_r:container_file_t:` and these are two different labels. If the pods have `spec.securityContext.seLinuxChangePolicy: MountOption`, kubelet correctly reports the conflict + refuses to run the second pod with something like:
```
Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[vol], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[vol]: conflicting SELinux labels of volume pvc-3f62d9ae-7ad0-47d4-8b5a-72656ace42e6: "system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2" and ""
```

However, the SELinux warning controller does not report any conflict and it should. 

### What did you expect to happen?

SELinux warning controller should emit something like:

```
SELinuxLabel "" conflicts with pod testpod-c2 that uses the same volume as this pod with SELinuxLabel ":::s0:c0,c2". If both pods land on the same node, only one of them may access the volume.
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run two pods, one with `spec.securityContext.seLinuxOptions.level = "s0:c0,c2"` and the second one with `nil`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The controller runs in KCM, who does not know the operating system defaults for SELinux labels and thus skips comparison of empty SELinux label components. It should compare at least the last one, with SELinux level and categories. Those are not defaulted by the OS.

title: Improving handling of Deprecated and Hidden metrics
body:
The current implication of [DeprecatedVersion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/metrics/opts.go#L60) for a metric(like [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.33/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/metrics/metrics.go#L83)) is confusing.

According to the [Metrics Deprecation Rules](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/deprecation-policy/#deprecating-a-metric) we want to first announce the deprecation of a metric and then stop serving them after a recommended period of time (for stable metrics, this is noted as: STABLE: 3 releases or 9 months (whichever is longer)). So seems like the metric should continue to function properly after its marked as deprecated.

But we recently caught an [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133405) that was 1.34.0 release blocking, where a STABLE metric marked as deprecated for 1.34.0 caused a panic in apiserver startup, because it was actually being removed in 1.34.0. It seems like the DeprecatedVersion here is actually behaving like RemovedVersion, where we stop serving the metric in K8s version greater than the specified value.


Questions:

1. What does the DeprecatedVersion mean here? Is it supposed to be the version where we mark the metric for deprecation but continue serving it for stated timeline in the guidelines, after which we actually remove the support for it? Or, is it the version post which we will stop serving the metric?

3. Based on the above, are we sure about the behaviour/support for `apiserver_storage_objects` metric (which was what caused [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133405) issue) that will be reflected in 1.34.0 ?

title: Temporary volumes (emptyDir, configMap, secrets) created with 0777 permissions – Security concern and compliance question
body:
### What happened?

Hello Kubernetes team,
A vulnerability scan (SHC) has flagged a potential misconfiguration (ID: RIES-693, also known as "Riesgo 55 en Misuri") due to temporary directories being created with 0777 permissions inside Kubernetes pods.

We have observed that:

    The issue affects volumes created from emptyDir, configMap, and secret.

    It is reproducible and not random, and seems to be part of Kubernetes' standard behavior.

    These directories are being created with world-writable (0777) permissions, which conflicts with various internal security and hardening policies.

    This behavior is not caused by the container runtime. We use CRI-O (Kubernetes v1.32.7), which is the recommended runtime, and the issue appears to originate in Kubernetes core.

We have reviewed the following related issue:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125876

In that thread, it is acknowledged that Kubernetes is assigning these permissions, and there's a TODO in the codebase suggesting it is known but not yet addressed. However, it's still unclear whether:

    This behavior is intentional and accepted, or

    It is a pending security enhancement or known issue under consideration.
Request:
Due to compliance requirements, we kindly request one of the following:

    Confirmation that this behavior is expected and accepted by the Kubernetes project, ideally with links to relevant documentation or design decisions.

    OR, confirmation that this is a known issue, and any information about plans to address it or a suggested mitigation.

We need this as evidence that the issue has been escalated to the Kubernetes maintainers.
🔧 Environment:

    Kubernetes version: v1.32.7

    Container runtime: CRI-O

  Thank you

Thank you in advance for your time and guidance. We understand this may be a deeply technical or legacy-driven decision, but any clarification or support you can provide will be extremely helpful to us and likely to others in regulated industries.

Kind regards,

### What did you expect to happen?

We expected the temporary directories created by Kubernetes for emptyDir, configMap, and secret volumes to have more restrictive default permissions — for example, 0755 or 0700 — instead of 0777, which grants world-writable access.

This expectation is based on common security hardening practices and compliance standards, which typically discourage the use of world-writable permissions (0777) in production environments, especially for sensitive volumes managed by the container orchestration platform.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

title: static pod will be kill first when node shutdown even if highest priority
body:
### What happened?

there are kube-proxy static file, and set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical`, like below

```
...
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  priorityClassName: system-node-critical
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  containers:
  - name: kube-proxy
    image: hyperkube:v1.32.2
...
```

set kubelet log level 1(--v=1), when node shutdown, will print log

```
I0808 17:22:43.086972   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:154] "Shutdown manager killing pod with gracePeriod" pod="kube-system/kube-proxy-node-2" gracePeriod=60
...
I0808 17:23:02.791204   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:172] "Shutdown manager finished killing pod" pod="kube-system/kube-proxy-node-2"
...
I0808 17:23:43.087167   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:216] "Shutdown manager pod killing time out" gracePeriod=60 priority=0
...
I0808 17:23:43.087658   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:154] "Shutdown manager killing pod with gracePeriod" pod="kube-system/csi-rbdplugin-pp9gl" gracePeriod=30
I0808 17:23:43.471530   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:172] "Shutdown manager finished killing pod" pod="kube-system/csi-rbdplugin-pp9gl"
I0808 17:23:44.680175   57909 nodeshutdown_manager.go:213] "Done waiting for all pods in group to terminate" gracePeriod=30 priority=2000000000
```

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy-node-2 should be deleted at `priority=2000000000` group, but it not.

The problem lies in determining priority, as static pods do not have priority locally in kubelet, only priority names exist, see:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8e6d788887034b799f6c2a86991a68a080bb0576/pkg/kubelet/nodeshutdown/nodeshutdown_manager.go#L273C1-L275C5

```
		if pod.Spec.Priority != nil {
			priority = *pod.Spec.Priority
		}

		// Find the group index according to the priority.
		index := sort.Search(len(groups), func(i int) bool {
			return groups[i].Priority >= priority
		})
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1 update static pod, and set `spec.priorityClassName=system-node-critical`
2 set kubelet log level 1
3 reboot node

### Anything else we need to know?


related issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109998. Due to the first deletion of the `kube-apiserver`, the inability to update the pod resulted in an endpoint leak

There are actually multiple solutions here:
1Respect static pod priorityClassName, thus make static pod deleted as second group
2 Add a separate one at the end of the group to store the static pod, which make sure static pod will deleted at final order.

title: GatedPods metric negative
body:
### What happened?

Kube-Scheduler currently provides a PreEnqueue plugin that prevents pods from entering ActiveQ or BackoffQ before they meet the scheduling requirements. This plugin is currently used to support the SchedulingGate feature. However, the Kube-Scheduler implementation does not seem to account for the possibility of pods becoming Gated from non-Gated state, resulting in some anomalies in GatedPods metrics. 

The problematic code is as follows. When GatedBefore is false and PreEnqueue returns a failure, a pod is generated with the metric "UnschedulablePods" but the actual podInfo.Gated = true. When this pod is deleted, the Gated metric may become negative.

```go
func (p *PriorityQueue) moveToActiveQ(logger klog.Logger, pInfo *framework.QueuedPodInfo, event string) bool {
	gatedBefore := pInfo.Gated()
	// If SchedulerPopFromBackoffQ feature gate is enabled,
	// PreEnqueue plugins were called when the pod was added to the backoffQ.
	// Don't need to repeat it here when the pod is directly moved from the backoffQ.
	if !p.isPopFromBackoffQEnabled || event != framework.BackoffComplete {
		p.runPreEnqueuePlugins(context.Background(), pInfo)
	}

	added := false
	p.activeQ.underLock(func(unlockedActiveQ unlockedActiveQueuer) {
		if pInfo.Gated() {
			// Add the Pod to unschedulablePods if it's not passing PreEnqueuePlugins.
			if unlockedActiveQ.has(pInfo) {
				return
			}
			if p.backoffQ.has(pInfo) {
				return
			}
			if p.unschedulablePods.get(pInfo.Pod) != nil {
				return
			}
			p.unschedulablePods.addOrUpdate(pInfo, event)
			logger.V(5).Info("Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue, because the pod is gated", "pod", klog.KObj(pInfo.Pod), "event", event, "queue", unschedulableQ)
			return
		}
		if pInfo.InitialAttemptTimestamp == nil {
			now := p.clock.Now()
			pInfo.InitialAttemptTimestamp = &now
		}

		unlockedActiveQ.add(pInfo, event)
		added = true

		p.unschedulablePods.delete(pInfo.Pod, gatedBefore)
		p.backoffQ.delete(pInfo)
		logger.V(5).Info("Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue", "pod", klog.KObj(pInfo.Pod), "event", event, "queue", activeQ)
		if event == framework.EventUnscheduledPodAdd.Label() || event == framework.EventUnscheduledPodUpdate.Label() {
			p.AddNominatedPod(logger, pInfo.PodInfo, nil)
		}
	})
	return added
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

GatedPods Metric should be correct!

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Implement a custom PreEnqueue Plugin, attempting to update it to make it gated from ungated, then delete it.

title: Frequent churn between EndpointSlice objects
body:
### What happened?

We are running a single control-plane k3s cluster in our lab. The cluster has about 56 high-power bare metal nodes. The cluster is used primarily by our developers and our CICD. We create kubevirt VMs for dev and testing. 

Recently as our cluster grew to serve a 100+ kubevirt VMs (running in pods), we noticed significant uptick in the number of ssh and nslookup failures by our CICD system when trying to communicate with the VMs. On average, we would see 1 in 100 or so attempts fail to resolve the VMs IP address. The lookups happened based on the VM name. We use a single headless Service for all of our VMs. 

We wrote a small script to see if we could reproduce the issue. The script would send DNS lookups (dig) to all running healthy VMs (VM status = ready). We noticed that coredns would occasionally return NXDOMAIN for perfectly healthy VMs. Importantly, those VMs were not going through any state transition. The NXDOMIANs would be short-lived, usually < 10 seconds and then it go back to resolving correctly. Again, it's important to note that the VMs(and their pods) for which the NXDOMAIN was received were not transitioning states during this period. 

To see why coredns would behave this way, we wrote another program to watch for updates on the EndpointSlice object. What we noticed was that when the number of endpoints per slice grew greater than 100 (the default value), then, as expected, a new slice would be created. However, what would happen next was surprising. The two endpointslices would start to exhibit significant churn, where endpoints would be frequently be removed from one slice and added to the other. Here is a snippet for the two slices: tortuga-4frcm and tortuga-sxqh9. The program logs the type of event (e.g. MODIFIED) and what changed (i.e. it does a diff between the old and new object). Some additional information that may be helpful:
1. We noticed that the control plane was complaining with these errors:

```
Aug 06 22:20:32 node-name-foo k3s[2663]: time="2025-08-06T22:20:32Z" level=warning msg="Proxy error: write failed: io: read/write on closed pipe"
Aug 06 22:20:42node-name-foo k3s[2663]: I0806 22:20:42.363009    2663 endpointslice_controller.go:337] "Error syncing endpoint slices for service, retrying" key="jenkins/tortuga" err="EndpointSlice informer cache is out of date"
```

2. We are running a single control-plane k3s cluster in our lab. It's certainly possible that this node when under load cannot send out events fast enough to all services (like coredns). However, we would expect that the system should continue to resolve valid VMs to their IPs. 

How does this tie into the coredns issue of returning NXDOMAIN for valid VMs?

Coredns also uses endpointslice objects. One theory would be that there is a significant time gap between the slice update events. Using the example above, an update where one slice removes a (valid) VM is received and then after a delay of several seconds, the update for the second slice, which includes the previously removed VM, is received. Between these two updates, coredns returns NXDOMAIN for the valid VM. 

Other thoughts:
1. The moving of endpoints between slices seems racy to me. If there is significant delay between propagating updates of the two slices, then services like coredns will have temporary inconsistencies. 
2. Is there a corner case where the endpointslice controller frequently balances endpoints across slices? Can this balancing be disabled?
3. Should coredns (and other consumers of endpointslice) be enhanced to detect stale cache entries?  
4. Is this expected behavior? I hope not. 

### What did you expect to happen?

We expect that coredns should reliably resolve IPs for VMs/Pods that are healthy.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unfortunately, this is not easy to produce, primarily because the issue seems to arise when the control-plane is under load and is having a hard time sending updates to all informers. 

### Anything else we need to know?

Our current workaround has been to increase endpoints pers slice from 100 (default) to 200. This has mitigated the issue for the time being, but we would like to scale to 500+ endpoints. Single slice approach may not be appropriate at that point.

title: Topology Spread should greedily allow scheduling to a node that doesn't make a bad skew worse
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Hi,

I'm starting this as a thought on how Topology Spread should work when it is already failing (having skew above max): I think the answer is it should consider scheduling any single pod that doesn't make situation worse, and preferably improves the skew even if it doesn't meet the max skew requirement, instead of a direct no (current behavior). Do let me know if this is already discussed as alternative to [#3990](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3990). I think this can be an easier and coherent approach that doesn't break what's already working, and to leave space for other components to improve stuff other than skew.

Given that this is different from existing behavior never-the-less, it might be a good idea to add a toggle (e.g., whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotScheduleWorse/ScheduleImprovements/ScheduleNoWorse)

/sig scheduling

### Why is this needed?

Given situation below as a 3 zone spread with max skew of 1, for simplicity sake, each pod schedules on a separate node (with minDomains 3 configured):

zone 1: 3 pods
zone 2: 3 pods
zone 3: 3->0 pods caused by zone failure
3 pending pods due to zone 3 failure

How this proposal helps:

1. No pending pods will be scheduled to zone 1 or zone 2, since a single schedule will make skew worse (3 -> 4).
2. When zone 3 recovers, this proposal is coherent on bringing new nodes back gradually, as scheduling any of the pending pods improves the skew (3 -> 2), which is a lower requirement than considering scheduling 2 pods at once, makes the skew under max, and eventually can recover.
3. If zone 2 encounters additional 1 node failure, this proposal helps bringing a new node into zone 2 (potentially through cluster-autoscaler), which improves replica count and doesn't make skew worse (3 -> 3).

Overall it makes this approach still somewhat rigor and limiting on maintaining the spread (not falling back to ScheduleAnyway), but helpful during and post zonal outage without human intervention.

Do let me know if any counter-examples.

title: RS controller created a pod that does not belong to it
body:
### What happened?

We execute a task once a week through a cronjob. We restart the pod by adding an annotation to the deployment. There are four cronjobs that add annotations to four deployments respectively at the same time point to trigger the restart. The next day after the cronjob was executed, we found that one of the deployments failed to restart and got stuck at the 1/2 status. The failure of the first replica to restart caused the rolling update to stop. The RS of this deployment created a pod that did not belong to it, and then it was deleted by other controllers.

1.The way to add the annotation is as follows: 
```

title: Race condition in kubelet's PodCertsManager might lead to memory leaks
body:
### What happened?

Introduced in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/4624cb9bb92186358e001be392e50e5d23b5cdd9, and only observable after enabling the `PodCertificateRequest` feature gate.

When https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2825 gets called, it queues PCRs for a given pod to be handled by a `podcertificate.Manager` instance.

However, if the queue keys for these PCRs get async-processed before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2826 is called, the `podcertificate.Manager` will never again attempt to clear its internal state for these PCRs as kept in its `Manager.credStore` map.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet's state gets cleaned for a given pod when the pod is removed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a unit test that runs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/790393ae92e97262827d4f1fba24e8ae65bbada0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2822, expose the `podcertificate.Manager{}.credStore` variable, and observe what happens to the `credStore` variable when a cached PCR's state is supposed to get removed. Run a couple hundred times to make sure the race condition appears.

### Anything else we need to know?

Discussed at https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C05MW3382US/p1754992465556979

title: Scheduler does not consider pod-deletion-cost during rollout, leading to pod imbalance
body:
### What happened?

During rollout of a Deployment with a `rollingUpdate` strategy (`maxSurge: 3`, `maxUnavailable: 0`) and `podAntiAffinity` based on `pod-template-hash`, the Kubernetes Scheduler does not take the `pod-deletion-cost` annotation into account. This leads to an imbalance where two pods with different `pod-template-hash` values are scheduled on the same node for an extended period. Specifically, the Scheduler should prioritize scheduling on nodes with existing pods of lower-cost pods in a manner that maintains a balanced distribution across nodes.

For example, in a setup with 6 replicas across 6 nodes, when a rollout begins, new pods are scheduled alongside existing ones without considering their deletion costs, resulting in a situation with two pods on one node and none on others, thus leading to an undesired imbalance throughout the rollout.


### What did you expect to happen?

I expected that the Scheduler would take `pod-deletion-cost` into account when scheduling new replicas during a rollout, ensuring that it removes lower-cost pods first and maintains balanced distribution across nodes to comply with `podAntiAffinity` rules.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Deployment with the following configuration:
    ```yaml
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: foo
    spec:
      replicas: 6
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: foo
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: foo
        spec:
          affinity:
            podAntiAffinity:
              requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
              - labelSelector:
                  matchExpressions:
                  - key: app.kubernetes.io/name
                    operator: In
                    values:
                    - foo
                matchLabelKeys:
                - pod-template-hash
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          containers:
          - name: foo
            image: foo:latest
    ```
2. Annotate the pods with pod-deletion-cost as shown below:
```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 | pod4 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 | pod5 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod6 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2c |
```

3. Do a rollout restart, it surges and it could do the following:
```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeA1 | pod7 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeB1 | pod8 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 | pod4 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 | pod5 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod6 | foo-123           | 998               | us-west-2c |
| NodeC2 | pod9 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2c |
```

This will put two pods (with different pod-template-hash) onto the same node, but take down the pods with lower cost, leading to:

```
| node   | pod  | pod-template-hash | pod-deletion-cost | Zone       |
| NodeA1 | pod1 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2a |
| NodeA1 | pod7 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2a |  
| NodeB1 | pod2 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2b |
| NodeB1 | pod8 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2b |
| NodeC1 | pod3 | foo-123           | 999               | us-west-2c |
| NodeA2 |      |                   |                   | us-west-2a | 
| NodeB2 |      |                   |                   | us-west-2b |
| NodeC2 | pod9 | foo-124           | <not-set-yet>     | us-west-2c |
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The current behavior gives rise to an imbalance in pod distribution across nodes, ultimately leading to resource underutilization in some zones while overloading others. 
- This issue seems particularly problematic in configurations where there's a custom tooling that adds pod-deletion-cost to workloads

title: Debian now deprecates public key file used for K8s APT repo
body:
Hi, the K8s repo at https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/ uses a public key file having a hashing algorithm which Debian APT no longer considers safe.  The message emitted by APT (in response to command `apt update`) is:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
```
The command `apt update --audit` outputs:
```
Warning: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Policy will reject signature within a year, see --audit for details
Audit: https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.33/deb/InRelease: Sub-process /usr/bin/sqv returned an error code (1), error message is:
   Error: Policy rejected packet type
   Caused by:
       Signature Packet v3 is not considered secure since 2026-02-01T00:00:00Z
```
As I understand it, this would be because the public key is hashed using SHA1, rather than SHA256 or SHA512.  

I can suppress this warning (presumably until 1 February 2026) by copying file `/usr/share/apt/default-sequoia.config` to new file (in new parent directories) `/etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/apt-sequoia.config`, and changing the date in the last line from `2026-02-01` to `2027-02-01`.

title: Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies
body:
It's becoming increasingly common to add new feature gates for extensions on features that still have a feature gate. Today we handle this in an ad-hoc way, where we sometimes check both feature gates (the one directly controlling the new extension, and the one for the original feature), but in lots of cases we just check the direct feature gate.

Rather than checking multiple feature gates wherever the extension feature is used, I propose:
1. Codify inter-FeatureGate dependencies, so if feature B depends on feature A, we make this explicit in the feature gate spec, and validate it on startup
    - Only allow a feature to be enabled if all it's dependent features are also enabled. Enforced in [`featureGate.Validate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9da4b7ecfb60ea484f8e6c89c42e63506571bc68/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go#L304).
    - Only allow a feature to graduate, if all it's dependent features are at least the same level of maturity. In other words, if feature A is beta, feature B can graduate to beta, but it cannot graduate to GA. (What does this mean for deprecation?). Enforced in unit test.
3. Wherever we need to check if feature B is enabled, we only check feature B, and rely on the validation to ensure that feature A is also enabled.

For an example, the new `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling` (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/132919) depends on _both_ `InPlacePodVerticalScaling` and `PodLevelResources`.

/kind feature
/sig architecture
/cc @JoelSpeed @liggitt @jpbetz @siyuanfoundation

title: Service Multi-Protocol Port Configuration Test Report
body:
### What happened?
#### Background
Starting from Kubernetes 1.24, Service support multiple ports with different protocols, with this feature becoming stable in version 1.26. This report examines the constraints and behaviors when configuring multiple ports with different combinations of port numbers, protocols, and nodePort values.

**Related Issue:** [Service port duplication and patch exception](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105610)

#### Test Methodology
Test Environment: v1.28.3
1. **Creation Tests:** Create NodePort Services with various port configurations to observe creation success and effectiveness
2. **Patch Tests:** Modify existing Services to test patch behavior and port functionality

#### Key Findings

##### Service Creation Behavior
- ✅ **Allowed:** Different protocols with different ports and nodePorts
- ✅ **Allowed:** Same protocol with different ports and different nodePorts  
- ✅ **Allowed:** Different protocols with same port but different nodePorts
- ❌ **Blocked:** Same protocol with same port (port conflict)
- ❌ **Blocked:** Same protocol with same nodePort (nodePort conflict)
- ❌ **Blocked:** Any configuration with port conflicts regardless of protocol

##### Patch Operation Behavior
Patch operations exhibit more complex behavior:
- **Normal cases:** Same as creation rules for basic scenarios
- **Anomaly:** When protocols differ but ports/nodePorts conflict, patch commands execute successfully but only the first port item becomes effective

##### Special Cases
1. **Auto-assigned nodePorts:** When protocols differ and ports are the same without specifying nodePorts, Kubernetes assigns the same nodePort value, causing patch anomalies on subsequent operations
2. **Recovery mechanism:** A second patch operation typically resolves the issue by assigning different nodePort values

#### Conclusions

##### Port Configuration Constraints
- **Same Protocol:** Both port and nodePort must be unique across all entries
- **Different Protocols:** Recommend ensuring both port and nodePort uniqueness to avoid patch anomalies

##### Recommendations
1. Always specify unique port and nodePort combinations regardless of protocol differences
2. Be aware of patch behavior anomalies when dealing with protocol-mixed configurations


### What did you expect to happen?

 Ideal scenario is:
(1) When the protocol types are different, the same PORT number should allow the use of the same nodePort, and this state should be achievable through both creation and PATCH.
Or (2) When the protocol types are different, the same PORT number should not allow the use of the same nodePort.

A technician previously raised a similar  [issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105610). I would like to report this situation to community now and track the resolution of it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. do `$ kubectl apply -f example.yaml` , creation is ok.
```yaml

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: multi-protocol-service
spec:
  type: NodePort
  ports:
  - name: udp-port
    port: 80
    targetPort: 300
    protocol: UDP
  - name: tcp-port
    port: 80
    targetPort: 300
    protocol: TCP
  selector:
    app: myapp
```

title: Deprecations are not marked correctly
body:
### What happened?

I noticed that in client-go there are some deprecations that are not marked correctly. Accordingly e.g. staticcheck or Intellij are not detecting the deprecations and are not producing findings for usage of deprecated code. I assume this also affects other parts of the code base.

Correct deprecation:
```go
	// CreateWithEventNamespace is the same as a Create, except that it sends the request to the event.Namespace.
	//
	// Deprecated: use CreateWithEventNamespaceWithContext instead.
```
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.4/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/typed/core/v1/event_expansion.go#L33-L36

Incorrect deprecation: (deprecation is not in its own paragraph)
```go
// NewFilteredSharedInformerFactory constructs a new instance of sharedInformerFactory.
// Listers obtained via this SharedInformerFactory will be subject to the same filters
// as specified here.
// Deprecated: Please use NewSharedInformerFactoryWithOptions instead
func NewFilteredSharedInformerFactory(client kubernetes.Interface, defaultResync time.Duration, namespace string, tweakListOptions internalinterfaces.TweakListOptionsFunc) SharedInformerFactory {
```
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.4/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/informers/factory.go#L116-L120

xref: https://go.dev/wiki/Deprecated
related thread in Slack: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EG7JC6T/p1754999884784489

### What did you expect to happen?

All deprecations should be detected correctly by tools like staticcheck / Intellij.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

One way is to fix one of the incorrect deprecations and then running statichcheck (usually via golangci-lint) should report all usages of the deprecated func now.

### Anything else we need to know?

It would be great if we could lint for incorrect deprecations, so we can find all current occurences and avoid this in the future.

I think fixing this issue is absolutely essential to enable consumers of k/k Go code to migrate away early from deprecated code.

title: Make healthCheckNodePort Optional for On-Premises LoadBalancer Services with externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Introduce a way to disable automatic allocation of healthCheckNodePort for LoadBalancer services when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, particularly for on-premises environments where external load balancers do not rely on this port.

### Why is this needed?

In on-premises Kubernetes/OpenShift clusters using MetalLB with BGP and external load balancers (e.g., F5), the healthCheckNodePort is not used. However, Kubernetes still allocates and exposes this port when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set.

**This leads to:**

Unnecessary open ports on nodes.
Potential security concerns.
Port exhaustion risks in large-scale clusters.
Operational confusion for administrators.
There is currently no native way to disable this behavior while preserving externalTrafficPolicy: Local, which is often required for source IP preservation.

**Proposed Solution**
Introduce an opt-out mechanism for healthCheckNodePort allocation, such as:

**Option 1: Annotation-based opt-out**

metadata:
  annotations:
    service.kubernetes.io/disable-healthcheck-nodeport: "true"

**Option 2: API field**

spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  disableHealthCheckNodePort: true

**Risks and Mitigations**
Misconfiguration could lead to traffic being sent to unhealthy nodes if the external load balancer is not properly configured.
Clear documentation and validation should accompany the feature to ensure safe usage.
**Additional Context**
This enhancement would benefit on-premises setups where:

MetalLB is used with BGP.
External load balancers perform their own health checks.
healthCheckNodePort is not required and adds unnecessary complexity.

The following assertion fails https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources_test.go#L1864-L1865

The test setup does add the claim objects in advance and waits for the cache to sync
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources/dynamicresources_test.go#L2088-L2105

I dug a little deeper, and it seems that the assumed cache adds an event handler to sync itself with the informer's store
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/pkg/scheduler/util/assumecache/assume_cache.go#L206-L215

The test does not wait until the registered handler returned from the `AddEventHandler` has synced.  The wait  in `tc.informerFactory.WaitForCacheSync(tc.ctx.Done())` does not include the handler used by the assumed cache.

See the informer doc:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L192-L195

This creates a race condition where the test may start execution while the assumed cache has not caught up with the initial store via the informer yet.

This does not seem to be an issue with the production code, since the registered handler from the `NewAssumeCache` gets included in the list of handlers to sync
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L441-L443  

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/17d6c9c551f917b63797cb1cfe9bbc4b01ea6a43/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L580-L586

title: Kubelet Volume Manager can erroneously mark volume as unmounted.
body:
### What happened?

We observed an edge case where an API server transient issue can cause a volume to be marked as unmounted in the volume manager's ASW, and making the subsequent `NodeVolumeUnstage` calls to fail due to dangling publish mounts.

The sequence of events is:
1. A map volume operation is kicked off.
2. The API server has a transient issue, causing the map volume operation to fail with `Error: MapVolume.MarkVolumeAsMounted failed while expanding volume for volume $PVC`. This error happens after the `MapPodDevice` (and therefore the `NodePublishVolume`) call has already succeeded. This causes the volume mount to be marked as uncertain and the map to be requeued.
3. When the operation retries,  the api server issue causes the MapPodDevice to fail with `blockMapper.publishVolumeForBlock failed to get NodePublishSecretRef`
4. This error causes `markVolumeErrorState` to be called. The logic here[0] falls into a branch that marks the volume as unmounted in ASW, since the mount is marked uncertain.
5. At this point the pod is deleted, so the map operation doesn't happen again. Since the volume is marked unmounted, the VM reconciler doesn't call unpublish for this pod and volume pair.

[0] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/56dd5ab10ff19aa9ebe438122a00472c4135de23/pkg/volume/util/operationexecutor/operation_generator.go#L819


### What did you expect to happen?

All volumes are unpublished correctly after the pod is deleted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Once `MapPodDevice` completes, trigger pod deletion and inject API failures. This should cause the pod to be deleted without unpublish being called.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: [FG: EnvFiles] Proposal for env file syntax extension and improvement
body:
When implementing the KEP and the corresponding code, we referred to a specification for .env files that is not widely recognized as authoritative. 
Current syntax: https://smartmob-rfc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/2-dotenv.html#formal-specification
  
Moreover, the scope of this specification is quite simplistic and does not appear to cover all use cases.

For example, we have the following user scenarios:
1. Users need to define a PEM-formatted private key as the value of an environment variable. This requires support for multi-line values (since the PEM format requires at least three lines: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privacy-Enhanced_Mail, and no extraneous characters should be inserted into the multi-line values. This necessitates the ability to insert multi-line values losslessly.
2. In a multi-container pod, multiple containers need to use the same environment variable defined by an initContainer, but each container needs to substitute the value based on its own variables. This requires the ability to interpolate environment variables.

Therefore, we propose to extend and modify the current envFile format:
1. Multi-line values containing line breaks can be enclosed in double quotes. Parsing should not terminate until the second corresponding double quote is encountered.
Example:
    ```
      PRIVATE_KEY="-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
      ...
      -----END DSA PRIVATE KEY-----"
    ```
2. During parsing, environment variables should support interpolation.
Example:
    ```
    DATABASE_URL="mysql://${USER}@localhost/my_database"
    container1: USER=user1 -> mysql://user1@localhost/my_database
    container1: USER=user2 -> mysql://user2@localhost/my_database
    ```

I believe the first point is a necessary addition, and the current method of introducing multi-line values (where a line ending with a backslash "" indicates the value continues on the next line, and implementations must concatenate lines without line endings, treating the backslash as a single space) should be deprecated.

The second point is an improvement feature request. We can choose to implement it, or remind users to define multiple similar environment variables as a workaround.

title: ServiceCIDR is known to not work in some clusters, but blocking it via VAP violates conformance
body:
The ServiceCIDR API requires support from non-core-k8s components in some clusters, and thus is not guaranteed to work in all clusters. The [ServiceCIDR documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/network/extend-service-ip-ranges/#preventing-unauthorized-servicecidr-creation-update-using-validating-admission-policy) explains how you can use VAP to block usage of the API in this case. (Though there are some problems and https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/51748 updates those docs.)

However, it turns out that doing this violates conformance, because the test `[sig-network] ServiceCIDR and IPAddress API should support ServiceCIDR API operations [Conformance]` requires that `e2e.test` is able to modify the default ServiceCIDR.

The test case just adds an annotation, so we could hack up the VAP to allow the specific change that the conformance test makes, but this seems like cheating, and would also be fragile.

Does it make sense for conformance to require ServiceCIDR to be available as an API, given that it doesn't work in some clusters and we explicitly document how to disable it? (FWIW I guess the same question could be asked about NetworkPolicy, except that everyone has gotten used to the fact that the NP API exists even in clusters where it doesn't work so no one tries to disable it...)

/sig network
/area conformance
/triage accepted
/priority important-soon
cc @aojea
