title: [Flaky test] TestPriorityAndFairnessWithPanicRecoveryAndTimeoutFilter flakes on APF header assertions
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

`k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/apiserver/pkg/server/filters` unit tests. Observed in:

- ci-kubernetes-unit-ppc64le
- ci-kubernetes-unit-1-34
- ci-kubernetes-unit-1-32

### Which tests are flaking?

`TestPriorityAndFairnessWithPanicRecoveryAndTimeoutFilter` Specifically sub-tests involving timeout scenarios:

- `priority_level_concurrency_is_set_to_1,_request_times_out_and_inner_handler_hasn't_written_to_the_response_yet`
- `priority_level_concurrency_is_set_to_1,_inner_handler_panics_after_the_request_times_out`

### Since when has it been flaking?

Intermittently observed

### Testgrid link

https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?text=TestPriorityAndFairnessWithPanicRecoveryAndTimeoutFilter&test=k8s.io%2Fapiserver%2Fpkg%2Fserver%2Ffilters

### Reason for failure (if possible)

There is an inherent race condition in the test setup between the TimeoutHandler and the APF (Priority and Fairness) tracking logic.

The test expects APF headers (like X-Kubernetes-PF-FlowSchema-UID) to be present on all responses. However, when a request times out (Status 504), the outer TimeoutHandler takes over, writes the response, and closes the stream/context.

If the TimeoutHandler finalizes the response before the inner APF handler has a chance to write its tracking headers, the headers will be missing from the response. The test currently fails an assertion when these headers are missing.

Sample Failure Log:

`priority-and-fairness_test.go:788: Expected APF headers to match, but got: expected HTTP header X-Kubernetes-PF-FlowSchema-UID to have value "test-fs", but got: ""`

### Anything else we need to know?

I have successfully reproduced this flake locally on x86 environments. I have a fix prepared which updates the test helper (`headerMatcher.inspect`) to skip APF header assertions if the request context is already cancelled or timed out.

### Relevant SIG(s)

/sig api-machinery

title: fake client-go: support ResourceVersion in Watch
body:
### What would you like to be added?

fake.Clientset suffers from a race condition related to informers: it does not implement resource version support in its Watch implementation and instead assumes that watches are set up before further resource changes are made.

If a test waits for caches to be synced and then immediately adds an object, that new object will never be seen by event handlers if the race goes wrong and the Watch call hadn't completed yet (can be triggered by adding a sleep before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b53b9fb5573323484af9a19cf3f5bfe80760abba/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L431).

Example test:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3c2e339be8a7dbed3f3918c8a33edf41726f22f9/pkg/controller/replicaset/replica_set_test.go#L1214-L1234

This is becoming more of a problem in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135395 because it makes `informerFactory.WaitForCacheSync` return more quickly, thus increasing the risk that the race goes wrong.

There are two workarounds:

- Explicitly wait for watches:

```Go
	var numWatches atomic.Int32
	clientSet.PrependWatchReactor("*", func(action core.Action) (handled bool, ret watch.Interface, err error) {
		var opts metav1.ListOptions
		if watchActcion, ok := action.(core.WatchActionImpl); ok {
			opts = watchActcion.ListOptions
		}
		gvr := action.GetResource()
		ns := action.GetNamespace()
		watch, err := clientSet.Tracker().Watch(gvr, ns, opts)

title: EndpointSlice API returns `endpoints: null` even though OpenAPI schema defines `endpoints` as required array
body:
### What happened?

When a Service has zero backing Pods (e.g., Deployment scaled to 0 or no Pods ever matched the selector), the EndpointSlice object returned by the API server contains:
```
{
  "kind": "EndpointSliceList",
  "apiVersion": "discovery.k8s.io/v1",
  "metadata": {
    "resourceVersion": "828044619"
  },
  "items": [
    {
      "metadata": { ... },
      "addressType": "IPv4",
      "endpoints": null,  // null here
      "ports": null
    }
  ]
}
```
This breaks clients / validators that rely on the published OpenAPI schema where `endpoints` is treated as a required field and modeled as an array (not nullable).

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the API Spec, `endpoints` should be a JSON array. For the “no endpoints” case, it should be an empty array.
```
"endpoints": []
```
Ref.: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/api/openapi-spec/v3/apis__discovery.k8s.io__v1_openapi.json#L228-L231



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
kubectl scale rs/replicaset.apps/demo-5f6c9cb999 --replicas=0
```

### Anything else we need to know?

- The API type defines `Endpoints []Endpoint` without `omitempty`, so it’s expected to be present and modeled as a list in generated schema/docs: https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/discovery/v1#EndpointSlice
- A related client breakage report (Java client) describing the same behavior: https://github.com/kubernetes-client/java/issues/3226

title: Add net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle and net.ipv4.tcp_notsent_lowat to the safe sysctl list
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to propose adding net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle and net.ipv4.tcp_notsent_lowat to the list of "safe" sysctls in Kubernetes.

Both of these sysctls are namespaced in the Linux kernel:

tcp_slow_start_after_idle has been namespaced since Linux 3.11.

tcp_notsent_lowat has been namespaced since Linux 3.12.


### Why is this needed?

As with the recently accepted change for TCP read/write buffers https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125234, modern high-performance applications require fine-grained control over the networking stack that cannot always be applied globally at the node level.

1. net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle for long-lived connections that have idle periods (like database pools or persistent API streams), the default behavior is to reset the congestion window after an idle period. Disabling this (0) is important for applications that need to maintain high throughput immediately upon resuming transmission without waiting for a slow-start ramp-up.

2. net.ipv4.tcp_notsent_lowat This is important for HTTP/2 and gRPC services. It limits the amount of unsent data in the write queue, which significantly reduces "bufferbloat" and improves responsiveness/latency for real-time streams. Setting this per-pod allows latency-critical microservices to coexist on the same node as throughput-oriented bulk transfer services.

Allowing these as safe sysctls enables developers to optimize their application's networking behavior via the Pod securityContext without requiring administrative intervention to modify Kubelet configuration or host-level sysctls.

Note: Text was formatted and edited with Google Gemini.

title: Consider CSIStorageCapacity when scheduling pods with already-bound PVCs
body:
Is it possible to extend `CSIStorageCapacity` tracking so that the scheduler also considers it when scheduling pods whose PVCs are already bound?

When a node hosting a pod is drained (for example, during maintenance or upgrades), the pod needs to be rescheduled. Currently, the scheduler does not use `CSIStorageCapacity` information for pods with bound PVCs. For storage backends that support volume rebuild or migration, it would be useful if the scheduler could prefer nodes with sufficient available storage capacity, so that the new node can accommodate the original volume and keep the pod and volume co-located for better I/O performance. At the moment, this is not supported, and pods can occasionally be scheduled onto nodes where volumes cannot be rebuilt.

Do you think this should be addressed on the Kubernetes side, or does it need to be handled by the storage backend? If on the Kubernetes side, this could potentially be implemented by adding a new field to StorageClass.

/sig storage
/sig scheduling

title: Error-level logs incorrectly use verbosity levels
body:
Currently, some components in Kubernetes have been migrated (or partially migrated) to [contextual logging](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/3077-contextual-logging/README.md). However, an incorrect pattern was introduced during the migration: Error-level logs are being called with verbosity methods (e.g., .V()).

The underlying package go-logr/logr, which contextual logging relies on, ignores the verbosity level when printing Error-level logs. For example, in the statement `logger.V(8).Error(nil, "Readiness probe already exists for container", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "containerName", c.Name)`, the error log will be printed regardless of the verbosity level set.

This can lead to error log flooding, which may hinder users' ability to review normal logs for troubleshooting. More critically, according to the [Kubernetes logging policy](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), logs should only be recorded when the information requires action from an administrator. This directly contradicts the practice of setting verbosity levels for Error logs, as administrators using the default logging level might miss these actionable errors. Therefore, these instances need to be fixed.

title: Support compression for WATCH responses
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I propose adding compression support for WATCH responses in the Kubernetes API server. This feature is necessary to maintain parity with the bandwidth efficiency of the legacy LIST method as clients transition to WatchList.

The proposal includes:

1. **Compression for WATCH:** Implement the capability for the server to provide compressed streaming data for WATCH connections.
2. **Algorithm Registration Interface:** Introduce an interface allowing custom compression algorithms to be registered. This ensures client-go remains lightweight and does not force new mandatory dependencies on all users.
3. **Default Realtime Compression:** Kubernetes binaries (e.g., kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kubectl) should include and support a realtime data compression like [s2] by default to maximize throughput.

[s2]: https://github.com/klauspost/compress/tree/master/s2

### Why is this needed?

The default enablement of WatchList for clients in Kubernetes 1.35 has fundamentally changed how initial object sets are fetched. While LIST operations are compressed, WATCH operations are not, leading to a massive spike in control plane outbound traffic.

### Key Impacts:
* Bandwidth Explosion: For most clusters communicating over a network, control plane outbound traffic can increase by 5x.
* Scalability Bottleneck: This increased data transfer is a critical blocker for the "Resource Size" scalability dimension proposed in [issue #134375](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134375).

### Why not gzip?
* Performance Regression: Standard library GZIP implementation often slows data transfer by 2x due to CPU overhead. However, modern algorithms like [s2] can actually increase throughput by 2.5x while significantly reducing volume.
* Breaking Change Risk: Most clients are configured to send Accept-Encoding: gzip by default, but they do not expect a compressed response for WATCH. Enabling GZIP without a negotiation mechanism would break these clients.

### Comparison: Performance and Volume

| Method | Compression | Data Volume (lower better) | Throughput (higher better) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **LIST** (Legacy) | GZIP | 1x (Baseline) | 1x (Baseline) |
| **WATCH** (1.35 Default) | None | **5x Increase** | Network-bottlenecked |
| **WATCH** (Proposed [s2]) | [s2] | **8x Decrease** | **2.5x Increase** |

[s2] was selected as it showed much better throughput over other tested algorithms (pgzip, zstd,br,lz4)

### **Goals**
*   Avoid the 5x increase in data transfer volume as clients switch to `WatchList`.
*   Ensure no new mandatory dependencies are added to the `client-go` library.

### **Non-Goals**
*   Supporting every available compression algorithm.
*   Improving the performance of the standard Go GZIP library.

### **Open Questions**
*   How should this effort be tracked and coordinated given that the original GZIP KEP ([#2338](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2338)) is currently stale?
*  Should we directly go to https://github.com/minio/minlz instead of [s2] as it written by the same author based on the collected experience.

/kind feature
/sig api-machinery
/sig scalability
/cc @liggitt @p0lyn0mial @wojtek-t @mborsz @jpbetz

title: containerStatuses ready stays true while started is false after container restart at the first time
body:
### What happened?

In pods' ContainerStatuses, there are two state fields, ready: controlled by readinessProbe, started: controlled by startupProbe.

As designed, readinessProbe won't start working until startupProbe is succeed.

Normally the field 'ready' won't be true if 'started' is still false.

But if the container in the pod exited, and the restartPolicy is Always or OnFailure, kubelet will try restart the container process immediately without changing the state of the pod. 

That cause ContainerStatuses 'ready' stays true while 'started' is false after container restart at the first time.

### What did you expect to happen?

Set the ready state to false when the container restart at the first time.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I reproduced this issue with a busybox configured as below, the startupProbe will pass after 30s, livenessProbe will kill the container after 60s, you can get the pod yaml after it restarted at the first time to see the fields: 

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: busybox
  name: busybox
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: busybox
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: busybox
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: busybox
        image: busybox:latest
        command:
          - bash
          - -c
          - sleep 30 && echo 1 > /started && sleep 3600

title: Potential goroutines leak in staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go
body:
### What happened?

Goroutine 1:If the method distribute() is invoked first, a goroutine holds the **RLock()** and calls listener.add(obj).
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L863-L874
The goroutine get blocked at the `p.addCh <- notification `
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1015-L1020

Goroutine 2:After that, The method shouldResync() is invoked, and the goroutine get blocked at `p.resyncLock.Lock()` , waiting for the **RLock()** to be released.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1090-L1099

Goroutine 3: Because the goroutine 2 tries to get Lock() and Write lock has a higher priority. So p.listenersLock.RLock() get blocked, which results in p.wg.Start(listener.pop) can't get executed.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L881-L890

And the `<-p.addCh` in listener.pop() can't be executed.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L1037

In the situation, these three goroutines are all blocked. The interleaving sequence that triggers the bug is as follows:
```
G1                                            G2                             G3
p.resyncLock.RLock()
p.addCh <- notification 
                                            p.resyncLock.Lock()
                                                                               p.resyncLock.RLock()                                 
                                                                                <-p.addCh                  
```

### What did you expect to happen?

No goroutines leak.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Adding time.Sleep(time.Second * 7) before `p.listenersLock.RLock()`. This step is to ensure that Lock is executed before RLock.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer.go#L881-L883

```
time.Sleep(time.Second * 7)
p.listenersLock.RLock()
```
2. Using goleak to detect the bug in the test function.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f36be36c76192c9ccaf8c22d61ec9ed3c0a2f978/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/shared_informer_test.go#L210

```
func TestListenerResyncPeriods(t *testing.T) {
	defer goleak.VerifyNone(t)
```

title: Standard numeric format validation (int32, int64, float, double) is not enforced in CRDs
body:
### What happened?

CRDs that use standard numeric formats for both integer and number types do not actually enforce these constraints during validation. 

This is a follow up issue of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/133880

### What did you expect to happen?

Reject invalid integer/number following the defined formats.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Scenario A (Integer/int32):
1. Create a CRD with a field: type: integer, format: int32.
2. Apply a Custom Resource with the value 2147483648.
3. Observed Behavior: Resource is accepted. Expected Behavior: Rejected (out of range).

Scenario B (Number/float):
1. Create a CRD with a field: type: number, format: float.
2. Apply a Custom Resource with the value 3.5e+38.
3. Observed Behavior: Resource is accepted. Expected Behavior: Rejected (out of range).

### Anything else we need to know?

The lack of enforcement is caused by a combination of two gaps in the validation pipeline:

1. Format Stripping: In pkg/apiserver/validation/formats.go, the StripUnsupportedFormatsPostProcessorForVersion function strips these formats from the schema because they are not explicitly whitelisted for numeric types. This prevents the validator from even knowing a format was requested.
2. Validator Initialization Gap: In k8s.io/kube-openapi/pkg/validation/validate/schema.go, the `numberValidator` is initialized without the Type and Format fields from the schema. Even if the format isn't stripped, the validator lacks the context to call IsValueValidAgainstRange correctly.
```go
func (s *SchemaValidator) numberValidator() ValueValidator {
	return &numberValidator{
		Path:             s.Path,
		In:               s.in,
		Default:          s.Schema.Default,
		MultipleOf:       s.Schema.MultipleOf,
		Maximum:          s.Schema.Maximum,
		ExclusiveMaximum: s.Schema.ExclusiveMaximum,
		Minimum:          s.Schema.Minimum,
		ExclusiveMinimum: s.Schema.ExclusiveMinimum,
	}
}
```

title: Promote old HPA alpha metrics to Beta
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The HPA currently exposes several metrics that are still marked as alpha, even though they have met the [requirements for promotion to beta](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/9de615daee15bdee370a825dc0ef150eac189700/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/metric-instrumentation.md#graduating-to-beta). Given their maturity and longevity, I believe the following metrics should be promoted to beta:

- `reconciliations_total` (introduced in #116010)
- `reconciliation_duration_seconds` (introduced in #116010)
- `metric_computation_total` (introduced in #116326)
- `metric_computation_duration_seconds` (introduced in #116326)

All of the metrics listed above have sufficient test coverage and have existed for a long time without significant issues, satisfying the criteria for promotion to beta.

### Why is this needed?

Ref: #135726

title: Discrepancy between `kubectl top pod` and the sum of Rss in `/proc/[pid]/smaps`
body:
We encountered inconsistencies among various memory metrics in our production environment. On the front-end monitoring page, we use `kubectl top pod` to display memory usage. Its output is as follows:
```
kubectl top pod clickhouse-keeper-0 
NAME                  CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)   
clickhouse-keeper-0   1314m        7117Mi   
```
Afterwards, we entered the pod:
```
kubectl exec -it clickhouse-keeper-0 bash
```
We then checked the cgroup memory statistics inside the pod, which showed:
```
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.stat 
cache 1650110464
rss 6907166720
rss_huge 6092226560
shmem 0
mapped_file 8028160
dirty 140435456
writeback 0
swap 0
pgpgin 9951374731
pgpgout 9954750697
pgfault 4135903411
pgmajfault 297
inactive_anon 0
active_anon 6906904576
inactive_file 1098760192
active_file 551292928
unevictable 0
hierarchical_memory_limit 8589934592
hierarchical_memsw_limit 9223372036854771712
total_cache 1650110464
total_rss 6907166720
total_rss_huge 6092226560
total_shmem 0
total_mapped_file 8028160
total_dirty 140435456
total_writeback 0
total_swap 0
total_pgpgin 9951374731
total_pgpgout 9954750697
total_pgfault 413590319
total_pgmajfault 297
total_inactive_anon 0
total_active_anon 6906904576
total_inactive_file 1098760192
total_active_file 551292928
total_unevictable 0
```
Finally, we examined the Rss metric in the `smaps` file of the pod's only process, summed it up, and the result was:
```
grep Rss /proc/1/smaps | awk '{sum+=$2} END {print sum " kB"}'
5579016 kB
```
The anonymous huge page memory usage was:
```
grep AnonHuge /proc/1/smaps | awk '{sum+=$2} END {print sum " kB"}'
3330048 kB
```
Based on the data above, the memory usage value from `kubectl top pod` is largely consistent with the `Rss` value from the `cgroup` inside the pod. However, there is a significant discrepancy compared to the sum of `Rss` from the `smaps` of that process inside the pod.

What I would like to know is: Why is there a difference between the sum of RSS in `smaps` and the memory usage reported by `kubectl top pod`?

Looking forward to your reply. Thanks.

title: Pod stuck in terminating state
body:
### What happened?

When deleted, the pod moves to terminating state and gets stuck. The one container is in state "terminated" so there should be nothing preventing shutdown. Per https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/51835#issuecomment-780923556 I'm opening a new issue and attaching pod info (this yaml?) and kubelet logs.

I'm not sure about the timestamps, but the pod delete was triggered at around 12:53 utc.

[kubeletlogs.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24567897/kubeletlogs.txt)
[podstatus.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24567898/podstatus.txt)

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod should move to terminated state/disappear

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

TBD

### Anything else we need to know?

I was in the process of destroying the cluster with terraform, but the control nodes and all dependent infrastructure are still up. The pod was running on control nodes (which are still alive). The container had an EBS volume attached.

title: Support for OFFLINE volume expansion using CSI driver using a rolling upgrade strategy
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Some CSI drivers (e.g. https://github.com/outscale/osc-bsu-csi-driver up to v1.7.0) support OFFLINE volume expansion only. If the users would like to resize PVC for pods controlled by StatefulSet, they should manually scale down all replicas before the external-resizer controller can resize the volumes. Otherwise, the StatefulSet controller creates the new Pod immediately without giving a chance for the _AttachDetachController_ to detach the volume from the worker.

It would be good to support OFFLINE volume expansion using the StatfulSet rolling upgrade strategy.

### Why is this needed?

Deployments with CSI drivers that support OFFLINE volume resize can still benefit from application no-downtime using a StatefulSet rolling upgrade strategy.

title: Stale conntrack entries on network disconnect and reconnect
body:
### What happened?

In a Kubernetes cluster (k3s 1.33.5) using a kube-vip and NodePort for UDP services, we observed that UDP traffic does not reliably recover after a prolonged network disconnection and reconnection.

When the network interface (LAN) is disconnected for an extended duration (e.g. 15–20 minutes) while UDP traffic continues from an external client, the kernel accumulates UNREPLIED UDP conntrack entries toward the VIP. After the network is restored and the VIP becomes reachable again, new UDP packets continue to match these existing conntrack entries, and traffic may remain disrupted until the entries naturally expire or are manually deleted.

Manually clearing the relevant conntrack entries immediately restores traffic.
This issue is intermittent, and does not occur 90% of the times during the tests. 

### What did you expect to happen?

	•	Existing UDP conntrack entries created during the outage should be invalidated, refreshed.
	•	Manual intervention (conntrack flush) should not be required to restore connectivity.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

 1. Setup a single node k3s cluster with a separate IP for kube-vip (Static IP)
 2. Deploy a UDP application on the cluster
 3. Start a UDP client in another machine which sends traffic to the UDP application 
 4. Unplug the network cable 
 5. Wait for 5 minutes
 6. Plug back the network cable
 7. Observe that the connectivity from UDP client to UDP application on the server is disrupted.

title: Support async moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue in scheduler
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Kube-Scheduler uses scheduling hint to determine whether the pods should be moved to ActiveQ. Scheduler will lock and traverse all pods in unschedulableQ to find which pods might become schedulable due to the incoming event. Many operation on SchedulingQueue will be blocked if the events come too frequently.

For example, if someone updates assigned pod in a high frequency, the SchedulingQueue will be blocked by assignedPodUpdate() and new pods can not be added into the activeQ, result in scheduler hang.

I want to make moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue run in a background goroutine, check multi cluster events once a time, and limit its frequency to avoid influencing other SchedulingQueue operation.

### Why is this needed?

If someone updates assigned pod in a high frequency, the SchedulingQueue will be blocked by assignedPodUpdate() and new pods can not be added into the activeQ, result in scheduler hang.

title: kubernetes is reconfiguring iptables/netfilter data structures with bad settings
body:
### What happened?

Hello,

I've been debugging issues with my Kubernetes nodes having very high CPU usage in network components.

I've finally traced down the origin to that block of code, which is overriding sysctl settings for iptables with insanely high values.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/conntrack/sysctls.go#L62

The default is for the kernel to configurable iptables data structures based on available memory. Typically 32k-256k buckets and 256k max entries (this may be a tad low for the most busy servers). 

**Problem: Kubernetes is reconfiguring the iptables data structures based on the number of CPU cores. It's broken on machines with many CPU.
On my servers with 512 cores, I am seeing Kubernetes reconfigure the kernel to have 16M iptables entries with a 4M hash table.
That's a 32 MB hash table that can't fit in CPU cache, with 6 GB of entries. It's ridiculous.**

The large data structure is causing constant thrashing of the CPU cache on all cores, as every network packet has to lookup the table multiple times, and network packets are distributed across all CPU cores for processing.

Some operations need to go over the whole hashtable, for read or write (write has locks), which is affected by the large size of the table. This is why you've been having issues with nginx proxy (among other bugs), you've got bug tickets investigating performance issue with processing/updating that table, but nobody pointing out that it should not have millions of items, no wonder it's slow to process!

Can you please correct this code?

This should be set to a fixed value. I think 256k buckets, 1M max entries is a good default value that should work for >99% of users.
If anyone reaches that limit, they should check with `netstat` what is consuming active entries, then they probably need to reduce the sysctl timeout to evict these entries faster, as the default is keeping them for too long.

```
net.nf_conntrack_max = 1048576
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_buckets = 262144
```

Regards.

### What did you expect to happen?

iptables should have reasonable configuration

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

you can look at sysctl settings on any kubernetes nodes with many cores and see the problem

title: The timeout behavior of the WaitForAPIServer function is abnormal.
body:
### What happened?

In my program, I have referenced the k8s.io/controller-manager repository. I will use the `WaitForAPIServer`  method within it to wait for the new Kubernetes cluster to become ready.

However, I often find that some Kubernetes clusters that have failed to access properly do not terminate their waiting process within the expected timeout period.



### What did you expect to happen?

I believe that the `WaitForAPIServer` method should always return immediately after the execution exceeds the time corresponding to the timeout value.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A program needs to be written to call the WaitForAPIServer method, set the timeout value to 5 seconds, and make it access an unreachable APIServer (for example, using an unreachable IP to check the total time consumed when calling this method)


````
	// build a client to a unreachable apiserver
	clientBuilder := NewKubernetesClientBuilder("basic-cluster-mesh/", restConfig)
	versionedClient := clientBuilder.Client("test-cli")
	
	tNow := time.Now()
	if err := app.WaitForAPIServer(versionedClient, 5*time.Second); err != nil {
		return ControllerContext{}, err
	}
	apiTime := time.Now()
	klog.Infof("WaitForAPIServer time-used: %v", apiTime.Sub(tNow))

````

### Anything else we need to know?

https://github.com/kubernetes/controller-manager/blob/master/app/helper.go#L35
````
// WaitForAPIServer waits for the API Server's /healthz endpoint to report "ok" with timeout.
func WaitForAPIServer(client clientset.Interface, timeout time.Duration) error {
	var lastErr error

	err := wait.PollImmediate(time.Second, timeout, func() (bool, error) {
		healthStatus := 0
         ....
````

We can see that here, PollImmediate is called. This function first calls the conditionFunc and then starts the timeout poller. This means that the time consumed by the first conditionFunc will not be taken into account.

title: [KubeProxy-Windows] RequireDualStack Service intermittently misprogrammed in Windows kube-proxy
body:
### What happened?

When creating a Service with ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack or PreferredDualstack on Windows nodes, kube-proxy sometimes programs incorrect load balancers.

The issue manifests in two main ways:

1. Incorrect backend selection
    - IPv6 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv4 VIPs
    - IPv4 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv6 VIPs
    - This results in traffic blackholing or connection failures

2. Incorrect load balancer flags
   - IPv6-specific HNS flags are sometimes applied to IPv4 load balancers
   - IPv4 flags are sometimes applied to IPv6 load balancers
   - This causes inconsistent behavior and unexpected failures in datapath programming

These issues appear intermittent and are more frequently observed under:

- Endpoint updates
- Service updates
- Rapid pod churn 

### What did you expect to happen?

For a RequireDualStack Service:

- IPv4 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv4 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv4-specific HNS flags

- IPv6 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv6 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv6-specific HNS flags

The programming behavior should be deterministic and consistent, matching the dual-stack service semantics defined in the Kubernetes dual-stack KEP.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Windows cluster with:
    - Dual-stack networking enabled
    - Windows nodes using winkernel kube-proxy
2. Create a Service:
 
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test-dualstack-lb
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
    - IPv6
  selector:
    app: test
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```
 
3. Deploy dual-stack pods with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
4. Trigger updates:
    - Scale pods up/down
    - Restart kube-proxy
    - Update endpoints or service annotations
5. Observe HNS load balancers and backend programming

### Anything else we need to know?

- This issue appears to be specific to Windows kube-proxy (winkernel).
- This issue violates the dual-stack contract defined in the Kubernetes dual-stack KEP.

title: kube-apiserver fails to start because start-service-ip-repair-controllers PostStartHook fails
body:
### What happened?

When upgrading a Kubernetes cluster from v1.32 to v1.33 by creating new control plane nodes with v1.33 manifests, the kube-apiserver fails to start with admission errors. 
```
0115 20:56:16.106534   # log start
...
E0115 20:56:24.741991       1 repairip.go:372] "Unhandled Error" err="the ClusterIP [IPv4]: 10.211.95.185 for Service <namespace foo>/<service bar>is not allocated; repairing" logger="UnhandledError"
...
Trace[295533714]: ---"Write to database call failed" len:247,err:ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io "10.211.95.185" is forbidden: not yet ready to handle request 10000ms (20:56:34.744)
Trace[295533714]: [10.000527316s] [10.000527316s] END
E0115 20:56:34.745027       1 repairip.go:235] "Unhandled Error" err="ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io \"10.211.95.185\" is forbidden: not yet ready to handle request" logger="UnhandledError"
I0115 20:56:34.746095       1 repairip.go:236] Shutting down ipallocator-repair-controller
I0115 20:56:34.834949       1 healthz.go:280] informer-sync,poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers check failed: readyz
[-]informer-sync failed: 4 informers not started yet: [*v1.Pod *v1.ServiceAccount *v1.Secret *v1.Namespace]
[-]poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers failed: not finished
...
I0115 20:57:06.335471       1 healthz.go:280] informer-sync,poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers check failed: readyz
[-]informer-sync failed: 1 informers not started yet: [*v1.Secret] # v1.Namespace informer is ready  
[-]poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers failed: not finished
...
F0115 20:57:18.630248       1 hooks.go:204] PostStartHook "start-service-ip-repair-controllers" failed: unable to perform initial IP and Port allocation check

```

We think this is a race condition introduced by new code path when `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is enabled by default in v1.33.  
`start-service-ip-repair-controllers` reads clusterIPs from all `Services` objects and creates `IPAddresses` objects if they are not found from cache. Since we are upgrading from v1.32, where `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is disabled, ETCD does not contain any `IPAddresses` objects. 
`start-service-ip-repair-controllers` therefore does not read any existing `IPAddresses` objects from cache and attempts to create them. However, at this point, the `ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io` API is not yet ready. As a result, `start-service-ip-repair-controllers` failes and the kube-apiserver never becomes ready.

Because we have a large number of namespaces, `v1.Namespace` informer takes more time to become ready, which increases the likelihood of this issue occurring in our cluster.
In v1.32 `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is disabled. The `start-service-ip-repair-controllers`  implementation only invokes the internal `RangeRegistry` API, which is initialized earlier, so this issue did not exist.



### What did you expect to happen?

The kube-apiserver should start successfully and the repair controller should create missing `IPAddress` objects for existing `Services`, either by:
1. Waiting for admission plugins to be ready before attempting writes
2. Deferring repair work until after startup completes
3. Retrying failed operations instead of terminating

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prerequisites:
- Cluster with large number of `Namespaces` and `Services` 
- `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` feature gate previously disabled

Steps:
1. Prepare v1.33 kube-apiserver manifests with `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` enabled by default
2. Start kube-apiserver
3. Observe API server fails to start

_No response_

title: Container fail to create when env var contains $ followed by non-ASCII character (invalid UTF-8 gRPC error)
body:
### What happened? After upgrading our Kubernetes cluster from v1.33.5 to v1.34.2 (AWS EKS), pods scheduled on nodes running v1.34.2 fail during container creation with the following error: ```bash grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8 ``` The pods are created successfully, but containers fail to create. Important observation: Pods scheduled on nodes still running v1.33.5 continue to work correctly with the same manifests and environment variables. The failure occurs only on nodes upgraded to v1.34.2, strongly indicating a regression. Through isolation and testing, we observed that the failure occurs when an environment variable value contains a $ immediately followed by a non-ASCII character. This behaviour did not occur on v1.33.5 and appears to be a regression introduced in v1.34.x. ### What did you expect to happen? Pods and containers should start successfully when environment variable values contain valid UTF-8 characters, including non-ASCII characters and literal $ characters. This configuration worked as expected on v1.33.5 nodes, even within the same cluster during a rolling upgrade. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Create a pod (or deployment) with an environment variable containing: - a $ - immediately followed by a non-ASCII UTF-8 character 3. Schedule the pod on a v1.34.2 node 4. Observe container creation failure with: - `grpc: error while marshaling: string field contains invalid UTF-8` Minimal reproducible example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: utf8-env-repro spec: containers: - name: test image: busybox command: ["sh", "-c", "echo started && sleep 3600"] env: - name: TEST_ENV value: "$£FOO" ``` Observed result: ❌ Fails on v1.34.2 nodes ✅ Works on v1.33.5 nodes Expected result: Container starts normally on all versions. ### Anything else we need to know? - We run a custom CRD/operator that propagates env vars from the CR spec into Deployments and multi-container Pods. - The failure occurs after Pod creation, during container creation / runtime interaction. - This reproduces across all containers in the pod that receive the env var. - This is reproducible in a mixed-version cluster: - Pods on v1.33.5 nodes work - Pods on v1.34.2 nodes fail ### Kubernetes version

title: Zero value Kubelet PSI metrics emitted even if underlying OS doesn't enable it
body:
### What happened?

In Kubernetes 1.34, the KubeletPSI feature gate was set to true. However, when running Kubernetes on an OS that does not have PSI enabled, the PSI metrics are not expected to be generated. Here are the counts of the metrics observed during a test:
```
# for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do echo "=== Node: $node ==="; for metric in cpu_waiting cpu_stalled memory_waiting memory_stalled io_waiting io_stalled; do echo -n "container_pressure_${metric}_seconds_total: "; kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$node/proxy/metrics/cadvisor" | grep "container_pressure_${metric}_seconds_total" | wc -l; done; done
=== Node: ip-10-0-11-217.us-east-2.compute.internal ===
container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total:      267
container_pressure_io_stalled_seconds_total:      267
```
I suspect this part of the code:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/cadvisor_linux.go#L105C53-L105C63
```
	if utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.KubeletPSI) {
		includedMetrics[cadvisormetrics.PressureMetrics] = struct{}{}
	} 
```
and prometheus does this: https://github.com/google/cadvisor/blob/master/metrics/prometheus.go#L1842
```
	if includedMetrics.Has(container.PressureMetrics) {
		c.containerMetrics = append(c.containerMetrics, []containerMetric{
			{
				name:      "container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total", 
```

cc: @haircommander @bitoku 

### What did you expect to happen?

There should be no PSI metrics when underlying OS never enables it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run k8s 1.34 and above and use grafana to monitor PSI metrics

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a good to have. Doesn't really impact anything as cardinality is also negligible. This zero value confuses the end-user as it gives a visual impression that PSI is enabled when looking at grafana charts.

I can propose a fix on this.

title: Duplicate ports with different protocols in pod spec get merged after pod spec update
body:
### What happened?

When I add a port with a duplicate port number but different protocol (UDP instead of TCP) to an existing Deployment, one of these two ports get removed.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect both to be present.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: test
        image: busybox
        command:
        - sleep
        - infinity
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
```

Then `kubectl edit` the `Deployment`, duplicating the containerport, but with UDP, like this:

```
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: UDP
```

And you'll observe that one of the two ports is gone in the `Deployment`.

### Anything else we need to know?

There are no mutating webhooks involved. Even with all hooks removed, I still observ this.

When you `get deploy -o yaml`, edit the yaml, `apply --server-side -f /the/yaml`, it does seem to get applied.

My guess is it is due to (only) `containerPort` being the merge key in types.go.

This is very similar to #105610, but that issue is about `Services`.

### Kubernetes version

I've observed this in 1.34.2, 1.33.6 and 1.32.4

### Cloud provider

self hosted Talos

### OS version

Talos Linux, various versions

Talos Linux

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Readiness Observations & Recommendations (Research)
body:
This issue shares research-based observations on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness
in Kubernetes, based solely on publicly available code and documentation.

This is NOT a vulnerability report and does not include exploitation, attack paths, or
sensitive configuration details. The intent is awareness, future-readiness, and community
discussion aligned with NIST PQC transition guidance.

Observations:
• Cryptographic usage is distributed across multiple layers
• There is no centralized crypto inventory or ownership map
• No defined crypto agility or PQC migration framework
• No governance-level visibility into algorithm lifecycle

Recommendations:
• Consider adding a crypto inventory layer
• Define crypto ownership and lifecycle policy
• Track NIST PQC migration readiness
• Introduce crypto agility abstractions
• Document PQC roadmap for operators

Why this matters:
Quantum-safe transitions are multi-year efforts. Early visibility reduces long-term risk.

Happy to refine or contribute to documentation if helpful.

title: Export `validateAffinity()` as `ValidateAffinity()` for external validation consistency
body:
**Problem Statement**:
The `validateAffinity()` function in `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/apis/core/validation` package is currently _private_ (unexported), which forces external projects that need to validate Affinity configurations to duplicate ~200 lines of validation logic.

If we need to validate Affinity, then we have to replicate the entire `validateAffinity()` logic along with its helper functions (`validateNodeAffinity`, `validatePodAffinity`, `validatePodAntiAffinity`, etc.) to pre-validate user-provided affinity configurations before deploying pods.
This duplication:
- Creates maintenance burden (keeping in sync with upstream changes)
- Risks validation drift between client-side and server-side logic
- Duplicates code that already exists and is well-tested in Kubernetes

_Similar Functions ARE already exported_:
The same package has validation methods exported for NodeSelector(`ValidateNodeSelector`), Tolerations(`ValidateTolerations`), but not for affinity.

**Proposed Solution**:
A simple, non-breaking wrapper following the existing pattern:
```
// ValidateAffinity checks if given affinities are valid.
func ValidateAffinity(affinity *core.Affinity, opts PodValidationOptions, fldPath *field.Path) field.ErrorList {
    return validateAffinity(affinity, opts, fldPath)
}
```

_Implementation impact_:
- Zero changes to internal logic : the private function remains unchanged
- Full backward compatibility : existing code paths unaffected
- Follows established pattern : mirrors how `ValidateTolerations` and `ValidateNodeSelector` are exported.

**Benefits**:
- Bug Discovery: External projects using server-side validation logic help identify bugs earlier. The same validation code is used by kube-apiserver, so bugs found externally benefit the entire ecosystem.
- Validation Accuracy: Pre-validating configurations using the exact same logic as the API server ensures users get consistent error messages and behavior.

**Addressing the use of** `k8s.io/kubernetes`
While `k8s.io/kubernetes` is not officially intended for use as an external library, the following points justify its use in this context:
- High Community Reliance: Per `pkg.go.dev`, over 1,900 projects import this validation package, demonstrating that many maintainers rely on it despite its "internal" designation.
- Functional Availability: The package exports numerous validation functions, making it a viable—and often necessary—resource for maintaining consistency with Kubernetes' internal validation logic.
- Community Guidance: Developer discussions frequently suggest leveraging these helpers to avoid diverging from core Kubernetes behavior, as re-implementing these complex rules from scratch is error-prone.

I’m happy to contribute the changes mentioned above. I wanted to align on the approach first to ensure it meets the project's standards—please let me know if you’d like me to open a PR.

/sig scheduling
/kind feature
/area api

title: best-effort topolopgy mgr NUMANodeAffinity hint doesn't consider amount of devices per NUMA node
body:
### What happened?

### Very simply put: 

Given a 2 NUMA node server with 3 devices split across each node, (1 on node 0, 2 on node 1), is it possible to configure the topology manager to select the NUMA node in which 2/3 GPUs presides when requesting a pod with all 3 devices ? 

### Context:

In our current setup we would like to schedule NUMA localized pods in a best-effort manner, meaning pods can span multiple NUMA nodes without failing.

We have a server with 128 cores, dual socket, configured as two NUMA nodes. 

```
NUMA:
  NUMA node(s):              2
  NUMA node0 CPU(s):         0-31,64-95
  NUMA node1 CPU(s):         32-63,96-127

```

This server has 3 GPUs. We have written our own device manager plugin (as we want to enable vfio passthrough) and this plugin advertises which node each GPU is on. (0x10de is nvidia vendor)

```
root@gpu3:~# for d in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*; do
  [[ -f "$d/vendor" && "$(cat $d/vendor)" == "0x10de" ]] && \
  printf "%s -> NUMA %s\n" "$(basename $d)" "$(cat $d/numa_node)"
done
0000:25:00.0 -> NUMA 0
0000:81:00.0 -> NUMA 1
0000:e2:00.0 -> NUMA 1
```

This setup works exactly as desired when requesting resources which fit into a single NUMA node. 

- Example, deploy pod 2 GPUs & 8 CPUs

title: [Bug] kube-apiserver: `--audit-log-maxsize=0` does not disable rotation as documented, but defaults to 100MB via lumberjack**
body:
### What happened?

When configuring `kube-apiserver` with audit logging enabled, setting `--audit-log-maxsize=0` results in audit logs being rotated when they reach **100MB**, instead of growing indefinitely (or not rotating based on size) as implied by the documentation.

Since default values for `--audit-log-maxbackup` and `--audit-log-maxage` are also `0` (meaning "retain all" and "retain forever"), the result is not a single large file, but an accumulation of many 100MB log files until disk exhaustion.

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the `kube-apiserver` help text and documentation:

> `--audit-log-maxsize`: The maximum size in megabytes of the audit log file before it gets rotated. **If this is 0, the log file is not rotated.**

I expected the `audit.log` file to grow indefinitely without rotation when `maxsize` is set to `0`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start `kube-apiserver` with the following flags:
```bash
--audit-log-path=/tmp/k8s-audit.log
--audit-log-maxsize=0

```
2. Generate audit events sufficient to exceed 100MB (e.g., using a load testing tool or simply `dd` appending if testing the library directly, or heavy API usage).
3. Observe that the log file is rotated (renamed with a timestamp) once it hits approximately 100MB.

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue lies in the interaction between `k8s.io/apiserver` and the underlying logging library `gopkg.in/natefinch/lumberjack.v2`.

1. **Kubernetes Implementation**:
In `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/audit/log/backend.go`, the backend is initialized with the user-provided `MaxSize`:
```go
func NewBackend(filename string, maxBackup, maxAge, maxSize int) audit.Backend {
    writer := &lumberjack.Logger{
        Filename:   filename,
        MaxSize:    maxSize,    // Passed as 0
        // ...
    }
    return backend.NewBackend(writer)
}

```


2. **Lumberjack Implementation**:
The `lumberjack` library treats `MaxSize: 0` not as "unlimited", but as "use default".
Reference: `lumberjack.go` in `natefinch/lumberjack`:
```go
const defaultMaxSize = 100 // megabytes

func (l *Logger) max() int64 {
    if l.MaxSize == 0 {
        return int64(defaultMaxSize * megabyte)
    }
    return int64(l.MaxSize) * int64(megabyte)
}

```
Consequently, passing `0` effectively sets the rotation threshold to 100MB.

title: Support TLS Server Name overrides in EgressSelectorConfiguration
body:
## What would you like to be added?

Add a `tlsServerName` field to the `TLSConfig` structure in `EgressSelectorConfiguration` to allow overriding the hostname used for TLS certificate verification, similar to the existing `tls-server-name` field in kubeconfig (added in[ #88769](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88769)).

## Precedent

This functionality already exists in:
- **kubeconfig files**: The `tls-server-name` field was added in #88769 for similar use cases
- **kubectl**: The `--tls-server-name` flag provides command-line access
- **Go's `tls.Config`**: The underlying `ServerName` field supports this

The egress selector `TLSConfig` would benefit from the same capability for consistency.

## Why is this needed?

### Use Case

This addresses scenarios where components using EgressSelectorConfiguration connect through Kubernetes Service DNS names (e.g., proxy.svc.cluster.local) but that hostname is not included in the server certificate's Subject Alternative Names (SANs), which define which hostnames a certificate is valid for.

**Example scenario:**
- Egress selector is configured to connect to: `https://konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local:8443`
- The proxy's TLS certificate contains SANs for: `proxy.example.com`
- Connection fails because `konnectivity-service.example.svc.cluster.local` is not in the certificate SANs

### Current Workaround Limitations

The current workaround of updating certificates to include all possible service DNS names has significant drawbacks:
- Requires certificate regeneration and rotation across many clusters
- Service names may vary across environments (dev, staging, prod)
- Certificate management becomes complex in multi-tenant environments
- May require coordination with external PKI infrastructure

### Proposed Solution

Add an optional `tlsServerName` field to override the hostname used for certificate verification:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: EgressSelectorConfiguration
egressSelections:
- name: cluster
  connection:
    proxyProtocol: HTTPConnect
    transport:
      tcp:
        url: "https://proxy-service.example.svc.cluster.local:8443"
        tlsConfig:
          caBundle: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
          clientCert: /etc/kubernetes/pki/client.crt
          clientKey: /etc/kubernetes/pki/client.key
          tlsServerName: "proxy.example.com"  # <-- New field
```
This would allow connecting via the service DNS name while verifying the certificate against the actual hostname in the SANs.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/028015267e30a5f4f975c9a57f91f53ddd79eca5/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/rest/update.go#L138-L145

title: [Cleanup] Default KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET to true in GCE cluster scripts
body:
### What happened?

While auditing stale TODO comments in the GCE configuration scripts (following my recent merged cleanup PR #136379), I identified a 9-year-old TODO at line 525 of cluster/gce/config-test.sh. The environment variable KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET still defaults to false, causing kube-proxy to be deployed as static pods in certain GCE test configurations.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expect GCE cluster configurations to align with modern Kubernetes standards (like kubeadm), where kube-proxy is managed as a DaemonSet by default. This change will allow for the future removal of legacy static-pod logic in cluster/gce/gci/configure-helper.sh, significantly reducing technical debt.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Inspect cluster/gce/config-test.sh at line 527.
2. Observe KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET=${KUBE_PROXY_DAEMONSET:-false}.
3. This stems from Commit 1102656 (PR #50705) from 2017, where the variable was introduced as an experimental option but never flipped to the default.

### Anything else we need to know?

I am a DevOps Engineer and am happy to take ownership of this transition. My plan is to:

1. Flip the default to true.
2. Monitor CI signal (pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce) to ensure no regressions.
3. Submit a follow-up PR to deprecate the false code path once verified.

title: Kubectl apply does not remove manually added env vars, causing permanent drift between manifest and live Deployment
body:
### What would you like to be added?

What happened?

We manage Deployments declaratively using kubectl apply (server-side apply) from GitOps pipelines.

In production, a user manually edited a Deployment (kubectl edit deployment) and added an extra environment variable directly under:
spec.template.spec.containers[].env

Later, the Deployment was redeployed using kubectl apply -f <manifest.yaml> with a manifest that does not contain this manually added env var.

Despite successful apply and no reported conflicts, the manually added environment variable remains present in the live Deployment.

This results in permanent configuration drift between the manifest and the cluster state.


### Why is this needed?

We expected the live Deployment to exactly match the applied manifest, such that:
Environment variables not present in the manifest are removed from the Deployment
kubectl apply enforces declarative state, even for mergeable lists like env
The applied manifest becomes the source of truth

In short:
After apply, the cluster state should be fully in sync with the manifest.

**How can we reproduce it**
1. create a deployment

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: sample-app
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          app: sample
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: sample
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: app
            image: nginx
            env:
            - name: Testing
              value: "working"
    
    kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

2. Manually edit the Deployment

    kubectl edit deployment sample-app
  
    env:
    - name: Testing2
      value: workingNot

  kubectl describe deployment sample-app

3. Re-apply the original manifest
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

4. Observe the result
kubectl describe deployment sample-app
❌ Testing2=workingNot still exists, even though it is not in the manifest.

**Anything else we need to know?**
Even tried with the below commands 
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml --server-side --force-conflicts --field-manager=gitops
Still it is not able to remove the additional env variables. 

There is currently no supported way to say:
“This list must exactly match the manifest.”
using kubectl apply

**Kubernetes version**
1.32.6

**Cloud provider**
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)

title: NewUnmounter always returns error while deleting pod after node reboot
body:
### What happened?

1. node reboot
2. kubelet starts and reconstructs a csi volume `uncertain`
3. kubelet calls `NodePublishVolume`  and gets `rpc error: code = InvalidArgument desc = rpc error: code = Internal desc = mount failed: exit status 255` , this is a final error, then kubelet calls `removeMountDir` to remove the volume directory and vol_data.json, but the volume in asw is still uncertain as it is a reconsructed volume
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/091d147008c4aecce64fe4d9bbef84ab95d74bc7/pkg/volume/csi/csi_mounter.go#L317-L320
5. the pod is deleting
6. kubelet starts to unmount the volume, but the volume dir has been deleted, `NewUnmounter` would always return error
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/091d147008c4aecce64fe4d9bbef84ab95d74bc7/pkg/volume/csi/csi_plugin.go#L558-L561
7. the pod keeps terminating

title: Feature Request: Use e2e --prefix flag to identify namespaces/resources created by an e2e run
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Enable the existing e2e framework --prefix flag (defined in TestContext) to be applied to namespaces created during e2e test execution, so that all resources created by an e2e run can be deterministically identified.

### Why is this needed?

1. Downstream CI systems, hosted environments, and long-running clusters executing upstream e2e tests need a reliable and supported mechanism to identify and clean up all resources created by a specific e2e run.
2. After e2e run on the environment, it leaves many cluster-scoped / namespace-scoped resources, which affect the cluster state for the next execution. Right now, we don't have any specific way to identify all leftover resources after e2e run, so we need some logic to identify such resources for clean up. 

**Currently:**

Namespace names vary per test

There is no common identifier tying them to a run

Cleanup often relies on heuristics (time-based, managedFields, etc.)

The framework already exposes a --prefix flag, but it has no effect today.

**Background / Current State**

**Prefix flag exists:**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/test_context.go#L427

Originally introduced (GCE use case), but usage later removed:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/899cf360bad0d9575124a46da455e048b6dfbeb1

Flag is still passed by e2e scripts but currently unused:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/hack/ginkgo-e2e.sh#L278

Namespace creation flow today

Most e2e namespaces are created via:

CreateTestingNS
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/util.go#L323

Although comments suggest using NewFramework, the call chain eventually reaches CreateTestingNS.

The namespace base name comes from hardcoded test definitions, for example:

taints.go (taint-single-pod)
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/node/taints.go#L161

**Other examples:**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/kubectl/exec.go#L57

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e_node/proc_mount_test.go#L40

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/storage/testsuites/capacity.go#L90

**As a result:**

Namespace naming is test-specific

There is no run-level grouping mechanism

**Proposed enhancement (for discussion)**

CreateTestingNS already has access to TestContext and uses other context variables:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/test/e2e/framework/util.go#L362

**Proposal:**

When TestContext.Prefix is non-empty, prepend it to the namespace base name

title: [Scheduler] Add an extension after PostFilter that will always execute
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I am a plugin developer, the plugin will have different actions according to the preemption result. For example, mark the podGorup (API in schedule-plugins) as failed and reject all the pods when failed to preempt, or I will mark the pods as schedulable (I will limit the number of times to schedule any pods in PodGroup for the performance).
But when any of the plugin return code other than fwk.Unschedulable, scheduler will skip all plugins after that. This makes difficult to implement the PostFilter:
- If we run coscheduling before preemption, we can not know the preempt result.
- If we run coscheduling after preemption and preempt return error (for example the pod is deleted when in schedulingCycle), we are not able to reject the podGroup because the scheduling stop the iteration for the PostFilter.

### Why is this needed?

Mentioned above.

title: [Declarative Validation] Make it so +k8s:required and +k8s:optional can be placed on non-pointer structs
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently declarative validation tags +k8s:required and +k8s:optional cannot be placed on non-pointer structs.  This should be updated as open API +required and +optional are allowed on non-pointer structs and we are hoping to have lint rules to validate both tags are added in pairs.  Related code:

`+k8s:required`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ebc5660fa5c37e5e2f4bc85aff7f181d03955a9c/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/required.go#L102-L108

`+k8s:optional`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ebc5660fa5c37e5e2f4bc85aff7f181d03955a9c/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/required.go#L173-L179



### Why is this needed?

This is needed as without this we are unable to create a linter that ensures "For any field that has +optional/+required, you must also have +k8s:optional/+k8s:required" as we cannot place the declarative validation +k8s:[optional|required] tags on non-pointer structs

title: Add validation around Pod IP Address
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Today we make assumptions around the Pod IP address coming back from the PodSandboxStatus RPC. This RPC is responsible for returning the ip addresses to the kubelet. The assumptions we make around the current handling of pod ip addresses from containerd and crio, while they do some validation if the pod ip address exists, it possible to return an empty string as the pod ip address. It probably makes sense to do validation in the SyncPod function (link below) to ensure this scenario cannot happen. The function should fail, right now the pod is constantly scheduled without a useful error message. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4b5e40aacd021aa1485d29c4965893b3de017697/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1596

### Why is this needed?

Without any validation, its possible for a pod to come up and have no ip address from the K8s perspective.

title: setcap build image shouldn't require a shell
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Building with a more vanilla setcap image shouldn't require a shell in the image to run the command 


in `build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile`

```sh
# We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
# non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
```

this command requires the `SETCAP_IMAGE` have a shell in order to:
1) RUN a command that isn't in the form of ["/usr/sbin/setcap", "..."] 
2) shell expand the `${BINARY}` argument


### Why is this needed?

By making this change you can eliminate the need of having a shell in the setcap image:


```diff
diff --git a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
index 27129d29bd9..acfe8c26f22 100644
--- a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
+++ b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
@@ -20,11 +20,11 @@ ARG SETCAP_IMAGE
 # to setup qemu for the builder.
 FROM --platform=linux/$BUILDARCH ${SETCAP_IMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /${BINARY}
+COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /set_cap_binary
 # We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
 # non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
-RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
+RUN ["setcap", "cap_net_bind_service=+ep", "/set_cap_binary"]
 
 FROM --platform=linux/$TARGETARCH ${BASEIMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --from=0 /${BINARY} /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
+COPY --from=0 /set_cap_binary /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
```

title: Feature Request: Reduce PSI Metric Cardinality to eliminate the impact to prometheus RSS
body:
**Summary**
I did a performance evaluation for enabling PSI at scale. with 500+ test containers on a cluster, enabling PSI causes Prometheus pod RSS increase up to 1.3+ GB on each Prometheus pod.
I noticed the "" and "POD" containers are included in the PSI metrics. Dropping them would eliminate approximately 66% of the PSI series.

**Analysis**
[PSI metrics](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/): Kubernetes lets you configure the kubelet to collect Linux kernel Pressure Stall Information (PSI) for CPU, memory, and I/O usage. The information is collected at node, pod and container level, exposed at the /metrics/cadvisor endpoint.

For each pod, PSI metrics are emitted not only for application containers but also for two additional containers:

- container="" (pause container - infra)
- container="POD" (pod cgroup)

Here is an example of one of the 3 PSI metrics for a pod
```
container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice",image="",name="",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 1.456709 1769503672619

container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="POD",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice/crio-d9ee10c5cdfc43b2bf36c7af5e34cffd4c353e09de52556c06ab98ee25d89310",image="",name="k8s_POD_perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77_node-density-heavy-0_43e94c3b-60b2-463c-bb0c-bb10d153e49d_0",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 0 1769503667734

container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total{container="perfapp",id="/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod43e94c3b_60b2_463c_bb0c_bb10d153e49d.slice/crio-cf24cfb805081bc45e300e9c041d123b78bc97167e43831d83bb1b1c1bfd7609.scope",image="quay.io/cloud-bulldozer/perfapp:latest",name="k8s_perfapp_perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77_node-density-heavy-0_43e94c3b-60b2-463c-bb0c-bb10d153e49d_0",namespace="node-density-heavy-0",pod="perfapp-1-1-bc966c69-h6c77"} 1.295762 1769503671596
```

cAdvisor emits PSI metrics for every relevant cgroup. For a pod with a single application container, this means:
3 containers × 6 PSI metric types = 18 total PSI metrics per pod.

- container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total
- container_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total
- container_pressure_io_stalled_seconds_total
- container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total

I investigated other container-level metrics and found inconsistent behavior—some include these two additional containers while others only include a subset of containers. 

Configure Prometheus metric relabeling to drop PSI metrics for non-application containers can help to reduce the prometheus resource consumption. But the kubelet.metricRelabelings field is not among the supported parameters in OpenShift until the 4.20 release.
The OpenShift Cluster Monitoring Operator only exposes a subset of Prometheus configuration parameters. According to the [Config Map Reference for the Cluster Monitoring Operator](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/monitoring_stack_for_red_hat_openshift/4.20/html-single/config_map_reference_for_the_cluster_monitoring_operator/index#clustermonitoringconfiguration%20%20https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/monitoring_stack_for_red_hat_openshift/4.20/html-single/config_map_reference_for_the_cluster_monitoring_operator/index):
"Not all configuration parameters for the monitoring stack are exposed. Only the parameters and fields listed in this reference are supported for configuration."

**Proposal**
Configure Kubernetes/cAdvisor/CRI-O to suppress PSI metrics for pause and pod cgroups("" and "POD" containers ) at the source. 
Dropping the "" and "POD" containers would eliminate approximately 66% of the PSI series from the source.

**Open Question**
- Is there strong reason to avoid dropping "" and "POD" containers because they are still meaningful to PSI metrics?
- The effort to drop them v.s. the additional resource consumption them bring.

title: fake.NewClientset should track status and spec independently
body:
### Description

The generated client-go fake clientset (e.g., k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes/fake) does not correctly model the separation between spec and status when using server-side apply.

When the same manager performs:

1. Apply() to update spec-owned fields
2. ApplyStatus() to update status-owned fields

the second call overwrites fields from the first call. This diverges from real apiserver behavior, where spec and status are separate subresources and are merged independently.

### Reproducer

````go
client := NewClientset()
namespace := "default"

pod, err := client.CoreV1().Pods(namespace).Apply(context.Background(),
	v1ac.Pod("foo", namespace).WithFinalizers("foo-finalizer"),
	meta_v1.ApplyOptions{FieldManager: "test-manager"})
require.NoError(t, err)
require.Equal(t, pod.Finalizers, []string{"foo-finalizer"})

pod, err = client.CoreV1().Pods(namespace).ApplyStatus(context.Background(),
	v1ac.Pod("foo", namespace).WithStatus(v1ac.PodStatus().WithPhase(v1.PodPending)),
	meta_v1.ApplyOptions{FieldManager: "test-manager"})
require.NoError(t, err)
require.Equal(t, pod.Status.Phase, v1.PodPending)
require.Equal(t, pod.Finalizers, []string{"foo-finalizer"})
````

### Actual behavior

The second call (ApplyStatus) overwrites the object stored in the fake tracker, causing fields set via Apply() (e.g. metadata.finalizers) to be lost.

This indicates that:

- Apply() and ApplyStatus() are not tracked independently
- The fake client does not model the /status subresource
- Server-side apply merge semantics are not respected

### Expected behavior

The fake client should behave like a real apiserver:

- Apply() updates spec/metadata fields
- ApplyStatus() updates only the status subresource
- Fields written by Apply() must remain intact after ApplyStatus()

This behavior is correctly observed when running the same code against a real API server (e.g. via envtest or a real cluster).

### Why this matters

- Controllers commonly update spec and status in separate calls
- Unit tests using fake.NewClientset produces false failures
- This encourages incorrect controller patterns (single combined updates) to work around fake behavior
- The divergence is subtle and easy to miss

### Notes

The root cause appears to be that the fake client’s ObjectTracker does not implement subresource semantics for /status, even for built-in types that support it.

Should probably be considered as a feature request, as the general advice is to write envtest when real apiserver behavior is required. At the same time, many developers prefer to use fake clients - even for more than just simple unit tests, mainly because a fake client is faster and easier to use/bootstrap.

Follow-up after https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125560.

For inspiration, this has been "solved" when using the controller-runtime fake client: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/pull/2259.
