title: api-server does not always refetch JWKS on unknown key ID
body:
### What happened?

We're performing regular key rotation of our signing keys used to sign tokens issued by our OIDC provider. Unfortunately the api-server does not properly refetch new signing keys.

The openid specification states that:
> The signer can begin using a new key at its discretion and signals the change to the verifier using the kid value. The verifier knows to go back to the jwks_uri location to re-retrieve the keys when it sees an unfamiliar kid value.

Source: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#RotateSigKeys

However, as written above the api-server does not comply with that. Currently the api-server is using the coreos/go-oidc v2 library which only reloads keys when the cache-control max-age is reached. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected api-server to comply with the openid spec and immediately refetch keys if an unknown kid is seen.

This behaviour has already been changed in v3 of coreos/go-oidc library with https://github.com/coreos/go-oidc/pull/259. Keys are immediately refreshed if an unknown key id is seen.

However, this change has the potential to DDOS the issuer when someone brings an invalid token or a token meant to be for another cluster if the api-server (or the coreos/go-oidc library) does not rate limit such requests (as far as I can tell go-oidc does not rate limit). So some additional work might be needed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can try to put together a reproducer later but I don't think it is needed at this point.

### Anything else we need to know?

On #sig-auth slack channel I found [this](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EN96KUY/p1667778735333849) old thread from 2022 describes a similar/related problem. I believe all recent Kubernetes versions are affected by this bug. This would be fixed by #134454

```console
$ kubectl version
```

title: DRA: allocator clears DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests too aggressively, widening a per-request config to the whole claim
body:
### What happened?

The DRA structured allocator post-processes allocated configs to drop a `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` list to `nil` when the config "applies to all requests" (the *empty means all* semantic). It decides this with a length comparison:

```go

for i := range allocationResult.Devices.Config {
    if len(allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests) {
        allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests = nil
    }
}
```

`len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)` is **not** equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim", because `config.Requests` entries may be sub-request references of the form `"<request>/<subRequest>"`  the allocator matches them that way a few lines earlier:

```go
subRequestName := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", request.Name, subRequest.Name)
if slices.Contains(config.Requests, subRequestName) { ... }
```

A config that references **N sub-requests of a single parent request** has `len(config.Requests) == N`. If the claim has **N top-level requests**, the lengths match even though the config covers only one of them  so its `Requests` is cleared and the config is silently re-scoped to **every** request in the claim.

The same defect is present in all three production implementations:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go` (the cleanup loop)
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`

### What did you expect to happen?

A config that references only sub-requests of one request should remain scoped to that request. `Requests` should be cleared to `nil` (the "applies to all" form) only when the config actually covers **all** top-level requests in the claim.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to the shared table in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` (`TestAllocator`) and run `go test ./structured/internal/experimental/ -run 'TestAllocator/repro-config-subrequests-not-all'` (fails identically for `incubating` and `stable`):

```go
"repro-config-subrequests-not-all": {
    features: Features{PrioritizedList: true},
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(
            requestWithPrioritizedList(req0,
                subRequest(subReq0, classA, 1),
                subRequest(subReq1, classB, 1),
            ),
            deviceRequest(req1, classA, 1), // second top-level request, unrelated to the config
        ).withConfigs(objects(
            // references BOTH sub-requests of req0 only; must NOT apply to req1
            deviceClaimConfig([]string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo")),
        )),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA), class(classB, driverB)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
        device(device1, nil, nil), device(device2, nil, nil),
    )),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{allocationResultWithConfigs(
        localNodeSelector(node1),
        objects(
            deviceAllocationResult(req0SubReq0, driverA, pool1, device1, false),
            deviceAllocationResult(req1, driverA, pool1, device2, false),
        ),
        []resourceapi.DeviceAllocationConfiguration{{
            Source:              resourceapi.AllocationConfigSourceClaim,
            Requests:            []string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, // expected: stays scoped to req0
            DeviceConfiguration: deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo"),
        }},
    )},
},
```

Device allocation comes out exactly as expected (`req-0/subReq-0` → `device-1`, `req-1` → `device-2`); the **only** difference is the config scope:

```text
expected: Requests: ["req-0/subReq-0", "req-0/subReq-1"]
actual:   Requests: nil      # == applies to ALL requests, including the unrelated req-1
```

title: [sig-network] Conntrack proxy implementation should not be vulnerable to the invalid conntrack state bug [Privileged] failing due to bug in test, again
body:
This is a reincarnation of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134116.

I have recently started to notice `[sig-network] Conntrack proxy implementation should not be vulnerable to the invalid conntrack state bug [Privileged]` flakes in downstream OpenShift CI jobs, statistically more significant in dual-stack (but not only).

We got a fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134164 for this which introduced tracking via

```
ipPort := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", addr.String(), pkt.DestPort)
[...]
pending[ipPort] = pkt.Seq + 1
```

instead of only

```
pending[addr.String()] = pkt.Seq + 1
```

however from my brief analysis it seems that we should be actually tracking by

```
ipPort := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", addr.String(), pkt.SrcPort)
```

so that we create a key using client's ephemeral port, not the server's listening port.

title: resource.Quantity.AsApproximateFloat64 returns NaN for a zero value with a large scale
body:
#### What happened?

`resource.Quantity.AsApproximateFloat64()` returns `NaN` for a quantity whose value is exactly zero but whose scale is large (roughly `|scale| >= 309`).

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go`, the function short-circuits only when `exponent == 0`, then returns `base * math.Pow10(exponent)`. For a zero value, `base` is `0` and `math.Pow10(scale)` overflows to `+Inf`, so it returns `0 * +Inf`, which is `NaN`.

#### What did you expect to happen?

A zero-valued quantity should approximate to `0` regardless of scale. The sibling `AsFloat64Slow()` returns `0` for the same input, and the two are meant to agree (their test tables are annotated to be kept in sync).

#### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
q := resource.NewScaledQuantity(0, 500) // value 0, scale 500
fmt.Println(q.AsApproximateFloat64())   // got NaN, want 0
```

Equivalently, a table row `{intQuantity(0, 500, DecimalSI), 0.0}` added to `TestQuantityAsApproximateFloat64` fails with "expected 0, got NaN", while the same row passes in `TestQuantityAsFloat64Slow`.

#### Anything else we need to know?

The result is `NaN` only for an exactly-zero value at a large scale. Non-zero values are unaffected (a tiny non-zero value that underflows still returns `0`, which is the documented approximate behavior).

#### Kubernetes version

master (the code is unchanged across released versions).

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery
/assign

title: Document caveats related to re-using the PodGroup name
body:
### What happened?

/sig scheduling

A pod group may be recreated with the same names, for example:

* Delete Pod A
* Delete PodGroup B
* Create PodGroup B
* Create Pod A

These events may be observed by the scheduler in a different order:

* Delete Pod A
* Create Pod A
* Delete PodGroup B
* Add PodGroup B

If Pod A gets scheduled before PodGroup B is observed as re-created, it may break immutability assumptions, and cause unexpected scheduler behavior (both initially and in the following cycles).

### What did you expect to happen?

This problem arises from the fact that the PodGroup API uses resource names as parent links instead of UIDs, making it impossible to tell from the scheduler perspective whether the pod belongs to the old (deleted) PG or the new (created) PG if those PGs use the same name.

Since the scheduler handles pods with the same name but different UIDs fine, it could be understandable that users may assume the same for the higher-level hierarchies (PodGroups or CompositePodGroups). Because the actual behavior may be unexpected, it should be clearly described, and the recommendation to always assign new names to PodGroups (and CompositePodGroups) should be present somewhere, as otherwise there is no guarantee that the higher-level scheduling constraints will be respected by the scheduler.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Re-create the PG using the same names but with different PG field values. The order of events on the scheduler side is non-deterministic but can be:

1. Old pod is deleted
2. New pod is created
3. New pod is scheduled
4. Old pod group is deleted
5. New pod group is created, possibly with conflicting requirements with the newly scheduled pod

title: kubelet allocates hostUsers:false pod UID/GID range ending at UINT32_MAX, causing sandbox creation to fail indefinitely
body:
### What happened?

A pod using:

```yaml

spec:

  hostUsers: false
```
intermittently fails during pod sandbox creation when kubelet allocates the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

This maps container UID/GID 0..65535 to host UID/GID: 4294901760..4294967295
The final mapped value is:
```
4294967295 = 2^32 - 1 = UINT32_MAX
```

The pod then fails sandbox creation indefinitely with:
```
FailedCreatePodSandBox
failed to create network namespace for sandbox:
failed to start noop process for unshare:
fork/exec /proc/self/exe: invalid argument
```

The affected pod never starts its init container or app container. Volume setup succeeds, but sandbox creation fails before container execution.

I have reproduced/observed this again with in same configuration on different cluster:
```
namespace: pim-adapter
pod: pim-adapter-akeneo-attributes-queue-cronjob-29701755-5blmf
```
The kubelet persisted user namespace state for this pod confirms the same terminal range:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```
The persisted kubelet state is from:
```
/var/lib/kubelet/pods/<pod-uid>/userns
```

Other hostUsers: false pods on the same node with non-terminal UID/GID ranges run successfully.

### What did you expect to happen?

Either:

1. kubelet should not allocate a pod user namespace range that includes 4294967295 / UINT32_MAX, or
2. the runtime/kernel stack should successfully create the sandbox with this mapping, or
3. the pod should fail with a clear validation/allocation error instead of retrying sandbox creation indefinitely.

In particular, kubelet should probably avoid allocating the final 65,536-ID block:
```
4294901760..4294967295
```
if this range is not valid for pod user namespace mappings.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This appears to reproduce when kubelet assigns the terminal 65,536-ID user namespace range to a pod using hostUsers: false.

Minimal pod property:
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: userns-terminal-range-repro
  namespace: userns-terminal-range-repro
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/busybox:latest
      command: ["sh", "-c", "id && sleep 3600"]
```

The important condition is that kubelet allocates this persisted user namespace mapping:
```
{
  "uidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ],
  "gidMappings": [
    { "hostId": 4294901760, "containerId": 0, "length": 65536 }
  ]
}
```

Validation steps on an affected pod:
```
NS=userns-terminal-range-repro
POD=userns-terminal-range-repro

kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='hostUsers={.spec.hostUsers}{"\n"}node={.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}uid={.metadata.uid}{"\n"}phase={.status.phase}{"\n"}'

POD_UID=$(kubectl get pod -n "$NS" "$POD" -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
echo "$POD_UID"
```
On the node where the pod is scheduled:
```
sudo cat "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Boundary check:
```
sudo jq -r '
  .uidMappings[0] as $u |
  .gidMappings[0] as $g |
  "uid_hostId=\($u.hostId)",
  "uid_length=\($u.length)",
  "uid_end=\($u.hostId + $u.length - 1)",
  "gid_hostId=\($g.hostId)",
  "gid_length=\($g.length)",
  "gid_end=\($g.hostId + $g.length - 1)",
  "uid_hits_uint32_max=\(($u.hostId + $u.length - 1) == 4294967295)",
  "gid_hits_uint32_max=\(($g.hostId + $g.length - 1) == 4294967295)"
' "/var/lib/kubelet/pods/$POD_UID/userns"
```
Observed output:
```
uid_hostId=4294901760
uid_length=65536
uid_end=4294967295
gid_hostId=4294901760
gid_length=65536
gid_end=4294967295
uid_hits_uint32_max=true
gid_hits_uint32_max=true
```

Check kubelet events/logs:

```
kubectl describe pod -n "$NS" "$POD" | grep -A8 -B4 'FailedCreatePodSandBox\|CreatePodSandbox\|failed to create network namespace\|noop process\|invalid argument'
```

```
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|CreatePodSandbox|FailedCreatePodSandBox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
```
sudo journalctl -u containerd --since "6 hours ago" | grep -E \
"$POD|$POD_UID|RunPodSandbox|failed to create network namespace|noop process|invalid argument"
```
The failure occurs before CNI appears to run and before any init/app container starts.

### Anything else we need to know?

This looks like a boundary bug in the kubelet pod user namespace allocator or in validation of generated mappings.
The node can run other hostUsers: false pods successfully when kubelet assigns non-terminal ranges. Examples of working persisted mappings observed on the same node include:
```
{"hostId":416546816,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":1584726016,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4152492032,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":4130734080,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
{"hostId":3823566848,"containerId":0,"length":65536}
```

The affected pod is from a CronJob/Job. In one observed case, the pod stayed stuck for approximately 2 days and accumulated more than 13,000 FailedCreatePodSandBox events. It happened on two different clusters with same CronJob/Job.

Relevant pod spec properties:
```
spec:
  hostUsers: false
  restartPolicy: OnFailure
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
```

The affected workload does not use:
```
hostNetwork: true
hostPID: true
hostIPC: true
volumeDevices:
```
Relevant sysctls on the node:
```
user.max_user_namespaces = 62502
user.max_net_namespaces = 62502
```
Workaround:
```
hostUsers: true
```
or removing:
```
hostUsers: false
```
avoids the kubelet pod user namespace allocation path and prevents this failure for the affected workload.

title: CronJob controller: processNextWorkItem does not call queue.Forget on the  (nil, nil) sync path, leaving stale rate-limiter backoff count
body:
/sig apps

**Description**

In `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#processNextWorkItem` only resets the workqueue rate limiter (queue.Forget) inside the requeueAfter != nil branch. When sync() returns (nil, nil) — no error and no requeue — none of the switch branches run, so Forget is never called:

```
requeueAfter, err := jm.sync(ctx, key)
switch {
case err != nil:
    utilruntime.HandleError(...)
    jm.queue.AddRateLimited(key)
case requeueAfter != nil:
    jm.queue.Forget(key)
    jm.queue.AddAfter(key, *requeueAfter)
// err == nil && requeueAfter == nil: nothing runs, Forget is not called
}

return true

```

Some paths/conditions when nil, nil are returned are such as below:
- CronJob not found / already deleted (returned directly by sync)
- CronJob being deleted (DeletionTimestamp != nil)
- CronJob suspended (spec.suspend == true)
- invalid spec.timeZone
- unparseable or invalid spec.schedule


**Issue**
I took one example flow and say : 
Take a suspended CronJob: on any given sync it may or may not need a status write, and that write may or may not succeed.( in `pkg/controller/cronjob/cronjob_controllerv2.go#syncCronJob` )
- Status write fails → sync returns (nil, err) → processNextWorkItem takes the err != nil branch → AddRateLimited increments the failure count.
- Status write succeeds → sync returns (nil, nil) → no branch runs → the count is left unchanged.

So the same path that can drive the counter up (when its status write errors) never brings it back down (when its status write succeeds).


**What happens if this isn't fixed**

I would be honest, i dont want to oversell this and the severity/impact might be on the lower side but there is definitely an impact.

Consider a CronJob that accumulated some failures during an API incident and is then suspended . Because the suspended sync returns (nil, nil), the stale failure count is retained. When the CronJob is later resumed and its first reconcile hits a transient error, AddRateLimited computes the backoff from the stale count rather than from a clean baseline.
Also - since queue keys by namespace/name, a later CronJob recreated with the same name inherits the previous object's stale backoff.

**Potential Fix**
Its just a simple one liner.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139918

**How was this uncovered**

In the sprit of full transparency :

I found this while building my own open source case study [tool](https://github.com/somak2kai/beats) on golang structural fingerprints and potential outliers and I used Kubernetes (among many others oss repos) as test subjects.  
processNextWorkItem in cronjob_controllerv2 was marked as a potential outlier compared to its cousins  such as the below ( and all of the below follow similar pattern of .forget on queue)
certificates/clustertrustbundlepublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
processNextWorkItem	rootcacertpublisher	certificates/rootcacertpublisher/publisher.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/bootstrap/tokencleaner.go#processNextWorkItem
controller/certificates/certificate_controller.go#processNextWorkItem

The goal of the tool was not to find issues , but was to perform a case study. This particular issue stood out , hence raising it. No personal agenda behind this 🙏

title: Skip CriticalPodAdmissionHandler for resizes
body:
### Proposal

Skip the `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` when evaluating resize feasibility, contingent on the `SchedulerPreemptionForPodResize` feature gate.

### Background

The `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` forcefully evicts pods from the node to make room for system-critical priority pods. This admission handler acts as a backstop, incase there was a disconnect between scheduling and node admission (for example, a [scheduler race](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126891) or pod bypassing the scheduler).

This admission handler was included by default when we implemented in-place pod resize, meaning that resized critical pods will forcefully evict lower priority pods to make room for the resize.

### Motivation

The `CriticalPodAdmissionHandler` uses custom Kubelet preemption logic that differs form the scheduler preemption logic and doesn't consider PodDispruptionBudgets (PDBs), pod PreemptionPolicy, nor workload-aware scheduling.

Now that we're adding support for scheduler-based preemption on resize, I think we should stop triggering the Kubelet-managed system-critical preemptions on resize (but keep it as a backstop for new-pod admission).

/kind bug
/sig node
/assign @natasha41575

title: DRA: pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses not populated for pod.spec.resourceClaims[].resourceClaimName
body:
### What happened

When a Pod references an existing ResourceClaim via `pod.spec.resourceClaims[].resourceClaimName`, the resourceclaim controller does not publish a corresponding entry in `pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses`.

Entries in `pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses` are only populated for ResourceClaims that the controller itself creates from a `pod.spec.resourceClaims[].resourceClaimTemplateName`.

Meanwhile, the referenced ResourceClaim's `status.reservedFor` does list the pod, so the binding exists — it is just not observable from the pod side.

### What you expected to happen

`pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses` should contain an entry for every claim listed in `pod.spec.resourceClaims`, regardless of whether the claim was supplied via `resourceClaimName` or `resourceClaimTemplateName`.

For a `resourceClaimName` entry, the published status entry would be the trivial mapping:

```yaml
status:
  resourceClaimStatuses:
  - name: <pod.spec.resourceClaims[].name>
    resourceClaimName: <pod.spec.resourceClaims[].resourceClaimName>
```

### Why this matters

1. **Status should be the source of truth.**
Kubernetes controllers reconcile `spec` (desired) and report observed state in `status`. Today, only template-generated claims are reflected in `pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses`. A claim that the user created up-front and the pod references via `resourceClaimName` is invisible in pod status, even though the same ResourceClaim already lists the pod in its `status.reservedFor`. The pod status is therefore an inaccurate observation of the current state.


2. **There is the use case where a DRA driver needs to look up every ResourceClaim attached to a pod via pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses**
    The [dra-driver-image-configurator](https://github.com/gke-labs/dra-drivers/tree/main/dra-driver-image-configurator) is such a case. The image-configurator uses BindingConditions to hold the pod long enough to mutate its image based on the device picked via the prioritized list.

    The image-configurator operates as a controller that watches Pods, retrieves the ResourceClaims referenced in `pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses`, and reads the necessary information from them.

    Imagine a case where the same ResourceClaim is shared across multiple Pods.

    If a Pod consumes a ResourceClaim with BindingConditions already set, it does not trigger any scheduling wait. Therefore, ResourceClaims for BindingConditions should be created separately from those for devices, and should be created per Pod.

    However, with the current behavior the driver can only see the template-generated claim through `pod.status.resourceClaimStatuses`, and it is not possible to read the information required for image mutation from the ResourceClaim.

```
+------------------+                  +-----------------+
| Pod foo          |                  | Pod bar         |
| spec:            |                  | spec:           |
|  rctemp->gpu/cpu |                  |  rcName ->gpu   |
|  rctemp->img-cfg |                  |  rctemp->img-cfg|
| status:          |                  | status:         |
|  device ->gpu    |                  |                 |
|  img-cfg->foo..  |                  |  img-cfg->bar.. |
+--+----------+----+                  +--+----------+---+
   |          |                          |          |
   |          +----------+    +----------+          |
   v                     v    v                     v
+-------------+       +-------------+       +-------------+
|ResourceClaim|       |ResourceClaim|       |ResourceClaim|
|foo-img-cfg  |       |shared-gpu   |       |bar-img-cfg  |
|status:      |       |config:      |       |status:      |
| BindingCond |       | ImageConfig |       | BindingCond |
| reservedFor:|       |reservedFor: |       | reservedFor:|
|  [foo]      |       |  [foo, bar] |       |  [bar]      |
+------+------+       +------+------+       +------+------+
       |                     |                     |
       |                     +---------+           |
       +----------+   +--------------- | ----------+
                  |   |                |
                  v   v                v
           +-----------------+ +-----------------+
           |ResourceSlice    | |ResourceSlice    |
           |image-config     | |gpu.example.com  |
           | BindingCondition| |                 |
           |                 | |                 |
           +-----------------+ +-----------------+
```

title: [IPPR] Deferred resizes can overestimate request footprint
body:
/kind bug

When the scheduler computes the aggregate resources of a Pod, it uses the maximum of desired, allocated and actual resources for each container.

The problem is we're doing this before the aggregation step. Consider this case:

Pod with 2 containers, c1 & c2
  - Desired:
    - c1: 1 CPU
    - c2: 2 CPU
  - Allocated:
    - c1: 2 CPU
    - c2: 1 CPU

The max of desired & allocated _should_ be 3 CPU, but the scheduler will compute 4 CPU since the max for c1 is 2, and the max for c2 is also 2.

To fix this we should aggregate desired requests, allocated requests, and actual requests separately, and use the max of the aggregated values. We just need to make sure that actual falls back to allocated, which falls back to desired (per-container).

/sig node
/cc @natasha41575 @pravk03

title: EasyCLA blocks website main to dev branch-sync PRs on kubernetes-prow[bot] merge commits
body:
### What happened?

Weekly "Merge main branch into dev-1.37" sync PRs against `kubernetes/website` fail the **EasyCLA** check with `Missing CLA Authorization`, and the only committer flagged is the bot identity `kubernetes-prow[bot]`.

These sync PRs merge `main` into the release dev branch, which by design pulls in the merge commits that Prow created when merging earlier PRs. EasyCLA evaluates every commit author in the PR, finds the `kubernetes-prow[bot]`-authored merge commits, and reports them as not covered by a signed CLA. Every human contributor on the branch passes; only the bot fails.

Key detail: in the same EasyCLA report, the older bot identity **`k8s-ci-robot` (name "Kubernetes Prow Robot") passes** the CLA check, while the newer GitHub App identity **`kubernetes-prow[bot]` fails**. So merge commits that used to be authored by the CLA-authorized `k8s-ci-robot` are now authored by `kubernetes-prow[bot]`, which has no CLA association - that identity change appears to be what newly breaks these sync PRs.

Examples:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/56271 — EasyCLA `fail`. `k8s-ci-robot` ✅ (e.g. `373112ed5c7fe7c2a5e502bb61b3aad9b917cf87`), but `@kubernetes-prow[bot]` ❌ (35 merge commits, e.g. `1797afad91da7d36ecf0ca3ed975a71e6716a860`).
- https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/56300 — fresh sync PR, same failure on the same bot identity.

This blocks the routine weekly branch sync during the v1.37 cycle: `tide` reports "Not mergeable. Needs ... cncf-cla: yes" because the bot commits aren't CLA-authorized.

### What did you expect to happen?

Merge commits authored by `kubernetes-prow[bot]` that arrive via a `main` → `dev-*` sync merge should not block EasyCLA / the `cncf-cla: yes` label - the same way the older `k8s-ci-robot` identity is already treated - so the routine weekly branch sync can proceed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Follow the [documented weekly branch-sync flow](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/blob/master/release-team/role-handbooks/docs/Release-Timeline.md#weekly-branch-sync-prs) for `kubernetes/website`: fetch `upstream/main` and `upstream/dev-1.37`, fast-forward `dev-1.37`, then `git merge upstream/main` onto a `merged-main-dev-1.37` branch.
2. Push the branch and open a PR targeting `dev-1.37`.
3. The merge brings in `kubernetes-prow[bot]` merge commits from `main`.
4. EasyCLA runs and reports `Missing CLA Authorization`, flagging only `@kubernetes-prow[bot]` (while `k8s-ci-robot` on the same PR passes).

### Anything else we need to know?

Rebasing/squashing is not a viable fix here: the entire purpose of the sync PR is to carry `main`'s merge history into the dev branch, so dropping those bot merge commits would defeat the sync. Looking for guidance on the right path - e.g. giving `kubernetes-prow[bot]` the same CLA treatment that `k8s-ci-robot` already has (allowlisting the bot identity in EasyCLA), an admin merge/override for sync PRs, or a different recommended sync procedure that avoids carrying bot-authored merge commits.

Filing as a tracking issue per advice in Slack to get direction from the owning SIG. Marking priority critical-urgent for now since it blocks the v1.37 weekly docs branch sync; happy to lower it once a fix path is confirmed.

title: Preemptor pod gets stuck in unschedulable queue when preempting a pod in PreBind/Permit phase
body:
# Description
When the SchedulerAsyncPreemption feature gate is enabled, a race condition in the scheduler can cause a high-priority preemptor pod to become stuck in the unschedulableEntities queue indefinitely after preempting a victim pod that is currently in the PreBind phase (or is a WaitingPod in the Permit phase).

# The Race Condition
## 1.Goroutine A (Async Preemption):
Starts and adds the preemptor pod to the scheduler's internal preempting set to guard against concurrent preemption attempts.
Determines the victim pod is in the PreBind phase and cancels its context (CancelPod), bypassing the API delete call (skipAPICall = true).
## 2. Goroutine B (Victim's Binding Cycle):
Detects context cancellation, aborts the PreBind phase, and fails.
Calls handleBindingCycleError, which removes the victim from the scheduler cache and broadcasts the framework.EventAssignedPodDelete event to the SchedulingQueue to reschedule pending pods.
## 3. Goroutine A (Cleanup):
Removes the preemptor pod from the preempting set.

If Goroutine B emits the EventAssignedPodDelete event before Goroutine A removes the preemptor from the preempting set:
- The scheduler's PreEnqueue check (IsPodRunningPreemption) evaluates the preemptor.
- Because the preemptor is still in the preempting map, and the victim pod still exists in the API server (since no API delete was performed, it just failed binding), the preemptor is rejected as "still running preemption" and remains in the unschedulable queue.
- Since no API delete was performed, no further informer events will arrive to wake up the preemptor. The preemptor remains stuck.


For normal preemption (API delete), this race is mitigated because the API delete eventually triggers an informer delete event after the preemption goroutine has finished, or isRunningPreemption correctly detects that the victim's DeletionTimestamp is set. However, for PreBind/Waiting cancellations, no API delete is performed, and the cancellation event is the only trigger.

# Real-World Evidence (Log Analysis)
Below are log entries showing the race occurring in a real-world scenario (anonymized):
```
INFO 2026-06-09T06:39:12.986658Z "Preemptor rejected a pod in preBind" preemptorType="pod" preemptor="preemptor-ns/preemptor-pod" podInPreBind="victim-ns/victim-pod" node="node-1"
INFO 2026-06-09T06:39:12.987537Z "Updating pod condition and nominated node name" pod="preemptor-ns/preemptor-pod" conditionType="PodScheduled" conditionStatus="False" conditionReason="Unschedulable" nominatedNodeName="node-1" nominatingMode=1
INFO 2026-06-09T06:39:12.990319Z "Async Preemption finished completely" preemptor="preemptor-ns/preemptor-pod" node="node-1" result="success"
INFO 2026-06-09T06:40:28.390704Z "Waited before sending request" pod="preemptor-ns/preemptor-pod" delay="1m15.402593375s" reason="client-side throttling, not priority and fairness" verb="PATCH" URL="https://kube-apiserver.example.com/api/v1/namespaces/preemptor-ns/pods/preemptor-pod/status"
```

# Timeline and Mechanics Analysis:
1. 06:39:12.986658Z: Goroutine A (Async Preemption) executes CancelPod for the victim pod (victim-ns/victim-pod).
2. Goroutine B (Victim Binding Cycle) detects the cancellation, fails the binding cycle, and immediately emits the EventAssignedPodDelete event. This event is queued in the preemptor's in-flight events.
3. Thread 1 (Scheduling Preemptor) scheduling cycle fails and enters handleSchedulingFailure.
- It calls AddUnschedulablePodIfNotPresent.
- The queueing logic evaluates the in-flight EventAssignedPodDelete event.
- It checks IsPodRunningPreemption for the preemptor. Because Goroutine A is still active (it only finishes at .990), this returns true.
- The event is ignored/discarded, and the preemptor is placed in unschedulableEntities.
4. 06:39:12.987537Z: Thread 1 logs "Updating pod condition..." and starts patching the status.
5. 06:39:12.990319Z: Goroutine A (Preemption Cleanup) finally completes and removes the preemptor from the preempting map.
6. 06:40:28.390704Z: The status patch started in step 4 finally completes after being client-side throttled for 1m 15s.

At step 3, the scheduling queue discarded the requeueing event because the preemption was still marked as running. After step 5, the preemption was marked as completed, but the event was already lost, causing the preemptor to get stuck.

/sig-scheduling

title: kubectl: `cluster-info dump --output-directory` writes pod logs (with embedded secrets) as world-readable
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP` writes every dump file via `setupOutputWriter`, which does:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126 (func setupOutputWriter)
file, err := os.Create(fullFile)
```

`os.Create` opens files `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` with mode `0666` before umask. With the very common `0022` umask that is `0644` (world-readable); with `0002` (common on shared systems / some distros) it is `0664` (group- and other-readable). Parents are created `0755` (`os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)` at line 124), so the directory tree is traversable by "other".

Pod logs are dumped verbatim to `{DUMP}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt` (line 295 → `writer.Write(data)` at line 287, raw bytes straight from the `log` API). Pod logs routinely contain application secrets: bearer tokens, DB connection strings, cloud credentials, signed URLs, signed certificate/key material, etc.

### What did you expect to happen?

Dump files should be created owner-only (`0600`), and the dump directory tree owner-only (`0700`) when it contains pod logs or other potentially sensitive cluster state, so that an unprivileged local user cannot read the operator's cluster dump.

Preconditions on the victim host: another local user can traverse the path to DUMP (the typical case — DUMP in a home dir, `/tmp`, a shared scratch dir, or a CI artifact dir whose parents are `0755`). The attacker needs **no Kubernetes API credentials at all** — only filesystem read on files kubectl itself just created.

1. Authorized/privileged operator runs kubectl once:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP --all-namespaces
   ```
   kubectl creates DUMP and all nested dirs `0755`, and every `logs.txt` (and `nodes.txt`, `events.txt`, …) `0644`/`0664`, with full pod-log contents — across **all** namespaces requested.
2. A second unprivileged local user reads the logs directly:
   ```bash
   cat $DUMP/*/leaky/logs.txt        # 044-mode readable + traversable parents (0755) => readable by "other"
   ```
   No exploit primitive required — ordinary filesystem ACLs. `--all-namespaces` widens the blast radius to logs from every namespace, including ones the attacker has no RBAC right to read.
3. Extract whatever secret the logs leaked (token, password, cert+key), then use it against the cluster or upstream systems:
   ```bash
   kubectl --token=<LEAKED> ...        # if a bearer token was logged
   # or use a leaked DB connection string / cloud credential against the corresponding backend
   ```
   → access beyond the attacker's normal reach, often as a high-privilege workload identity.

Exposure is **durable**: the files persist at `0644`/`0664` on disk under DUMP until someone manually tightens permissions or deletes them, and re-running the dump re-creates them the same way. On a shared host captured by automation, the window can stay open indefinitely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run this single self-contained snippet from the root of a Kubernetes checkout. It spins up a fake API server that returns one pod whose `log` endpoint serves a secret marker, then runs the real `kubectl cluster-info dump` and reports the resulting file mode + leak. It uses an already-built `kubectl` (`_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl` or `_output/bin/kubectl`).

```bash
set -e
KUBECTL="${KUBECTL:-_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl}"
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || KUBECTL=_output/bin/kubectl
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || { echo "build kubectl first: make kubectl"; exit 1; }

python3 - "$PWD/$KUBECTL" <<'PY'
import http.server, json, os, pathlib, socket, stat, subprocess, sys, tempfile, threading, urllib.parse
kubectl_bin = sys.argv[1]
secret = "TOKEN=cluster-log-secret-12345\n"
def list_obj(kind, items=None):
    return {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": items or []}
def apps_list(kind):
    return {"apiVersion": "apps/v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": []}
pod = {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": "Pod",
       "metadata": {"name": "leaky", "namespace": "default", "uid": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"},
       "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "app", "image": "busybox"}]}, "status": {"phase": "Running"}}

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): return
    def send_json(self, obj):
        d = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(d))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(d)
    def do_GET(self):
        p = urllib.parse.urlparse(self.path).path
        if p == "/api": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIVersions", "versions": ["v1"], "serverAddressByClientCIDRs": []})
        if p == "/api/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/apis": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIGroupList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groups": [{"name": "apps", "versions": [{"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}], "preferredVersion": {"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}}]})
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "apps/v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/api/v1/nodes": return self.send_json(list_obj("NodeList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/events": return self.send_json(list_obj("EventList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/replicationcontrollers": return self.send_json(list_obj("ReplicationControllerList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/services": return self.send_json(list_obj("ServiceList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods": return self.send_json(list_obj("PodList", [pod]))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/daemonsets": return self.send_json(apps_list("DaemonSetList"))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments": return self.send_json(apps_list("DeploymentList"))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/replicasets": return self.send_json(apps_list("ReplicaSetList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/leaky/log":
            d = secret.encode(); self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(d))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(d); return
        self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(("not found: " + p).encode())

with socket.socket() as s:
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); port = s.getsockname()[1]
srv = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), H)
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
out = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="cluster-info-dump-poc-"); os.chmod(out, 0o755)
try:
    cmd = [kubectl_bin, f"--server=http://127.0.0.1:{port}", "--kubeconfig=/dev/null",
           "cluster-info", "dump", "--namespaces=default", "--output-directory=" + out, "-o", "json"]
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print("ERROR: kubectl cluster-info dump failed", file=sys.stderr)
        print(r.stdout, file=sys.stderr); print(r.stderr, file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(r.returncode)
    lp = pathlib.Path(out) / "default" / "leaky" / "logs.txt"
    content = lp.read_text(); mode = stat.S_IMODE(lp.stat().st_mode)
    print(f"kubectl        : {kubectl_bin}")
    print(f"dump_dir       : {out}")
    print(f"log_file       : {lp}")
    print(f"log_mode       : {mode:04o}")
    print(f"contains_secret: {secret.strip() in content}")
    print(f"other_readable : {bool(mode & 0o004)}")
    if (mode & 0o004) and secret.strip() in content:
        print("VULNERABLE: log dump file is readable by other users and contains the secret marker")
finally:
    srv.shutdown()
PY
```

Expected output (observed; mode depends on umask — `0644` under `0022`, `0664` under `0002`, both other-readable):

```text
kubectl        : .../kubectl
dump_dir       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX
log_file       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX/default/leaky/logs.txt
log_mode       : 0664
contains_secret: True
other_readable : True
VULNERABLE: log dump file is readable by other users and contains the secret marker
```

The pod log containing the secret marker is written to a mode-`0664` (or `0644`) file readable by other local users. No API binding or real cluster is involved.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Sink: `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126`, `func setupOutputWriter`, called from the dump path (e.g. pod logs at line 295; also nodes/events/services/pods/etc.). Parents created `0755` at line 124.
- Same class as the already-reported client-go kubeconfig migration (`0666`→`0644`) and kubeadm/kube-scheduler config writers — sensitive runtime output written `0666` before umask instead of owner-only.
- Suggested fix: create dump files `0600` (`os.OpenFile(fullFile, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC, 0600)`) and the dump directory tree `0700` when writing pod logs / sensitive cluster state.

title: Failure cluster [046b4ed3...] ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-rootless failure
Job admission plugin checks gang-scheduling parallelism guard when only one of GenericWorkload/WorkloadWithJob is enabled
body:
<!-- This issue was generated with AI assistance -->

## What happened?

The `validateParallelismChange` admission check in `plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go` uses an AND condition to skip validation:

```go
if !p.genericWorkloadEnabled && !p.workloadWithJobEnabled {
    return nil
}
```

This means the gang-scheduling parallelism guard is active when **either** feature gate is enabled. Disabling only `WorkloadWithJob` (or only `GenericWorkload`) is not sufficient to bypass the check — both must be disabled.

If a user disables `WorkloadWithJob` expecting to opt out of gang-scheduling admission behavior, the check still fires because `GenericWorkload` is enabled (or vice versa).

## What did you expect to happen?

Disabling the relevant feature gate for the code path being exercised should be sufficient to skip the validation. For example, the `SchedulingGroup`-based path (line 133) only makes sense with `GenericWorkload`, and the owner-reference scan path (line 148) only makes sense with `WorkloadWithJob`. Each branch should be gated independently on its corresponding feature gate, rather than both branches being gated on the OR of the two gates.

## How can we reproduce it?

1. Disable `WorkloadWithJob` feature gate, leave `GenericWorkload` enabled.
2. Create a Job that has an owner-created PodGroup with gang scheduling.
3. Attempt to update the Job's parallelism.
4. Observe `is forbidden: cannot change parallelism for a Job referencing gang-scheduled PodGroup` even though `WorkloadWithJob` is disabled.

## Relevant code

`plugin/pkg/admission/job/admission.go`, `validateParallelismChange` function.

/kind bug

title: kubelet logs --manifest-url-header credentials (Authorization / API keys) to runtime logs
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet is configured with `--manifest-url` and credential-bearing `--manifest-url-header` values (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer …` or `X-API-Key: …`), those header values are written to kubelet runtime logs at startup, in cleartext.

At static-pod source init, `makePodSourceConfig` copies the config map into a plain `http.Header` and logs it directly:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:372-393
manifestURLHeader := make(http.Header)
if len(kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader) > 0 {
    for k, v := range kubeCfg.StaticPodURLHeader {
        for i := range v {
            manifestURLHeader.Add(k, v[i])          // values copied into a plain http.Header
        }
    }
}
...
if kubeCfg.StaticPodURL != "" {
    logger.Info("Adding pod URL with HTTP header", "URL", kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, "header", manifestURLHeader)  // <-- sink
    config.NewSourceURL(logger, kubeCfg.StaticPodURL, manifestURLHeader, ...)
}
```

The codebase already knows this field is secret and masks it elsewhere:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/apis/config/types.go:107
StaticPodURLHeader map[string][]string `datapolicy:"token"`
```

…and the *config-dump* path redacts it before logging the full `KubeletConfiguration` (`cmd/kubelet/app/server.go:287-290` masks the map to `<masked>`). But `makePodSourceConfig` logs the **runtime `http.Header` copy**, not the config map — so neither the `datapolicy:"token"` tag nor the logging-mask applies, and the header values ship out verbatim. (`datapolicy` only fires on a strongly-typed field argument; here the value has been flattened into an `http.Header` passed as a generic `"header"` argument.)

### What did you expect to happen?

`makePodSourceConfig` should not log the header values. The `datapolicy:"token"` tag and the `server.go:287-290` config-mask both express the intent that `StaticPodURLHeader` is secret; this code path bypasses both by logging a runtime copy. The sink should mask/drop the `header` field (e.g. log only that headers are present, or redact like the config-dump path does). Redaction must not depend on operators avoiding sensitive headers, since the field is the documented place to put upstream auth.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Copy-paste into a shell **inside the kubernetes repo** (auto-detects root). It drops a same-package Go test under `pkg/kubelet` that calls the real `makePodSourceConfig` with a custom `logr` sink capturing klog output, sets `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret`, and asserts the secret appears in the captured logs. Cleans up after itself; no cluster or running kubelet needed.

```bash
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
F="$ROOT/pkg/kubelet/zz_poc_staticpodheader_logleak_test.go"
trap 'rm -f "$F"' EXIT
cat >"$F" <<'GOEOF'
package kubelet

import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/go-logr/logr"
	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	kubeletconfiginternal "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/apis/config"
	kubeletutil "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/util"
	"k8s.io/klog/v2"
)

type pocSink struct{ buf *bytes.Buffer }

func (s *pocSink) Init(logr.RuntimeInfo)          {}
func (s *pocSink) Enabled(int) bool               { return true }
func (s *pocSink) Info(_ int, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) Error(err error, msg string, kv ...interface{}) {
	fmt.Fprintln(s.buf, append([]interface{}{msg, err}, kv...)...)
}
func (s *pocSink) WithValues(kv ...interface{}) logr.LogSink { return s }
func (s *pocSink) WithName(string) logr.LogSink              { return s }

func TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak(t *testing.T) {
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	ctx := klog.NewContext(context.Background(), logr.New(&pocSink{buf: &logs}))

	const secret = "Bearer static-pod-url-secret"
	kubeCfg := &kubeletconfiginternal.KubeletConfiguration{
		StaticPodURL:        "http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml",
		StaticPodURLHeader:  map[string][]string{"Authorization": {secret}},
		HTTPCheckFrequency:  metav1.Duration{Duration: time.Hour},
	}
	deps := &Dependencies{PodStartupLatencyTracker: kubeletutil.NewPodStartupLatencyTracker()}

	if _, err := makePodSourceConfig(ctx, kubeCfg, deps, "node-a", func() bool { return true }); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("makePodSourceConfig: %v", err)
	}
	if !strings.Contains(logs.String(), secret) {
		t.Fatalf("secret NOT in logs:\n%s", logs.String())
	}
	t.Logf("VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs\n%s", logs.String())
}
GOEOF
( cd "$ROOT" && go test ./pkg/kubelet -run TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak -count=1 -v 2>&1 | grep -E 'VULNERABLE|Adding pod URL|PASS|FAIL|ok ' )
```

Expected: printed lines show the secret in the kubelet log output, then `PASS`:

```text
VULNERABLE: static pod URL header secret written to kubelet logs
    Adding pod URL with HTTP header URL http://127.0.0.1:1/static-pods.yaml header map[Authorization:[Bearer static-pod-url-secret]]
--- PASS: TestPOCStaticPodURLHeaderLogLeak (0.00s)
ok  	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet
```

i.e. the `Authorization: Bearer static-pod-url-secret` value is logged verbatim by `Adding pod URL with HTTP header`.

### Anything else we need to know?

- This is secret disclosure of upstream-manifest credentials to kubelet logs, at default verbosity. It is a duplicate of the same finding already recorded internally as `kubelet_staticpodurlheader_log_leak`.
- Distinct from `kubelet_configz_staticpodurlheader_leak` (the `/configz` JSON path, different sink and code path) — both leak the same `StaticPodURLHeader` field but via different endpoints; both capitalize on the fact that `makePodSourceConfig`/`setConfigz` bypass the `datapolicy`/config-mask that `server.go:287-290` applies.
- Affects kubelet configured with `--manifest-url` + `--manifest-url-header`. Nodes using only `--pod-manifest-path` are not affected.

```console
v1.37.0-alpha.2-121-ga0b6070d29d   # current master; reproducer verified at a0b6070d29d
```

title: kube-apiserver exits during storage initialization with etcdclient: failed to connect to the etcd server: context deadline exceeded on v1.37.0-alpha.2
body:
### Issue
Kubernetes v1.37.0-alpha.0: kubeadm init completes successfully and the control plane boots.
Kubernetes v1.37.0-alpha.1: kube-apiserver consistently exits during storage initialization with error creating storage factory: `etcdclient: failed to connect to the etcd server: context deadline exceeded.`
Kubernetes v1.37.0-alpha.2: Same behavior.

### What happened:

During kubeadm init, the control plane bootstrap consistently fails because kube-apiserver exits during startup before becoming ready.
kubeadm successfully completes the following phases:

```
Preflight
Certificate generation
kubeconfig generation
Static Pod manifest generation
kubelet startup
```

However, kube-apiserver never reaches a Ready state and repeatedly exits with:

`error creating storage factory: etcdclient: failed to connect to the etcd server: context deadline exceeded
`
As a consequence, kubeadm eventually times out waiting for the control plane and fails while attempting to create the bootstrap ClusterRoleBinding.
The ClusterRoleBinding failure appears to be a downstream symptom of the API server never becoming available.

### What you expect to happen:

kubeadm init should complete successfully and the control plane should become Ready.

How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Environment:

```
Kubernetes: v1.37.0-alpha.2
kubeadm: v1.37.0-alpha.2
Runtime: CRI-O
OS: SLES
Kernel: <kernel version>
Reproduced on:
Bare metal
OpenStack VMs
```
The issue is consistently reproducible in both environments.

### Anything else we need to know:
kube-apiserver logs
```
I0630 12:16:40.343858       1 server.go:151] Version: v1.37.0
...
E0630 12:17:00.759028       1 run.go:72] "command failed" err="error creating storage factory: etcdclient: failed to connect to the etcd server: context deadline exceeded"
```

The apiserver exits approximately 20 seconds after startup.

etcd status
```
starts successfully
becomes leader
reports "ready to serve client requests"
continues running

```
It does not continuously crash.


**Connectivity verification**

The following checks were performed:
Both etcd and kube-apiserver are static pods using hostNetwork: true
kube-apiserver is configured with:
--etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
etcd listens on:
127.0.0.1:2379
<node-ip>:2379

Using the same client certificate and key configured for kube-apiserver:

```
curl \
  --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt \
  --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key \
  https://127.0.0.1:2379/health

returns

{"health":"true"}
```
indicating that etcd is reachable and accepts the same client credentials used by kube-apiserver.


**Resource validation**
The node does not appear to be resource constrained.
```
~22 GiB RAM
~12 GiB available memory
CPU remains approximately 95–98% idle during bootstrap
No OOM events observed
```


**Additional observations**
Increasing kube-apiserver verbosity to --v=8 does not produce additional diagnostics before the process exits.
kube-apiserver repeatedly exits while etcd continues running.
The failure reproduces consistently on multiple environments.

**Kubernetes version**
```
$ kubeadm version
v1.37.0-alpha.2
$ kube-apiserver --version
v1.37.0-alpha.2
```

title: Excessive "Label not found" V(4) logs for optional container annotations flood kubelet logs and cause rapid disk space consumption
body:
### What happened?

When kubelet runs with `--v=4` (a common debug level), the log is continuously flooded with lines like:

```plaintext
I0627 08:10:30.787761    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 08:10:30.787766    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 08:10:30.787771    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
...
I0627 09:00:34.694549    9911 labels.go:293] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.pod.deletionGracePeriod"
I0627 09:00:34.695552    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.preStopHandler"
I0627 09:00:34.695745    9911 labels.go:304] "Label not found" label="io.kubernetes.container.ports"
```

In a kubemark cluster, this was observed to run continuously and consume disk space rapidly, with approximately 220 pods (2 containers per pod) running on each node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Logging "Label not found" for optional annotations at V(4) might be too verbose, since these labels are typically absent for many containers. It would be better to raise the log level so it doesn't appear during typical debug verbosity, or perhaps consider removing the line entirely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run kubelet with --v=4.
2. Schedule a high density of pods on the node (e.g., ~200 pods), whose containers have no preStop handler, no ports, and whose pod has no deletionGracePeriodSeconds (i.e. almost every pod).
3. Observe the three "Label not found" lines being emitted continuously during pod syncs, consuming disk space rapidly.

### Anything else we need to know?

> Commit [ab839c93](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/ab839c93ff85072b2cc289a5826f61ff409b937a)

In `pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/labels.go`, the "Label not found" logs are emitted by `getInt64PointerFromLabel` and `getJSONObjectFromLabel` whenever a label is absent.

These labels are only written conditionally in `newContainerAnnotations`:

`podDeletionGracePeriodLabel` — only if `pod.DeletionGracePeriodSeconds != nil`
`containerPreStopHandlerLabel` — only if `container.Lifecycle.PreStop != nil`
`containerPortsLabel` — only if `len(container.Ports) > 0`
Since these conditions are not met for most containers, the labels are expected to be missing. However, `getContainerInfoFromAnnotations` is called on every status lookup, triggering the log on the normal path.

title: DRA: Consumable Capacity PolicyRange doesn't support fractional value
body:
### What happened?

Discussion Thread in slack: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0409NGC1TK/p1782398632052059

This issue is originally reported by @liggitt 

> Looking at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139698, I was digging into consumable capacity policy range step validation more ... it looks like the validation and use is coercing the requested values and steps to integers before determining if max-min divides evenly by step, etc. Was that intended? I didn't see anything in the design or validation of min / max that required integer values

Currently, the step alignment logic evaluates quantities using resource.Quantity.Value(). Because .Value() automatically ceils any fractional metric to the next whole integer, fractional steps (such as 0.5 or 2.5 core allocations) lose precision. For example, if a Step of 0.5 is processed, it is evaluated as 1, causing step math to behave incorrectly and misalign requested allocations.

### What did you expect to happen?

The system should either explicitly disallow fractional quantities with clear documentation, or it should preserve fractional values during conversion.

We should either 
- keep integer-only constraints with Value() conversion but update the documentation to explicitly state that fractional quantities are not supported 
- or update the internal logic to preserve fractional precision with a reasonable performance tradeoff. For example, we can use resource.Quantity.MilliValue() to support milli-scale metrics (like millicores).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Define RangePolicy with fractional quantities

title: e2e: Pod InPlace Resize Container (resource-quota)/(limit-ranger) tests use hardcoded resource sizes too large for resource-constrained nodes
body:
### What happened?

The `Pod InPlace Resize Container (resource-quota)` and `Pod InPlace Resize Container (limit-ranger)` e2e tests in `test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go` (`doPodResizeResourceQuotaTests` / `doPodResizeLimitRangerTests`) hardcode a base container size of `300m CPU / 300Mi memory`. Each test creates **2 Guaranteed-QoS pods via `CreateBatch`** at that size, requiring 600m CPU / 600Mi memory combined just to get through test setup, before any resize/quota/limit-range logic under test even runs.

On resource-constrained schedulable nodes -- e.g. a compact 3-node control-plane topology where masters also run workloads -- this is often more headroom than is actually free, and the second pod fails to schedule:

```
FailedScheduling: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu. no new claims to deallocate,
preemption: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```

This causes the tests to permafail on such clusters, even though the ResourceQuota/LimitRange enforcement logic actually under test is unrelated to node size. Some "valid increase" `ginkgo.Entry` cases also patch containers up to 350-400m/Mi and must be **actuated** on a node (`WaitForPodResizeActuation`), which needs even more headroom.

By contrast, sibling tests in the same file (`doPodResizeSchedulerTests`, `doPodResizeRetryDeferredTests`) already avoid this by sizing pods as fractions of the node's actual allocatable/available capacity (`e2enode.GetNodeAllocatableAndAvailableQuantities`) instead of hardcoded absolute values, and `test/e2e/common/node/pod_resize.go`'s generic resize tests use a much smaller footprint (~20m/35Mi).

Observed downstream in OpenShift CI on `periodic-ci-openshift-release-main-nightly-5.0-e2e-agent-compact-fips`:
- 0% pass rate across 14 runs (Sippy), with these tests the largest contributor.
- Failures reproduced a week apart, same root cause each time.

### What did you expect to happen?

These tests should be able to run on resource-constrained nodes (small VMs, compact/control-plane-schedulable topologies) without needing several hundred millicores/mebibytes of headroom just for setup pods, since the actual behavior under test (quota/limit-range admission math) is independent of absolute resource size.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run a cluster where schedulable nodes have less than ~600m CPU / 600Mi memory free (e.g. a compact 3-node cluster with control-plane pods co-located and no dedicated workers).
2. Run the `Pod InPlace Resize Container (resource-quota)` / `(limit-ranger)` e2e suites (`test/e2e/node/pod_resize.go`, `pod-resize-resource-quota-test` / `pod-resize-limit-ranger-test`).
3. Observe the second `CreateBatch` pod fail to schedule with `Insufficient cpu`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Related OpenShift bugs (for reproduction data/context, not something a k/k SIG should need to track directly):
- https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-96515
- https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPBUGS-96708

title: kube-apiserver 1.35+ never shuts down on SIGTERM when its identity Lease cannot be created (e.g. hostname longer than 63 bytes)
body:
### What happened?

On hosts with hostnames longer than 63 bytes, `kube-apiserver` does not shut down after `SIGTERM`. It keeps serving until `SIGKILL`.

This reproduces consistently with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 binaries on Linux and macOS. v1.34 shuts down normally on the same hosts.

The hostname matters because the apiserver identity Lease is labeled with `kubernetes.io/hostname`, and Kubernetes label values are limited to 63 bytes. When the hostname exceeds that limit, Lease creation is rejected forever. Since v1.35, shutdown waits on that retry loop, causing a deadlock.

The retry loop logs:

```
    E0705 16:05:59 controller.go:201] "Failed to ensure lease exists, will retry"
    err="Lease.coordination.k8s.io \"apiserver-...\" is invalid: metadata.labels:
    Invalid value: \"sat12-dp146-...-FE94C5DD19A3.local\":
    must be no more than 63 bytes" interval="7s"
```
A goroutine dump after `SIGTERM` shows the shutdown hook blocked in `Stop()` while the lease controller is still retrying:

```
    goroutine 1 [sync.Mutex.Lock]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).Stop(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:131
    k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver.completedConfig.New.func10()
            k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/server.go:279
    k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server.(*GenericAPIServer).RunPreShutdownHooks(...)

    goroutine 3459 [select]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).backoffEnsureLease(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:203
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).sync(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:174
```

The deadlock is:

1. `sync()` holds `reconcilingLock` and calls `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)`.
2. `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)` retries forever because the Lease can never be created.
3. On `SIGTERM`, the pre-shutdown hook calls `controller.Stop()`.
4. `Stop()` blocks waiting for `reconcilingLock`.
5. The retry context is only canceled after pre-shutdown hooks return.
6. Pre-shutdown hooks cannot return because `Stop()` is blocked.

This is not specific to hostnames. Any permanent `ensureLease` failure can block shutdown the same way.

This appears to have been introduced by #134514, shipped in v1.35.0. It is present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x, and not present in v1.34.x.

Fix: #140241. With that fix applied, the same setup exits about 2 seconds after `SIGTERM`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`SIGTERM` should shut down `kube-apiserver` within seconds.

If the identity Lease cannot be created, the identity feature should be degraded, but apiserver shutdown should not be blocked.

### How can we reproduce it?

Option A: component-level test

Run the regression test from #140241:

```
    TestStopDoesNotBlockWhenLeaseCannotBeCreated
```

in:

```
    staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller_test.go
```
Without the `controller.go` fix from that PR, `Stop()` never returns and the test times out after 30 seconds. With the fix, it passes quickly.

Option B: real binaries in containers

Adjust `arm64`/`amd64` as needed.

```
    mkdir repro && cd repro

    curl -sLo kube-apiserver https://dl.k8s.io/v1.36.2/bin/linux/arm64/kube-apiserver
    chmod +x kube-apiserver

    curl -sL https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/releases/download/v3.6.4/etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64.tar.gz \
      | tar xz --strip-components=1 etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64/etcd

    openssl genrsa -out sa.key 2048
    openssl rsa -in sa.key -pubout -out sa.pub

    cat > test.sh << 'EOF'
    #!/bin/bash

    /repro/etcd \
      --data-dir=/tmp/etcd \
      --listen-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --advertise-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      >/tmp/etcd.log 2>&1 &

    sleep 3

    /repro/kube-apiserver \
      --etcd-servers=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cert-dir=/tmp/certs \
      --secure-port=6443 \
      --bind-address=127.0.0.1 \
      --advertise-address=$(hostname -i) \
      --authorization-mode=RBAC \
      --disable-admission-plugins=ServiceAccount \
      --service-cluster-ip-range=10.0.0.0/24 \
      --allow-privileged=true \
      --service-account-issuer=https://127.0.0.1:6443/ \
      --service-account-key-file=/repro/sa.pub \
      --service-account-signing-key-file=/repro/sa.key \
      >/tmp/apiserver.log 2>&1 &

    PID=$!

    sleep 20

    echo "lease errors: $(grep -c 'Failed to ensure lease exists' /tmp/apiserver.log)"

    kill -TERM $PID

    for i in $(seq 45); do
      kill -0 $PID 2>/dev/null || {
        echo "RESULT: exited ${i}s after SIGTERM"
        exit 0
      }
      sleep 1
    done

    echo "RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM"
    EOF
```

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*61+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result with a 64-byte hostname:

```
    RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM
```

For comparison, a 63-byte hostname exits normally:

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*60+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result:

    RESULT: exited 2s after SIGTERM

### Anything else we need to know?

This was found in Kubebuilder CI, which runs controller tests against real `kube-apiserver` and `etcd` binaries through controller-runtime envtest. Teardown sends `SIGTERM` and later `SIGKILL`; there is no kubelet or container runtime involved.

Public examples:

- macOS runner with a 68-byte hostname:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28746565395/job/85238353306?pr=5836
- Ubuntu runner with hostname set to 64 bytes:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28747687942/job/85241306371?pr=5836

This does not appear to be connection draining. There are no in-flight or watch requests, and no shutdown activity begins.

It also does not appear to be signal delivery. `etcd`, started the same way on the same host, exits in under a second on `SIGTERM`, and the hung apiserver handles `SIGQUIT` normally.

Full goroutine dumps and `-v=4` logs are available if helpful.

### Kubernetes version

Reproduced with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 release binaries.

Introduced in v1.35.0 by #134514.
Present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x.
Not present in v1.34.x.

### Cloud provider

None. Plain host processes on GitHub Actions runners and a laptop.

### OS version

Reproduced on macOS 15 arm64 and Ubuntu 24.04 amd64/arm64.

The deciding variable is hostname length, not OS. Linux caps hostnames at 64 bytes, so only a 64-byte hostname exceeds the 63-byte label value limit.

### Install tools

None. Official release binaries executed directly.

### Container runtime (CRI) and version

N/A

### Related plugins

N/A

title: KEP-5491: `matchAttribute` constraint fails to allocate devices when backtracking is required (DRAListTypeAttributes)
body:
/wg device-management
/sig scheduling
KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5491

_This bug is originally reported by @pohly in a private communication._

### What happened?

When using `DRAListTypeAttributes` is enabled (list-type device attributes),  `matchAttribute` fails the device allcation even when a valid combination of devices exists.

For example, given four devices where attributes are lists of values:
- `dev1: attr=[1,2]`
- `dev2: attr=[1]`
- `dev3: attr=[2]`
- `dev4: attr=[2]`

The device allocator fails to find the valid allocation  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`  because after removing  `dev2` during backtracking,  the intersection kept in the allocator is still  `{1}`  (stale from when  `dev2`  was added), causing  `dev3`  and  `dev4`  to be incorrectly rejected as below:

1. Add  `dev1`  → intersection becomes  `{1,2}` 
1. Add  `dev2`  → intersection shrinks to  `{1}` 
1. Try  `dev3`  →  `{2} ∩ {1} = ∅`  → rejected
1. Try  `dev4`  → same rejection
1. Backtrack: remove  `dev2`  →  only`numDevices`  goes to 1, but intersection is still  `{1}` (BUG) 
1. Retry  `dev3`  → rejected (wrong!  `{1,2} ∩ {2} = {2}`  is valid)
1. Allocation fails despite  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`  being a valid solution

### What did you expect to happen?

The allocator should successfully return a valid set of 3 devices that satisfies the  `matchAttribute` constraint, such as  `{dev1, dev3, dev4}`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable the `DRAListTypeAttributes`  feature gate
2. Create devices with list-type attributes as described above (4 devices,  `attr` attribute as a list)
3. Create a  `ResourceClaim` requesting 3 devices with a `matchAttribute`  constraint on  `attr`
4. Observe that allocation fails despite `{dev1, dev3, dev4}` being a valid solution

### Anything else we need to know?

### Root cause (allocator internals):

The bug is in [`matchAttributeConstraint`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L865-L878) in [the experimental allocator](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go).

The allocator uses recursive depth-first search with backtracking. When a device is tentatively added to the `matchAttributeConstarint`, [`add()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L880) narrows the intersection to the running intersection of all device attribute sets. However, when the allocator backtracks and calls [`remove()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.2/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go#L965), the intersection is _never_ restored. Subsequent candidates are then evaluated against a stale, over-restricted intersection and incorrectly rejected.

Note: _`distinctAttributeConstraint` does not have this bug_ — it stores per-device attributes in a [`map[requestName]attribute` and correctly removes entries on backtrack](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/constraint.go#L41).

### Proposed fix approaches:

#### Option A: Intersection stack

Push the intersection before narrowing in `add()`, pop it back in `remove()`.

- ✅ `O(1)` per add/remove
- ⚠️ Relies on the allocator's device search order (it works today due to Depth-First search structure in the allocator, but is fragile to future refactors)

#### Option B: Store per-device sets, recompute on remove

Keep a `map[deviceID]deviceAttributeSet`; recompute the intersection from scratch in `remove()`. It is a similar approach to the `distinctAttributeConstraint` implementation

- ✅ Correct regardless of removal order
- ✅ Consistent with existing patterns in the codebase
- ⚠️ `O(n)` per remove — impact could be limited in practice since the number of search target devices would typically be single digits

Generally, _Option A_ would be preferred. I'd be glad to have feedback!

title: When a node restarts, only the first init container is executed.
body:
### What happened?

Our pod has two init containers. After the node restarted, the first init container ran again, but the second init container did not execute, and the main container started running.
The reason is that when the power is cut off, all init containers have been successfully executed, the main container has been created, but it is not running and remains in the create state.
```
[root@taocanmaster1host ~]# crictl ps -a | grep node-ag
c184da0ba17b5       cd62784d2eb2b       4 days ago          Running             agent                 1                   81af3eb568823       agent-g6hzd
ee5aef279cc06       cd62784d2eb2b       4 days ago          Created             agent                 0                   33cfe0399befe      agent-g6hzd
```
According to the code, after the node is restarted, the sandbox is re-created. In this case, the first init container is directly started.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1064-L1071
When entering computePodActions for the second time, there was an issue when calculating which init container needs to be started.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1017-L1052
As shown in the preceding figure, the computeInitContainerActions method first checks the container status. If the container is in the created or running state, the pod is considered to have been initialized.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/93248f9ae092f571eb870b7664c534bfc7d00f03/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go#L1083-L1087
Here, it is considered that initialization has already been completed, and subsequent operations will not be executed, causing other init containers to not execute.I think this is a bug.

### What did you expect to happen?

After the node is restarted, all init containers need to be executed again.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

After the master container is created, power off and then power on the container to ensure that the container is in the created state.

title: Flaky test: pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler uncertain mount tests time out waiting for detach
body:
#### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit (top job in the k8s-metrics flake feed for this package; 3 jobs total)

#### Which tests are flaking?

`Test_UncertainDeviceGlobalMounts` and `Test_UncertainVolumeMountState` in `pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler`, with occasional knock-on failures in other tests of the same package.

#### Since when has it been flaking?

At least the week of 2026-07-06: 9 failures across 3 jobs for `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/volumemanager reconciler` in the flake feed.

#### Reason for failure (if possible)

Both tests run their table cases as parallel subtests, and each subtest starts a reconciler goroutine (`reconciler.Run`) with a stop channel that is never closed. Every finished subtest therefore leaks a reconciler that keeps spinning at the test's 1ns loop interval. The leaked reconcilers starve the remaining subtests; under load their wait helpers exceed the ~36s exponential backoff budget and fail with:

```
reconciler_test.go: Timed out waiting for volume "fake-plugin/timeout-setup-volume" to be detached.
```

Reproducible locally with:

```
go test ./pkg/kubelet/volumemanager/reconciler -race -count=30 -timeout=45m
```

On an otherwise idle 16-core machine this failed `Test_UncertainVolumeMountState` in 7 of 30 runs and `Test_UncertainDeviceGlobalMounts` in 2 of 30, plus knock-on failures in `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeFSResizeControllerAttachEnabled` and `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeUnmapControllerAttachEnabled`, and the leak roughly triples the package runtime by the later iterations.

#### Anything else we need to know?

Fix is straightforward: stop each reconciler when its subtest returns (the pattern `Test_Run_Positive_VolumeFSResizeControllerAttachEnabled` already uses) and create the ktesting context per subtest. PR to follow.
