title: kubelet: DRA health watch error-spams every 5s for drivers that don't implement DRAResourceHealth (Unimplemented not handled)
body:
### What happened?

With the `ResourceHealthStatus` feature gate (beta, on by default since 1.36), the kubelet logs an `ERROR` every 5 seconds, per DRA driver, for every driver that does not implement the optional `DRAResourceHealth` gRPC service:

```
E0709 17:55:32.410673 kubelet manager.go:1038] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="gpu.nvidia.com"
E0709 17:55:32.413349 kubelet manager.go:1038] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="dra.cpu"
```

I hit this while running `kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-cpu` (`dra.cpu`) and the NVIDIA GPU driver (`gpu.nvidia.com`) on a 1.36 node; both are logged every 5s, indefinitely. On a two-driver node that is 24 `ERROR` lines per minute forever. The DRAResourceHealth kubelet gRPC API is still `v1alpha1` and driver adoption is a tracked prerequisite (#139475), so essentially every DRA driver today (NVIDIA GPU, `dra-driver-cpu`, `dranet`, ...) returns `Unimplemented` and triggers this.

### What did you expect to happen?

`codes.Unimplemented` is a definitive, permanent signal that the server does not implement this method for the life of the connection; retrying it cannot succeed. Since DRA health is an optional feature, the kubelet should handle it gracefully: log once at low verbosity (e.g. "driver does not implement DRA health monitoring") and stop the per-driver health watch until the plugin re-registers, instead of re-establishing the stream every 5 seconds and logging at `ERROR` each time.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a cluster:
1. A 1.36 node with `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled (beta, default on).
2. Install any DRA driver that does not implement `DRAResourceHealth` (all current drivers, since the API is still `v1alpha1`, #139475).
3. `journalctl -u kubelet` shows the `manager.go` "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" / `Unimplemented` line for that driver every 5 seconds.

I also reproduced the logic in isolation with the same two primitives the kubelet uses (a real gRPC server with no health service, driven by `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait.UntilWithContext(..., period)`). It emits the byte-identical error and re-logs it every period:

```
[V2] Successfully started WatchResources health stream
[ERROR] Error receiving from WatchResources stream: rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth
[V2] Successfully started WatchResources health stream
[ERROR] Error receiving from WatchResources stream: rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth
... (repeats every period)
=== mode=current -> ERROR logs emitted: 5 (in 5s at 1s period) ===
```

Adding a `codes.Unimplemented` check that logs once and stops the loop drives this to `0` repeated errors.

### Root cause

The health watch is retried on a fixed 5s period with no backoff and no handling of `Unimplemented`.

`pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go` (identical on `release-1.36` and `master`):

```go
wait.UntilWithContext(streamCtx, func(ctx context.Context) {
    logger.V(4).Info("Attempting to start WatchResources health stream")
    stream, err := p.NodeWatchResources(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        logger.V(3).Info("Failed to establish WatchResources stream, will retry", "err", err)
        return
    }
    logger.V(2).Info("Successfully started WatchResources health stream")
    err = pm.streamHandler.HandleWatchResourcesStream(ctx, stream, driverName)
    logger.V(2).Info("WatchResources health stream has ended", "error", err)
}, 5*time.Second)
```

`NodeWatchResources` creates the gRPC stream lazily and returns no error, so the code reaches `HandleWatchResourcesStream`, where the first `Recv()` returns `Unimplemented`. `pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go` treats it as an unexpected error:

```go
resp, err := stream.Recv()
if err != nil {
    if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) || errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) { ...; return err }
    if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { ...; return nil }
    // Other errors are unexpected, log & return.
    logger.Error(err, "Error receiving from WatchResources stream")   // Unimplemented lands here
    return err
}
```

`wait.UntilWithContext(..., 5*time.Second)` ignores the returned error and re-runs the whole thing 5s later, so the `Unimplemented` is re-hit and re-logged at `ERROR` forever. At default verbosity only the `ERROR` line is visible (the `V(2)` context lines are not), so an operator sees a bare error loop with no explanation. Neither `release-1.36` nor `master` checks for `codes.Unimplemented` in either file.

### Proposed fix

When the stream fails with `status.Code(err) == codes.Unimplemented`, treat it as a graceful, terminal condition for that driver: log once at `V(2)`/Info that the driver does not implement DRA health monitoring, and stop the per-driver retry loop (cancel `streamCtx` / return without rescheduling) rather than re-running every 5s. The watch restarts naturally when the plugin re-registers. Happy to send a PR.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Feature gate `ResourceHealthStatus`: `1.31` Alpha (default off) -> `1.36` Beta (default on).
- Related: #139475 (promote the DRAResourceHealth API to `v1beta1`); until drivers adopt it, every DRA node is affected.

### Kubernetes version

`v1.36.1` (kubeadm). Confirmed the same code on `release-1.36` and `master`; the running kubelet's `manager.go:1038` matches the `release-1.36` source line exactly.

### Cloud provider

None (bare-metal kubeadm).

### OS version

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17; containerd 2.2.1.

title: kube-scheduler event recording can cause unbounded goroutine and memory growth
body:
### What happened?

In a large cluster under a burst of pending Pods and scheduling failures, kube-scheduler memory, CPU, and goroutine count kept increasing. Monitoring showed scheduler memory continuously rising and peaking at about 30 GiB. The goroutine count also kept growing and peaked at about 3 million. The scheduler eventually appeared unhealthy: scheduling throughput dropped to zero for a period, and monitoring data had gaps during the incident window.

The most suspicious retained memory was not from scheduler preemption itself, but from the Kubernetes event recording path in client-go:

```
k8s.io/client-go/tools/events.(*eventBroadcasterImpl).recordToSink
k8s.io/client-go/tools/events.(*eventBroadcasterImpl).attemptRecording
```

### pprof analysis

I will share detailed redacted pprof output later. The current pprof summary is below.

A goroutine profile captured from the scheduler showed about 65,977 goroutines in that sample. About 62,465 goroutines were blocked around client-go/tools/events.(*eventBroadcasterImpl).recordToSink while contending on the event cache mutex. Thousands of goroutines were also waiting in client-side rate limiting or writing requests to the apiserver:

```
~62,465 goroutines: eventBroadcasterImpl.recordToSink / event cache path
~3,293 goroutines: golang.org/x/time/rate.(*Limiter).Wait
~6,587 goroutines: net/http2 writeRequest
```

The corresponding heap profile showed about 7.08 GiB in-use heap in that sample. This is much lower than the ~30 GiB memory usage observed from monitoring, and I do not yet know why there is such a large gap between the monitored process/container memory and the Go pprof inuse_space value. The largest retained objects visible in the heap profile were from the event recording path and goroutine stacks:

```
events.k8s.io/v1.(*Event).DeepCopy                ~2,198 MiB, ~31%
runtime.malg                                      ~1,431 MiB, ~20%
fmt.Sprintf                                       ~1,015 MiB, ~14%
recordToSink.func1.1 + newEvents + makeEvent       ~650 MiB,  ~9%
```

Roughly 5.4 GiB (~76%) of the sampled in-use heap appeared to be directly related to the event broadcaster goroutine buildup.

During the same window, scheduler logs showed client-side throttling while writing events:

```
client-side throttling: 109 occurrences
POST event requests:    66
PATCH event requests:   43
main paths:
  /apis/events.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/<workload-namespace>/events
  /apis/events.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/kube-system/events

observed delay:
  avg: 134.539s
  p50: 140.211s
  p95: 280.442s
  max: 304.833s
```

The scheduler was also doing expensive scheduling and preemption work. A CPU profile showed high CPU in these paths:

```
workqueue.ParallelizeUntil                         ~52%
preemption.(*Evaluator).DryRunPreemption           ~39.5%
framework.(*NodeInfo).SnapshotConcrete             ~28%
runtime.gcBgMarkWorker / gcDrain                   ~39%
```

Those paths likely created heavy transient allocation and GC pressure, but the dominant retained heap and goroutine growth in the sampled pprof came from the event broadcaster path.

The relevant upstream code shape appears to be:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/events/event_recorder.go
func (recorder *recorderImpl) eventf(...) {
    event := recorder.makeEvent(...)
    go func() {
        defer utilruntime.HandleCrash()
        recorder.Action(watch.Added, event)
    }()
}

// staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/events/event_broadcaster.go
func (e *eventBroadcasterImpl) recordToSink(ctx context.Context, event *eventsv1.Event, clock clock.Clock) {
    eventCopy := event.DeepCopy()
    go func() {
        evToRecord := func() *eventsv1.Event {
            e.mu.Lock()
            defer e.mu.Unlock()
            eventKey := getKey(eventCopy)
            isomorphicEvent, isIsomorphic := e.eventCache[eventKey]
            if isIsomorphic {
                if isomorphicEvent.Series != nil {
                    isomorphicEvent.Series.Count++
                    isomorphicEvent.Series.LastObservedTime = metav1.MicroTime{Time: clock.Now()}
                    return nil
                }
                isomorphicEvent.Series = &eventsv1.EventSeries{Count: 2, LastObservedTime: metav1.MicroTime{Time: clock.Now()}}
                return isomorphicEvent.DeepCopy()
            }
            e.eventCache[eventKey] = eventCopy
            return eventCopy.DeepCopy()
        }()
        if evToRecord != nil {
            e.attemptRecording(ctx, evToRecord)
        }
    }()
}
```

When FailedScheduling or related events are generated much faster than the event sink can create/patch events, this design seems able to accumulate one goroutine per event. If writes are slow or client-side throttled, those goroutines can live for a long time in attemptRecording, while Event.DeepCopy objects and goroutine stacks retain a large amount of memory.

### What did you expect to happen?

Event recording should not be able to create unbounded goroutine and heap growth inside kube-scheduler when the apiserver event sink is slow or client-side throttled.

Expected behavior would be one of the following, or something equivalent:

```
- bounded concurrency for event sink writes
- bounded queue length with explicit drop/coalescing behavior
- stronger aggregation before spawning long-lived goroutines
- separate backpressure protection so event recording cannot make scheduler memory unbounded
```

Scheduling failures may produce many events, but event delivery should degrade in a bounded way instead of risking scheduler instability.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We do not yet have a small deterministic reproducer. The issue has been observed in multiple Kubernetes versions, including vendor builds based on upstream v1.28.15 and v1.34.1.

The clusters where this happened were not extremely large. A representative cluster size was roughly:

text
Nodes:        ~100
Pods:         ~5,000 total
Pending Pods: ~3,000

When the issue happened, the common signals were:

```
- kube-scheduler Patch Pods QPS was relatively high, roughly around 100
- scheduler backoff queue had significant backlog, usually >1,000
- scheduler unschedulable QPS was high, roughly around 100
- pending Pods and scheduling failures stayed elevated for a sustained period
```

I tried to reproduce this locally with stress tests, but have not yet reproduced the continuous goroutine and memory growth.

One stress setup used for exploration was:

```
Kubernetes: vendor build based on upstream v1.34.x
Nodes:      500
Pods:       20k total
Pending:    10k pending Pods
Priority:   10k high-priority Pods and 10k low-priority Pods
Scheduler:  client qps/burst around 60/110
Scenario:   periodically scale workloads up/down to create frequent Pod create/delete activity and scheduling failures/preemption attempts
Result:     scheduler periodically updated events, but goroutine and memory did not keep growing continuously
```

The suspected trigger is a sustained high rate of FailedScheduling or similar scheduler events while event create/patch requests are throttled or slow. Artificially lowering scheduler client QPS/burst, slowing event writes, keeping a large scheduler backoff queue, or creating many distinct unschedulable Pods may make the issue easier to reproduce.

title: TestSubmitPodGroupAlgorithmResult/One_unschedulable` flakes on Windows due to non-deterministic pod ordering in PodGroup scheduling
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master

### Which tests are flaking?

- `TestSubmitPodGroupAlgorithmResult/One_unschedulable`
- `TestSubmitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` (parent)


### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `8eb66b73ef2` ("Add support for PodGroups in scheduling queue", 2026-04-24), which introduced `PodGroupMemberPodsOrderingFunc` without a deterministic tie-breaker for pods with equal priority, attempts, and timestamp. The test itself was introduced in `6233b259071` ("Introduce Workload Scheduling Cycle", 2026-01-28).


### Testgrid link

_No response_

### Reason for failure (if possible)

`PodGroupMemberPodsOrderingFunc` in `pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go` orders pods within a PodGroup by priority, then by attempts, then by timestamp. When all three are equal (as is the case in the test where p1, p2, p3 are created with identical priority and timestamps), the function returns 0, leaving the order non-deterministic — it depends on Go map iteration order, which is randomized and differs across platforms (notably on Windows).

The test `TestSubmitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` builds `podResults` as a positional slice `[result_for_p1, result_for_p2, result_for_p3]` and then iterates over `podGroupInfo.QueuedPodInfos` using the index `i` to assign each result to a pod. When the queue returns pods in a different order (e.g., `[p2, p1, p3]` instead of `[p1, p2, p3]`), the "unschedulable" result (intended for p2) gets assigned to p1, causing:

```
Expected bound pods: map[p1:{} p3:{}], but got: map[p2:{} p3:{}]
Expected failed pods: map[p2:{}], but got: map[p1:{}]
```

title: Non-deterministic victim ordering in pod group preemption causes flaky `TestPodGroupEvaluator_SelectVictimsOnDomain`
body:
### Which jobs are flaking?

`pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master`

### Which tests are flaking?

`[sig-scheduling] k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/framework: preemption` — `TestPodGroupEvaluator_SelectVictimsOnDomain/Efficiency:_Preempt_minimum_number_of_victims`

### Since when has it been flaking?

Since commit `00f22436be9` ("Reimplement WAP with in place filter reprieval", 2026-06-23), which rewrote `selectVictimsOnDomain` and its tests.

### Testgrid link

_No response_

### Reason for failure (if possible)

`moreImportantVictim` sorts victims by `EarliestStartTime` as a tie-breaker when priority and workload type are equal. When pods lack `Status.StartTime`, `GetPodStartTime` falls back to `time.Now()`, which is called separately for each victim during domain construction. This produces non-deterministic ordering that depends on clock resolution and OS scheduling. On Windows (lower timer resolution), the sort order differs from Linux, causing the reprieve loop to preempt different victims than expected.

The test "Efficiency: Preempt minimum number of victims" creates 4 pods (p1–p4) without `StartTime` and expects `{p3, p4}` as victims. Depending on the non-deterministic sort order, the reprieve loop may instead preempt `{p1, p4}` or other combinations.

title: DRA: define an upper bound or overflow-safety contract for device request count
body:
## Summary

For `DeviceAllocationModeExactCount`, the device request `Count` is an `int64` and is currently validated only for its lower bound.

Both `ExactDeviceRequest.Count` and `DeviceSubRequest.Count` flow through `validateDeviceAllocationMode`:

```go
case resource.DeviceAllocationModeExactCount:
    if count <= 0 {
        allErrs = append(allErrs,
            field.Invalid(countFldPath, count, "must be greater than zero"))
    }
```

There is no upper bound, so the API accepts the entire positive `int64` range, including:

```text
9223372036854775807
```

I verified this behavior against Kubernetes v1.36.1.

This issue is not asserting that every positive `int64` value is invalid, nor that Kubernetes itself must necessarily impose a small device-count limit. The question is whether the API should define a practical upper bound, or at least explicitly document an overflow-safety contract for consumers.

## Motivation

Several independent DRA consumers have treated `Count` as an ordinary device quantity and aggregated or multiplied it using unchecked `int64` arithmetic.

Because one request may contain `math.MaxInt64`, even two requests are sufficient to wrap a running sum negative.

I audited three independent scheduler and quota-accounting codebases, and each had independently written unchecked `int64` aggregation of `Count`. To be clear, the reports and fixes below are all mine, so this is one audit across three projects rather than three separate discoveries. The point is that three separately maintained codebases each missed the same thing:

| Project                     | Observed path                                                            | Current status                                     |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| kubernetes-sigs/kueue       | Per-DeviceClass DRA quota count; two `MaxInt64` requests wrapped to `-2` | #12896, fixed through #12897 and related hardening |
| volcano-sh/volcano          | Device count addition, gang-size multiplication, and quota comparison    | #5621; release-1.15 backport #5626 merged          |
| kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler | GPU count accumulation into queue and parent fair-share accounting       | reported in #1873; fix #1874 under discussion      |

In the reproduced Kueue and KAI cases, the oversized requests did not result in real device allocation or resource theft. The requests were impossible to satisfy, and no cross-tenant resource escalation was demonstrated.

On the KAI fix specifically, a maintainer has reasonably questioned whether it is worth the added complexity given the trigger is currently unreachable. That is a fair question, and it is exactly the kind of call that becomes easier to make once the API states its intended contract, which is what this issue asks for.

The observed impact is therefore accounting integrity and robustness:

* negative quota or fair-share values;
* an impossible workload being admitted by an out-of-tree quota layer;
* corrupted queue accounting while the workload remains pending;
* additional defensive fixes being needed independently in multiple consumers.

This is a low-severity correctness and API-contract issue, not a security report.

## Why unschedulability does not fully contain the problem

A request for `math.MaxInt64` devices cannot be satisfied by a real cluster.

However, the affected out-of-tree implementations process and aggregate the request while it is still pending, before successful device allocation or node binding. Therefore, the fact that no node can satisfy the request does not prevent the request from corrupting quota or fair-share bookkeeping.

No equivalent overflow in an in-tree scheduler or allocator path has been demonstrated here. The confirmed impact so far is in out-of-tree consumers.

## Current API contract

DRA already places explicit limits on several collection sizes, such as the number of devices in an individual `ResourceSlice`, counter sets, counters, selectors, and subrequests.

Those limits are not directly equivalent to a semantic limit on the total number of devices requested, and other DRA scalar `int64` fields are also not necessarily upper-bounded.

Therefore, the absence of an upper bound on `Count` is not by itself proof of a validation bug.

Notably, the in-tree structured allocator explicitly guards this exact-count path and comments on it directly (`dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`):

```go
case resourceapi.DeviceAllocationModeExactCount:
    numDevices := request.count()
    if numDevices > math.MaxInt {
        // Allowed by API validation, but doesn't make sense.
        return requestData, fmt.Errorf("... exact count %d is too large", ...)
    }
```

That check is a cast-safety guard before `int(numDevices)`; on a 64-bit platform `math.MaxInt == math.MaxInt64`, so it is a no-op for the values here. What actually protects the in-tree allocator is that it draws from a bounded pool of real devices, so an impossible count simply fails to allocate. Out-of-tree quota and fair-share accounting has no such natural bound and sums the counts directly, which is why the same input wraps their books negative. The concern is recognized in-tree (the comment says as much), but only implicitly, and the consumers that most need the contract are precisely the ones without the pool's protection.

The recurring downstream failures instead suggest that the intended arithmetic contract is currently too easy for consumers to miss:

* Is the full positive `int64` range intentionally valid?
* Must all consumers use checked or saturating addition and multiplication?
* Or should obviously impossible counts be rejected at the API boundary?

## Possible approaches

### A. Document the full-range contract and audit consumers

Keep the field unbounded, but update the API godoc and DRA documentation to state explicitly that:

* `Count` may contain any positive `int64` value;
* consumers must treat it as untrusted input;
* additions and multiplications must use checked or saturating arithmetic;
* unschedulability must not be relied upon to protect accounting code.

This is compatible and makes the intended responsibility clear.

It may also be useful to audit in-tree consumers for unchecked aggregation, even though no in-tree overflow has been demonstrated in this report.

### B. Add a practical API upper bound

Define and validate a maximum device count, similar in form to other DRA validation constants.

This would reject obviously impossible requests at the source and reduce the range that every consumer must handle.

However:

* the maximum requires a defensible semantic justification;
* this changes validation for an existing API field;
* compatibility treatment for already stored objects requires SIG API Machinery review;
* the relevant native-type declarative-validation work is KEP-5073, not CRD validation ratcheting under KEP-4008;
* a per-request upper bound does not eliminate the need for checked arithmetic when counts are multiplied or aggregated across claims and pods.

### C. Do both

Document that consumers must always use overflow-safe arithmetic, while separately considering a practical API bound as defense in depth.

This avoids treating validation as a replacement for safe consumer arithmetic.

## What I'm asking

To keep this concrete and small: would SIG Node accept a short godoc note on `Count` (and `DeviceSubRequest.Count`) stating that it is unbounded up to `MaxInt64`, that consumers must aggregate and multiply it with overflow-safe arithmetic, and that unschedulability must not be relied on to protect accounting code? I am happy to open that PR.

A hard API upper bound (approach B) is a larger, separate question: it changes validation on a GA field and would need a KEP plus SIG API Machinery review, so I am not proposing it here. Whether in-tree consumers should also be audited is likewise secondary and can be split out.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind feature

title: DRA structured allocator double-counts a shared counter for a persisted allow-multiple device recorded only by share ID
body:
### What happened?

When a device both allows multiple allocations (`DRAConsumableCapacity`) and consumes shared counters (`DRAPartitionableDevices`), a persisted shared allocation can cause the device's counters to be accounted for twice during a later scheduling cycle.

This occurs when the earlier allocation result contains a `ShareID` but no `ConsumedCapacity`. In that state, the device is represented in `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, but it has no entry in `AggregatedCapacity`.

When a later claim attempts to share the same device, the structured allocator rejects it with:

```text
Insufficient counters device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
Device not usable device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
```

The persisted allocation has already caused the device's counters to be subtracted from the pool. The new allocation attempt nevertheless charges the same counters again, causing a false counter exhaustion.

### Root cause

`allocateDevice` skips the counter availability check for an allow-multiple device only when `deviceCapacityInUse` returns true:

```go
skipCounterCheck := allowMultipleAllocations && alloc.deviceCapacityInUse(device.id)
```

`deviceCapacityInUse` only checks persisted aggregated capacity and capacity reserved during the current allocation search:

```go
func (alloc *allocator) deviceCapacityInUse(deviceID DeviceID) bool {
    _, found := alloc.allocatedState.AggregatedCapacity[deviceID]
    return found || alloc.allocatingCapacityForAnyClaim(deviceID)
}
```

A persisted shared allocation without consumed capacity has:

```text
AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs: contains device1/share-A
AggregatedCapacity:       no entry for device1
```

Counter availability is initialized through `IsDeviceAllocated`, which does recognize `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`. Therefore, the persisted allocation already causes device1's counters to be subtracted from the available pool.

However, `deviceCapacityInUse` does not recognize `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`. Consequently:

```text
persisted share ID
    ↓
IsDeviceAllocated(device1) == true
    ↓
device1's counters are subtracted from availableCounters
    ↓
deviceCapacityInUse(device1) == false
    ↓
skipCounterCheck == false
    ↓
checkAvailableCounters charges device1's counters again
    ↓
false "Insufficient counters"
```

This appears to be a remaining edge case after #134103. That change added the counter-check skip when some device capacity is already in use, but a shared allocation without a persisted `AggregatedCapacity` entry is not covered by that predicate.

### What did you expect to happen?

The existing allocation already represents device1 as a shared, allow-multiple device, and its shared counters have already been accounted for.

Because the device permits multiple allocations and the new allocation consumes no per-share capacity, a second claim should be able to share device1 without charging its physical shared counters again.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The following case can be added to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

```go
"partitionable-consumable-capacity-shared-device-counter-not-recharged": {
    features: Features{
        PartitionableDevices: true,
        ConsumableCapacity:   true,
    },
    // device1 already has a persisted shared allocation. It is represented
    // only by a share ID, with no AggregatedCapacity entry.
    allocatedSharedDeviceIDs: sets.New(
        internal.MakeSharedDeviceID(
            MakeDeviceID(driverA, pool1, device1),
            &fixedShareID,
        ),
    ),
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claimWithRequests(claim0, nil, request(req0, classA, 1)),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        sliceWithDevices(
            slice1,
            node1,
            resourcePool(pool1, 2),
            driverA,
            device(device1, nil, nil).
                withAllowMultipleAllocations().
                withDeviceCounterConsumption(
                    deviceCounterConsumption(
                        counterSet1,
                        map[string]resource.Quantity{
                            "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                        },
                    ),
                ),
        ),
        sliceWithCounterSets(
            slice2,
            node1,
            resourcePool(pool1, 2),
            driverA,
            counterSet(
                counterSet1,
                map[string]resource.Quantity{
                    "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                },
            ),
        ),
    ),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{
        allocationResult(
            localNodeSelector(node1),
            deviceRequestAllocationResult(
                req0,
                driverA,
                pool1,
                device1,
            ).withConsumedCapacity(&fixedShareID, nil),
        ),
    },
},
```

The shared test harness replaces generated share IDs with `fixedShareID` before comparing results. The expected `fixedShareID` above therefore does not imply that the new allocation reuses the persisted allocation's actual share ID.

On commit `16e45f3b5e6a76a1ac741550e3a65980eea783c2`, this case fails with no allocation result and logs:

```text
Insufficient counters device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
Device not usable device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
```

It passes when the counter-check skip also recognizes that device1 already has a persisted shared allocation.

The failure is reproduced in the incubating allocator, which is selected for this feature combination, and in the experimental allocator, which carries the same predicate. The stable allocator does not support `ConsumableCapacity` and is not affected.

### Anything else we need to know?

The skip predicate needs to recognize a persisted shared allocation represented by `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, even when the device has no entry in `AggregatedCapacity`.

A narrow fix could add a lookup for the underlying `DeviceID` in the persisted shared-device state while retaining the existing `deviceCapacityInUse` behavior for allocations with consumed capacity and allocations created during the current search.

Because this check runs in the allocator's per-candidate search path, it may be preferable to precompute a `Set[DeviceID]` from `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` when constructing the allocator rather than scanning every shared ID for each candidate.

Regression coverage should retain the existing #134103 cases and add this persisted, capacity-less shared-allocation case.

This is separate from #140431:

* #140431 addresses reserved state that is not rolled back within one allocation search.
* This issue concerns persisted shared state reconstructed between scheduling cycles.

title: DRA structured allocator counter caches are keyed by pool name and collide across drivers
body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator scopes resource pools by both driver and pool name, but its shared-counter caches are keyed by the pool name alone.

When two different drivers publish pools with the same name on the same node, and devices in both pools consume counters, their counter accounting collides. Allocating a device from the first driver's pool can cause an otherwise available device from the second driver's independent pool to be rejected with `Insufficient counters`.

For example:

```text
driver-a / pool-1
driver-b / pool-1
```

are distinct resource pools, but both currently use the same cache key, `pool-1`.

#### Root cause

`checkAvailableCounters` drops the driver from the pool identity:

```go
pool := device.pool
poolName := pool.PoolID.Pool

availableCountersForPool, found := alloc.availableCounters[poolName]
...
consumedCountersForPool, found := alloc.consumedCounters[poolName]
```

The associated maps are also keyed only by the pool name:

```go
availableCounters map[draapi.UniqueString]counterSets
consumedCounters  map[draapi.UniqueString]counterSets
```

Elsewhere, resource pools are correctly identified and grouped with:

```go
PoolID{Driver, Pool}
```

Therefore, `driver-a/pool-1` and `driver-b/pool-1` share the same entries in both counter maps.

The first pool that initializes `availableCounters[poolName]` determines the cached counter definitions. During allocation, `consumedCounters[poolName]` then aggregates in-flight consumption from devices belonging to both drivers.

In the minimal reproduction below, both pools have an independent `counter-set-1/c: 1`. After `driver-a/pool-1/device-1` consumes its own counter, the allocator incorrectly treats that consumption as belonging to `driver-b/pool-1` too and rejects `device-2`.

With different counter definitions or limits, the same key collision may also cause a device to be evaluated against another driver's counter set.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pools belonging to different drivers must have independent shared-counter accounting, even when their pool names are identical.

Both of these devices should allocate:

```text
driver-a/pool-1/device-1
driver-b/pool-1/device-2
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add the following case to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

<details>
<summary>Regression test</summary>

```go
"partitionable-devices-counter-sets-scoped-per-driver": {
    features: Features{
        PartitionableDevices: true,
    },
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claimWithRequests(claim0, nil, request(req0, classA, 1)),
        claimWithRequests(claim1, nil, request(req1, classB, 1)),
    ),
    classes: objects(
        class(classA, driverA),
        class(classB, driverB),
    ),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        // driverA / pool-1 has its own counterSet1 (c:1) and device1.
        sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverA,
            device(device1, nil, nil).withDeviceCounterConsumption(
                deviceCounterConsumption(
                    counterSet1,
                    map[string]resource.Quantity{
                        "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                    },
                ),
            ),
        ),
        sliceWithCounterSets(slice2, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverA,
            counterSet(
                counterSet1,
                map[string]resource.Quantity{
                    "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                },
            ),
        ),

        // driverB / pool-1 has the same pool and counter-set names, but is an
        // independent pool because it belongs to a different driver.
        sliceWithDevices(slice3, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverB,
            device(device2, nil, nil).withDeviceCounterConsumption(
                deviceCounterConsumption(
                    counterSet1,
                    map[string]resource.Quantity{
                        "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                    },
                ),
            ),
        ),
        sliceWithCounterSets(slice4, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 2), driverB,
            counterSet(
                counterSet1,
                map[string]resource.Quantity{
                    "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                },
            ),
        ),
    ),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{
        allocationResult(
            localNodeSelector(node1),
            deviceAllocationResult(
                req0,
                driverA,
                pool1,
                device1,
                false,
            ),
        ),
        allocationResult(
            localNodeSelector(node1),
            deviceAllocationResult(
                req1,
                driverB,
                pool1,
                device2,
                false,
            ),
        ),
    },
},
```

</details>

From `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation`, run:

```console
go test ./structured/... \
  -run 'TestAllocator/partitionable-devices-counter-sets-scoped-per-driver' \
  -count=1 \
  -v
```

On current master, the allocation fails. At verbosity level 7, the allocator logs show that the second driver's device is rejected after the first driver's independent device is allocated:

```text
Device allocated device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
Insufficient counters device="driver-b/pool-1/device-2"
Device not usable device="driver-b/pool-1/device-2"
```

The test passes after changing the counter-cache keys and their lookups from the pool name to the complete `PoolID`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The proposed fix is to key both maps by `PoolID`:

```go
availableCounters map[PoolID]counterSets
consumedCounters  map[PoolID]counterSets
```

and use:

```go
poolID := pool.PoolID
```

for all lookup, insertion, and counter-deallocation paths.

This matches the identity already used when the allocator gathers and groups resource pools.

The same pool-name-only counter-cache shape is present in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants, so all three variants should be updated together and covered by the shared allocator test.

This bug is independent of the reserved-state rollback addressed by #140431.

The reproduction is allocator-only and does not require a running cluster, DRA driver, container runtime, or cloud provider.

title: DRA structured allocator leaks reserved counters and constraints when it rejects or backtracks a candidate device
body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator can leave reserved state behind when it stops considering a candidate device, which can make a schedulable pod fail to schedule.

`allocateDevice` reserves a device's shared counters and adds claim constraints before it may reject the candidate on a device taint or a claim constraint. For a candidate it accepts, it also reserves consumable capacity, and the backtracking search later has to undo all of that. Some of these paths did not reverse what they had done:

- A candidate rejected on a device taint or a claim constraint kept its reserved shared counters.
- The success undo for an allow-multiple device released its capacity but not the counters it had reserved on its first allocation, so backtracking leaked them.

A leaked counter reservation makes the allocator treat a counter set as exhausted, so it fails to allocate a device combination a node can satisfy, and a schedulable pod stays pending.

The consumable-capacity rejection path does not leak capacity, because the capacity check runs before the reservation. What it can leave behind is the claim constraint added just before the check.

### What did you expect to happen?

When the allocator rejects or backtracks a candidate, every reservation it made for that candidate (shared counters, claim constraints, device marking, consumable capacity) should be released, so a later candidate combination is evaluated against the correct available state.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Four cases in the shared `allocatortesting` table reproduce it. Each asserts the exact allocated devices:

- `partitionable-devices-taint-releases-counter`
- `partitionable-devices-constraint-releases-counter`
- `partitionable-consumable-capacity-backtrack-releases-counter`
- `consumable-capacity-rejection-rolls-back-constraints`

These cases are added by the fix PR, so to reproduce, apply only the `allocator_testing.go` test additions from #140431 onto the reported master commit, then run:

```console
cd staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation

go test \
  ./structured/internal/stable \
  ./structured/internal/incubating \
  ./structured/internal/experimental \
  -run 'TestAllocator/(partitionable-devices-taint-releases-counter|partitionable-devices-constraint-releases-counter|partitionable-consumable-capacity-backtrack-releases-counter|consumable-capacity-rejection-rolls-back-constraints)$' \
  -count=1
```

With only the regression-test changes applied, these cases fail on the reported master commit. They pass with the implementation changes from #140431.

The default feature configuration selects the incubating allocator (ConsumableCapacity and the device binding and status gates are on by default, and stable does not support them), so this is reachable on default clusters. The stable and experimental variants carry the same shape.

### Anything else we need to know?

Proposed fix: #140431.

That PR records what each `allocateDevice` call mutated in a `deviceRollbackState` value and reverses it with one `rollbackDevice` method, called on every rejection path after a counter reservation (including the `must` error path) and returned as the success undo, so the rejection cleanup and the backtracking undo can no longer drift apart. All three allocator variants are fixed together.

Two further cases in the same test table cover the fix rather than reproduce the master bug, so they pass on the reported master commit:

- `partitionable-empty-capacity-multiple-share-backtrack-keeps-counter-ownership`: for an allow-multiple device with no consumable capacity, its capacity-map entry doubles as the marker that lets a later share skip the counter check. The rollback must not delete it while another share is still active; doing so recharges the device's counter for a later share and rejects that share wrongly. This guards the new rollback against over-removing the marker.
- `partitionable-all-mode-constraint-must-error-with-reserved-counter`: exercises the `must` error path with a reserved counter. That error aborts the allocation, so the case locks the error contract and runs the rollback branch rather than reproducing a leak.

title: DRA: distinctAttribute constraint can allocate duplicate attribute values when a single request allocates multiple devices
body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator can return a device set that violates a `distinctAttribute` constraint when a single request allocates more than one device.

`distinctAttributeConstraint` tracks the attribute values it has already seen in a map keyed by the request name:

```go
attributes map[string]resourceapi.DeviceAttribute
```

When a request allocates several devices, every device of that request is added under the same request-name key, so each device overwrites the previous one:

```go
// add(), first device of the request
m.attributes[requestName] = *attribute
...
// add(), later devices of the same request
if !m.matchesAttribute(*attribute) {
    return false
}
m.attributes[requestName] = *attribute // overwrites the earlier device's value
```

`matchesAttribute` then only compares a new device against the surviving (most recent) value, not against all devices already chosen for the request. A device can therefore duplicate the value of an earlier device of the same request and still be accepted.

#### Example

One request asks for three devices with `distinctAttribute` on `numa`, and the pool offers `numa` values `1, 2, 1, 3`:

```text
device-1 numa=1
device-2 numa=2
device-3 numa=1
device-4 numa=3
```

The allocator accepts `device-1`, `device-2`, then `device-3`:

- add `device-1` → `attributes[req0] = 1`
- add `device-2` → `2 != 1`, accepted, `attributes[req0] = 2`
- add `device-3` → only `2` remains in the map, so `1 != 2`, accepted, `attributes[req0] = 1`

The result is `device-1`, `device-2`, `device-3`, in which `device-1` and `device-3` both have `numa=1`. This breaks the constraint, which requires the value to be unique across the request's devices.

#### Relationship to #140300

#140300 fixes a different constraint (`matchAttribute` list-intersection restore on backtrack) and notes that `distinctAttributeConstraint` is unaffected because its `remove` correctly deletes the request's map entry on backtrack. That is accurate for the backtracking path and for a request that contributes a single device. The case here is separate: it is `add` overwriting an earlier device of the same multi-device request, so the map never holds more than one of the request's values at a time. `remove` is not involved.

### What did you expect to happen?

When one request allocates multiple devices under a `distinctAttribute` constraint, all of those devices must have distinct values for the attribute.

For the example above, the correct allocation skips `device-3` (a duplicate of `device-1`) and takes `device-4`:

```text
device-1 numa=1
device-2 numa=2
device-4 numa=3
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add the following case to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

<details>
<summary>Regression test</summary>

```go
"distinct-constraint-single-request-multiple-devices": {
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claimWithRequests(claim0,
            []resourceapi.DeviceConstraint{{DistinctAttribute: &intAttribute}},
            request(req0, classA, 3),
        ),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
            device(device1, nil, map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resourceapi.DeviceAttribute{
                "numa": {IntValue: ptr.To(int64(1))},
            }),
            device(device2, nil, map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resourceapi.DeviceAttribute{
                "numa": {IntValue: ptr.To(int64(2))},
            }),
            device(device3, nil, map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resourceapi.DeviceAttribute{
                "numa": {IntValue: ptr.To(int64(1))},
            }),
            device(device4, nil, map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resourceapi.DeviceAttribute{
                "numa": {IntValue: ptr.To(int64(3))},
            }),
        ),
    ),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    // device1 (1) and device2 (2) are distinct; device3 (1) duplicates
    // device1 and must be skipped; device4 (3) completes the distinct set.
    expectResults: []any{allocationResult(
        localNodeSelector(node1),
        deviceAllocationResult(req0, driverA, pool1, device1, false),
        deviceAllocationResult(req0, driverA, pool1, device2, false),
        deviceAllocationResult(req0, driverA, pool1, device4, false),
    )},
},
```

</details>

From `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation`, run:

```console
go test ./structured/... \
  -run 'TestAllocator/distinct-constraint-single-request-multiple-devices' \
  -count=1 \
  -v
```

On current master the case fails on all variants. At verbosity level 7 the allocator logs show `device-3` being accepted even though it duplicates `device-1`:

```text
distinctAttributeConstraint: Constraint satisfied by device device="driver-a/pool-1/device-3" numDevices=3
Device allocated device="driver-a/pool-1/device-3"
```

The allocated set is `device-1`, `device-2`, `device-3` instead of the expected `device-1`, `device-2`, `device-4`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Keying the seen-values map by the request name records only one value per request, which is enough when each request contributes one device but not when a request allocates several devices. Re-keying by `DeviceID` alone is not sufficient either, because an allow-multiple device can be allocated more than once. A fix likely needs to record each successful `add` separately (for example a per-request list or a stack) so that all of a request's chosen values are compared, and so `remove` undoes exactly the value added by the candidate being backtracked.

The same shape is present in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants, so all three would need the change and coverage in the shared allocator test.

The type's doc comment (`All devices must share the same value ... We don't need to track *which* devices are part of the set, only how many`) describes match semantics rather than distinct semantics and looks copied from `matchAttributeConstraint`.

This is independent of the reserved-state rollback in #140431. The reproduction is allocator-only and does not require a running cluster, DRA driver, container runtime, or cloud provider.

No feature gate is required for the scalar `distinctAttribute` constraint; it is part of the GA `resource.k8s.io/v1` API. The default feature configuration selects the incubating allocator variant, which has this behavior.

title: DRA: consumable-capacity roundUpRange overflows int64 for a large capacity request, allocating a device it cannot satisfy
body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator's consumable-capacity rounding overflows int64 for a large capacity request, so a device is allocated for a request it cannot satisfy and its consumed capacity is recorded as a negative value.

`roundUpRange` (in `structured/internal/{incubating,experimental}/consumable_capacity.go`) rounds a request up to the next `Min + n*Step` using int64 arithmetic:

```go
requestedInt64 := requestedVal.Value()
step := validRange.Step.Value()
min := validRange.Min.Value()
added := (requestedInt64 - min)
n := added / step
mod := added % step
if mod != 0 {
    n += 1
}
val := min + step*n
return *resource.NewQuantity(val, resource.BinarySI)
```

For a request near `math.MaxInt64` with a `ValidRange` that has a `Step`, `min + step*n` exceeds `math.MaxInt64` and wraps to a negative value. That negative consumed capacity then passes both the policy check (`violateValidRange`: a negative value is below `Max`) and the over-capacity check (`clone[name].Cmp(cap.Value)`: a negative value is below the device capacity), so the device is accepted.

#### Impact

- A request far larger than the device's capacity is accepted instead of rejected.
- The device's consumed capacity for that allocation is recorded as a large negative quantity, which corrupts the running total for that shared allow-multiple device, so later requests can over-consume it.

#### Reachability

The request capacity is not bounded by validation. `validateExactDeviceRequest` (`pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`) validates the device class, selectors, allocation mode, count, and tolerations, but not the `Capacity` field, so a claim may carry any positive int64 in `request.capacity.requests[name]`. The device-side policy is validated (`Min + Step <= capacity`), but that does not bound the request. The default feature configuration selects the incubating allocator, which has this behavior.

### What did you expect to happen?

A capacity request far larger than the device capacity should be rejected, and consumed capacity should never be negative.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

<details>
<summary>Regression test</summary>

```go
"consumable-capacity-range-policy-step-request-overflow": {
    features: Features{
        ConsumableCapacity: true,
    },
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(deviceRequest(req0, classA, 1).withCapacityRequest(resource.NewQuantity(9223372036854775807, resource.BinarySI))),
    ),
    classes: objects(classWithAllowMultipleAllocations(classA, driverA, true)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
            device(device1, nil, nil).withAllowMultipleAllocations().withCapacityRequestPolicyRange(map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resource.Quantity{capacity0: four}),
        ),
    ),
    node:          node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{},
},
```

</details>

From `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation`, run:

```console
go test ./structured/... \
  -run 'TestAllocator/consumable-capacity-range-policy-step-request-overflow' \
  -count=1 -v
```

The device has capacity 4 with a `Min=2, Step=2, Max=4` policy, and the claim requests `math.MaxInt64`. Expected: no allocation. On current master, `device-1` is allocated (the logs show `Device allocated` and a negative `consumed capacity`), because `roundUpRange` overflowed to a negative value. The case fails on the incubating and experimental variants; stable does not support ConsumableCapacity.

### Anything else we need to know?

`roundUpRange` and `violateValidRange` both convert `resource.Quantity` to int64 via `.Value()` and do plain int64 arithmetic. #140161 reworks `CapacityRequestPolicyRange` for fractional quantities but does not touch this overflow. A fix could compute the rounding with `resource.Quantity` arithmetic (or saturate at `math.MaxInt64`), and validation could additionally bound the request against the device capacity.

The reproduction is allocator-only and does not require a running cluster, DRA driver, container runtime, or cloud provider.

Feature gate:

```text
DRAConsumableCapacity=true
```

`DRAConsumableCapacity` is beta and enabled by default starting with Kubernetes 1.36.

title: DRA: CapacityRequestPolicy validValues rejects distinct fractional values as duplicates
body:
### What happened?

A `CapacityRequestPolicy` with distinct fractional `validValues` is rejected by API validation as if the values were duplicates.

`validateRequestPolicyValidValues` deduplicates the values with `validateSet` using `quantityKey`:

```go
func quantityKey(item apiresource.Quantity) string {
	return strconv.FormatInt(item.Value(), 10)
}
```

`Quantity.Value()` rounds up to the nearest integer away from zero, so any two sub-integer quantities collapse to the same key. For example `100m` and `200m` both have `Value() == 1`, so a policy that lists both is reported as a duplicate on the second value.

The rounding at allocation time is not affected: `roundUpValidValues` compares with `Cmp`, which distinguishes `100m` from `200m`. The problem is only in the validation-layer dedup key, so a policy that the allocator would handle correctly cannot be created.

### What did you expect to happen?

A discrete policy that lists distinct fractional values, for example `validValues: [100m, 200m]` with `default: 100m` on a device with capacity `1`, should be accepted.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this test to `pkg/apis/resource/validation`:

<details>
<summary>Repro test</summary>

```go
func TestFractionalValidValuesFalseDuplicate(t *testing.T) {
	pol := &resource.CapacityRequestPolicy{
		Default:     ptr.To(apiresource.MustParse("100m")),
		ValidValues: []apiresource.Quantity{apiresource.MustParse("100m"), apiresource.MustParse("200m")},
	}
	errs := validateRequestPolicy(apiresource.MustParse("1"), pol, field.NewPath("requestPolicy"))
	if len(errs) != 0 {
		t.Errorf("valid fractional validValues policy rejected: %v", errs.ToAggregate())
	}
}
```

</details>

On the current code this fails with:

```text
requestPolicy.validValues[1]: Duplicate value: "1"
```

`100m` and `200m` are two distinct, sorted, in-range values, and `default` is present, so the policy is valid, but it is rejected because both map to the key `"1"`.

### Anything else we need to know?

A dedup that preserves fractional distinctness is enough. Since `validValues` is capped at a small maximum, an `O(n^2)` comparison with `Cmp` is a simple option, or a canonical representation that keeps `100m` and `200m` distinct while still treating `1Ki` and `1024` as equal.

The same `quantityKey` is also present on #140161, which reworks `CapacityRequestPolicyRange` for fractional quantities, so that PR does not fix this.

This is an API validation issue reproduced with a unit test; it does not require a running cluster, DRA driver, container runtime, or cloud provider.

Feature gate:

```text
DRAConsumableCapacity=true
```

`DRAConsumableCapacity` is beta and enabled by default starting with Kubernetes 1.36.

title: DRA: node-allocatable footprint uses the wrong driver's device when two drivers share a pool and device name
DRA: validate and reject negative capacity across consumable and node-allocatable accounting
body:
### What happened?

Two DRA capacity maps are missing non-negative API validation and feed overlapping accounting paths: `ResourceClaim.spec.devices.requests[*].exactly.capacity.requests` (and the `firstAvailable[*].capacity.requests` variant), and `ResourceClaim.status.allocation.devices.results[*].consumedCapacity`.

For plain consumable capacity, `CapacityRequirements.Requests` is resolved by `calculateConsumedCapacity` and recorded as consumed capacity. Before #140442, a negative resolved value could reduce accounting. Current master rejects a resolved negative value and aborts allocation in both allocator variants, but the API server still accepts a negative request.

Persisted `DeviceRequestAllocationResult.ConsumedCapacity` is also used when reconstructing cluster-wide consumed-capacity state. A negative stored value must make that reconstruction fail. Silently dropping the value would under-count already consumed capacity, and validating only the aggregate would let a positive entry mask a negative one for the same device and capacity key.

For DRA node-allocatable resources, `addDeviceMapping` reads `DeviceRequestAllocationResult.ConsumedCapacity[CapacityKey]`, applies `Device.NodeAllocatableResources[resource].Mapping.CapacityMultiplier`, and adds the result to the pod's mapped node-allocatable demand. A negative source or computed value can become a negative resource footprint and bypass positive-demand fit checks.

The original description used pre-Alpha-2 field names. #140009 changed the API to `NodeAllocatableResources` and `CapacityMultiplier`, and it already validates the multiplier fields as positive.

### What did you expect to happen?

The system should fail closed at each boundary that can still receive an old, malformed, or corrupt object:

- API validation rejects a negative `CapacityRequirements.Requests` for new or changed values, with ratcheting so an existing object that already passed weaker validation stays valid.
- API validation rejects a negative `DeviceRequestAllocationResult.ConsumedCapacity` when a new allocation result is stored.
- `calculateConsumedCapacity` rejects a negative raw request and allocation aborts.
- Reconstruction of existing consumed-capacity state returns an error when any individual stored value is negative, rather than a generic helper silently skipping it.
- `addDeviceMapping` rejects a negative source value and a negative value after applying `CapacityMultiplier`.

### How can we reproduce it?

The node-allocatable regression test should use the current Alpha-2 API (`Device.NodeAllocatableResources[resource].Mapping.CapacityKey` and `CapacityMultiplier`) and expect an error instead of accepting a negative mapped quantity.

The plain consumable-capacity regression for a negative request is covered by #140442. Additional coverage is needed for a negative persisted `ConsumedCapacity` while gathering allocated state: the invalid allocation being the first capacity inserted for a device, the invalid allocation inserted after a valid one, a positive allocation otherwise masking the negative value, an invalid in-flight allocation, and removal of the invalid claim clearing the stored error.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a correctness and fail-closed accounting issue, not evidence that an ordinary namespace workload author directly controls allocation status.

The spec-side request can be user-provided, but current master rejects a resolved negative value at allocation time via #140442. Admission validation is still needed for early rejection and API integrity. The status-side path requires an authorized status writer, an allocator bug, or a legacy object created before stricter validation.

Related: #140441, #140442, #140563, #140009, #140650, and #140084.

title: DRA: re-preparing a claim after a kubelet restart appends duplicate devices (unbounded checkpoint growth)
body:
### What happened?

When the kubelet restarts while a pod using a ResourceClaim is still running, the DRA manager re-runs `NodePrepareResources` for that claim and appends the returned devices onto the checkpoint-restored `DriverState.Devices` instead of replacing them. The device list grows by one full set on every restart, and duplicate `CDIDeviceIDs` are surfaced to the runtime and persisted to the checkpoint.

`newClaimInfoFromState` restores every checkpointed claim with `prepared: false`:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/claiminfo.go
func newClaimInfoFromState(state *state.ClaimInfoState) *ClaimInfo {
	info := &ClaimInfo{
		ClaimInfoState: *state.DeepCopy(),
		prepared:       false,
	}
	return info
}
```

`prepared` is unexported and not part of the checkpoint, so it is always `false` after a restart. In `prepareResources` the skip guard then does not fire:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go
if claimInfo.isPrepared() { // false after a restart, so not skipped
	continue
}
```

`NodePrepareResources` runs again and the response is added with `addDevice`, which appends without checking for devices already present:

```go
// pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/claiminfo.go
func (info *ClaimInfo) addDevice(driverName string, deviceState state.Device) {
	...
	driverState.Devices = append(driverState.Devices, deviceState)
	info.DriverState[driverName] = driverState
}
```

The cached ClaimInfo it appends to is the one restored from the checkpoint (`prepareResources` uses `m.cache.get` and only builds a fresh ClaimInfo when the entry does not exist), so the list doubles. `setPrepared` then checkpoints the doubled list, and the next restart doubles it again.

### What did you expect to happen?

Re-preparing an already-prepared claim after a restart should be idempotent: the manager should not accumulate duplicate devices, and the checkpoint should not grow across restarts.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A unit test in `pkg/kubelet/cm/dra` that drives the real `Manager`: prepare a claim, then build a second `Manager` on the same state directory (which restores the checkpoint), then prepare the same pod again. `DriverState.Devices` goes from 1 to 2. Making `addDevice` idempotent (or resetting the driver's devices before re-adding) keeps it at 1.

```
after first prepare: 1 device(s) in DriverState
after restart + re-prepare: 2 device(s) in DriverState
```

I have the test and am glad to attach it or open a PR.

### Anything else we need to know?

Not tenant-triggered and node-local. The concrete effect is unbounded growth of `DriverState.Devices` and the checkpoint for a long-lived pod on a kubelet that restarts (upgrades, crashes, config reloads), plus duplicate `CDIDeviceIDs` passed to the runtime and to device-health tracking.

Suggested direction: make re-prepare idempotent, either by resetting the driver's `DriverState.Devices` before re-adding the `NodePrepareResources` response (the response is the authoritative set) or by deduping in `addDevice`. Restoring with `prepared: false` and re-calling the driver is fine; the manager just should not accumulate.

title: DRA: ResourceSlice validRange.step of 2^64 re-panics with integer divide by zero (bypasses the #139698 Sign() guard via Value() truncation)
body:
### What happened?

`ResourceSlice` validation panics with `integer divide by zero` on a `capacity.requestPolicy.validRange.step` whose value is a positive multiple of 2^64 (for example `18446744073709551616`).

This re-opens the panic that #139653 reported and #139698 fixed. That fix added a guard using `Quantity.Sign()`, but the arithmetic still uses `Quantity.Value()`, and the two disagree for values that do not fit in int64:

```go
// pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go
if valueRange.Step.Sign() <= 0 {            // :1178  Sign() is exact -> 2^64 has Sign()==1, passes
    ...
} else {
    ... validateRequestPolicyRangeStep(...) // :1186
}

func validateRequestPolicyRangeStep(value, min, step apiresource.Quantity, ...) {
    stepVal := step.Value()   // :1197  Value() == big.Int.Int64(), truncates 2^64 -> 0
    ...
    if added%stepVal != 0 {   // :1201  added % 0 -> integer divide by zero
```

`resource.MustParse("18446744073709551616").Sign()` is `1` but `.Value()` is `0`, so a step of 2^64 passes the `Sign() <= 0` guard and then divides by zero. Same for `2^65`, `2^128`, and milli-scaled values like `18446744073709551616000m`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Validation should return a field error for an out-of-range step, never panic.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create (or have a DRA driver publish) a `ResourceSlice` whose device has `allowMultipleAllocations: true` and a capacity with:

```yaml
requestPolicy:
  default: "0"
  validRange:
    min: "0"
    step: "18446744073709551616"   # 2^64
```

Driving the real `validateRequestPolicyRange` with `step = 2^64` panics:

```
PANIC: runtime error: integer divide by zero
```

I have the test and can open a PR.

### Anything else we need to know?

The apiserver's panic-recovery middleware catches this and returns HTTP 500 for the offending create/update, so the apiserver does not crash; the effect is repeated 500s and log spam on the affected request. `CapacityRequestPolicy` lives only on `ResourceSlice.Spec`, which NodeRestriction limits to a node writing its own slice, so the realistic trigger is a buggy or malicious DRA driver publishing a slice (or a cluster-admin), not an unprivileged namespace tenant. It is gated by `DRAConsumableCapacity`, which is beta and on by default in 1.36, so the default configuration is affected.

There is a sibling wrong-accept in the same function: `added := value.Value() - min.Value()` (`:1200`) is an int64 subtraction that can wrap for near-`MaxInt64` `min`/`value`, producing an incorrect "not a multiple" result. Same root cause (int64-truncating `Value()` arithmetic).

Suggested fix: do the step/multiple math with `Quantity.Cmp` / `big.Int` (like the `Sign()` guard) instead of `Value()`, or reject a step whose `Value() <= 0` in addition to `Sign() <= 0`. Related `Value()`-truncation validation issue in the same file: #140457.

title: resource: PodRequests/PodLimits report a zero-valued pod-level resource on an infeasible resize
PodRequests/PodLimits insert an explicit zero for pod-level resource keys absent from actuated resources
body:
**What happened**:

`PodRequests` and `PodLimits` (`staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/resource/helpers.go`) compute pod-level aggregation by iterating `pod.Spec.Resources.{Requests,Limits}` and assigning the value from the *effective* (actuated) resources for each supported pod-level resource:

```go
for resourceName, quantity := range pod.Spec.Resources.Limits {
    if IsSupportedPodLevelResource(resourceName) {
        limits[resourceName] = quantity
        if effectiveLims != nil {
            limits[resourceName] = effectiveLims[resourceName]
        }
    }
}
```

When a resource key is present in the spec but absent from the effective map, `effectiveLims[resourceName]` returns a zero-valued `resource.Quantity`, so the key is inserted into the result with an explicit zero.

This happens in practice when an in-place resize *adds* a pod-level request/limit (adding a key is permitted by validation; only removal is blocked) and the resize is marked `PodResizePending` / `Infeasible`: `determineEffective{Requests,Limits}` then returns the actuated-only map, which does not contain the newly added key.

Container-level aggregation (`AggregateContainerRequests` / `AggregateContainerLimits`) iterates the *effective* map via `addResourceList` and therefore omits keys that are not actuated. The two paths disagree on the resulting key set for the same input.

**What you expected to happen**:

Pod-level aggregation should omit a key that is not present in the effective/actuated resources, matching container-level aggregation, rather than inserting an explicit zero.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Build a pod with pod-level resources (`Spec.Resources.{Requests,Limits}` = `{cpu, memory}`), status resources actuated to `{cpu}` only, and a `PodResizePending` / `Infeasible` condition; call `PodLimits` / `PodRequests` with `UseStatusResources` and `InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScalingEnabled` set. The returned map contains `memory: 0` (explicit), whereas `AggregateContainer{Requests,Limits}` on the same pod omits `memory`.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

This is a consistency issue and is not currently observable through any cgroup/enforcement path. The paths that write cgroup values (`ResourceConfigForPod`, `calculateSandboxResources`) do not set `UseStatusResources`, and the consumers that do set it read through `.Cpu()` / `.Memory()` accessors, where an explicit zero and an absent key are equivalent. The only presence-checking consumer (`ResourceConfigForPod`, which checks `limits[v1.ResourceMemory]`) does not use those options. Filing ahead of the pod-level in-place resize GA work so the two aggregation paths stay consistent.

title: kube-controller-manager panics (nil pointer dereference) when a StorageVersionMigration targets a resource not present in the RESTMapper
body:
### What happened?

Creating a `StorageVersionMigration` for a resource, then removing that resource from the cluster (e.g. deleting the CRD) while the migration is still pending, makes the `kube-controller-manager` panic and enter `CrashLoopBackOff`.

The storage-version-migrator controller's `sync` dereferences a nil `*schema.GroupVersionResource`:

```
E0714 13:08:33 "Observed a panic" panic="runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference"
	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator.(*SVMController).sync(...)
		pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator/storageversionmigrator.go:227
...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
```

In `sync`, `resourceFor` returns `(nil, false, nil)` when the resource is not in the RESTMapper (this is the normal "unknown resource" return, not an error), and the following line logs `gvr.String()` on that nil pointer:

```go
gvr, exists, err := resourceFor(svmc.restMapper, toBeProcessedSVM.Spec.Resource)
if err != nil { return err }
if !exists {
    logger.V(4).Info("resource does not exist in our rest mapper", "gvr", gvr.String()) // gvr is nil -> panic
    ...
}
```

`GroupVersionResource.String()` has a value receiver, so calling it on a nil pointer dereferences it. The arguments of `logger.V(4).Info(...)` are evaluated unconditionally, so this happens regardless of the log verbosity. The panic crashes the whole controller-manager (all controllers stop) until the offending `StorageVersionMigration` is removed.

Note: the sibling function in the same package (`ResourceVersionController.sync` in `resourceversion.go`) handles the exact same `!exists` case without touching `gvr`, which is what makes this look like an oversight.

### What did you expect to happen?

The controller should handle a missing resource gracefully (it already intends to: it requeues for up to one minute, then marks the migration failed) without panicking or crashing the controller-manager.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a cluster with the `StorageVersionMigrator` feature enabled and the `storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1` API served:

```bash
# 1. A CRD (migrating a CRD to a new storage version is a documented use case)
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: widgets.example.com}
spec:
  group: example.com
  names: {plural: widgets, singular: widget, kind: Widget, listKind: WidgetList}
  scope: Namespaced
  versions: [{name: v1, served: true, storage: true, schema: {openAPIV3Schema: {type: object}}}]
YAML

# 2. Request a storage version migration for that resource
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageVersionMigration
metadata: {name: migrate-widgets}
spec: {resource: {group: example.com, resource: widgets}}
YAML

# 3. Delete the CRD (it leaves the RESTMapper) while the migration is pending
kubectl delete crd widgets.example.com
```

Within ~30-60s the kube-controller-manager panics and goes into CrashLoopBackOff:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager   # restartCount increasing, CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl -n kube-system logs <kcm-pod> --previous | grep -A2 "nil pointer"
```

Removing the `StorageVersionMigration` (`kubectl delete storageversionmigration migrate-widgets`) lets the controller-manager recover.

A unit-level reproduction (fake client, no cluster) is also available if you want it.

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause is a single line (`gvr.String()` on a nil pointer). Trigger requires cluster-admin rights (StorageVersionMigration is cluster-scoped) plus the target resource disappearing from the RESTMapper, so this is not a privilege-escalation issue, but the crash takes down the entire controller-manager.

I have a fix ready (a one-line change: log the migration's `spec.resource` instead of the nil `gvr`) plus a regression test that panics without the fix and passes with it, and I'm happy to open a PR.

title: kubectl explain: add an -o skeleton output format for a copy-pasteable YAML starting point
body:
cc @kubernetes/sig-cli-feature-requests

## What would you like to be added?

A new `kubectl explain <type> -o skeleton` output format that renders a
resource's schema as a concise, editable YAML skeleton (field names with
placeholder values) instead of the verbose field-by-field prose that
`plaintext`/`plaintext-openapiv2` produce.

A companion `-o skeleton-comments` renders the same skeleton with short
inline `# ...` comments for fields that need explaining: `# required`,
`# enum: A|B|C`, `# map[string]string`, and a drill-down hint for fields
collapsed for depth (see below).

Example, `kubectl explain deployments.spec.template.spec.containers -o skeleton`:

```yaml
containers:
- name: "<required>"
  args:
  - ""
  command:
  - ""
  env: []
  envFrom: []
  image: ""
  imagePullPolicy: ""
  lifecycle: {}
  livenessProbe: {}
  ports: []
  readinessProbe: {}
  resources: {}
  securityContext: {}
  startupProbe: {}
  stdin: false
  stdinOnce: false
  terminationMessagePath: ""
  terminationMessagePolicy: ""
  tty: false
  volumeDevices: []
  volumeMounts: []
  workingDir: ""
```

Design notes:
- Placeholder values come from the schema's own `default`, else the first
  `enum` value, else `example`, else a type-appropriate zero value. A
  required field with none of those (typically a bare string) gets the
  literal `"<required>"` sentinel so it isn't mistaken for an intentionally
  empty optional field.
- The `status` subresource and server-managed `metadata` fields
  (`resourceVersion`, `uid`, `managedFields`, etc.) are omitted, since nobody
  hand-authors those.
- To keep output readable on resources with deep optional structure (Pod's
  `affinity`/`tolerations`/`securityContext`, CRD validation schemas), each
  optional field spends against a small budget before its own optional
  children collapse to a placeholder with a drill-down hint (e.g.
  `# optional, nested further -- see: kubectl explain pods.spec.affinity -o skeleton`).
  Required fields are free, so a load-bearing chain like
  `containers[].image` always expands regardless of depth.
- Implemented as one more template in the existing `pkg/explain/v2`
  template-based generator (same mechanism as `plaintext-openapiv2`), so it
  only touches the openapiv3 explain path.

## Why is this needed?

`kubectl explain` today is documentation-first: it's great for looking up
what a field means, but not for the common case of "I want to write a
Deployment/CRD manifest and need a skeleton to fill in." Today's next-best
alternatives (`kubectl create deployment ... --dry-run=client -o yaml`,
hand-copying from docs, or `explain --recursive`) either only cover a
handful of built-in kinds, produce output flooded with every field
regardless of relevance, or don't work at all for CRDs.

`-o skeleton` gives a fast, copy-pasteable starting point for any resource
the cluster serves an OpenAPI v3 schema for, including CRDs, while staying
short enough to read. The optional-depth budget means you see the fields
that actually need decisions (`containers[].image`) without also seeing
every leaf of `affinity`/`tolerations` you probably don't need today, and
you can always drill into a collapsed field with a normal
`explain <type>.<field> -o skeleton` call.

This is proposed as a proof of concept with a working implementation and
test suite already in hand (unit tests covering required/optional
ordering, enums, maps, `$ref` cycles, field-path drill-down, and the
depth-budget behavior). Happy to open the PR once there's SIG CLI agreement
on the approach/flag naming.

|---|---|---|---|
| [2077438447429095424](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-gce-scale-performance-5000/2077438447429095424) | 07-15 | `nodes-us-east1-d-8blj` | scale-30 |

All three stragglers are in **us-east1-d** — a different instance each run, across two different boskos projects — while nodes in us-east1-b/c all join. * A rerun alone is unlikely to help: 3/3 runs each lost a different VM, so going green likely needs the zone issue to clear or a validation-side mitigation (e.g. `kops validate` tolerating N un-joined machines at scale, or replacing un-joined instances during validation so the MIG recreates them).
