title: [Failing test] apisnoop-conformance-gate red since 2026-07-23: getLifecycleAPIGroup untested — pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml is not consumed by the gate
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

- `apisnoop-conformance-gate` (periodic, every 3h)
- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-conformance#apisnoop-conformance-gate
- https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate

### Which tests are failing?

The gate itself:

```
==================
UNTESTED ENDPOINTS
getLifecycleAPIGroup

==================
ERROR: You have 1 untested endpoints
==================
```

### Since when has it been failing?

First red build: [2080099338675032064](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080099338675032064) (2026-07-23 01:15 UTC).
Last green build: [2080053868456054784](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080053868456054784) (2026-07-22 22:14 UTC).
Every run since has failed (~60 consecutive builds as of 2026-07-30), and `testgrid-num-failures-to-alert: '1'` means this alerts on every run.

### Reason for failure

#137050 (merged 2026-07-23 00:33 UTC, 42 minutes before the first red build) added the `lifecycle.k8s.io/v1alpha1` group (EvictionRequest). The group discovery path `/apis/lifecycle.k8s.io/` has no version in it, so its operation `getLifecycleAPIGroup` registers as **stable** in apisnoop even though the group only serves an alpha version. No conformance test can hit it (the group is not served in a default/conformance cluster), so the gate flags it as an untested eligible endpoint.

#137050 anticipated this and added `getLifecycleAPIGroup` to [`test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml) — **but the `apisnoop-conformance-gate` job never reads that file**. The gate (snoopdb image) only loads `ineligible_endpoints.yaml`:

- [`303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql) fetches only `test/conformance/testdata/ineligible_endpoints.yaml`
- the untested list is `conformance.new_endpoint` = stable endpoints in the latest release minus `ineligible_endpoint` ([`207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql), [`203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql))
- [`docker-entrypoint.sh`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/docker-entrypoint.sh) exits 1 if that list is non-empty

`pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` is only consumed by:
- test-infra's [`experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py) (the `conformance-audit` jobs in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-arch/conformance-audit.yaml`)
- the apisnoop web UI ([`apps/web/src/lib/constants.js`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/web/src/lib/constants.js))

### Anything else we need to know?

- #140923 was filed for this failure and closed as a duplicate of #140523, but #140523 tracks adding EvictionRequest CRUD tests — that cannot turn this gate green while the group is alpha-only (the endpoint is not served in a conformance cluster, and alpha APIs cannot have conformance tests). #140897 was closed unmerged. So nothing currently open unblocks the job.
- Precedent for exactly this situation is an entry in **`ineligible_endpoints.yaml`** (the file the gate does consume). `getInternalApiserverAPIGroup`, `getResourceAPIGroup`, and `getStoragemigrationAPIGroup` all have entries there with reason *"The endpoint is part of a group that has no stable endpoints yet, reporting as a stable endpoint in apisnoop."* (see also kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop#859, the identical failure for `storagemigration`).

Proposed fix:

1. **Short term (unblocks CI):** move `getLifecycleAPIGroup` from `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` to `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` with the same reason/link as the existing `get*APIGroup` entries, and remove it once `lifecycle.k8s.io` serves a stable version with conformance coverage (#140523).
2. **Longer term:** make snoopdb's gate also honor `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` (kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop), so the documented escape hatch actually applies to `apisnoop-conformance-gate`, or document that only `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` gates CI.

title: Memory Manager pod-scope restore compares container blocks with the pod request
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager, after a kubelet restart, Memory Manager finds a restored container allocation and calls `regenerateHints` with that container's blocks and the whole Pod memory request.

For a multi-container Pod, those values differ, so `regenerateHints` returns no hint instead of restoring the Pod's previous NUMA hint. This can cause an existing Pod to fail admission under `restricted` or `single-numa-node`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-scope hint restoration should use the restored pod-level allocation and preserve the previous NUMA hint.

### How can we reproduce it?

Use a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory resources and two containers, allocate it with static Memory Manager, restart from the checkpoint, then call `GetPodTopologyHints`. The current code returns no regenerated hint because it compares one container's blocks with the Pod request.

title: gofmt in go1.26.5 gives different output on amd64 and arm64, which breaks ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary (the only verify job that runs on arm64 nodes, on the AKS build cluster)

### Which tests are failing?

verify-gofmt.sh

### Since when has it been failing?

First failure 2026-07-20 17:12 UTC, a few hours after #140000 merged. The job then alternated between green and red depending on which node it landed on. It has failed every run since 2026-07-29 17:06 UTC because every pod since then has landed on arm64 nodes.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-k8s-infra-canaries#verify-master-canary

### Reason for failure (if possible)

gofmt from go1.26.5 does not produce the same output on amd64 and arm64 for one struct literal in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go` (added in #140000). The amd64 build of gofmt accepts the code as checked in. The arm64 build wants the short fields aligned to the long `enableInPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption` line. Each build rejects the form the other one wants, so running update-gofmt cannot produce a form both accept.

This is a bug in Go, not in the release binaries. The gofmt binaries in the CI image match the official go.dev tarballs, and building gofmt from unmodified go1.26.5 sources reproduces the difference purely by changing GOARCH. The cause is in go/printer, which decides where to break column alignment using a geometric mean computed with `math.Log` and `math.Exp` (nodes.go lines 232 to 287 in go1.26.5). Those functions can differ in the last bit between architectures, and the field lengths in this literal sit exactly on the 2.5 ratio threshold, so the decision flips. Presubmits run on amd64, which is why the change merged cleanly.

Evidence: the last green run (build 2082497666687700992, amd64 node) and the first red run of the streak (build 2082513014723973120, arm64 node) tested the same commit 7fbcad5e8ec.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix on our side is to restructure the literal so the long field is assigned after the struct is built. I verified that form is accepted by gofmt from go1.26.5 on linux amd64, linux arm64, and darwin arm64, and by go1.27rc2. I will send a PR and file a golang/go issue for the printer bug.

title: kubectl rollout history: printer errors silently dropped when listing all revisions with -o flag
body:
### What happened?

When running kubectl rollout history deployment/foo -o yaml (without --revision), errors returned by printer.PrintObj are silently discarded. The loop that iterates over all revisions calls printer.PrintObj(historyInfo[k], o.Out) without checking the error return value, so a broken pipe, a closed writer, or any other IO failure during output is invisible to the caller — the command exits 0 regardless.

**Relevant code:**
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/rollout/rollout_history.go#L195-L197

`go
for _, k := range sortedKeys {
    printer.PrintObj(historyInfo[k], o.Out)  // error return ignored
}
`

Compare with the single-revision path immediately above it (lines 186–188), which does handle the error correctly:

`go
if err := printer.PrintObj(revision, o.Out); err != nil {
    return err
}
`

### What did you expect to happen?

Any error from printer.PrintObj in the all-revisions loop should be returned and propagated, causing the command to exit non-zero, consistent with how every other code path in the same function behaves.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The easiest way to trigger this in a real cluster is to pipe the output to a program that exits early (causing a broken pipe):

`
kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp -o yaml | head -1
`

On Linux this will log a broken-pipe write error at the OS level, but kubectl will still exit 0 because the error from PrintObj is swallowed.

A unit test can inject a writer that returns an error to confirm the bug programmatically.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix is straightforward: wrap the PrintObj call in the loop the same way the single-revision branch already does.

The existing test TestRolloutHistoryWithOutput in ollout_history_test.go covers the happy-path for yaml all revisions but has no case that injects a failing writer, so the bug is not caught by the test suite today. A test covering printer-error propagation should be added alongside the fix.

title: DRA: ExtendedResourceCache serves stale mappings and can drop the winner across DeviceClass updates and collisions
body:
The extended resource cache (`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/deviceclass/extendedresourcecache/extendedresourcecache.go`, behind `DRAExtendedResource`) loses information it needs to keep `resourceName2class` correct across DeviceClass updates and explicit-name collisions. `updateResourceName2class` treats the class currently cached under an explicit name as a collision peer and arbitrates by creation timestamp and name, but that same path also runs when a class updates itself, and the removal paths delete by key without checking which class owns the entry.

Cases I traced on master:

1. A same-class update serves a stale object. On `OnUpdate` for a class that keeps its `ExtendedResourceName`, `updateResourceName2class` finds the cached (old) object under that name, sees an equal timestamp and equal name, and returns before replacing the pointer or re-adding the default mapping. `resourceName2class` keeps pointing at the old object while `class2ResourceName` is updated, so `GetDeviceClass(name)` returns the pre-update DeviceClass (stale selectors/config) until some unrelated event rewrites it.

2. A collision loser never gets its own implicit mapping. When the new class loses the explicit-name arbitration, the early `return` also skips the "Always add the default mapping" at the end, so `deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/<loser>` (which is unique and cannot collide) is never registered. The loser is then unreachable even by its own implicit name.

3. Deleting the loser removes the winner. `removeResourceName2class` deletes `resourceName2class[loser.ExtendedResourceName]` without checking that the entry belongs to the loser, so when a winner holds that explicit key, deleting the loser drops the winner's mapping.

4. Deleting the winner does not promote the runner-up. The cache only stores the current winner, not the candidate set, so once the winner is deleted nothing can restore the next class for that explicit name.

5. Renaming or updating the loser removes another class's mapping. The remove-old step deletes `resourceName2class[old.ExtendedResourceName]` unconditionally, so if the winner now owns that old key, updating the loser drops the winner's mapping.

The common root is that the cache keeps only the materialized winner per explicit name and mutates it in place, with no per-class ownership check and no record of the other candidates. The migration case the code intends to support (two DeviceClasses sharing an explicit `ExtendedResourceName`, newer wins) is exactly where these break.

I think the fix is to retain the candidate DeviceClasses per explicit name (or re-derive the winner from the full set on each event), keep implicit mappings independent of explicit-name arbitration, and remove a mapping only when it belongs to the class being changed. I am happy to send a fix and regression tests covering same-class update, loser add, loser delete, winner delete with runner-up promotion, winner and loser rename, and the equal-timestamp tie-break.

title: kubectl patch: 'map does not contain declared merge key' error lacks actionable context
body:
## What happened

When using `kubectl patch` with a strategic merge patch on a list field without providing the required merge key, users see the following error:

```
Error from server: map: map[hostPath:map[path:/var/lib/kubelet/pods]] does not contain declared merge key: name
```

## What I expected

The error should explain:
1. **Which field** requires the merge key
2. **What** a merge key is and why it is required
3. **How to fix it** — i.e. include the merge key field in each list item
4. A short example of the correct format

## Reproduction

```bash
# Attempt to patch a container list without providing the "name" merge key
kubectl patch pod mypod --type=strategic -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"image":"nginx:1.25"}]}}'
```

Expected: helpful error explaining that each list item needs `"name": "<container-name>"`
Actual: `map: map[...] does not contain declared merge key: name`

## Root cause

The error originates from `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/mergepatch/errors.go` line 36:

```go
func ErrNoMergeKey(m map[string]interface{}, k string) error {
    return fmt.Errorf("map: %v does not contain declared merge key: %s", m, k)
}
```

The message prints the full map contents (potentially verbose) but provides no guidance on what the user needs to do to fix the patch.

## Suggested improvement

Something along the lines of:

```
Error: strategic merge patch requires merge key "name" in each list item.
When patching list/array fields, each item must include the merge key field so Kubernetes knows which item to update.
Example: {"spec": {"containers": [{"name": "my-container", "image": "nginx:1.25"}]}}
```

## Environment

- Kubernetes version: any (error message unchanged across recent versions)
- Component: `kubectl patch` / `apimachinery` strategic merge patch

/area kubectl
/kind documentation

title: kubectl get: PrintObj errors are silently discarded in human-readable output loop
body:
### What happened?

When running kubectl get pods -o yaml (or any human-readable/structured output that goes through the per-object printer loop), errors returned by printer.PrintObj are silently discarded. The loop in Run() that iterates over fetched objects calls printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w) without checking the error return value, so a broken pipe, a closed writer, or any other IO failure during output is invisible to the caller. the command exits 0 regardless.

Relevant code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/get/get.go#L569

```go
for _, info := range infos {
    ...
    printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w) // error return ignored
}
```


This is notable because the surrounding function already has an error-aggregation mechanism in place for this exact purpose. ToPrinter errors a few lines earlier are collected into an allErrs[] error slice and returned via utilerrors.NewAggregate(allErrs) at the end of Run(). The plumbing exists; PrintObj's return value just isn't fed into it.

A second occurrence of the identical pattern exists at staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/prune.go#L137 printer.PrintObj(obj, p.out) inside a loop, in a function that returns error, with the result likewise ignored.



### What did you expect to happen?

Any error from printer.PrintObj in the loop should be captured, added to allErrs, and ultimately returned via the existing utilerrors.NewAggregate(allErrs) call, causing the command to exit non-zero consistent with how the ToPrinter error path in the same function already behaves:


```go
if err := printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w); err != nil {
    if !errs.Has(err.Error()) {
        errs.Insert(err.Error())
        allErrs = append(allErrs, err)
    }
}
```


### How can we reproduce it?

The easiest way to trigger this in a real cluster is to pipe the output to a program that exits early (causing a broken pipe):

```console
$ kubectl get pods -A | head -1
```


On Linux this triggers a broken-pipe write error at the OS level, but kubectl will still exit 0 because the error from PrintObj is swallowed.

A unit test can inject a writer that returns an error to confirm the bug programmatically.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix is small: wrap the PrintObj call in the loop with the same error-collection pattern already used for ToPrinter errors a few lines above it in the same function. The same bug class exists in apply/prune.go:137 and should ideally be fixed alongside this, or filed as a linked follow-up.
Existing tests for get.go's output path cover the happy path only; none inject a failing writer, so this isn't caught by the current suite. A test covering printer-error propagation should be added with the fix.

title: DRA: GatherPools completeness is order-dependent when ResourceSliceCount values disagree
body:
### What happened?

`GatherPools` determines whether a pool generation is complete by comparing the number of retained slices with `slicesForPool[0].Spec.Pool.ResourceSliceCount`, so the declared count comes from the first retained slice for that pool generation. When two ResourceSlices in the same driver, pool, and generation disagree on `ResourceSliceCount`, the same set of objects can be classified differently under different input permutations. In my direct allocator reproduction, `slice-a` declares `resourceSliceCount: 1` and contains one device, while `slice-b` declares `resourceSliceCount: 2` and contains one device. With `[slice-a, slice-b]`, the generation is treated as incomplete and its devices are not offered; with `[slice-b, slice-a]`, it is treated as complete and is built. Only the input order changes.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pool-generation completeness should be invariant under permutations of the ResourceSlice input. ResourceSlices in the same `(driver, pool, generation)` describe one pool revision and should agree on the total `ResourceSliceCount`. When they do not, `GatherPools` should fail closed deterministically—for example, by treating the generation as invalid or otherwise unavailable for allocation—rather than accepting the contradictory revision in one ordering and rejecting it in another. Slice order may legitimately affect candidate preference, but it should not determine whether a revision is complete.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Construct two ResourceSlices in the same `(driver, pool, generation)`: `slice-a` with `resourceSliceCount: 1` and one device, and `slice-b` with `resourceSliceCount: 2` and one device. Invoke the structured allocator with a claim for one device, once with each ResourceSlice input order. `[slice-a, slice-b]` yields no allocation because the pool is considered incomplete, while `[slice-b, slice-a]` allocates. Two controls isolate the count disagreement from device capacity: consistent counts `{2, 2}` allocate in both orders, while consistent counts `{1, 1}` with two slices are incomplete in both orders. I reproduced the same order-dependent result in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants.

### Anything else we need to know?

The slower completeness path does not remove the order dependence because it also compares the number of discovered slices against `slicesForPool[0].Spec.Pool.ResourceSliceCount`. The source already contains `Future TODO: detect inconsistent ResourceSliceCount, also in poolIsInvalid`; this report concerns the observable consequence of not yet performing that check, rather than merely requesting implementation of the existing TODO. Per-object API validation does not detect the condition because each slice's count can be individually valid while the set is cross-object inconsistent.

This is a library-level observation against `GatherPools`. I reproduced it by invoking the structured allocator directly and did not verify the input ordering of any specific production consumer, so whether a particular consumer encounters the order-dependent result in practice depends on the order in which it supplies ResourceSlices.

A possible fix requires no API change: during the initial scan, track the expected `ResourceSliceCount` for each `(driver, pool, generation)`, fail closed when another slice declares a different value, apply the same behavior in all three allocator variants, and add regression coverage for both permutations. Whether the disagreement should be represented as invalid, incomplete, or otherwise unavailable for allocation is a maintainer decision. I am happy to send a PR if that direction sounds right.

title: hack/README.md: punctuation errors (comma splice and missing space) in vestigial redirection notice
body:
**What happened?**

`hack/README.md` contains punctuation errors that affect the readability of the documentation.

**Line 15–16 — Comma splice:**
A comma is used where a period is required; "Please" begins a new sentence and should not be joined to the previous one with a comma.

    This script is a vestigial redirection, Please do not add "real" logic.

**Line 17 — Missing space between sentences:**
There is no space between the period and the following sentence.

    The `true` target of this makerule is `hack/make-rules/update.sh`.It is equivalent to `make update`.

**What did you expect to happen?**

Both sentences should be separated correctly with a period and a single space, consistent with standard English punctuation:

    This script is a vestigial redirection. Please do not add "real" logic.

    The `true` target of this makerule is `hack/make-rules/update.sh`. It is equivalent to `make update`.

**Anything else we need to know?**

This is a documentation-only fix — no code or behavior is affected. A PR with the corrected punctuation is ready to follow this issue.

title: Liveness probe failure container restart leads to container starting up with started=true and liveness probes starting before startup probes have run
body:
### What happened?

The full details of the repro can be seen in the Bash script below, but roughly:

1. Start a container with startup and liveness probe.
2. Wait for both to succeed. All normal so far.
3. Flip liveness probe to fail.
4. Container restarts.
5. New container sees liveness probe before startup probe.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the new container to first need to pass its startup probes before liveness probes begin, as per the docs here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/#startup-probe.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproduction bash script:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

CLUSTER="probe-repro-$$"
K3S_IMAGE="rancher/k3s:v1.36.2-k3s1"
KIND_IMAGE="kindest/node:v1.36.1@sha256:3489c7674813ba5d8b1a9977baea8a6e553784dab7b84759d1014dbd78f7ebd5"
MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION="v1.36.2"
POD="probe-repro"
ENVIRONMENT="k3s"
KIND_KUBECONFIG=""

usage() {
  echo "usage: $0 [--k3s | --minikube | --kind]" >&2
}

if (($# > 1)); then
  usage
  exit 2
fi

case "${1:---k3s}" in
  --k3s) ENVIRONMENT="k3s" ;;
  --minikube) ENVIRONMENT="minikube" ;;
  --kind) ENVIRONMENT="kind" ;;
  --help)
    usage
    exit
    ;;
  *)
    usage
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

if [[ "$ENVIRONMENT" == "kind" ]]; then
  KIND_KUBECONFIG=$(mktemp)
fi

cleanup() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker rm --force "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    minikube) minikube delete --profile "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
    kind) kind delete cluster --name "$CLUSTER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true ;;
  esac
  if [[ -n "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" ]]; then
    rm -f "$KIND_KUBECONFIG"
  fi
}
trap cleanup EXIT

k() {
  case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
    k3s) docker exec --interactive "$CLUSTER" /bin/kubectl "$@" ;;
    minikube) minikube --profile "$CLUSTER" kubectl -- --context="$CLUSTER" "$@" ;;
    kind) kubectl --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" "$@" ;;
  esac
}

c() {
  k exec "$POD" -- "$@"
}

echo "Booting $ENVIRONMENT..."

case "$ENVIRONMENT" in
  k3s)
    command -v docker >/dev/null
    docker run --detach --privileged --name "$CLUSTER" "$K3S_IMAGE" \
      server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb >/dev/null
    ;;
  minikube)
    command -v minikube >/dev/null
    minikube start \
      --profile "$CLUSTER" \
      --driver=docker \
      --container-runtime=containerd \
      --kubernetes-version="$MINIKUBE_KUBERNETES_VERSION" \
      --keep-context
    ;;
  kind)
    command -v kind >/dev/null
    command -v kubectl >/dev/null
    kind create cluster \
      --name "$CLUSTER" \
      --image "$KIND_IMAGE" \
      --kubeconfig "$KIND_KUBECONFIG" \
      --wait 120s
    ;;
esac

until k get serviceaccount default >/dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 0.2
done

echo "Applying manifest..."

k apply -f - >/dev/null <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: probe-repro
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 2
  volumes:
    - name: state
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name: test
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: [sh, -c]
      args:
        - |
          instance=initial
          if test -f /state/container-seen; then
            instance=replacement
          else
            touch /state/container-seen
          fi
          echo "$instance" > /state/instance
          printf '%s  %-11s  container started\n' \
            "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
          on_term() {
            printf '%s  %-11s  received SIGTERM\n' \
              "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" >> /state/events
            exit 0
          }
          trap on_term TERM
          sleep 3600 &
          wait $!
      volumeMounts:
        - name: state
          mountPath: /state
      startupProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=failure
              test "$instance" = initial && result=success
              printf '%s  %-11s  startup probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 100
      livenessProbe:
        exec:
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              instance=$(cat /state/instance)
              result=success
              if test "$instance" = initial && test -f /state/fail-liveness; then
                result=failure
              fi
              printf '%s  %-11s  liveness probe: %s\n' \
                "$(date -u '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ')" "$instance" "$result" >> /state/events
              test "$result" = success
        periodSeconds: 1
        failureThreshold: 1
EOF

k wait "pod/$POD" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}'=true \
  --timeout=120s >/dev/null

FIRST_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')

echo "First container ID: $FIRST_ID"
echo "Waiting 2 seconds to allow some probe successes..."

sleep 2

echo "Failing liveness probe..."
c touch /state/fail-liveness

echo "Waiting for container to restart..."

SECOND_ID="$FIRST_ID"
for _ in {1..600}; do
  SECOND_ID=$(k get pod "$POD" \
    -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID}')
  [[ -n "$SECOND_ID" && "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]] && break
  sleep 0.1
done

[[ "$SECOND_ID" != "$FIRST_ID" ]]

echo "Second container ID: $SECOND_ID"

STARTED=$(k get pod "$POD" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].started}')
c sh -c \
  'printf "%s  %-11s  Kubernetes status started=%s\n" "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" replacement "$1" >> /state/events' \
  sh "$STARTED"

echo "Waiting 3 seconds for some probes to happen..."

sleep 3

echo "Event log:"

c cat /state/events
```

Save as repro.sh and here are the results of me running it:

```

2026-08-04T08:27:19Z  initial      container started
2026-08-04T08:27:19Z  initial      startup probe: success
```

## Reason for failure (if possible)
All failing steps are kubetest infrastructure lifecycle steps, not individual test failures. The job is configured with `--timeout=120m` within a 2h20m Prow deadline. On flaky runs the test suite hits the timeout, causing a cascade: `kubetest.Test` → `kubetest.Timeout` → `kubetest.TearDown` → `kubetest.DumpClusterLogs`. `kubetest.Up` and `kubetest.listResources After` flakes on separate runs suggest GCP Boskos project provisioning slowness.

title: Security implications of named ports in NetworkPolicy
body:
In our setup, NetworkPolicies are owned by the platform team. Users can create ML inference services via a self-service REST API that accepts almost all pod spec fields, including port names and numbers. 

When a platform-owned NetworkPolicy uses a named port (e.g. port: http), any API user can create a pod with that port name mapped to an arbitrary port number — effectively controlling what traffic the NetworkPolicy permits without platform team visibility or approval.

Example:

The platform team defines a NetworkPolicy allowing port: http for inference service pods. A user creates an inference service and assigns the name http to an unintended port:

User-defined via REST API — matches platform NetworkPolicy
- name: http
  containerPort: 9000

The platform NetworkPolicy now permits traffic to an unintended service on port 9000 — with no policy change, no audit event, and no platform team approval.

Why we can't simply use numeric ports:

The platform team doesn't control what port number each user's workload listens on. Different model servers use different ports. Named ports were attractive because they decouple policy from the user's choice of port number — but this means the policy's effective scope is controlled by the pod spec, not the policy itself.

Questions:

1. What use cases does named port support in NetworkPolicy serve that numeric ports cannot?
2. Is there any official guidance on named vs. numeric ports in NetworkPolicy from a security standpoint?

title: DRA: per-device nodeSelector with multiple terms passes validation and aborts the scheduling cycle
body:
### What happened?

A per-device `nodeSelector` on a ResourceSlice device may contain more than one node selector term.

ResourceSlice API validation accepts such an object, even though the API contract requires exactly one term. When structured allocation selects that device, the allocator rejects the selector with a hard error.

The error is not wrapped with `ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`. The DynamicResources Filter plugin therefore returns a framework Error instead of rejecting only the current node. A Filter error cancels the remaining node search and aborts the current scheduling cycle.

Subsequent retries can reproduce the same failure while the malformed ResourceSlice remains unchanged and allocation continues to select that device.

### Where validation and the allocator disagree

Both node selector fields are documented as single-term selectors:

- `ResourceSliceSpec.NodeSelector`: "Must use exactly one term."
- `Device.NodeSelector`: "Must use exactly one term."

The slice-level selector enforces this contract in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`:

```go
allErrs = append(allErrs,
    corevalidation.ValidateNodeSelector(spec.NodeSelector, false, fldPath.Child("nodeSelector"))...,
)
if len(spec.NodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms) != 1 {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(
        fldPath.Child("nodeSelector", "nodeSelectorTerms"),
        spec.NodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms,
        "must have exactly one node selector term",
    ))
}
```

The per-device path in `validateDevice` only calls `ValidateNodeSelector`:

```go
if device.NodeSelector != nil {
    setFields = append(setFields, "`nodeSelector`")
    allErrs = append(allErrs,
        corevalidation.ValidateNodeSelector(device.NodeSelector, false, fldPath.Child("nodeSelector"))...,
    )
}
```

`ValidateNodeSelector` requires at least one valid term but does not limit the selector to one term. A selector with two or more valid terms therefore passes this validation path.

The allocator later assumes validation has enforced the single-term invariant. In `createNodeSelector`:

```go
default:
    // This shouldn't occur, validation must prevent creation of such slices.
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", len(nodeSelector.NodeSelectorTerms))
```

The caller wraps that error with `%w`, but not with `ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter plugin treats it as a fatal framework Error and the scheduler cancels the remaining Filter work for that scheduling cycle. The same `createNodeSelector` branch exists in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants.

### What did you expect to happen?

ResourceSlice API validation should reject a per-device `nodeSelector` whose `nodeSelectorTerms` length is not exactly one, matching the existing validation for `ResourceSliceSpec.NodeSelector`. Malformed ResourceSlices should not be admitted and then deferred until scheduler allocation, where they can abort a scheduling cycle.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Publish a ResourceSlice with `perDeviceNodeSelection: true` and a device whose `nodeSelector` has two individually valid terms (one of them matching a real node), then a ResourceClaim and Pod that select it:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: nsrepro-class
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel:
      expression: 'device.driver == "nsrepro.example"'
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata:
  name: nsrepro-slice
spec:
  driver: nsrepro.example
  pool: {name: nsrepro-pool, generation: 1, resourceSliceCount: 1}
  perDeviceNodeSelection: true
  devices:
  - name: dev0
    attributes:
      type: {string: repro}
    nodeSelector:
      nodeSelectorTerms:                 # two terms; one matches a node in the cluster
      - matchExpressions:
        - {key: kubernetes.io/hostname, operator: In, values: [<a-node-in-your-cluster>]}
      - matchExpressions:
        - {key: kubernetes.io/hostname, operator: In, values: [nonexistent-node]}
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata: {name: nsrepro-claim}
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: req0
      exactly: {deviceClassName: nsrepro-class, allocationMode: ExactCount, count: 1}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: nsrepro-pod}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  resourceClaims: [{name: c, resourceClaimName: nsrepro-claim}]
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10, resources: {claims: [{name: c}]}}]
```

The ResourceSlice is accepted, confirming API validation does not reject the two-term per-device selector:

```text
deviceclass.resource.k8s.io/nsrepro-class created
resourceslice.resource.k8s.io/nsrepro-slice created
```

The Pod then stays `Pending`, and the scheduler reports it via the Pod event and the kube-scheduler log:

```text
# kubectl get event (Pod nsrepro-pod)
running "DynamicResources" filter plugin: create NodeSelector for claim nsrepro-claim: unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with 2 terms

# kube-scheduler log
E ... schedule_one.go:279] "Error selecting node for pod" err="running \"DynamicResources\" filter plugin: create NodeSelector for claim nsrepro-claim: unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with 2 terms" pod="default/nsrepro-pod"
E ... schedule_one.go:1243] "Error scheduling pod; retrying" err="..." logger="UnhandledError" pod="default/nsrepro-pod"
```

The `schedule_one.go:279` "Error selecting node for pod" path (rather than a node-local `Unschedulable` status), and the `UnhandledError` logger, confirm the failure aborts the scheduling cycle rather than filtering out one node.

### Anything else we need to know?

The primary fix appears to be enforcing the same exact-one-term constraint in the per-device validation path in `validateDevice`, plus a regression test in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation_resourceslice_test.go`.

For already-stored malformed ResourceSlices, update validation may need to ratchet an unchanged old `nodeSelector` value so that unrelated updates are not blocked. That update-compatibility detail can be handled in the fixing PR.

A defensive allocator change could also be considered for malformed objects that predate the validation fix, but it should not replace enforcement of the API invariant.

### Kubernetes version

Source references (`file:line`) are from master (commit `7f71d2e`). The runtime reproducer above was captured on a real cluster running v1.36.2, where `DRAPartitionableDevices` is Beta and enabled by default (since v1.36).

/kind bug
/sig scheduling
/wg device-management

title: DRA: allocator should fail closed (per-node) on a malformed ResourceSlice nodeSelector term count
body:
### What happened?

Follow-up to #141212 and #141213. The validation fix in #141213 stops a new or modified ResourceSlice from carrying a per-device `nodeSelector` whose term count is not exactly one. It ratchets the new constraint, so a slice with a multi-term selector that was stored before the fix, or accepted by an older API server during a version-skewed rolling upgrade, is still admitted on an unchanged update.

Those already-stored multi-term slices can still reach the structured allocator. `createNodeSelector` handles the term count like this:

- `len == 0`: no-op. This is not reachable through a normal allocation. `ValidateNodeSelector` already rejects a zero-term selector ("must have at least one node selector term"), and even a stored one matches no node, because `nodeaffinity`'s `Match` returns false when there are no terms, so `isSelectable` filters the device through `NodeMatches` before `createNodeSelector` runs. Rejecting zero terms here would be defense in depth, not a fix for a demonstrated available-everywhere allocation.
- `len == 1`: merged.
- `len > 1`: returns `fmt.Errorf("unsupported ResourceSlice.NodeSelector with %d terms", ...)`.

The `> 1` error is not wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so the DynamicResources Filter plugin treats it as a framework error rather than an `Unschedulable` result for that node. A framework error from Filter cancels the remaining node search and aborts the scheduling cycle, and it recurs on retry while the malformed slice stays in place. #141212 has a v1.36.2 reproducer.

There is also an ordering edge. `createNodeSelector` returns as soon as it sees a result with a `nodeName`, so a multi-term selector on a device that appears after a `nodeName` device is never inspected, while the same selector before it returns the hard error. Whether a malformed slice aborts the cycle therefore depends on result order.

### What did you expect to happen?

Admission-time validation cannot retroactively fix a slice that was already stored, and version skew lets an older API server accept one during an upgrade, so the allocator should degrade gracefully instead of aborting the scheduling cycle for the whole Pod.

Proposed change, in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants (or their shared source):

- Treat a term count greater than one as a classified per-node failure: return an error wrapped with `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`, so Filter reports `Unschedulable` for that node and keeps searching the rest.
- Check the term count for every selected result before the `nodeName` early return, so result order does not decide whether a malformed slice is caught.
- Optionally reject zero terms in the same place as defense in depth, even though the normal path filters it earlier.

Tests would assert that a more-than-one-term selector returns an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` with the malformed selector both before and after a `nodeName` device, and that a single term keeps its current behavior.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is intentionally kept out of #141213 to keep that admission fix small and reviewable during the v1.37 freeze. Linking here so the allocator gap is not lost when #141212 is closed by #141213.

/kind bug
/sig node

title: Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles CoreDNS v1.13.1 — 3 minor versions behind upstream v1.14.6, exposing clusters to 49+ known CVEs
body:
## Summary

Kubernetes v1.35.1 bundles `registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1` as the
default DNS provider. The upstream CoreDNS project has since released v1.14.6,
which addresses the vast majority of known vulnerabilities present in v1.13.1.

Since Kubernetes controls which CoreDNS version ships with each release, and
cluster administrators rely on the officially bundled version, we are requesting
that the CoreDNS version be bumped in an upcoming Kubernetes patch release.

/sig network
/area dns
/kind bug
/priority important-soon

## Environment

- **Kubernetes Version:** v1.35.1
- **Bundled CoreDNS:** registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.13.1
- **Latest Upstream CoreDNS:** v1.14.6
- **OS:** Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.0 (Coughlan)
- **Scanners:** Dependency-Track, Trivy

## Why This Matters

Cluster administrators installing Kubernetes v1.35.1 via kubeadm or other
official tooling receive CoreDNS v1.13.1 by default. Most organizations
rely on the officially bundled versions and do not independently upgrade
individual control plane components.

While it is technically possible to manually upgrade CoreDNS to v1.14.6,
this is:
- Not documented as a supported configuration for v1.35.1
- A burden on every individual cluster administrator rather than a fix at source

## Vulnerability Comparison: v1.13.1 vs v1.14.6

We scanned both versions to quantify the security impact.

| CVE-2026-26018 | HIGH | 1.14.2 | DoS via predictable PRNG |
| CVE-2026-32934 | HIGH | 1.14.3 | DoS due to unbounded resource growth |

## Remaining Vulnerabilities in v1.14.6

Even after upgrading to v1.14.6, a small number of issues remain. We are

title: CPU Manager incorrectly spans sockets with distribute-cpus-across-cores and align-by-socket enabled
body:
### What happened?

When using CPU Manager with `static` policy and both of the following options enabled:
- `distribute-cpus-across-cores=true` (distributes CPUs evenly across NUMA nodes)
- `align-by-socket=true` (prefers NUMA nodes within the same socket)

CPUs may be allocated across multiple sockets instead of staying within a single socket. This violates the socket affinity guarantee that `align-by-socket=true` is supposed to provide.

For example:
- Socket 0: NUMA 0-3 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 0: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 1: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 2: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 3: (30 CPUs available)

- Socket 1: NUMA 4-7 (126 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 4: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 5: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 6: (32 CPUs available)
  - NUMA 7: (30 CPUs available)

Result: CPUs are allocated from NUMA 0,1,3,6 across both sockets.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `align-by-socket=true`, the 120 CPUs should be allocated entirely from Socket 0 (NUMA 0,1,2,3) (which has 126 available CPUs).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Configure kubelet with:
--cpu-manager-policy=static
--cpu-manager-policy-options="distribute-cpus-across-cores=true,align-by-socket=true"

title: LimitRange maximum can be exceeded by declaring hugepages at the pod level
body:
### What happened?

A `LimitRange` of type `Pod` with a `max` for `hugepages-*` does not constrain a Pod that
declares its hugepages through pod-level resources (`spec.resources`). Such a Pod is admitted
even when its effective hugepages consumption exceeds the configured maximum.

The LimitRanger admission plugin keeps a private copy of the "is this a pod-level resource?"
predicate that lists only cpu and memory:

```go
// plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger/admission.go
var supportedPodLevelResources = sets.New(api.ResourceCPU, api.ResourceMemory)

func isSupportedPodLevelResource(name api.ResourceName) bool {
	return supportedPodLevelResources.Has(name)
}
```

The canonical predicate in component-helpers also matches the `hugepages-` prefix. Because of the
drift, `podRequests`/`podLimits` skip the pod-level override for hugepages and evaluate the
aggregated **container** values instead.

API validation explicitly permits the pod-level value to exceed the container aggregate (it only
rejects the reverse: "pod level limit for %s is insufficient to cover the aggregated container
and node-allocatable DRA limits"), so the two numbers can legitimately differ.

### What did you expect to happen?

The Pod-scoped `LimitRange` maximum should be enforced against the effective pod-level hugepages
value, the same way it is enforced when the value is written at container level.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Requires the `PodLevelResources` feature gate (Beta, on by default since 1.34).

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: hugepages-max
  namespace: demo
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Pod
      max:
        hugepages-2Mi: 4Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: over-the-limit
  namespace: demo
spec:
  resources:                 # pod-level: 8Gi, twice the LimitRange max
    requests:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
    limits:
      hugepages-2Mi: 8Gi
  containers:
    - name: c1
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
      resources:             # container aggregate stays within the max
        requests:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
        limits:
          hugepages-2Mi: 2Gi
```

Observed: the Pod is admitted.
Expected: rejected, as with `maximum hugepages-2Mi usage per Pod is 4Gi, but limit is 8Gi` -
which is exactly what happens if the same `8Gi` is written on the container instead.

Equivalent unit-level reproduction in `plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger`:

```go
err := PodValidateLimitFunc(&limitRange, &pod)  // returns nil; expected an error
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The duplicated helper carries a `TODO(ndixita): Find alternatives to avoid duplicating the code`
and a comment saying it exists "to avoid conversion of v1.Pod to api.Pod". That rationale does not
apply to this function - it takes only a resource name - so it can simply delegate to
`resourcehelper.IsSupportedPodLevelResource`.

The neighbouring duplicated helpers (`podRequests`, `podLimits`, `addResourceList`,
`maxResourceList`) carry the same TODO and are worth auditing for similar drift.

Found by source inspection plus a unit test at commit `b882c60b402` (v1.37.0-rc.0).

```console
# Affects any release where PodLevelResources is enabled (Beta / default-on since 1.34).
```

title: CPU manager exclusive allocation metrics drifts
body:
### What happened?

The static policy in CPU Manager maintains the `CPUManagerExclusiveCPUsAllocationCount` and `CPUManagerSharedPoolSizeMilliCores` gauges by applying per-event deltas, and updates `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` only for the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation. This drifts away from the actual allocation state in several scenarios:

1. Init container CPU reuse is double counted (container scope). When an app container reuses the CPUs of a non-restartable init container, `allocateCPUs` returns the full allocation including the reused CPUs, which stay assigned to the init container too. The allocation path adds the full size of both allocations, counting the reused CPUs twice. The release path correctly subtracts the sibling-adjusted sets, so after the pod is removed the gauge keeps a permanent positive residue equal to the number of reused CPUs. The shared pool gauge has the mirrored problem: the allocation delta subtracts CPUs which have never been taken out of the default CPU set.

2. Fresh allocations and restarts disagree. During a kubelet run the exclusive allocation gauge accumulates deltas with the duplicates described above, while after a restart `initializeMetrics` recomputes it as the union of the checkpointed assignments (no duplicates). The same node state can therefore report two different values before and after a kubelet restart.

3. Pod-level (pod scope) allocations can leak on partial failure. `allocatePodForAdd` updates the metrics and stores the pod-level CPU set, but a failure while partitioning the bubble among the containers (takeByTopology) returns an error without releasing anything: the bubble stays out of the default CPU set, the gauge stays inflated, and nothing can ever clean it up, because `RemoveContainer` returns early for a pod with no container assignments and `removeStaleState` only iterates over container assignments.

4. Pod-level releases can drift the gauge below the real value. `RemoveContainer` subtracts the whole pod-level CPU set when the last container assignment is removed, but after a kubelet restart `initializeMetrics` only accounts the union of the remaining container assignments, which is smaller than the bubble if some containers have already been removed before the restart. Releasing a pod which died while the kubelet was down then over-subtracts the difference.

5. `initializeMetrics` ignores the pod-level CPU sets. After a restart the gauge is seeded only from the container assignments, so the part of a pod-level bubble not covered by any container assignment is not counted, even though it is excluded from the default CPU set.

6. `CPUManagerAllocationPerNUMA` never drops back to zero. The update loop only writes the NUMA nodes present in the current allocation, so once the last exclusively allocated CPU of a node is released, the node keeps reporting its last non-zero value forever. The metric is also fed only with the container assignments, making a pod-level bubble invisible at allocation time, because the container assignments are stored later than the pod-level CPU set.

### What did you expect to happen?

Metrics always present valid current state of exclusive CPUs allocations.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The scenarios are described in issue.
They are also fully covered by unit tests.
Running unit tests without changes to the code will reveal the problems.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: [DRA] ResourceClaim controller can re-reserve terminal Pods
body:
### What happened?

The ResourceClaim controller can oscillate `status.reservedFor` when a terminal, already scheduled Pod still references an allocated static claim that remains in use by another Pod.

The controller has two conflicting paths:

1. `enqueuePod` recognizes a `Succeeded` or `Failed` Pod and queues each referenced claim so terminal reservations can be removed.
2. The same Pod can still satisfy `podNeedsWork` when `spec.nodeName` is set and its allocated claim no longer reserves it.
3. `syncPod` then enters the pre-scheduled-Pod path and restores the terminal Pod's consumer reference.

The claim cleanup path removes that reference again. Under sustained reconciliation this produces repeated `ResourceClaim/status` writes and conflicts while the static allocation remains valid for another consumer.

A manually managed static ResourceClaim shared by multiple Pods is a documented DRA use case; the terminal consumer should be cleanup-only rather than re-reserved.

### What did you expect to happen?

A terminal Pod must never be added or restored to `ResourceClaim.status.reservedFor`.

Claim work should still be enqueued so an existing terminal-Pod reservation is removed. The Pod itself should not be queued for reservation work, and `syncPod` should be safe if an already queued terminal Pod reaches it.

### How can we reproduce it?

A controller unit test can reproduce this with:

1. An allocated, manually managed ResourceClaim.
2. One nonterminal Pod already present in `status.reservedFor`, keeping the allocation live.
3. A second Pod which:
   - references the same claim;
   - has `spec.nodeName` set;
   - is `Succeeded` or `Failed`; and
   - is absent from `status.reservedFor` because cleanup already ran.
4. Sync the terminal Pod key.

On current behavior, the terminal Pod is appended to `reservedFor`. The expected claim status contains only the live consumer.

The minimal correction is to exclude terminal Pods from `podNeedsWork` and to make `syncPod` return before any reservation work. `enqueuePod` already queues referenced claims for terminal-Pod cleanup before applying the Pod work predicate.

### Anything else we need to know?

This was observed as a control-plane hot loop rather than a one-time stale status. A focused regression test fails against Kubernetes `v1.36.2` by showing the extra terminal consumer and passes with the terminal-Pod guard. The complete `pkg/controller/resourceclaim` unit-test package also passes with that correction.

The status field is maintained by Kubernetes core; no DRA vendor-driver behavior is required to reproduce the controller interaction.

/sig node
/kind bug

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.36.2+k3s1
```

The relevant ResourceClaim controller paths were also still present in current upstream source when checked on 2026-08-08.

title: compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test always fails since the 1.37 cut: validator ignores MinCompatibilityVersion
body:
**What happened**:

The periodic job [`ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test`](https://prow.k8s.io/?job=ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test) has failed on every run since 2026-08-06 12:48 UTC. The failure rate is 100 percent.

The validator reports one failure:

```
Validating features for emulated_version=1.37, current_version=1.38...
FAIL: feature 'DRAFractionalCapacityRange' expected value 1, got 0
```

The trigger is the release-1.37 branch cut, not a code change. The `v1.37.0-rc.0` tag moved master from `v1.37.0-beta.0` to `v1.38.0-alpha.0`. That shifted the version pair the job validates:

| | Build | Time (UTC) | k/k SHA | Validated pair |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Last green | [2085330939616956416](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416) | 2026-08-06 11:45 | `4f5591ab57b` | emulated 1.36, current 1.37 |
| First red | [2085346290606018560](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560) | 2026-08-06 12:48 | `b882c60b402` | emulated 1.37, current 1.38 |

The commit window holds one commit, `b882c60b402 CHANGELOG: Update directory for v1.37.0-rc.0 release`. It changes only CHANGELOG files, so it is not the cause.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is absent from the `release-1.36` reference list. The job therefore never checked the gate before the cut.

**Root cause**

The kubelet and the control plane report the correct value. The validator expects the wrong one.

`pkg/features/kube_features.go` declares two specs at the same version:

```go
DRAFractionalCapacityRange: {
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
	{Version: version.MustParse("1.37"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta, MinCompatibilityVersion: version.MustParse("1.37")},
},
```

`SetEmulationVersion` sets the minimum compatibility version to `emulated - 1`. See `staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/featuregate/feature_gate.go`. The job passes only `--emulated-version=1.37`, so the minimum compatibility version is 1.36. The second spec needs 1.37 or higher. The runtime therefore selects the first spec and reports `0`. This matches the documented behavior of `MinCompatibilityVersion` and the plan in kubernetes/kubernetes#140594, which schedules the on-by-default promotion for 1.38.

Two problems in the tooling make the validator disagree:

1. The generator `test/compatibility_lifecycle/cmd/feature_gates.go` in kubernetes/kubernetes does not write `minCompatibilityVersion` into `versioned_feature_list.yaml`. In that file the two specs differ only in `default`, so no consumer can tell them apart.

   ```yaml
   - name: DRAFractionalCapacityRange
     versionedSpecs:
     - default: false
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
     - default: true
       lockToDefault: false
       preRelease: Beta
       version: "1.37"
   ```

2. `get_target_spec` in `experiment/compatibility-versions/versioned_specs_util.sh` takes `last` of the matching specs. It selects the `default: true` spec and expects `1`.

`DRAFractionalCapacityRange` is the only feature in kubernetes/kubernetes that uses `MinCompatibilityVersion`. That is why the problem appears now.

**What you expected to happen**:

The job passes. The validator selects the spec that applies at the minimum compatibility version the job actually runs with.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

```bash
SPECS='[{"default":false,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"},
        {"default":true,"lockToDefault":false,"preRelease":"Beta","version":"1.37"}]'

# current get_target_spec behavior
echo "$SPECS" | jq -r --arg ver 1.37 \
  '[ .[] | select((.version|tonumber) <= ($ver|tonumber)) ] | last | .default'
# => true   (validator expects 1)

# what the control plane reports at --emulated-version=1.37
# kubernetes_feature_enabled{name="DRAFractionalCapacityRange",stage="BETA"} 0
```

**Please provide links to example occurrences, if any**:

- First red build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085346290606018560
- Last green build: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test/2085330939616956416
- TestGrid tab: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-api-machinery-emulated-version#compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test

Of the 229 builds still in GCS, 150 passed and 79 failed. Every pass is before the boundary. Every failure is after it. No build interleaves, so this is not a flake.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Control that isolates the cause.** The job `ci-kubernetes-e2e-kind-compatibility-versions-feature-gate-test-n-2` runs the same validator against the same master build, but it validates emulated 1.36 against current 1.38. It stays green. The break is specific to the 1.37 spec pair.

**Suggested fix, in two parts.**

Part 1 clears CI. Change `get_target_spec` to take the first spec at the highest matching version instead of the last. That selects the spec that applies at the default minimum compatibility version.

```jq
[ .[] | select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) <= ($ver|sub("^v";"")|tonumber)) ] as $c
| ($c | map(.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) | max) as $m
| ($c | map(select((.version|sub("^v";"")|tonumber) == $m)) | first)
```

I checked this against normal features at 1.31, 1.33 and 1.35. The result does not change. The result changes only when two specs share a version.

This part is necessary, not only convenient. The `release-1.37` reference list is frozen. It will never carry `minCompatibilityVersion`. The validator must therefore fall back to first-wins for the 1.37 pair whatever else changes.

Part 2 prevents the next occurrence. Write `minCompatibilityVersion` from the kubernetes/kubernetes generator, then compare against it in the validator for 1.38 and later.

**Related.** This validator has missed a feature gate lifecycle pattern twice before. See kubernetes/test-infra#34396 and kubernetes/test-infra#35179. Expect the problem to return at the 1.38 cut if the gate is promoted per kubernetes/kubernetes#140594 without matching validator work.

Owner is SIG API Machinery. The alert address on the job is `compatibility-version-test@google.com`. Feature owners are @sunya-ch and @pohly.

title: MemoryQoS: add effective-state conformance coverage
body:
/sig node

While validating MemoryQoS in Netflix's Kubernetes and cgroup v2 environment, we found that checking the configured feature and reservation policy alone was not sufficient to establish the effective runtime state. A configuration change can be accepted while existing workloads retain their previously materialized cgroup controls until a workload lifecycle event occurs.

MemoryQoS already has node-e2e coverage for protection, throttling, configuration changes, and rollback behavior. Operators still need to correlate three layers when verifying the feature:

1. the final admitted Pod resource shape;
2. the deployed kubelet MemoryQoS configuration;
3. the effective cgroup v2 controls on the running Pod and container.

The individual controls are tested, but there is no single conformance check that derives the expected Pod/container state and compares all relevant controls with the effective cgroup state. Missing read-back evidence should also be distinguishable from a real mismatch.

I have a draft change that adds a small conformance helper with explicit `FULFILLED`, `DRIFTED`, and `INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE` results, plus a node-e2e scenario for a Burstable Pod that validates `memory.min`, `memory.low`, `memory.high`, and `memory.max` at both Pod and container scope.

Would SIG Node consider this useful coverage for KEP-2570, and is `test/e2e_node/memory_qos_test.go` the preferred home?

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos
