title: [Bug] Device taint NoExecute eviction does not evict pods using DRA-backed extended-resource claims (pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus)
body:
### What happened?

**TL;DR:** the device-taint eviction controller (`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction`) only discovers which
claims a pod is using by reading `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. A pod that got its device through the newer
Extended Resource Backed by DRA path (KEP-5004, `DRAExtendedResource`) has its claim reference in
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus` instead — a field this controller never looks at. Both
`DRADeviceTaints` and `DRAExtendedResource` are Beta and **default-on since v1.36**, so this affects any
cluster running a stock 1.36+ apiserver/controller-manager with a DRA driver installed — no unusual
configuration required.

Live-reproduced on a `kind` cluster (full steps and output below): two pods, each holding one device from the
same driver, then a single `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` applied against that driver:

| Pod | Requests its device via | Claim reference lives in | Result after `NoExecute` taint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pod-to-be-evicted` | `ResourceClaimTemplate` | `pod.spec.resourceClaims` | Evicted within ~10s (correct) |
| `pod0` | plain `resources.limits` extended-resource request | `pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus` | **Still `Running`, untouched** — the bug |

The `DeviceTaintRule`'s own status confirms only one pod was ever considered:
`"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace"` → `"1 pod evicted since starting the controller"`.

**Scope note, to save a maintainer the round-trip:** this is specifically about the *post-allocation eviction*
path. Allocation-time taint enforcement (a **new** pod being blocked from a `NoSchedule`/`NoExecute`-tainted
device it doesn't tolerate) is unaffected and works correctly for both request styles. The bug is
narrowly in the separate, already-allocated-pod eviction controller.

**Couple of affected use cases**
- GPU health-triggered auto-remediation. A node-health/GPU-health controller (e.g. something reacting to Xid/ECC errors, similar in spirit to NVIDIA GPU Operator's health checks) detects a failing GPU and applies a NoExecute DeviceTaintRule to force workloads off it before quarantining or repairing the device. Any pod still using the classic nvidia.com/gpu: 1-style request — which is the majority of existing GPU workloads, since KEP-5004's entire purpose is letting them keep working unmodified under DRA — is never evicted, and keeps running on a known-bad GPU instead of being cleanly rescheduled. Worst case: silently corrupted training/inference output rather than a clean failure.
- Targeted single-device maintenance on a multi-GPU node. An admin wants to service or replace one GPU on a node without draining the whole node (disruptive to the node's other GPUs/workloads), so they taint just that device NoExecute instead of cordoning the node. Any pod holding that device via an extended-resource request keeps running through the "drain," so the device can't actually be safely pulled for maintenance without an admin separately hunting down and manually killing those pods — defeating the point of device-level (vs. node-level) maintenance tooling.
- Clusters mid-migration from device plugins to DRA. KEP-5004 exists specifically so clusters can adopt DRA drivers without immediately rewriting every pod spec — meaning a long transitional period where legacy extended-resource-requesting Deployments/Jobs and newer ResourceClaim-based workloads coexist on the same devices. During that period, any device-taint-based enforcement (decommissioning a device, isolating a suspect one) only works for the already-migrated minority of workloads, silently failing for everyone else — undermining the mechanism cluster-wide for as long as the migration takes, which for large fleets could be months.

### What did you expect to happen?

A `NoExecute` device taint should evict every pod actually consuming the tainted device, independent of which
API surface the pod used to request it. An admin tainting a failing/draining GPU for maintenance has no way to
know (and shouldn't need to know) whether a given consumer pod requested it via a `ResourceClaim` or via a
classic `resources.limits` extended-resource request — both end up running on the same physical device via
the same DRA driver and the same underlying `ResourceClaim` object. Today only one of the two is actually
evicted.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducible deterministically on a `kind` cluster with no real GPU hardware, using
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) (a maintained,
public example DRA driver that simulates GPUs). All manifests below are the driver's own unmodified example
manifests (`demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/` and
`demo/examples/extended-resource-request/`), just applied side by side.

**Prerequisites:** Docker, `kind` v0.20+, `helm` v3.7+, `kubectl`.

```bash
# 1. Create a kind cluster with the required feature gates and API version.
#    (DynamicResourceAllocation and DRAAdminAccess are already GA/locked-on by v1.36 and are
#    omitted; DRADeviceTaints/DRAExtendedResource are Beta+default-on in 1.36 but included
#    explicitly for clarity; DRADeviceTaintRules is Beta+default-OFF in 1.36 and must be set.)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  DRADeviceTaints: true
  DRAExtendedResource: true
  DRADeviceTaintRules: true
runtimeConfig:
  resource.k8s.io/v1beta2: "true"
containerdConfigPatches:
- |-
  [plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri"]
    enable_cdi = true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name dra-repro --image kindest/node:v1.36.1 --config kind-config.yaml --wait 3m

# 2. Install the example DRA driver (8 simulated GPUs, no real hardware, default values).
git clone --depth 1 --branch v0.4.0 https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver.git
helm upgrade -i --create-namespace --namespace dra-example-driver dra-example-driver \
  dra-example-driver/deployments/helm/dra-example-driver
kubectl -n dra-example-driver wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app.kubernetes.io/component=kubeletplugin --timeout=90s

# 3. Control pod: requests a GPU via a ResourceClaimTemplate (pod.spec.resourceClaims).
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/1-basic-resourceclaimtemplate.yaml
kubectl apply -f dra-example-driver/demo/examples/device-taints-tolerations/device-taint-pod-noexecute/2-pod-to-be-evicted.yaml
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod-to-be-evicted --timeout=60s

# 4. Treatment pod: requests a GPU via the classic extended-resource field. The scheduler
#    satisfies it via DRA and records the claim in pod.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus instead
#    of pod.spec.resourceClaims (confirmed with the jsonpath check below).
kubectl create namespace extended-resource-request
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: extended-resource-request
  name: pod0
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ctr0
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["export; trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
    resources:
      limits:
        deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com: 1
EOF
kubectl -n extended-resource-request wait --for=condition=Ready pod/pod0 --timeout=60s
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}{"\n"}'

# 5. Taint the whole driver's devices NoExecute — both pods' devices are in scope.
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta2
kind: DeviceTaintRule
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  deviceSelector:
    driver: gpu.example.com
  taint:
    key: gpu.example.com/unhealthy
    value: "true"
    effect: NoExecute
EOF

# 6. Observe.
sleep 15
kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted   # expect: NotFound (evicted+deleted)
kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide           # expect: still Running
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='{.status.extendedResourceClaimStatus}'
{"requestMappings":[{"containerName":"ctr0","requestName":"container-0-request-0",
"resourceName":"deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/gpu.example.com"}],
"resourceClaimName":"pod0-extended-resources-v77pc"}

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o jsonpath='spec.resourceClaims={.spec.resourceClaims}'
spec.resourceClaims=

$ kubectl apply -f device-taint-rule.yaml
devicetaintrule.resource.k8s.io/example created

$ kubectl get devicetaintrule example -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'
# immediately after creation:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:42Z","message":"1 pod needs to be evicted in 1 namespace.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"PodsPendingEviction","status":"True","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

# ~10s later:
[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-08-10T07:34:52Z","message":"1 pod evicted since starting the controller.",
"observedGeneration":1,"reason":"Completed","status":"False","type":"EvictionInProgress"}]

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get pod pod-to-be-evicted
Error from server (NotFound): pods "pod-to-be-evicted" not found

$ kubectl -n basic-resourceclaimtemplate get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -3
28s   Normal   DeviceTaintManagerEviction   pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Marking for deletion
28s   Normal   Killing                      pod/pod-to-be-evicted   Stopping container ctr0

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get pod pod0 -o wide
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
pod0   1/1     Running   0          69s   dra-repro-worker

$ kubectl -n extended-resource-request get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
# Scheduled / Pulled / Created / Started only — zero eviction-related events, ever.

$ kubectl get resourceclaim -A
NAMESPACE                   NAME                            STATE
extended-resource-request   pod0-extended-resources-v77pc   allocated,reserved
# (pod-to-be-evicted's generated claim is gone — cleaned up along with the deleted pod)
```

Only one of the two pods using tainted devices from the same driver was ever evicted. This reproduces every
time; there is no timing dependency.


### Anything else we need to know?

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`;
live-reproduced above on `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (closest publicly available `kind` node image to `v1.36.3` at
time of testing — same code, confirmed by reading).

**1. The eviction controller enumerates claims from exactly one field.**

`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go`, `podEvictionTime`
([current source](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go)),
is the *only* place this controller determines which claims a pod uses:

```go
func (tc *Controller) podEvictionTime(pod *v1.Pod) *evictionAndReason {
    if pod.Spec.NodeName == "" {
        return nil
    }
    var eviction *evictionAndReason
    for i := range pod.Spec.ResourceClaims {
        claimName, mustCheckOwner, err := resourceclaim.Name(pod, &pod.Spec.ResourceClaims[i])
        ...
    }
    return eviction
}
```

Grepping the full 1691-line file for `ExtendedResource` returns zero matches, on both the tag and master.

**2. The sibling `resourceclaim` controller already had to solve this exact problem.**

`pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go`, `enqueuePod`:

```go
// Check if pod has any resource claims to process.
// Extended resource claims are stored in pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus,
// not in pod.Spec.ResourceClaims, so we need to check both locations.
hasResourceClaims := len(pod.Spec.ResourceClaims) > 0
hasExtendedResourceClaims := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus != nil
...
// Without this, extended resource claims would never be cleaned up when
// pods complete, causing device resources to remain allocated indefinitely.
if hasExtendedResourceClaims {
    claimName := pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName
    ...
}
```

The device-taint eviction controller never received the equivalent treatment.

**3. Both contributing feature gates are Beta and default-on as of this release**
(`pkg/features/kube_features.go`):

```go
DRADeviceTaints: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.33"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
DRAExtendedResource: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
},
```

So this isn't an edge-case opt-in combination — it's the default state of a stock 1.36+ cluster with any DRA
driver and `DeviceTaintRule` usage.

**4. No test coverage exercises this interaction.** `test/integration/dra/device_taints.go` and
`pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction_test.go` (2926 lines) both have zero hits for
`ExtendedResource`.

**5. Allocation-time taint enforcement is unaffected (see "Scope note" above)** —
`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`,
`taintPreventsAllocation`, is reached identically for extended-resource and explicit-claim requests, since
`extendeddynamicresources.go` builds an in-memory claim for the extended-resource path before `Filter` runs.
Included here to preempt the natural "does this mean extended-resource claims ignore taints entirely?"
question — they don't; only post-allocation `NoExecute` eviction is blind.

### Suggested fix direction

Mirror the `resourceclaim` controller's dual-location check into `podEvictionTime` — i.e. also resolve
`pod.Status.ExtendedResourceClaimStatus.ResourceClaimName` when present, using the same claim lookup/ownership
logic already used for `pod.Spec.ResourceClaims`. This looks like a contained, well-scoped fix; happy to
attempt a PR once a maintainer confirms this is the intended approach (rather than, say, deprecating the
implicit extended-resource path's exemption from eviction on purpose — which seems unlikely given point 2
above, but worth confirming).



### Kubernetes version

<details>
Live reproduction (above): `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream via `kind`. Code paths involved confirmed
identical at tag `v1.36.3` (latest stable at time of this report) and master HEAD
`94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f` by direct source comparison.
</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
None — plain `kind` (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster.
</details>


### OS version

<details>
Whatever the `kind` node image ships (containerized, not relevant to this bug).
</details>


### Install tools

<details>
`kind` v0.32.0, Helm v3.7+ (for the example driver chart).
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd (as shipped in the `kind` node image), with `enable_cdi = true` (required by the example DRA
driver to advertise its simulated devices via CDI).
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
[kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0 — a
maintained, public example/reference DRA driver used purely to simulate GPU devices with no real hardware
dependency. Not specific to this driver: the bug is entirely in core `kube-controller-manager` code and would
reproduce identically with any DRA driver.
</details>

title: [Bug] Non-admin users can self-escalate to DRA device adminAccess by labeling their own namespace (no RBAC check on the capability itself)
body:
**TL;DR:** requesting `adminAccess: true` on a DRA device request only checks whether the containing
namespace carries the label `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`. It does **not** check whether the
*creating principal* has any elevated permission. `DRAAdminAccess` is GA and locked-on by default since v1.36,
so this is the live behavior of any stock cluster today.

**Self-escalation, verified live (details withheld here — see note at the end).** A principal holding only:
- ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` (needed to use DRA at
  all), and
- `get`/`patch` on exactly *one* `Namespace` object, by name, via `resourceNames` — a narrow, realistic
  self-service pattern many platforms grant so app teams can manage their own namespace's labels/annotations
  (chargeback tags, network-policy selectors, etc.), confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to grant **no**
  access to any other namespace and **no** unscoped `namespaces` access,

was able to label its own namespace with `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` and immediately have a
`ResourceClaim` with `adminAccess: true` accepted — a claim that had been rejected moments earlier with the
identical spec, before the namespace was labeled. No cluster-admin, no cluster-wide `namespaces` access, no
help from any other actor. This user granted *themselves* a capability that "ignores all ordinary claims to
the device with respect to access modes" (direct quote from the field's own doc comment), using a permission
scope that has nothing to do with device access and that many clusters already hand out for unrelated
self-service reasons.

**Baseline confirmation (no elevated permission of any kind).** Before the self-escalation test above, the
same claim was tried with *zero* `namespaces` access at all: a `ServiceAccount` bound to a `Role` granting
only ordinary `create/get/list/watch/delete` on `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — successfully
created the identical `adminAccess: true` claim in a namespace someone else had already labeled, and was
rejected with the exact same spec in an otherwise identical, unlabeled namespace:

| Namespace | Principal's RBAC | `adminAccess: true` claim |
|---|---|---|
| `admin-labeled` (pre-labeled by someone else) | create/get/list/watch/delete on `resourceclaims` only | **Created successfully** |
| `admin-unlabeled` (no label) | identical | Rejected: `Forbidden: admin access to devices requires the ` `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` ` label on the containing namespace` |
| `admin-unlabeled`, **after** the same principal is given narrow self-service `get`/`patch` on just that one namespace and labels it themselves | unchanged claim-related RBAC, +self-service namespace-metadata edit only | **Created successfully — self-escalation** |

**Contrast with the two other authorization checks in the same file.** `pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`
contains three related checks. Two of them go through the real authorizer against a dedicated synthetic
subresource:

```go
// AuthorizedForBinding checks if the caller is authorized to update
// status.allocation and status.reservedFor by verifying permission on the
// synthetic resourceclaims/binding subresource.
func AuthorizedForBinding(ctx context.Context, fieldPath *field.Path, authz authorizer.Authorizer, ...) field.ErrorList {
    ...
    attrs := &syntheticSubresourceAttrs{
        Attributes:  baseAttrs,
        subresource: resourcev1.SubresourceBinding,
        ...
    }
    if err := checkAuthorization(ctx, authz, attrs); err != nil { ... }
}
```

`AuthorizedForDeviceStatus` follows the same pattern against a `resourceclaims/driver`-style subresource. The
third — `AuthorizedForAdmin` — does not:

```go
// AuthorizedForAdmin checks if the request is authorized to get admin access to devices
// based on namespace label
func AuthorizedForAdmin(ctx context.Context, deviceRequests []resource.DeviceRequest, namespaceName string, nsClient v1.NamespaceInterface) field.ErrorList {
    ...
    ns, err := nsClient.Get(ctx, namespaceName, metav1.GetOptions{})
    ...
    if ns.Labels[resource.DRAAdminNamespaceLabelKey] != "true" {
        return append(allErrs, field.Forbidden(adminAccessPath, ...))
    }
    return allErrs
}
```

No `authorizer.Authorizer` call, no synthetic subresource — just a label read.

### What did you expect to happen?

One of two things, either of which would close this gap:

- `adminAccess` is gated the same way `binding`/`driver` status updates already are — a real RBAC check
  against a dedicated synthetic subresource (e.g. `resourceclaims/adminaccess`), so a cluster operator can
  scope *who* is allowed to request it independently of namespace labeling; or
- if the namespace-label design is intentional (e.g. because whoever can label a namespace is assumed to
  already be a namespace-level admin), that assumption does not hold up — see "Self-escalation" above.
  Ordinary `get`/`patch` on *one's own* `Namespace` object, scoped via `resourceNames` (a narrow self-service
  pattern, not "namespace-level admin" in any broad sense), is sufficient to set the label and immediately
  self-grant `adminAccess`. If the label-based design is kept, setting this *specific* label should require a
  permission distinct from ordinary namespace-metadata editing (which RBAC cannot currently express, since
  `namespaces` `patch`/`update` has no per-label-key granularity) — which argues for moving the check to a
  real subresource-based authorization instead.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducible deterministically on any `kind` cluster running v1.36+ with `DynamicResourceAllocation` and a
`DeviceClass` available (no real hardware or even a functioning driver required — this check happens at
`ResourceClaim` admission time, before any scheduling/allocation is attempted). General shape (exact manifests
and command transcript intentionally not included here — see closing note):

1. Two otherwise-identical namespaces, only one carrying `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true`.
2. An ordinary principal in each namespace, granted only `create/get/list/watch/delete` on
   `resourceclaims`/`resourceclaimtemplates` — confirmed via `kubectl auth can-i` to have no other permission
   (no `namespaces` access, no access to the real RBAC-protected `resourceclaims/binding` or
   `resourceclaims/status` subresources).
3. The identical `adminAccess: true` `ResourceClaim` attempted by that principal in both namespaces — succeeds
   only in the labeled one, confirming the label (not any RBAC permission) is the sole gate.
4. Follow-up: that same principal is then granted exactly one additional, narrow permission — `get`/`patch`
   on *only its own* `Namespace` object, by name — confirmed via `can-i` to grant nothing else (not access to
   any other namespace, not unscoped `namespaces` access). Using only that permission, the principal labels
   its own namespace and immediately passes the same check that had just rejected it — full self-escalation,
   with no cluster-admin or cluster-wide `namespaces` access involved anywhere.

This reproduces every time, has no timing dependency, and does not depend on the specific DRA driver used
(verified with a public example driver simulating GPUs — no real hardware needed).

**Sample output showing the baseline rejection (safe to share, does not enable exploitation on its own):**

```
$ kubectl -n admin-unlabeled apply -f claim.yaml --as=<ordinary-principal-with-no-namespaces-access>
The ResourceClaim "admin-claim" is invalid: spec.devices.requests[0].adminAccess: Forbidden: admin access to
devices requires the `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: true` label on the containing namespace
```

The full transcript showing the subsequent self-escalation (labeling the namespace, then the same claim
succeeding) is withheld from this public issue — see the note at the end.

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against tag `v1.36.3` and confirmed unchanged at master HEAD `94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f`;
live-verified on `kindest/node:v1.36.1`.

**1. `AuthorizedForAdmin`** (`pkg/registry/resource/utils.go`) — the check under discussion, shown in full
above. Invoked from `resourceclaimStrategy.Validate` on every `ResourceClaim` create
(`pkg/registry/resource/resourceclaim/strategy.go`) and the equivalent path for `ResourceClaimTemplate`.

**2. `AuthorizedForBinding` and `AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`**, same file — both go through
`authorizer.Authorizer` against a dedicated synthetic subresource (`resourceclaims/binding`,
`resourceclaims/driver`-style attributes respectively). These are the pattern `AuthorizedForAdmin` doesn't
follow.

**3. `DRAAdminAccess` feature-gate history** (`pkg/features/kube_features.go`):

```go
DRAAdminAccess: {
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.32"), Default: false, PreRelease: featuregate.Alpha},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.34"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.Beta},
    {Version: version.MustParse("1.36"), Default: true, PreRelease: featuregate.GA, LockToDefault: true}, // GA in 1.36; remove in 1.39
},
```

GA and `LockToDefault: true` since v1.36 — this is the permanent, non-optional behavior of the API going
forward, not something a cluster operator can currently disable even if they wanted to while a fix lands.

**4. What `adminAccess` actually grants**, per its own doc comment (`pkg/apis/resource/types.go`): it "ignores
all ordinary claims to the device with respect to access modes" — i.e. it's explicitly a
privilege-escalation-shaped capability (bypassing normal exclusivity/access restrictions on a device), which
is exactly the kind of thing the project already has a pattern (`AuthorizedForBinding`/`AuthorizedForDeviceStatus`)
for gating properly.

**5. Defaulting itself is safe** — `AdminAccess` is a `*bool`; unset/false means disabled, so there's no
fail-open default. The gap is specifically in the enforcement mechanism for the "true" case.

### Why this matters in practice

Two distinct real-world paths to the same outcome, in increasing order of how deliberate they need to be:

1. **Self-escalation (verified live above, the more serious path).** Any user with the narrow, common
   self-service permission to edit their own namespace's metadata — a pattern many platforms grant precisely
   so app teams don't need a ticket to add their own labels/annotations — can grant *themselves*
   `adminAccess` on demand, with zero involvement from any other actor. To be precise about what this
   permission is *not*: it isn't equivalent to cluster-admin or even namespace-admin — it grants nothing
   beyond editing metadata on that one `Namespace` object. But it is fair to say that, given this bug,
   granting it implicitly and silently also grants the DRA `adminAccess` capability for that namespace — a
   completely separate, undocumented capability the grantor never chose to hand out and most likely doesn't
   know exists. RBAC gives the grantor no way to decouple "edit your own namespace's labels" from "grant DRA
   device-privilege bypass in that namespace," since there is no per-label-key permission to withhold just
   the one label that matters.

2. **Incidental exposure via unrelated automation.** The namespace label is otherwise settable by anyone with
   plain `namespaces` `update`/`patch` RBAC, which in real clusters is often held more broadly still — GitOps
   reconcilers, PSA/Istio sidecar-injection automation — none of whom are necessarily making a considered
   decision to grant every current and future claim-creator in that namespace a device-privilege-escalation
   capability. Once labeled for any reason (including an unrelated automation reusing the same key by
   coincidence, or a namespace labeled once and never revisited), every principal with ordinary claim-create
   rights in that namespace silently gains `adminAccess` with no further signal, audit trail, or independent
   permission check.

Path 1 is the one to lead with when discussing severity — it doesn't require any misconfiguration or
carelessness, just a permission grant that is common, reasonable, and completely unrelated to device access
on its face.

### A note on what's not included here

The exact RBAC manifests and full `kubectl` command transcript that demonstrate the self-escalation
end-to-end have intentionally been left out of this public issue, to avoid publishing a ready-to-run
privilege-escalation script while this is unpatched. Everything needed to understand, locate, and fix the
underlying gap is above. Happy to provide the full reproduction (manifests + transcript) privately — already
shared with security@kubernetes.io — to any SIG Auth/SIG Node approver or Security Response Committee member
working this issue; just ask.

### Kubernetes version

<details>
Live reproduction: `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream via `kind`. Code paths involved confirmed
identical at tag `v1.36.3` (latest stable at time of this report) and master HEAD
`94c136764292cc5fac976c0de6587daaea56410f` by direct source comparison. `DRAAdminAccess` is GA since v1.36.
</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>
None — plain `kind` (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster.
</details>

### OS version

<details>
Whatever the `kind` node image ships (containerized, not relevant to this bug).
</details>

### Install tools

<details>
`kind` v0.32.0.
</details>

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd (as shipped in the `kind` node image).
</details>

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
A public example DRA driver (kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) — used only to provide a real
`DeviceClass` for the claim to reference. Not specific to this driver: the check under discussion runs
entirely in `kube-apiserver`'s registry/admission code, before any driver involvement, and would reproduce
identically with any DRA driver or even a `DeviceClass` with no working driver at all.
</details>

title: CVE-2026-19444: kubectl cp path traversal on Windows allows arbitrary file writes
body:
**CVSS Rating:** [CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:H/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:A/AC:L/PR:H/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N) - Medium (6.5)

### Description of vulnerability

A path traversal vulnerability exists in the `kubectl cp` command when it is run on Windows. `kubectl cp` copies files between containers and the user machine. To copy files *from* a container, Kubernetes runs `tar` inside the container to create a tar archive, copies it over the network, and `kubectl` unpacks it on the user's machine. If the `tar` binary in the container is malicious, it could run any code and output unexpected, malicious results.

An attacker who controls the contents of a container could use this to write files to arbitrary paths on the user's machine when `kubectl cp` is called, limited only by the system permissions of the local user. This issue only affects clients on Windows platforms.

### Am I vulnerable?

You are affected if you run the `kubectl` client on Windows and use `kubectl cp` to copy files *from* a container whose contents you do not fully control.

To determine whether your `kubectl` client is an affected version, run:

```shell
kubectl version --client
```

### Affected Versions

- kubectl v1.34.0 to v1.34.11
- kubectl v1.35.0 to v1.35.8
- kubectl v1.36.0 to v1.36.4

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by only copying files from containers you trust, or by avoiding `kubectl cp` from untrusted containers on Windows.

### Fixed Versions

- kubectl >= v1.34.12
- kubectl >= v1.35.9
- kubectl >= v1.36.5

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact [security@kubernetes.io](mailto:security@kubernetes.io)

### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by Moriel Harush @MorielHarush

The issue was fixed and coordinated by:
Marly Salazar @mpuckett159 
Maciej Szulik @soltysh 
Vyom Yadav @Vyom-Yadav

title: Succeeded pods cause incorrect HPA calculation
body:
### What happened?

Pods in a terminal `Succeeded` state are not excluded from HPA calculations. In most cases, data is unavailable, so they enter `missingPods`. The handling of `missingPods` means that when there are sufficient pods in `Succeeded` states they can damp out scaling.

Although pods controlled by replicasets are generally deleted upon termination rather than staying around in a terminal state, there are cases where `Succeeded` pods may be preserved. One notable example is the behavior noted in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118310, where node pressure eviction etc. can lead to pods transitioning to `Succeeded`.

This issue caused one of our workloads to have its HPA de-facto pinned to a fixed replica count for over a day despite usage varying widely (above and below) the target. Deletion of `Succeeded` pods caused normal expected scaling behavior to resume on the following reconciliation.

Elaboration on our specific case, and why it caused HPA replicas to be effectively pinned, can be found in the reproduction steps.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pods in a terminal phase should not participate in HPA replica calculations.

`Succeeded` pods should be treated similarly to deleted and `Failed` pods and [be ignored in HPA calculations](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L427-L430), especially when they have no resource metrics.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Inspection of the referenced code will make the issue clear.

As a concrete example, take this case which is derived from our observation in production:

Configure the calculator with:
- `currentReplicas = 24`
- CPU target `targetUsage = 1000m`
- 24 Ready and Running Pods with metrics
- 52 Succeeded Pods with `deletionTimestamp = nil`
- No metrics for the Succeeded Pods

`AverageValue` resource metrics enter `GetRawResourceReplicas` [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L596-L613)
The calculator [lists every Pod matching the scale target selector](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L193-L204)
`groupPods()` [ignores deleting and Failed Pods, but not Succeeded Pods](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L409-L427). The 52 Succeeded Pods therefore enter `missingPods`
#### Downscale case
Give each Running Pod a metric value of `600m`.
The initial ratio, calculated from the 24 metric-bearing Pods, is:
    r = 600 / 1000 = 0.6

Because this indicates a downscale, each missing Pod is [assigned the target value](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L226-L231) of `1000m`
The recalculated ratio is approximately:
    q = (24 * 600 + 52 * 1000) / (76 * 1000)
      = 0.874
The calculated replica count is approximately:
    ceil(q * 76) = 67

The ratio indicates a downscale, but `67` is greater than `currentReplicas=24`. The [consistency check returns 24](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L247-L259)

Expected raw proposal if Succeeded Pods were ignored:
    ceil(24 * 0.6) = 15
Actual proposal:
    24

#### Scale-up case
Give each Running Pod a metric value of `2000m`.
The initial ratio is:
    r = 2000 / 1000 = 2.0

Because this indicates a [scale-up, each missing Pod is assigned zero](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L232-L237)
The recalculated ratio is:
    q = (24 * 2000) / (76 * 1000)
      = 0.632

The i[nitial ratio indicates scale-up, while the recalculated ratio indicates scale-down. The direction check returns 24](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L247-L253)

Expected raw proposal if Succeeded Pods were ignored:
    ceil(24 * 2.0) = 48
Actual proposal:
    24

In both cases, the calculation returns successfully, so the HPA can report `ScalingActive=True` and `ValidMetricFound` while retaining the current replica count.

A controller unit test could reproduce this using 24 Running Pods with metrics, 52 Succeeded Pods without metrics, and `currentReplicas=24`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This appears related to #129866 and the unmerged fix in #129868. The impact is broader than the earlier issue descriptions because the current second-pass calculation can suppress both scale directions.

The affected v1.34.9 code:
- Metric evaluation and selection:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L303-L350
- `AverageValue` resource metric path:
  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/horizontal.go#L596-L613
- Succeeded Pods become missing Pods:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L409-L427
- Missing-Pod substitution:  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L226-L245
- Tolerance and consistency checks:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.34.9/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L247-L259

The same behavior remains in v1.36.3:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L422-L440
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/controller/podautoscaler/replica_calculator.go#L226-L259

title: Who should set the `DisruptionTarget` condition for pods that must be deleted outside the eviction API?
body:
The `DisruptionTarget` [condition](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions/#pod-disruption-conditions) is not set when a pod is deleted by a raw delete call, only by mechanisms such as the eviction API. Some controllers need to delete pods while enforcing a hard node termination deadline, overriding PDBs, which the eviction API does not do.

Karpenter does this when a node reaches its `terminationGracePeriod` deadline or is terminated by a node auto repair health issue. Those pods die without a `DisruptionTarget`, so a Job `podFailurePolicy`, for example, matching on it never fires and the failure is counted as an application level failure. Karpenter issue for more details and reproduction steps: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/karpenter/issues/3218

The Karpenter maintainers don't necessarily want to stamp a condition on the pod that they don't own, so we are asking:

- Should out of tree controllers set `DisruptionTarget` themselves?   
- If not, what is the recommended way for deletions overriding PDBs to put some kind of stamp on pods so other controllers can distinguish node level failures from application failures?

title: DRA structured allocator overflows the native-int device-count sum in the per-claim limit check
body:
### What happened

The structured allocator adds device counts in native `int` before comparing to `resourceapi.AllocationResultsMaxSize`. `allocateOne` forms `len(results) + requestData.numDevices - r.deviceIndex`, and the pre-flight `Allocate` loop accumulates `minDevicesPerClaim += numDevices`. `DeviceRequest.Count` is validated only as `> 0`, never against the result limit, so several large-but-valid counts sum past the limit and wrap. Two counts of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` wrap to a negative total, so `total > MaxSize` is false and the check is skipped; four wrap back near zero. A `FirstAvailable` request whose first alternative carries a huge count, sitting behind a device already allocated for the claim, drives the overflowing subtraction and misdirects the backtracking rather than pruning the oversized alternative.

### What you expected to happen

Each request is refused against the remaining capacity before the sum is formed, so no addition overflows and an oversized count is rejected with `number of requested devices exceeds the claim limit`.

### How to reproduce it

A single claim with two `ExactCount` requests of `math.MaxInt/2 + 1` each: the total overflows negative and is admitted today. A `FirstAvailable` request with a first subrequest of `math.MaxInt` behind one already-allocated device: the oversized alternative should be pruned and the small one taken. Both are covered by the tests in #141307, and the fix is applied identically across the stable, incubating, and experimental tiers.

### Anything else we need to know

`math.MaxInt` makes the counts overflow on 32-bit builds as well. This is worth a backport decision for the release branches that already carry the per-claim result-limit check.

### Related

This is the concrete in-tree instance behind #140424, which asks for an upper bound or overflow-safety contract on `DeviceRequest.Count`. #140424 observes that the structured allocator guards the single-count path; the gap here is the multi-count sum on that same path, one large count plus the devices already allocated for the claim, which was not guarded until #141307.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

_This issue was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. I checked the allocator paths and the overflow cases against the code and the tests myself._

title: PodTopologySpread silently ignores the constraint when `labelSelector` is an empty (non-nil) object `{}`
body:
### What happened?

When a `topologySpreadConstraint` is written with an **empty but non-nil** label selector (`labelSelector: {}`), the constraint is silently treated as a no-op. `maxSkew` and `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` have no effect at all: pods are placed as if the constraint were absent, with no error, event, or warning.

The root cause is a short-circuit in `countPodsMatchSelector` (`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/podtopologyspread/common.go`), introduced by commit `3dae9ba6d68` ("Optimize topology spreading for null selector"):

```go
func countPodsMatchSelector(podInfos []fwk.PodInfo, selector labels.Selector, ns string) int {
	if selector.Empty() {   // <-- wrong predicate
		return 0
	}
	...
}
```

`selector.Empty()` reports whether the selector **has any requirements**, not whether it **matches anything**. For the two degenerate selectors these two notions are exactly inverted.

The divergence originates in `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector`, which distinguishes a nil pointer (field unset) from a non-nil empty object by design:

```go
func LabelSelectorAsSelector(ps *LabelSelector) (labels.Selector, error) {
	if ps == nil {
		return labels.Nothing(), nil     // field unset      -> match nothing
	}
	if len(ps.MatchLabels)+len(ps.MatchExpressions) == 0 {
		return labels.Everything(), nil  // {} : no filter   -> match everything
	}
	...
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

`labelSelector: {}` means "select every pod in the namespace" (this is what `metav1.LabelSelectorAsSelector({})` returns, `labels.Everything()`). The spread constraint should count all pods in the namespace per topology domain and enforce `maxSkew` accordingly — i.e. it should behave identically to a `matchLabels` selector that happens to select the same set of pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproduced on a 2-node cluster (`controlplane` + `node01`). The idea: make `node01` the only schedulable node while a second, empty topology domain still participates in the count, then submit two constraints that select the *exact same* set of pods and observe that they behave oppositely.

```bash
# 1) Make node01 the only schedulable node.
#    (Other nodes stay cordoned but still count as empty topology domains,
#     because the default nodeTaintsPolicy is Ignore.)
WORKER=node01
kubectl get nodes -o name | grep -v "/$WORKER$" | xargs -r kubectl cordon
```

```yaml
# repro.yaml  (replace node01 with your worker node name if different)
# Seed: two app=demo pods pinned to the worker (nodeName bypasses the scheduler).
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: bg1, labels: {app: demo}}
spec:
  nodeName: node01
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: bg2, labels: {app: demo}}
spec:
  nodeName: node01
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9}]
---
# A) empty selector -> Everything() -> hits the bug
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: test-empty, labels: {app: demo}}
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: {}
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9}]
---
# B) equivalent matchLabels -> selects exactly the same pods as A
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: test-match, labels: {app: demo}}
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
    whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
    labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: demo}}
  containers: [{name: c, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9}]
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f repro.yaml
sleep 3
kubectl get pod bg1 bg2 test-empty test-match -o wide
```

Observed result:

```
root@controlplane:~/topology$ kubectl get pod bg1 bg2 test-empty test-match -o wide
NAME         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE     IP              NODE     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
bg1          1/1     Running   0          4m28s   192.168.1.42    node01   <none>           <none>
bg2          1/1     Running   0          4m28s   192.168.1.185   node01   <none>           <none>
test-empty   1/1     Running   0          4m28s   192.168.1.204   node01   <none>           <none> <-- labelSelector: {} : constraint ignored, scheduled onto the over-full node
test-match   0/1     Pending   0          4m28s   <none>          <none>   <none>           <none> <-- equivalent matchLabels : correctly rejected by the spread constraint
```

### Anything else we need to know?

**Scope — this is the `{}` path, not the `nil` path (please do not merge with #135797).** #135797 discusses the `nil` (field-omitted) case: a `nil` selector becomes `labels.Nothing()`, correctly counts 0 (it faithfully means "match nothing"), and the debate there is whether to reject it at API validation. That is a validation/design question, not a code defect. This report is strictly about `labelSelector: {}` → `Everything()`, where the semantic is "match all pods" but the code returns 0 — a functional correctness bug. The two share a symptom (constraint becomes a no-op) but have opposite root causes. The `nil` case is tracked separately in #135797 and is explicitly out of scope here.


I'm happy to work on the fix (one-line change + tests, drafted below) once the expected behavior is confirmed.

/kind bug

title: test/images/agnhost/Dockerfile lacks a fallback when golang:$GOLANG_VERSION tag isn't published yet
body:
### What happened?

test/images/agnhost/Dockerfile pulls its build-time Go toolchain via a tag-based reference — FROM golang:$GOLANG_VERSION AS preparer — where GOLANG_VERSION is derived from .go-version by test/images/image-util.sh (~lines 148–167).

When a release branch's .go-version is bumped as part of a Go patch release, the post-kubernetes-push-e2e-agnhost-test-images postsubmit job immediately tries to build agnhost against that new GOLANG_VERSION. If the corresponding golang:$GOLANG_VERSION tag hasn't been published to Docker Hub yet, the build fails outright, with no fallback (e.g. golang:latest + GOTOOLCHAIN=auto) to let Go resolve the actual toolchain version from go.mod/.go-version instead of depending on the base image tag existing.

Observed failure:
https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/post-kubernetes-push-e2e-agnhost-test-images/2087993003036643328

This is the gap left by kubernetes/kubernetes#136954, which fixed .go-version-driven bumps on release branches generally but explicitly excluded e2e test images like agnhost, deferring them to follow-up PRs (referenced in downstream bump PRs, e.g. openshift/kubernetes#2633).

Note: master's test/images/agnhost/Dockerfile has since moved to a digest-pinned base (FROM golang@sha256:...) with ARG GOTOOLCHAIN=go${GOLANG_VERSION}, so affected release branches appear to be missing this pattern.

### What did you expect to happen?

The post-kubernetes-push-e2e-agnhost-test-images build should succeed (or at worst degrade gracefully) even when the exact golang:$GOLANG_VERSION tag isn't yet published on Docker Hub — by resolving the Go toolchain via GOTOOLCHAIN=auto against go.mod/.go-version rather than requiring that exact base image tag to already exist at build time.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Would appreciate, if minor version release of Kubernetes versions, also updates tag of agnhost with latest dependency, So test images does not accumulate CVE.

title: A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in CreateContainerError after its node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.
body:
### What happened?

A pod using a Dynamic Resource Allocation claim got permanently stuck in `CreateContainerError` after its
node rebooted, with no automatic recovery.

Setup: a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim, already `Running` with its device allocated and
prepared. I rebooted the node (a full reboot — kubelet and the container runtime both restart, along with
every workload container on that node, including the DRA driver's own pod).

After the node came back:
- The driver re-registered and kubelet re-prepared the same already-allocated claim (confirmed via the
  driver's own logs — it logged a fresh "prepare" call for the exact same claim UID and returned success).
- Despite that, the pod's container repeatedly failed to start:
  ```
  Warning  Failed  Error: failed to create containerd container: CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices k8s.gpu.example.com/gpu=<uid>-gpu-0
  ```
- This did not resolve on its own. I watched it for 5+ minutes: kubelet kept retrying the identical
  container creation with the identical (still-unresolvable) device reference, backing off further each
  time. It never attempted to re-prepare the claim again.
- The only way I found to recover was deleting and recreating the pod, which allocates a fresh claim and
  works immediately.


Note: a plain `systemctl restart kubelet` alone (container runtime left untouched, containers kept running)
does **not** reproduce this — I tried that first and saw no re-prepare attempt at all over several minutes.
The container runtime itself needs to also restart (i.e. an actual node reboot, or restarting kubelet and
the container runtime together) for this to trigger.


### What did you expect to happen?

Either the pod should recover cleanly after the node comes back, or if the replayed prepare produces a
result that doesn't actually work, there should be some way to detect that and retry — an Event, a condition,
or another re-prepare attempt — rather than an indefinite retry loop with a generic container-runtime error
that gives no indication anything DRA-related happened.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up a DRA driver and create a pod with a `ResourceClaimTemplate`-based claim (used
   [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver) v0.4.0 for
   this repro). Confirm it reaches `Running` with the claim allocated.
2. Fully reboot the node the pod is running on (in a `kind` cluster: `docker restart <node-container>`; on a
   real cluster: an actual node reboot, or restarting the container runtime and kubelet together).
3. Wait for the node to report `Ready` again and the driver's pod to come back up and re-register.
4. Observe: `kubectl describe pod` shows repeated `CreateContainerError` / `CDI device injection failed:
   unresolvable CDI devices ...` events, with a growing `BackOff`. This does not resolve on its own.
5. Delete and recreate the pod — it comes up fine immediately with a fresh claim.


### Anything else we need to know?

I reproduced this the same way on a second, real (non-kind) cluster — same sequence of events, same
`CDI device injection failed: unresolvable CDI devices` error, same lack of self-recovery. A comparison pod
on a node that wasn't rebooted kept running the whole time, so this is specifically tied to the reboot, not
something intermittent.

Two things worth separating here, since I've only tested with one driver:

- Kubelet does not appear to remember, across a restart, that a claim was already successfully prepared —
  every claim gets treated as unprepared again after a reboot, and gets a fresh `NodePrepareResources` call
  regardless of which driver is behind it. This part reproduced identically on both clusters.
- Once that replayed call happens, kubelet accepts whatever the driver responds with and never re-checks or
  retries even after the resulting container creation keeps failing — it just repeats the identical failing
  attempt indefinitely. This also isn't specific to any one driver's behavior; it's what kubelet does with
  the response once it gets it, and I did not see it change over the retries.
- What I can't say for certain is whether every DRA driver would produce an unusable result the way this one
  did on replay. I tested only [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver).
  A driver with more robust logic may not have any visible symptom. But it seems that kubelet
  gives a driver no way to tell "this is a replay of something you already told me was ready" versus a fresh
  request, and never verifies or retries regardless. So any driver whose restart-recovery isn't airtight may hit
 this type of problem. This happened on the very first attempt, with the reference driver
  meant to demonstrate best practices, using nothing more unusual than a node reboot.


### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
kind v0.32.0, node image kindest/node:v1.36.1
```

</details>



### Cloud provider

<details>

Local `kind` cluster, not cloud-hosted.

</details>


### OS version

<details>

<details>

title: [Failing-test]: investigate host memory used while resolving Ubuntu images for DRA node jobs
body:
## Current status

The root cause has been confirmed.

`getGCEImage` used:

    gcloud compute images list --format=json --project=<project>

and buffered and unmarshaled the complete project listing.

For `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`, the real Prow measurement was:

- 12,558 images
- 283 MiB JSON
- runner VmHWM: 1,067 MiB
- lookup: 44.6s

The equivalent COS path returned 234 images / 1.5 MiB and the runner peaked at 43 MiB.

kubernetes/kubernetes#141590 added a gcloud-side family filter before the output reaches `exec.Output()`. With that fix, the same Ubuntu lookup returned 407 images / 17 MiB, the runner VmHWM dropped to 103 MiB, lookup time dropped to 5.8s, and the selected image remained unchanged.

The fix merged as:

    0edccb5d3e0c3a2efa310d7a2f1725b2a201e5ee

## Remaining work

The current 2Gi Prow limit remains the mitigation until resource rollback is validated.

kubernetes/test-infra#37770 is the first 1Gi canary. It changes only the two master-only Ubuntu alpha/beta periodics and leaves the release-1.37 jobs at 2Gi.

The issue stays open until:

1. the canary package is confirmed to contain #141590;
2. both canary jobs complete five consecutive runs with clear memory headroom;
3. the standard master Ubuntu jobs are validated at 1Gi;
4. no release-1.37 job is accidentally reduced.

<details>
<summary>Original investigation</summary>

### Which jobs are failing?

These four Ubuntu DRA node jobs was OOM killed before test can start:

* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-1-7-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra
* https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-node-e2e-containerd-2-0-ubuntu-dra-alpha-beta-features

The jobs run again after kubernetes/test-infra#37491 changed the Prow memory from 1Gi to 2Gi.

This issue is for investigate the root cause. The 2Gi change only mitigate it.

### Which tests are failing?

No one test.

The Prow pod was OOM killed while `e2e_node.test remote` was preparing the run. The GCE VM was not created yet, so this was not an OOM inside Ubuntu guest.

### Since when has it been failing?

The original report in #140701 was opened on 2026-07-16.

For root cause bisect, we still need confirm the last green and first red revisions again.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-dynamic-resource-allocation

### Reason for failure (if possible)

Known now:

* 1Gi was not enough for these Ubuntu jobs.
* 2Gi let the jobs run again.
* OOM happened in the host Prow pod before GCE VM creation.
* Ubuntu image config uses an image family and regex from `ubuntu-os-gke-cloud`.
* Before creating VM, the GCE runner calls `gcloud compute images list --format=json`.
* The command output is fully buffered, then Go unmarshals all image objects, filters it and sorts the matched images.

One possible reason is this image lookup use much more memory for the Ubuntu project than COS.

I made one local synthetic test with 250,000 image objects. The current full JSON path used about 149 MiB maximum RSS. A pre-filtered one-row input used about 1.6 MiB and selected the same image. This only show the current path can amplify memory. It does not prove the real Prow OOM root cause yet.

Proposed verification:

1. Run Ubuntu and COS with the same Kubernetes revision and 1Gi Prow limit.
2. Record cgroup `memory.current`, `memory.peak` and `memory.events`.
3. Record `/usr/bin/time -v` for `e2e_node.test` and the `gcloud` child.
4. Record the JSON output size and image count.
5. Compare current command with:

   * `--no-standard-images`
   * only `name`, `family` and `creationTimestamp`
   * a family filter when image family is configured
6. Verify both commands select the same Ubuntu and COS image.
7. Run at least three Ubuntu DRA canary jobs.

The fix is accepted when the selected image is unchanged, peak memory is reduced, and the Ubuntu jobs can complete repeatedly without OOM under the controlled limit.

### Anything else we need to know?

Related work:

* #140701 reported the original outage.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37308 reduced the node-job memory.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37309 raised it from 500Mi to 1Gi.
* kubernetes/test-infra#37491 raised it from 1Gi to 2Gi and mitigated the failure.

There is also a suspicious regex in the Ubuntu config:

```yaml
image_regex: ".*[^-cgroupsv1]$"
```

This is a negated character class. It does not mean “does not end with `-cgroupsv1`”. I think it should be checked separately because changing it together can change which image is selected and make the memory result hard to review.

I searched open and closed issues in `kubernetes/kubernetes` and `kubernetes/test-infra` with the four job names, `Ubuntu DRA OOM`, `e2e_node.test OOM` and the image project name. I did not find another issue tracking this root-cause investigation. GitHub search index can have delay.

This issue is opened separately as requested in #140701.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind failing-test
/assign @thc1006


</details>

title: [Failing-test]: ci-kind-dra-1-34 times out before DRA suite can finish
body:
> **Status 2026-09-14.** The comments below carry `[UPDATED]` notes and strike-through where they were wrong.
>
> - The failures are memory pressure at the 6Gi limit, not the CPU quota. Prow reports `Job pod was OOM killed by the cluster.` for both builds listed below (test container `OOMKilled`, exit 127 in the first) and for 22 of the 40 `ci-kind-dra-1-34` runs from 08-03 to 09-11, 21 of them after running into the 90 minute timeout. The kind node journals cannot see that kill, so I missed it at first.
> - The runner CPU quota problem was real but separate. kubernetes/test-infra#37733 (merged 08-21, in the job image since 09-07) copies the pod's `cpu.max` into the runner's `init` leaf. The release-1.34 binaries have `containermaxprocs=0` (`godebug default=go1.24`) and ignore it; with `GOMAXPROCS=2` in the runner env (kubernetes/test-infra#37731) my replica of the job still ran into the 6Gi limit (one run each way). Neither explains the OOM kills.
> - The apiserver leak claim is withdrawn. The memory comes from `ResourceSlice Controller creates slices`, which on release-1.34 and release-1.35 publishes 100 max-size ResourceSlices; master cut it to 10 in #136156 (1847d5b1a, "created too much load for an E2E test"). Same branch, count as the only change: about 2 GiB less non-reclaimable memory for the suite on both branches, 3.0 to 3.4 GiB in the 1.34 random seed runs that hit the scheduler log mode below.
> - Why 1.34 is worse than 1.35, and why the seed matters: the scheduler's experimental structured allocator logs the full ResourceSlice list at V(5) once per node it evaluates, per scheduling attempt (`structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, "Gathering pools"), about 74 MB per line while the 100 slices exist, and the jobs run kube-scheduler at `--v=5`. release-1.34 picks that allocator with the default gates (`DRAResourceClaimDeviceStatus`, beta); release-1.35 only when an alpha gate selects it (`DRADeviceBindingConditions` together with device status, or `DRAConsumableCapacity`), which the all-gates presubmit `pull-kubernetes-kind-dra-all` does. Master dropped the statement in #136588. In uncapped replays with random seeds the scheduler wrote 0.2 to 5.9 GB of log within about 30 s of that test; in job replicas at 2 CPUs, 0.2 to 4.3 GB, within about a minute at 12Gi and spread over 8 to 28 minutes in the 6Gi runs that thrashed; kube-scheduler at 1.0 to 1.7 GiB where it was sampled. With the statement deleted, the 100 slice presubmit replicas completed at 6Gi on both branches, still at 93 to 95% of the limit non-reclaimable.
> - Outcome (09-14): the remedy is the job memory, not branch code. #142082 (delete the log statement on release-1.35) and #142083 (the 100 to 10 change from #136156, release-1.35) were closed, they do not meet the cherry-pick guidelines; kubernetes/test-infra#37865 (6Gi to 12Gi for the 1.34 and 1.35 kind DRA jobs) merged on 09-14 06:25 UTC; the periodics run on a 24h interval and pick it up on their next runs, due around 14:20 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-34` and 20:17 UTC for `ci-kind-dra-1-35`. kubernetes/test-infra#37731 is closed. Whether the jobs stay green at 12Gi is what the next runs will show. First prow runs on the two PRs before they were closed (09-14): #142083 passed all three kind-dra presubmits; #142082 on its own passed the plain and `-all-slow` jobs; its `-all` job failed twice without an OOM kill (the first time with the apiserver stalling while the 100 slices were created and deleted, the second time on a different spec, a pod the kubelet rejected at device-plugin admission with the control plane quiet) and passed on the third run, so the log deletion alone leaves that job on the edge at 6Gi. The numbers are summarized in those PRs; I have the raw samples if anyone wants them.
>

title: kubelet: `dropCacheFor` does not invalidate name-keyed trust bundle cache entries when the ClusterTrustBundle has a `spec.signerName`
body:
### What happened?

[`dropCacheFor`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c44d2a82ef7f87c8b4278cd13af0a55614ed2a53/pkg/kubelet/clustertrustbundle/clustertrustbundle_manager.go#L208-L218) clears signer-keyed cache entries when the ClusterTrustBundle has a `spec.signerName`, and name-keyed entries otherwise. A bundle with a signer name can still be projected by name with `clusterTrustBundle.name`, and that name-keyed entry is cleared by no event, so it survives until the 5 minute cache TTL expires. For that window kubelet writes the pre-update trust anchors into the projected volume of running pods, and of pods that start on the same node.

### What did you expect to happen?

Every cache entry for a changed ClusterTrustBundle is invalidated, so a pod sees the new trust anchors within one `--sync-frequency` period.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproducer: https://gist.github.com/RafPe/3406b1a959b2104071c85fc8d7304a01

One pod projects the same bundle three ways at once, each in its own volume:

| arm | projected as | bundle | time until the pod sees the new anchors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | by `name` | has `signerName` | **290-374 s** |
| 2 | by `signerName` | has `signerName` | 0-95 s |
| 3 | by `name` | no `signerName` | 0-95 s |

Arm 1 minus arm 2 is 296, 290, 299 and 300 s over four runs. With `syncFrequency: 10s`, arms 2 and 3 converge in under 10 s and arm 1 takes 299-310 s.

### Anything else we need to know?

`AddFunc`, `UpdateFunc` and `DeleteFunc` all call `dropCacheFor`. The if/else is unchanged since 2022, so release-1.33 through master are affected, on both `certificates.k8s.io/v1beta1` and `v1`. Fix with tests in #141459.

Found while testing [pod-certificate-signer](https://github.com/RafPe/pod-certificate-signer).

### Kubernetes version

`kindest/node:v1.35.5`, `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (two clusters, one with `syncFrequency: 10s`), and v1.37.0-rc.0.9+9f489375110c8a built from `release-1.37`.

### Cloud provider

None, local `kind` clusters.

### OS version

Node: Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), kernel 7.0.14-orbstack (arm64). Host: macOS darwin/arm64.

### Install tools

`kind v0.32.0`. On 1.35 and 1.36 the config enables the `ClusterTrustBundle` and `ClusterTrustBundleProjection` gates and `runtimeConfig: certificates.k8s.io/v1beta1`; on 1.37 both gates are GA and default true. Config is in the gist.

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

`containerd://2.3.1`

title: Kubelet restart preserves stale readiness for a replaced container when the API server status is outdated
body:
### What happened?

Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141155#issuecomment-5272111983 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/141155#issuecomment-5274991536.

#141342 stops a replacement container from inheriting the previous container's `Started` by comparing container IDs in `convertToAPIContainerStatuses`. The same identity problem exists on the readiness side of the kubelet restart preservation logic (`ChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart=false`, the default since 1.35):

1. `worker.go` decides `isRestart` purely from the container start time being older than the kubelet start plus the 10s grace period, and in that case does not seed the initial `Failure` result for the new container ID: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94ece9779a9b1a07efd6cc986fa81ebb8947db28/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L257-L283
2. `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart` sets `ready=true` when there is no readiness result yet and the container predates the grace period, and only backs off if the `PodReady` condition in `pod.Status` is not True: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/94ece9779a9b1a07efd6cc986fa81ebb8947db28/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go#L312-L341

Neither checks whether the container the API server knew about is the same container the runtime is reporting. If container A is replaced by B while the kubelet cannot reach the API server, and the kubelet then restarts, B is treated as a container that survived the restart and inherits A's `Ready=true`. B is reported Ready before its own readiness probe has ever run, until the first real probe result lands, which is delayed by `initialDelaySeconds`.

Reproduced on kind v1.36.1 (readiness-only pod, `initialDelaySeconds: 60`, probe `test -f /tmp/ready` that only the original container satisfied):

```
15:01:03 worker->apiserver blocked (iptables), liveness failure triggered
15:01:06 runtime creates replacement B (8bb688...), A exited
15:01:12 API still shows A: ready=true restarts=0
15:01:12 kubelet stopped, wait 12s so B is older than the grace period
15:01:24 API unblocked, kubelet started
15:01:27 API shows B: ready=true started=true restarts=1 podReady=True
         ... B stays Ready for ~43s, its readiness probe never passed ...
15:02:10 first probe result after initialDelay: ready=false podReady=False
```

Containers with a startup probe are covered by #141342 because B stays `Started=false` until its startup probe passes and readiness is gated behind that. Containers with only a readiness probe are not.

### What did you expect to happen?

A replacement container should not inherit the previous container's `Ready` state. Readiness preservation across kubelet restart should only apply when the container ID in the API status matches the container ID reported by the runtime, consistent with the `Started` handling in #141342.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Two-node kind cluster (`kindest/node:v1.36.1`), pod pinned to the worker:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: q2
spec:
  nodeName: <worker>
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    readinessProbe:
      exec: {command: ["test","-f","/tmp/ready"]}
      initialDelaySeconds: 60
      periodSeconds: 2
    livenessProbe:
      exec: {command: ["test","!","-f","/tmp/die"]}
      periodSeconds: 1
      failureThreshold: 1
```

1. `kubectl exec q2 -- touch /tmp/ready`, wait for the pod to be Ready.
2. On the worker: `iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -j DROP` (and `ip6tables`), `ss -K dport = :6443`.
3. `kubectl exec q2 -- touch /tmp/die` so the kubelet replaces the container while the API is unreachable. Confirm with `crictl ps -a` that a new container is running.
4. `systemctl stop kubelet`, sleep 12s (keep the whole blocked window under the 40s node monitor grace period so the node lifecycle controller does not set PodReady=False for you).
5. Remove the iptables rules, `systemctl start kubelet`.
6. `kubectl get pod q2 -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].containerID} {.status.containerStatuses[0].ready}'` shows the new container ID with `ready=true` until `initialDelaySeconds` elapses.

### Anything else we need to know?

Proposed fix: apply the same container identity rule in both places above. `w.pod.Status.ContainerStatuses` / `InitContainerStatuses` (snapshot taken at `AddPod`) and `pod.Status` in `UpdatePodStatus` carry the pre-restart API view, so the old ID can be looked up by container name. If the known ID is non-empty and differs from the runtime ID, seed the initial readiness result and skip `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart`.

One interaction to keep in mind: in a multi-container pod where X is unchanged and Y is replaced, correctly marking Y NotReady flips `PodReady=False`, and on the next sync `setReadyStateOnKubeletRestart` will also drop X to NotReady if X's first probe result has not landed yet. That is an existing property of the preservation design, but worth covering in unit tests.

Unit tests in `worker_test.go` (`TestChangeContainerStatusOnKubeletRestart` already has isRestart fixtures) and `prober_manager_test.go` should be enough; an e2e is likely not practical.

title: Pod evicted for exceeding its ephemeral-storage limit is indistinguishable from successful completion
body:
### What happened?

When a Pod (`restartPolicy: Never`) is evicted for exceeding its **own** `ephemeral-storage` limit and its main container handles SIGTERM and exits 0, the resulting Pod object carries **no durable signal that it was evicted**. It is indistinguishable from a clean completion:

- `status.phase: Succeeded`
- `status.reason: ""`  (empty)
- conditions all `reason: PodCompleted` (`Ready`/`ContainersReady=False`)
- **no `DisruptionTarget` condition**
- no container `terminated.reason` (exit code `0`)

The only trace is a kubelet Event: `Warning Evicted Pod ephemeral local storage usage exceeds the total limit of containers <N>` …which is best-effort and GC'd after `--event-ttl` (default 1h).

### What did you expect to happen?

A **durable, machine-readable marker on the Pod** distinguishing an ephemeral-storage-limit eviction from a normal completion — mirroring how **OOM** is surfaced (`container.state.terminated.reason: OOMKilled`, exit `137`).

### The asymmetry

OOM and ephemeral-storage-limit breaches are *both* self-inflicted resource-limit violations, so I understand neither is a "disruption" and `DisruptionTarget` doesn't apply (per the disruptions docs).

For the ephemeral case, **both the pod phase and the container reason read as a clean finish**, and `pod.status.reason` is blank — zero signal at every level.

## Full mapping
| Scenario | `pod.status.phase` | `pod.status.reason` | `container…terminated.reason` / exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clean completion (exit 0) | `Succeeded` | `""` | `Completed` / 0 |
| **Ephemeral-limit eviction, app exits 0** | **`Succeeded`** | **`""`** | **`Completed` / 0** |
| OOM | `Failed` | `""` | `OOMKilled` / 137 |
| SIGTERM not handled (exit 143) | `Failed` | `""` | `Error` / 143 |
| **Node-pressure hard eviction** (SIGKILL / grace-0) | `Failed` | **`Evicted`** | `Error` / 137 (or `ContainerStatusUnknown`) |

So a controller/Job cannot tell "evicted for blowing its disk limit" from "finished successfully" without racing the ephemeral `Evicted` event.

### How to reproduce it (minimal)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: eph-evict }
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:latest            # nginx exits 0 on SIGTERM
    resources:
      limits: { ephemeral-storage: "1Gi" }
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/fill bs=1M count=2000 & exec nginx -g 'daemon off;'"]

title: Endpoints controller emits FailedToCreateEndpoint/FailedToUpdateEndpoint events with empty involvedObject.namespace
body:
### What happened?

`syncService` (`pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go`) builds a
placeholder Endpoints object without `Namespace` when the lister returns
NotFound:

```go
currentEndpoints = &v1.Endpoints{
    ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{
        Name:   service.Name,
        Labels: service.Labels,
    },
}

newEndpoints := currentEndpoints.DeepCopy() inherits the missing Namespace.
If the following Create() fails (e.g. AlreadyExists from a race), the
event is recorded against this object:

e.eventRecorder.Eventf(newEndpoints, v1.EventTypeWarning, "FailedToCreateEndpoint",
    "Failed to create endpoint for service %v/%v: %v", service.Namespace, service.Name, err)

Result: involvedObject.namespace is "" even though the message text and
involvedObject.name are correct — breaking any consumer that filters on
involvedObject.namespace.


### What did you expect to happen?

newEndpoints (and the earlier NotFound placeholder currentEndpoints) should have
Namespace: service.Namespace set, so involvedObject.namespace on the resulting
event matches the actual service namespace, consistent with the message text.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Cause a race where an Endpoints object with the target name already exists
   when the controller's lister still reports NotFound (e.g. concurrent create,
   or a stale informer cache), so Create() returns AlreadyExists.
2. kubectl get events -o json and inspect the FailedToCreateEndpoint event's
   involvedObject.namespace — it is empty, while the message field contains the
   correct "<namespace>/<name>" text.

title: macOS client releases are not signed
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `kubectl` binaries available for macOS via Homebrew / GitHub Releases are currently distributed without code signing. In restricted enterprise environments, unsigned binaries are blocked from running by default.

```sh
# Homebrew
codesign -dvv /opt/homebrew/bin/kubectl

Executable=/opt/homebrew/Cellar/kubernetes-cli/1.36.4/bin/kubectl
Identifier=a.out
Format=Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20400 size=476606 flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed) hashes=14891+0 location=embedded
Signature=adhoc
Info.plist=not bound
TeamIdentifier=not set
Sealed Resources=none
Internal requirements=none

# Direct download
tar -xzf kubernetes-client-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
codesign -dvv ./kubernetes/client/bin/kubectl

Executable=/Users/tturner/Downloads/kubernetes/client/bin/kubectl
Identifier=a.out
Format=Mach-O thin (arm64)
CodeDirectory v=20400 size=444382 flags=0x20002(adhoc,linker-signed) hashes=13884+0 location=embedded
Signature=adhoc
Info.plist=not bound
TeamIdentifier=not set
Sealed Resources=none
Internal requirements=none
```

Wondering if this has been explored as an option for making `kubectl` a trusted binary on macOS?


### Why is this needed?

To reduce risks posed by the execution of untrusted binaries, enterprises environments are beginning to enforce aggressive binary authorisation policies that restrict the execution of unsigned code. Having `kubectl` signed with a Developer ID certificate would allow folks to maintain these policies without disrupting engineers' workflows.

### Which tests are flaking?

`[sig-storage] CSI Mock volume attach When CSIDriver AttachRequired changes from true to false should cleanup VolumeAttachment properly [Slow]`

### Reason for failure (if possible)

When `CSIDriver.spec.attachRequired` changes from true to false, kubelet updates the volume’s desired-state attachability but does not update an already created actual-state entry.

If the volume was attached and mounted before the transition, kubelet continues reporting it as requiring controller attachment in `Node.Status.VolumesInUse`. As a result, the attach/detach controller does not delete the existing VolumeAttachment, and the e2e test times out.
