title: fake client-go: a deletion between List and Watch is lost, and the informer keeps the object forever
body:
### What happened? Follow-up to #135953, which was fixed by #135959 and #136143: a fake client no longer loses objects that are **created** between the reflector's `List` and its `Watch`, because `tracker.Watch` now replays stored objects whose resource version is newer than the one the `List` returned. A **deletion** in that same window is still lost, and unlike a lost create it can never be repaired: the informer's store keeps an object that no longer exists in the tracker, no `DeleteFunc` ever fires, and no relist happens, so every later read from that informer's lister returns a phantom object for the lifetime of the test. The cause is the asymmetry between the two paths: - `tracker.Watch` replays existing objects only ([`fixture.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/testing/fixture.go), the `addExisting` / `addFromRV` block): `for _, obj := range matchingObjs { if addFromRV < obj.resourceVersion { fakewatcher.Add(obj.Object) } }`. A deleted object is not in `t.objects` any more and the tracker keeps no tombstone, so there is nothing to replay. - `tracker.delete` sends `w.Delete(...)` only to the watchers that `getWatches` returns *at that moment*. A watcher registered a moment later never learns about it. `WaitForCacheSync` returning does not imply that the reflector has called `Watch`; it only means the initial `List` was processed. #135959 already notes that the window got easier to hit once `WaitForCacheSync` stopped polling (#135395). ### What did you expect to happen? A fake client + informer to converge on the tracker's contents regardless of the timing of `Watch`, for deletions as it now does for creations: either the deletion is delivered, or the watch is rejected so that the reflector relists. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? The existing `staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/testing/internal/listandwatch_test.go` is already built for this: it delays the reflector's `Watch` until the test has mutated the tracker, in a `synctest` bubble. The variant below deletes the object instead of creating a second one. `TestListAndWatch` passes, `TestListAndWatchDelete` fails: ``` delete_gap_test.go:64: I0101 08:00:00.000000] Deleted the ConfigMap delete_gap_test.go:41: I0101 08:00:00.000000] Continuing Watch... delete_gap_test.go:71: Unexpected item(s) in informer cache, want 0, got 1 = [&ConfigMap{ObjectMeta:{cm1 default ...}}] delete_gap_test.go:74: Expected the object to be added and deleted, got adds/updates/deletes 1/0/0 --- FAIL: TestListAndWatchDelete (0.04s) --- PASS: TestListAndWatch (0.00s) ```
staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/testing/internal/delete_gap_test.go ```go // Like TestListAndWatch, but the object is deleted after the cache sync and before // the Watch call in the reflector's ListAndWatch is allowed to continue. func TestListAndWatchDelete(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, testListAndWatchDelete) } func testListAndWatchDelete(t *testing.T) { logger, ctx := ktesting.NewTestContext(t) cm := &v1.ConfigMap{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: "cm1", Namespace: "default"}} client := fake.NewClientset(cm) stopCh := make(chan struct{}) defer close(stopCh) deleteDone := make(chan struct{}) f := informers.NewSharedInformerFactory(client, 0) configMapInformer := f.InformerFor(&v1.ConfigMap{}, func(client kubernetes.Interface, resync time.Duration) cache.SharedIndexInformer { return cache.NewSharedIndexInformer(cache.ToListWatcherWithWatchListSemantics(&cache.ListWatch{ ListFunc: func(options metav1.ListOptions) (runtime.Object, error) { return client.CoreV1().ConfigMaps("").List(context.Background(), options) }, WatchFunc: func(options metav1.ListOptions) (watch.Interface, error) { logger.Info("Delaying Watch...") <-deleteDone logger.Info("Continuing Watch...") return client.CoreV1().ConfigMaps("").Watch(context.Background(), options) }, }, client), &v1.ConfigMap{}, resync, nil) }) var adds, updates, deletes int if _, err := configMapInformer.AddEventHandler(cache.ResourceEventHandlerFuncs{ AddFunc: func(_ any) { adds++ }, UpdateFunc: func(_, _ any) { updates++ }, DeleteFunc: func(_ any) { deletes++ }, }); err != nil { t.Fatalf("Unexpected error adding event handler: %v", err) } store := configMapInformer.GetStore() f.Start(stopCh) f.WaitForCacheSync(stopCh) logger.Info("Caches synced") if err := client.CoreV1().ConfigMaps("default").Delete(ctx, "cm1", metav1.DeleteOptions{}); err != nil { t.Fatalf("Unexpected error deleting ConfigMap: %v", err) } logger.Info("Deleted the ConfigMap") close(deleteDone) // Wait for watch setup and event processing. synctest.Wait() if objs := store.List(); len(objs) != 0 { t.Errorf("Unexpected item(s) in informer cache, want 0, got %d = %v", len(objs), objs) } if adds != 1 || updates != 0 || deletes != 1 { t.Errorf("Expected the object to be added and deleted, got adds/updates/deletes %d/%d/%d", adds, updates, deletes) } } ```
Without touching client-go, the same thing shows up as a rare flake. A loop that builds a fake client holding one object, starts an informer factory, calls `WaitForCacheSync`, deletes the object through the client and then waits up to 300ms for the lister to lose it, reports on my laptop: ``` deletes never observed: 15-20/3000 (~0.5%), observed but slower than 10ms: 0 ``` It is binary — the event arrives within a few milliseconds or never. Inserting `time.Sleep(300 * time.Millisecond)` between `r.list(ctx)` and `r.watchWithResync(ctx, w)` in `Reflector.ListAndWatchWithContext` turns the same loop into 20/20 lost. ### Anything else we need to know? **How it shows up in a real test.** The symptom is not "an event is missing", it is a timeout inside the code under test, which makes it expensive to diagnose. Code that waits for an object to disappear from a lister (`k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/volume/csi`'s attacher waits for a `VolumeAttachment` to be gone before it recreates it under the same name) fails with its own timeout error, no replacement object is created, and every later assertion in the test fails as a consequence. Two rows of one table-driven test are affected, each failing about 0.5% of the time — and 100% of the time with the reflector sleep above. **Possible fixes**, roughly in order of faithfulness: 1. Keep an event log per GVR — resource version plus event type, including deletions — and have `Watch(rv)` replay everything newer than `rv`. This is what the real API server does and it makes creates, updates and deletes all behave, at the cost of the tracker retaining a bounded history. 2. Cheaper: remember the resource version of the most recent deletion per GVR (or simply that a deletion happened) and let `Watch` return `apierrors.NewResourceExpired(...)` when the requested resource version can no longer be served. The reflector then relists and converges, which is exactly the real behaviour for an expired watch, and needs no history. 3. At minimum, document the remaining gap next to the `resourceVersions` comment in `fixture.go`, which currently says the supported use case is "List (no resource version check ...) + Watch (Exact match for the ResourceVersion returned by List)" without noting that a deletion in between is dropped, and offer a supported way for tests to wait until the watch is registered. **Workaround for test authors** until then: take over the watch, so that the test can wait until the reflector has registered it. It has to forward `ListOptions`, otherwise the replay added by #135959 is disabled: ```go watching := make(chan struct{}) var once sync.Once client.PrependWatchReactor("volumeattachments", func(action core.Action) (bool, watch.Interface, error) { var opts metav1.ListOptions if watchAction, ok := action.(core.WatchActionImpl); ok { opts = watchAction.ListOptions } w, err := client.Tracker().Watch(action.GetResource(), action.GetNamespace(), opts) if err != nil { return false, nil, err } once.Do(func() { close(watching) }) return true, w, nil }) // ... factory.Start(...); factory.WaitForCacheSync(...) <-watching ``` Signalling from inside the reactor is enough even before `Tracker().Watch` is called, because `Fake.InvokesWatch` holds the `Fake` mutex for the whole reactor chain and every other client call needs the same mutex — measured: 0 lost deletes out of 3000 for both orderings, against 15-20 without the reactor. cc @pohly (#135959, #136143) /kind bug /sig api-machinery ### Kubernetes version
Reproduced on `master` at 738a65b9203 (`v1.37.0-rc.1`-ish); the fake client behaviour is the same since #136143 (v1.36) and the flake predates it, see #95372 and #87472.
### Cloud provider
N/A, unit tests only.
### OS version
Not OS specific; observed on darwin/arm64, go1.26.5.

title: PersistentVolume explicit binding compares capacities through overflowing Quantity.Value()
body:
`checkVolumeSatisfyClaim` in the PV controller compares a PV's capacity against a claim's request through `Quantity.Value()`:

```go
requestedQty := claim.Spec.Resources.Requests[v1.ResourceName(v1.ResourceStorage)]
requestedSize := requestedQty.Value()
...
volumeQty := volume.Spec.Capacity[v1.ResourceStorage]
volumeSize := volumeQty.Value()
if volumeSize < requestedSize {
    return fmt.Errorf("requested PV is too small")
}
```

`Value()` projects the quantity onto int64. A storage quantity can be larger than int64, and once it is, `Value()` overflows, so this comparison can order two such quantities wrongly. This is the check that runs when a PVC binds to a specific PV through `spec.volumeName`.

The automatic matching path does not share the bug. `FindMatchingVolume` compares the same two quantities with `Quantity.Cmp` (component-helpers `pv_helpers.go`), and its tests already cover quantities like `800E`.

### What happens

A PV with capacity `9223372036854775808` (2^63) reads back as a negative number through `Value()`. A `1Gi` claim that names it through `spec.volumeName` is rejected with `requested PV is too small` and stays Pending.

In the reverse direction, a claim whose request is past int64 wraps negative, the size check passes, and a PV smaller than the request can be bound to the claim.

### Why it is reachable

#141169 changed `validateBasicResource` to accept a PV capacity of 2^63, and the automatic path already treats these quantities as valid, so the explicit-binding path should agree with it. Neither value is something a normal cluster produces.

### Fix

Compare with `Cmp`, matching `FindMatchingVolume`:

```go
if volumeQty.Cmp(requestedQty) < 0 {
    return fmt.Errorf("requested PV is too small")
}
```

Part of #141166.

/sig storage
/kind bug

title: DeviceTaintRule with deviceSelector omitted blocks device allocation cluster-wide, including adminAccess claims, contradicting documented behavior
body:
### What happened?

A `DeviceTaintRule` with the `deviceSelector` field entirely omitted (not an empty `{}` object
-- the field itself absent) makes every device on every node, across every driver and pool,
untolerated and therefore unschedulable -- not just whatever devices the taint was meant to
target.

Live-verified on a freshly-created kind cluster running v1.37.0 GA with **no non-default
feature gates set at all** (`DynamicResourceAllocation`/`DRADeviceTaints`/`DRADeviceTaintRules`
are all GA and enabled by default at this release):

1. An ordinary `ResourceClaim` targeting one device (`gpu-0`) allocates and its Pod runs, with
   zero `DeviceTaintRule`s present.
2. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with `taint.effect: NoSchedule` and `deviceSelector` omitted:
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
   kind: DeviceTaintRule
   metadata:
     name: taint-no-selector
   spec:
     taint:
       key: example.com/no-selector-test
       value: "true"
       effect: NoSchedule
   ```
3. The exact same claim/Pod from step 1, recreated, now fails to schedule (`FailedScheduling`,
   `cannot allocate all claims`).
4. Also confirmed on a 4-device pool: every device becomes unschedulable, not just one --
   including a claim declaring `adminAccess: true`, which is otherwise documented to bypass
   ordinary device exclusivity but is not exempted from `DeviceTaintRule` enforcement.
5. Deleting only the `DeviceTaintRule` (no other change) immediately restores every
   previously-blocked claim to allocate successfully.



### What did you expect to happen?

According to the field's own documentation (`kubectl explain devicetaintrule.spec.deviceSelector`):

> The empty selector matches all devices. Without a selector, no devices are matches [sic].

A `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted should match **zero** devices and have no
scheduling effect -- the opposite of what actually happens.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?



1. Create a cluster running v1.37.0 (no special feature gates required).
2. Install any DRA driver advertising at least one device (repro used
   `kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver` v0.4.0).
3. Create an ordinary `ResourceClaim` + Pod referencing one device; confirm it runs.
4. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with any `taint` and `deviceSelector` omitted entirely.
5. Observe: any *new* claim against *any* device in the cluster -- including unrelated
   drivers/pools, and `adminAccess: true` claims -- fails to schedule.
6. Delete the `DeviceTaintRule`; confirm previously-blocked claims immediately allocate.



### Anything else we need to know?

- This appears specific to the `NoSchedule` enforcement path. Tested `NoExecute` separately: a
  `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted does **not** evict an already-running
  pod on an unrelated device (its `EvictionInProgress` condition stays `reason: NotStarted`
  indefinitely) -- confirmed the eviction mechanism itself works correctly in the same environment
  via a positive control (a `NoExecute` taint with a matching selector evicted the target pod
  within 5 seconds). So the nil-selector matching bug looks confined to whatever code path
  `NoSchedule` uses to block new allocation, not the separate eviction controller.
- Distinct from #141422 / the pending fix in #141425: that issue concerns a selector that is
  *present but empty* (`deviceSelector: {}`). This report is about the field being *absent*
  entirely -- confirmed by reading #141425's diff that its new validation only rejects the
  empty-but-present case and returns immediately with no error when the selector is nil, so it
  does not cover this scenario.
- Creating a `DeviceTaintRule` is a cluster-scoped permission not granted by any built-in
  `view`/`edit`/`admin` ClusterRole -- but this bug means anyone holding that permission can
  silently take down DRA scheduling cluster-wide with one missing field, when the documented
  default behavior should be a no-op.

title: Reconcile cloud-provider InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels periodically
body:
### What would you like to be added?

The cloud node controller should periodically reconcile node labels returned through `cloudprovider.InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels` for already initialized Nodes.

The reconciliation should:

* add labels that are missing from the Node;
* update labels whose values differ from the current instance metadata;
* preserve unrelated Node labels;
* continue rejecting labels in Kubernetes-reserved namespaces;
* not remove labels that are no longer returned by the cloud provider.

A proposed implementation is available in:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141616

Provider-side implementation:

https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack/pull/3166

Previous implementation attempts:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130888
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131096

### Why is this needed?

`InstanceMetadata.AdditionalLabels` are currently applied only during the initial synchronization of a Node carrying the external cloud-provider taint.

Consequently, labels introduced by a newer cloud provider are not added to already initialized Nodes, manually removed labels are not restored, and changed values remain stale.

One example is the OpenStack `hostId`, which identifies the physical compute host within a project. An OpenStack operator may live-migrate an instance while draining a hypervisor for maintenance. In this case, the provider returns a new `hostId`, but the existing Node label is not updated.

For `InstancesV2` implementations, the cloud node controller already periodically calls `InstanceMetadata()`. Reconciling `AdditionalLabels` therefore does not require an additional cloud-provider API request.

Existing Pods are not automatically rescheduled when a topology label changes. Updating the label still makes the current placement observable and ensures newly scheduled Pods use the current topology information.

/sig cloud-provider
/area cloudprovider

title: e2e_node/remote/gce: readiness polling drops terminal errors and shadows the ready instance
body:
`createGCEInstance` waits for a VM to report `RUNNING` and for containerd or CRI-O to become available. The current gcloud implementation can exhaust that polling loop without returning an error.

Inside the loop, `instance, err := getGCEInstance(name)` declares variables in the loop body, leaving the outer `instance` and `err` unchanged. Errors for a non-running VM or a missing runtime service are also assigned to `_`. After the loop, the function checks only the outer `err`, not whether readiness was reached. The affected code is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/55877941cfcadd07522f2199006bc9a89f40df6d/test/e2e_node/remote/gce/gce_runner.go#L591-L628

This has three different effects:

- If the VM never reaches `RUNNING`, `registerGceHostIP` will usually reject it later, but the useful provisioning error is lost.
- If the VM is `RUNNING` but its runtime service never appears, the later check does not catch it because it only checks the VM state. Setup can continue with a node that is not ready for node e2e.
- The outer `instance` remains nil and is passed to the kernel-argument path. That path is present in the source; I have not confirmed which current job configurations set `kernel_arguments`.

The pre-gcloud implementation assigned the observed instance and error to the outer variables, so this appears to have changed during #123006.

The readiness wait should return the exact instance that passed both checks, preserve the last failed observation, and return an error when polling expires or its context is canceled.

/sig node
/kind bug

title: Improve init container startup status visibility ( like pulling big image)
body:
### What would you like to be added?


Improve startup status visibility for init containers.

Today, `kubectl get pod` shows the same status for different stages:

```text
Init:0/1
```

For example:

- pulling the init container image
- creating the init container
- running the init container

Also, `initContainerStatuses` may only show:

```yaml
state:
  waiting:
    reason: PodInitializing
```

while the image is still being pulled.

It would be useful to distinguish these stages, similar to `ContainerCreating` for main containers.

For example:

```text
Init:Pulling
Init:ContainerCreating
Init:0/1
```

The exact status names are open for discussion.

Related:
- kubernetes/enhancements#5334 (KEP-5334: Image Pull Progress)
- kubernetes/enhancements#3542 (earlier image pull progress proposal)


### Why is this needed?


When an init container takes a long time to start or run, users cannot tell whether it is pulling the image, creating the container, or already running.

We had an init container image pull that took more than 50 minutes. `kubectl get pod` showed `Init:0/1`, and `initContainerStatuses` only showed `PodInitializing`.

The actual image pulling state was only visible from Pod Events.

This makes troubleshooting init containers harder than main containers.

/sig node
/sig cli

title: kubectl kuberc set accepts an empty option name
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl kuberc set` accepts an `--option` value whose flag name is empty, for example:

```console
kubectl kuberc set --section defaults --command get --option '=wide'
```

The command reports success and writes an entry with an empty `name` to the kuberc file. When the matching command is used later, kuberc attempts to apply that entry and returns an `invalid flag` error.

### What did you expect to happen?

`kubectl kuberc set` should reject an option with an empty flag name instead of persisting a kuberc configuration that breaks later commands.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run `kubectl kuberc set --section defaults --command get --option '=wide'` with kuberc enabled.
2. Inspect the generated kuberc file and observe an option with `name: ""`.
3. Run a matching `kubectl get` command and observe that kuberc rejects the empty flag name.

### Anything else we need to know?

The parser splits each option at `=` and strips leading dashes, but does not check whether the resulting name is empty. A focused unit test can cover this without a cluster.

title: [Failing Test] [sig-auth] Projected PodCertificate conformance test cannot bind port 443 under Restricted Linux settings
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

External Kubernetes v1.37.0 certified-conformance run.

This is not an upstream Kubernetes CI job. The failure is deterministic on Linux nodes using the default privileged-port setting:
`  net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=1024.`

### Which tests are failing?

[sig-auth] Projected PodCertificate [FeatureGate:PodCertificateRequest] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundle] [FeatureGate:ClusterTrustBundleProjection] should allow server and client pods to establish an mTLS connection [MinimumKubeletVersion:1.37] [Conformance]

### Since when has it been failing?

 Observed recently during a Kubernetes v1.37.0 certified-conformance run.

The affected test configuration was introduced during the Pod Certificates beta e2e work in September 2025 and promoted to conformance for v1.37.

### Testgrid link

_No response_

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test server container fails before the mTLS handshake:

`E0901 ... error while serving: while listening: listen tcp 0.0.0.0:443: bind: permission denied
`
The test creates the server with a Restricted security context (non-root, all capabilities dropped) but configures agnhost to listen on privileged port 443. On Linux with the default per-network-namespace setting:

 ```
 net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start = 1024
  CapEff: 0000000000000000
```

  binding port 443 requires root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE.

  The client therefore receives:

`  dial tcp <service-cluster-ip>:443: connect: connection refused
`
Validated fix: change the server listener to 8443 and explicitly set the Service targetPort to 8443 while retaining Service port 443. The original focused e2e test then passes with the actual PodCertificateRequest, ClusterTrustBundle projection, and mTLS flow.

### Anything else we need to know?

 ## Summary

  The v1.37 conformance test:

  [sig-auth] Projected PodCertificate ... should allow server and client pods to establish an mTLS connection

  fails deterministically on Linux nodes using the normal privileged-port boundary.

  The test creates the server with a Restricted security context, which runs it
  non-root with all capabilities dropped, while configuring agnhost to listen on
  `0.0.0.0:443`.

  ## Reproduction

  Kubernetes: v1.37.0
  OS: Oracle Linux 8.10
  Kernel: 5.15.0-322.203.3.5.el8uek.x86_64
  Runtime: CRI-O 1.36.3

  On each node, a Restricted non-root diagnostic pod reported:

  ```text
  /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_unprivileged_port_start: 1024
  CapEff: 0000000000000000

  The e2e server log:

  error while serving: while listening: listen tcp 0.0.0.0:443: bind: permission denied

  The client consequently reports:

  dial tcp <service-cluster-ip>:443: connect: connection refused

  ## Expected behavior

  The conformance test should pass on Linux nodes using the default privileged
  port boundary, without requiring a provider to relax it cluster-wide.

  ## Root cause

  test/e2e/auth/projected_podcertificate.go builds a Restricted security
  context, drops capabilities, and configures:

  "--listen=0.0.0.0:443",

  The Service has port 443 with no explicit targetPort, so it defaults to 443.

  ## Proposed fix

  Keep the Service port and client URL at 443, but use an unprivileged backend
  port:

  + "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/intstr"

  - "--listen=0.0.0.0:443",
  + "--listen=0.0.0.0:8443",

  - Ports: []v1.ServicePort{{Name: "https", Port: 443}},
  + Ports: []v1.ServicePort{{
  +   Name:       "https",
  +   Port:       443,
  +   TargetPort: intstr.FromInt(8443),
  + }},

  ## Validation

  We reran the original focused Sonobuoy test while applying only those two
  transient object changes. It passed with the real in-process signer,
  PodCertificateRequest issuance, projected certificates, ClusterTrustBundle
  projection, and mTLS assertion:

  passed: 8

title: DRA: Add audit-log visibility for the adminAccess self-escalation entry points (namespace labeling, claim creation)
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Follow-up to #141293, which established that a narrow, common namespace-metadata-edit permission is sufficient for a non-admin user to self-grant DRA's `adminAccess` — working as designed, RBAC gates verbs not field values. 

Two points in that self-escalation path leave no audit trail today:

1. A namespace gets labeled `resource.kubernetes.io/admin-access: "true"`.
2. A `ResourceClaim` with `adminAccess: true` gets created/admitted in that namespace.

Checked both directly against source (pinned `v1.37.0`) — neither has any distinguishing entries:
- `pkg/registry/resource/utils.go` (`AuthorizedForAdmin`, the namespace-label check): no audit
- `pkg/registry/resource/resourceclaim/strategy.go` (where `adminAccess` field handling lives): no audit here as well
- `pkg/registry/core/namespace/strategy.go` : no audit here also.

Live-verified on a real `v1.37.0` cluster with audit logging enabled (`RequestResponse` level for both resource types) to confirm this.

Performed both actions 
- labeled a namespace, 
- created an `adminAccess: true` claim in it 

Inspected the resulting audit events. Both show only the generic `authorization.k8s.io/decision`/`reason` annotations every audit event gets regardless of resource type. Nothing DRA- or adminAccess-specific. 

Also confirmed zero `Event` objects for either action via `kubectl get events` (this is actually good to avoid showing info to people who do not need to know, but audit log would be good).

I'd propose adding an audit-log entry at each point, using `AddAuditAnnotations`. 
AFAIK, this would match the behavior to PodSecurity admission which already does it for a similar purpose.

I don't have a strong opinion on exactly which code path should add each annotation (admission plugin vs. the relevant controller). 
That's a call best made by experts.
Please let me know in case I missed something.

P.S.:
A policy-engine-based mitigation ([kyverno/policies#1523](https://github.com/kyverno/policies/pull/1523)) covers similar ground, but
only on clusters that install it. 
Ideally, a native audit annotation that doesn't depend on any third-party component would be good.




### Why is this needed?

`adminAccess` bypassing ordinary exclusivity is settled, working-as-designed behavior (#141293). This issue doesn't reopen that. What's missing at these two points is any way for a cluster operator to *see* the chain starting: a namespace being labeled, and a claim requesting the capability. An operator doing a routine security review currently has no entry to find either by, natively, or even via `kubectl get events`, since nothing records it at all.

Likely SIG: sig-auth.

title: DRA: AllocationMode All errors for incomplete or invalid pools are not per-node failures
body:
### What happened?

An `AllocationMode: All` request returns a plain error when a pool gathered for the candidate node is incomplete or invalid. In `validateDeviceRequest`, same code in the stable, incubating and experimental variants:

```go
if pool.IsIncomplete {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
if pool.IsInvalid {
	return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently invalid", klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID)
}
```

Neither wraps `internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode`. `DynamicResources.Filter` maps only that sentinel to an `Unschedulable` result for the node; anything else becomes a framework `Error`, and `checkNode` in `findNodesThatPassFilters` cancels the remaining node checks when one shows up.

The other failing cases in the same suite do wrap it. Probe on master `a818af18fe2`, logging `errors.Is(err, ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)` for every case that errors:

```
all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool                                                false | claim claim-0, request req-0: asks for all devices, but resource pool driver-a/pool-1 is currently being updated
invalid-pool-is-error-if-no-other-device-can-be-allocated                          true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
duplicate-slice                                                                   true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-validation-error-on-non-targeting-slice                     true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-device-counter-consumption-references-unknown-counter-set    true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
partitionable-devices-same-counter-set-name-in-different-resource-slices           true  | invalid resource pools were encountered
```

Same in all three variants.

`IsIncomplete` does not need a malformed object. `GatherPools` sets it when the generation resolved for the node holds fewer slices than its declared `resourceSliceCount`, which is what a pool looks like while a driver is publishing a new generation.

### What did you expect to happen?

The check itself looks right and I would leave it alone: a slice that has not arrived may hold another device matching the request, so the allocator cannot know the full set yet.

The classification is the part that looks wrong. Wrapping the sentinel keeps the visible message, since it has no text of its own, and keeps the failure on one node:

```go
return requestData, fmt.Errorf("claim %s, request %s: asks for all devices, but resource pool %s is currently being updated%w",
	klog.KObj(claim), request.name(), pool.PoolID, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode)
```

Other nodes then keep being evaluated, and if all of them fail the Pod is `Unschedulable`. `EventsToRegister` already lists `ResourceSlice` `Add` and `Update`, so the slice update that finishes the rollout requeues it. The invalid branch wants the same treatment.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

`all-devices-of-the-incomplete-pool` in `allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` already reaches the incomplete branch. Adding this next to the existing `expectError` assertion produces the output above:

```go
if err != nil {
	t.Logf("PROBE %s errors.Is=%v", name, errors.Is(err, internal.ErrFailedAllocationOnNode))
}
```

No case covers the invalid branch today.

### Anything else we need to know?

Same classification shape as #141214 and #141338, different trigger. Those need a malformed stored per-device `nodeSelector`; this one fires during an ordinary generation rollout. Filing separately so the accepted scope of #141214 stays as it is.

@trungminhdo4-glitch offered on #141214 to fold this into #141338 if the maintainers would rather keep the per-node classification changes together. I am not opening a competing PR either way.

### Kubernetes version

Read and probed on master `a818af18fe2`. The code path is unchanged on current master.

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

---

This issue was written in part with the assistance of generative AI. I verified the code references and ran the probe above myself.

title: in-tree iSCSI: DetachBlockISCSIDisk fails permanently when the by-path link is already gone, stranding the volume in volumesInUse
body:
### What happened?

If the iSCSI session for a **block-mode** in-tree iSCSI volume is lost while the pod is still running, the teardown that follows never completes. `DetachBlockISCSIDisk` returns an error before it reaches its own logout, kubelet retries every 2m2s indefinitely, and the volume stays in `node.status.volumesInUse`:

```
kubelet[...]: Error: failed to validate devicePath: /dev/disk/by-path/ip-<portal>-iscsi-<iqn>-lun-0
kubelet[...]: Operation for "{volumeName:kubernetes.io/iscsi/<portal>:<iqn>:0 podName: nodeName:}" failed.
  No retries permitted until <t+2m2s> (durationBeforeRetry 2m2s).
```

Because the node still advertises the volume, the attach/detach controller will not attach it anywhere else:

```
Warning  FailedAttachVolume  attachdetach-controller
  Multi-Attach error for volume "<pv>" Volume is already exclusively attached to one node and can't be attached to another
```

Nothing is visibly wrong until the workload moves. A pod that stays on the same node keeps working, since the controller's view happens to match. We found this weeks later, when a pod was first scheduled to a different node and would not start.

### What did you expect to happen?

Teardown to complete. A missing device link is the state teardown is meant to clean up, and the code that gets skipped already handles it.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run a pod with a block-mode (`volumeMode: Block`) in-tree iSCSI PV on node A.
2. With kubelet still running, log the session out underneath it:
   `iscsiadm -m node -T <iqn> --logout`
3. Delete the pod.

Teardown then fails on every retry. `kubectl get node A -o jsonpath='{.status.volumesInUse}'` still lists the volume, with no pod referencing it, no session, and no `/dev/disk/by-path` link. Scheduling the workload to node B gives the Multi-Attach error above.

Note that restarting kubelet does not reproduce this. It clears it, because the actual state of the world is rebuilt from pod directories, so the stuck entry only exists in a running kubelet.

Two workarounds, both confirmed. Delete the volume's directory under
`/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/kubernetes.io/iscsi/volumeDevices/iface-default/`, which makes the function take its `PathExists` early return and complete in about 20 seconds. Or restart kubelet.

### Anything else we need to know?

The check is in `pkg/volume/iscsi/iscsi_util.go`, in `DetachBlockISCSIDisk`, and is the same on `master`:

```go
devicePath := getDevByPath(portals[0], iqn, lun)
klog.V(5).Infof("iscsi: devicePath: %s", devicePath)
if _, err = os.Stat(devicePath); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("failed to validate devicePath: %s", devicePath)
}
```

Three things suggest the check is unnecessary:

1. `devicePath` is not used after it. It is computed, logged at V(5), stat'd, then discarded. The detach that follows uses `portals`, `iqn`, `iface`, `volName` and `initiatorName`.

2. The code it prevents from running already handles a missing session. `detachISCSIDisk` wraps both the logout and the node record delete in `ignoreExitCodes(err, exit_ISCSI_ERR_NO_OBJS_FOUND, exit_ISCSI_ERR_SESS_NOT_FOUND)`. The guard against logging out a target another volume is using, `isSessionBusy`, counts plugin directories matching `portal-iqn` and does not look at `/dev`, so a missing link does not affect it either.

3. The filesystem-mode equivalent has no such check. `DetachDisk` is otherwise the same function, with the same `PathExists` early return, the same portal and IQN extraction, the same `isSessionBusy` guard and the same `detachISCSIDisk` call, and it goes from resolving portals to logout with no device check. The file contains only two `os.Stat` calls: this one, and one in `waitForPathToExistInternal` on the attach side where waiting for a device is the intent.

The check dates to a6d979dd88, the commit that added block volume support, and is unchanged since apart from a glog to klog rename.

The comment three lines above it reads "If we arrive here, device is no longer used, see if need to logout the target", so the function is meant to run when the device is gone, which is the condition the check rejects.

A possible fix, making the block path behave like the filesystem path:

```go
devicePath := getDevByPath(portals[0], iqn, lun)
klog.V(5).Infof("iscsi: devicePath: %s", devicePath)
if _, err := os.Stat(devicePath); err != nil {
    // The link is already gone if the session was lost before teardown ran.
    // detachISCSIDisk ignores ISCSI_ERR_NO_OBJS_FOUND and ISCSI_ERR_SESS_NOT_FOUND,
    // and isSessionBusy counts plugin directories rather than devices, so both
    // remaining steps work without it.
    klog.V(4).Infof("iscsi: devicePath %s already gone, continuing to detach", devicePath)
}
```

I built v1.33.13 with that change and ran it on the affected node, using the same reproduction steps on the same two volumes.

With the stock binary, teardown logs `Error: failed to validate devicePath: ...`, retries every 2m2s indefinitely, and the volumes stay in `volumesInUse` until the directory is removed or kubelet is restarted.

With the patched binary the same sequence logs:

```
iscsi_util.go:738] iscsi: log out target <portal> iqn <iqn> iface default
operation_generator.go:1365] UnmapDevice succeeded for volume "<boot pv>"
operation_generator.go:1365] UnmapDevice succeeded for volume "<storage pv>"
```

and both volumes leave `volumesInUse` on their own in about 40 seconds, with no `failed to validate devicePath` at all. So execution reaches `isSessionBusy` and `detachISCSIDisk`, and those handle the missing session as expected.

I am happy to send a PR if this looks right.

Possibly related, though CSI rather than in-tree iSCSI: #131410 reports the same downstream symptom, with `UnmountDevice started` and no matching success, the volume stuck in `volumesInUse`, Multi-Attach on another node, and resolution only by removing the node.

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.33.13
Server Version: v1.33.13
```
Also seen on v1.33.12. The code is the same on `master`.

### Cloud provider

None, bare metal on-premise.

### OS version

```console
$ cat /etc/os-release
NAME="openSUSE Leap"
VERSION="15.6"

$ uname -a
Linux <node> 6.4.0-150600.23.103-default #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

### Install tools

kubeadm

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

containerd 2.2.0

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

In-tree iSCSI volume plugin (`kubernetes.io/iscsi`), block mode, static PVs against an iSCSI array. The workloads are KubeVirt VMs, but nothing in the failure is KubeVirt specific and it reproduces with any pod using a block-mode iSCSI PV.

title: Node capacity/allocatable never advertise hugepages-* on Windows nodes
body:
# hugepages resources on Windows nodes - not applicable (closed)

## Summary
This issue requested support/clarity for `hugepages-*` resources on Windows nodes. After analysis, the conclusion is that **the Linux hugepages design does not apply to Windows**; the issue is therefore closed as not-applicable (see 'Decision' below).

## What was observed
On Windows the kubelet never reports `hugepages-*` in `Node.status.capacity`/`allocatable`. Root cause: `pkg/kubelet/cadvisor/util.go` only emits hugepages from `MachineInfo.HugePages`, and the Windows winstats provider (`pkg/kubelet/winstats/perfcounter_nodestats_windows.go`, `getMachineInfo`) never populates `HugePages`.

## The Linux design (why it exists)
Linux pre-allocates `hugetlbfs` pages at boot; Kubernetes advertises `hugepages-<size>` as a **schedulable, never-overcommitted node resource** and the `emptyDir medium:HugePages` plugin mounts the `hugetlbfs` filesystem into the container, with the kernel guaranteeing the pages. It is a host-kernel memory-accounting + per-container filesystem-mount mechanism.

## Why it does not apply to Windows
- No `hugetlbfs` and no hugetlb page allocator; process-isolated containers have no hugetlb guarantee.
- Windows 'large pages' (`VirtualAlloc(MEM_LARGE_PAGES)` + `SeLockMemoryPrivilege`) are a **process-address-space allocation**, not a schedulable node resource, not mountable, and not a per-container guarantee.
- There is no viable Windows design that Kubernetes could back with the same 'huge pages as a schedulable, guaranteed, mountable resource' semantics. The user-facing need (large/low-TLB memory) exists, but a different mechanism and a new KEP would be required, not the Linux hugepages design.

## Decision
Applying the policy 'if the same design does not apply to Windows, close'; if it could, suggest a new design - the same design is not applicable, so this issue is **closed** as not-applicable. Windows hugepages should be documented as Linux-specific/unsupported.

If sig-windows maintainers believe a Windows large-pages / non-paged-reservation model is worth an enhancement KEP, reopen and re-scope with such a design (distinct from the Linux hugetlbfs resource).

---
_AI-assisted analysis; reconcile with sig/windows + sig-node maintainers._

title: Node.status.volumesAttached[].devicePath is block-device/unix-specific; Windows semantics undefined
body:
# `volumesAttached[].devicePath` semantics on Windows nodes

## What would you like to be added?
A defined contract for `Node.status.volumesAttached[].devicePath` on Windows, and a fix for the dead platform-specific code that assumes a unix block device. On Windows the field currently carries effectively the CSI `VolumeID`/opaque per-driver handle, while the code paths (`hostutil.PathIsDevice`, block-volume `MapPodDevice`) assume a unix block-device node.

## Why is this needed?
On Linux, `devicePath` is the actual host block-device node (e.g. `/dev/xvdX`) that kubelet uses to mount/format and the block-volume plugin maps into the pod - validated and consumed semantically. Windows has no `/dev` device tree (volumes surface as volume-GUID paths or CSI VolumeID), so the field's meaning on Windows is undefined and the detach-path safety check is a silent no-op. Controllers, CSI drivers, and consumers need a reliable contract.

## Current state (source-verified)
- `pkg/volume/util/hostutil/hostutil_windows.go` `PathIsDevice` -> `(false, nil)` and `DeviceOpened` -> `(false, nil)` unconditionally.
- The detach path calls these (`operationexecutor/operation_generator.go` ~L883-891); on Windows the in-use recheck can never trigger.
- Block-volume mapping is linux-only: `volume_path_handler_linux.go` vs `volume_path_handler_unsupported.go` on Windows.
- CSI on Windows is GA (kubernetes/enhancements KEP-1122, milestone v1.22) but covers filesystem-volume mount, not the block-like devicePath semantics.

## Why the Linux design does not apply as-is
The Linux `devicePath` = a real, validated host block-device node used for mount/format and block-volume MapPodDevice. Windows has no device node tree; volumes are volume-GUID paths / CSI VolumeID, and WindowsPathIsDevice has nothing to test.

## Recommended new design for Windows (proposed under the 'suggest a new design' policy branch)
Because a viable Windows meaning exists, the issue is kept open:
1. **Redefine the contract**: on Windows, `Node.status.volumesAttached[].devicePath` should carry the **CSI `VolumeHandle` (volumeID)** - the attach identity - not a device path. Update the `AttachedVolume.DevicePath` doc in `staging/src/k8s.io/api/core/v1/types.go` to state the platform variance (Linux = block device node; Windows = CSI volumeID).
2. **Fix the dead detach safety check**: gate the `PathIsDevice`/`DeviceOpened` branch on platform (or document it does not apply on Windows) instead of leaving unreachable code.

title: [1.36] Kubelet retries DRA health streams for plugins that do not advertise health support
body:
### What happened?

On Kubernetes 1.36, kubelet starts a `NodeWatchResources` health stream for every registered DRA plugin whenever `ResourceHealthStatus` is enabled. It does this even when the plugin does not advertise the optional `DRAResourceHealth` service in its registration response.

When the service is not implemented, kubelet receives `codes.Unimplemented`, logs it as an error, and retries every five seconds:

```text
E0902 21:16:20.306285 manager.go:1045] "Error receiving from WatchResources stream" err="rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = device health reporting is not supported by this driver" logger="DRA registration handler.dra-manager" pluginName="compute-domain.nvidia.com"
```

`ResourceHealthStatus` is Beta and enabled by default in 1.36, so this occurs on the default feature-gate configuration when a DRA plugin does not implement health reporting.

This does not appear to affect DRA workload correctness, but it continuously emits error-level kubelet logs. At one retry every five seconds, each unsupported plugin produces 17,280 error records per day per node. This creates unnecessary log storage and ingestion costs and makes genuine kubelet errors harder to identify.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should only start the health stream when the plugin advertises a supported `DRAResourceHealth` service.

If a plugin advertises the service but returns `codes.Unimplemented`, kubelet should treat that as a terminal indication that health reporting is unsupported and stop retrying until the plugin re-registers.

This is the behavior in Kubernetes 1.37.

### How can we reproduce it?

This was reproduced with a kind v1.36.1 cluster using the head of:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/pull/1243

The GPU plugin streams health normally when its health reporting feature is enabled. Kubelet nevertheless continues attempting `NodeWatchResources` every five seconds for `compute-domain.nvidia.com`, which does not advertise the health service.

The same driver configuration is quiet on kubelet 1.37.

Full reproduction findings and logs:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/issues/1423#issuecomment-5532233065

Although the report uses the NVIDIA DRA driver, the behavior is generic to any DRA plugin that registers without the optional health service.

### Anything else we need to know?

In release-1.36, `RegisterPlugin` receives the plugin's `supportedServices`, but the health stream is started without checking that list:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L324-L334

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bf628307442eb90f0c503e6c8f9525bce1f14aa6/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/plugin/dra_plugin_manager.go#L387-L407

Kubernetes 1.37 fixed this as part of #139477 by:

- selecting an advertised health service during registration;
- starting the stream only when such a service was advertised;
- stopping retries when the stream returns `codes.Unimplemented`.

This issue is intended to track a targeted backport of that behavior to release-1.36, not the larger v1 health API and kubeletplugin helper changes from #139477.

The proposed 1.36 fix would:

1. Start `NodeWatchResources` only if the plugin advertises `v1alpha1.DRAResourceHealth`.
2. Treat `codes.Unimplemented` as non-error and stop retrying.
3. Add regression tests for an absent health service and an `Unimplemented` stream.

A backport to 1.35 or earlier is not requested because `ResourceHealthStatus` was Alpha and disabled by default there.

cc @shivamerla @guptaNswati @pohly

### Kubernetes version

```console
$ kubectl version
Server Version: v1.36.1
```

The current release-1.36 source remains affected. Kubernetes 1.37 is not affected.

### Cloud provider

kind

### Related plugins

NVIDIA DRA driver, although the kubelet behavior is driver-independent:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu/issues/1423

title: ResourceQuota admission admits over-quota requests when an unrelated quota's status update hits a Conflict
body:
### What happened?

With two ResourceQuota objects in one namespace covering disjoint resources, a request that exceeds one quota can be **admitted** if, in the same admission batch, another request's status update on the *other* quota returns 409 Conflict.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b2ec8b6fefac451a2dedafc4dd71f2f16c7a6abe/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/resourcequota/controller.go#L262-L264

On a Conflict, checkQuotas recurses with only the conflicted quota subset and re-evaluates every waiter in the batch. A waiter already denied by a different quota matches none of the subset, so this unguarded assignment replaces its determined `Forbidden` with success. The other re-resolution sites in the same function are guarded with `IsDefaultDeny`; this one is not


### What did you expect to happen?

A request denied for exceeding quota A stays denied regardless of Conflict retries on quota B. Quota status update conflicts are routine (the quota controller's `UpdateStatus`, HA apiservers, the evaluator's own workers racing), so the retry path is hot.

title: DRA ResourceSlice stays valid after its driver becomes unavailable, so the scheduler keeps binding pods onto capacity that can never be prepared
body:
### What happened?

If a DRA driver becomes unavailable on a node for any reason (it crashes, it's mid-restart, a rolling upgrade is in progress, etc.) while the node itself stays healthy, the `ResourceSlice` it was advertising stays exactly as-is. Nothing marks it stale or removes it. 

The scheduler keeps binding new pods to that node against those devices even though the driver is gone, with no warning that anything is wrong.

I reproduced this by simulating a driver outage on a node that was otherwise completely healthy (see the steps in the repro section). 
The `ResourceSlice` didn't change at all, before or after:

```
NAME                                                        NODE                            DRIVER            POOL                            AGE
00000-gpu.example.com-kubelet-stuck-prepare-worker3-6smqv   kubelet-stuck-prepare-worker3   gpu.example.com   kubelet-stuck-prepare-worker3   86m
```

same name, same age, driver pod gone. 

I then created a new pod with a fresh claim, pinned to the same node. It scheduled normally:

```
Normal   Scheduled                       Successfully assigned finding12/workload-a-dc5b9d4fd-9w4l4 to kubelet-stuck-prepare-worker3
Warning  FailedPrepareDynamicResources   Failed to prepare dynamic resources: prepare dynamic resources: DRA driver gpu.example.com is not registered
```

The scheduler had no way to know the device it just handed out belongs to a driver that isn't running anymore.

#### What's not affected?
- **An already running Pod:**  A pod that's already running when the driver goes away is unaffected. Its device access was
already set up before the driver disappeared, and I confirmed it keeps working.
- **Device Exclusivity:** This is unaffected. A slice advertising 2 devices still only lets 2 claims be allocated at once, driver up or down. Extra pods stayed unscheduled with the ordinary `FailedScheduling` reason (`cannot allocate all claims`as expected).

The bug isn't that counting breaks down. It's that the count itself keeps being treated as real no matter how long the driver's been gone. 
Once the driver came back, it resumes with the same slice. The slice had never been touched the whole time.

#### Impact

- What makes this worse than an ordinary capacity shortage: a real shortage leaves a pod visibly `Pending`, waiting, which could give it a chance to be scheduled on a node with a healthy driver. But the current behavior doesn't do this. The scheduler reports success, the pod gets bound, and it just never starts. As long as driver is down, the state is stuck.
- Once bound, nothing moves it. A pod's owning controller (ReplicaSet, Job, a gang scheduler's PodGroup) only checks pod count, not whether the pod is actually making progress, so a stuck pod is never replaced automatically.
- **Gang scheduling:** For a gang-scheduled job, one member landing on an orphaned slice is enough to keep the whole group below quorum indefinitely, with nothing to signal that anything is wrong beyond that one pod's own events.


### What did you expect to happen?

Once a `ResourceSlice`'s driver has been unreachable for a while, I'd expect the scheduler to stop treating it as available capacity, instead of only invalidating it when the whole Node object gets deleted.

A pod scheduled against a slice like this is doomed before it even starts. The slice isn't actually serving anything, yet the pod gets bound as if it were. 

And once that happens, there's no way for the pod to end up on a different, healthy slice by itself, even if other nodes have working drivers with free capacity. 
The only way out is the driver coming back (which depends entirely on what took it down in the first place) or someone stepping in manually.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy a DRA driver as a DaemonSet, targeted to a node via a `nodeSelector` label (I used
   [kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver)
   v0.4.0). Confirm its `ResourceSlice` exists.
2. Simulate the driver becoming unavailable: remove the `nodeSelector` label so the DaemonSet
   controller withdraws the driver pod. (This is just a convenient way to take the driver down on
   demand for this repro — a real crash, restart, or upgrade removes the same pod the same way;
   nothing about the label itself matters.)
3. Check the `ResourceSlice` again — still there, unchanged.
4. Create a pod with a fresh claim against the driver's `DeviceClass`, pinned to the same node.
   It gets scheduled and bound normally.
5. Repeat step 4 up to the number of devices the slice advertises. Each pod keeps landing on the
   same node, no warning, for as long as the driver stays down. One more beyond that count
   correctly stays unscheduled (`FailedScheduling: cannot allocate all claims`), same as it would
   with the driver present — exclusivity itself isn't affected, only whether the count should still
   be trusted at all.
6. Restore the label so the driver pod comes back. The slice was never touched throughout.


### Anything else we need to know?

This isn't specific to GPUs or to this driver. I checked, and the `ResourceSlice` type itself has no staleness, expiry, or heartbeat field for any resource type. It applies to any DRA-exposed device on any driver built on the standard `kubeletplugin` helper library, including NVIDIA's own production DRA driver.

The trigger here (driver pod down, node fine) isn't unusual. 
A crash loop, a bad config push, a hardware or firmware fault the driver can't recover from (GPU Xid/ECC errors are a well-known
example), or a rolling upgrade with `maxUnavailable > 0` all get you there.



### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
kind v0.32.0, node image kindest/node:v1.37.0
```

title: getKubeletMappings() picks a different user namespace ID range depending on whether kubelet was built with cgo
Add kubelet to KUBE_CGO_OVERRIDES in source-built race jobs once kubelet is a static binary
body:
Follow-up from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870, split out at @dims' request.

`-race` needs cgo, and [`kube::golang::build_binaries_for_platform()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/79f041dd524968a26c28398be9b5dc30ada1f841/hack/lib/golang.sh#L841-L884) only appends `KUBE_RACE` to the non-static and `.test` groups, so a kubelet in `KUBE_STATIC_BINARIES` cannot carry race instrumentation at all. The DRA and kind race jobs already override the components they care about for exactly this reason:

```yaml
# Normally control plane components are linked statically, which does not work with -race (needs CGO).
# We need to override the default for components of interest.
- name: KUBE_CGO_OVERRIDES
  value: kube-apiserver kube-controller-manager kube-scheduler
```

kubelet is absent from that list only because it did not need to be there. Once #135870 merges, the build log line @pohly used to verify #133834 goes from `cmd/kubelet (non-static, race detection)` to `cmd/kubelet (static)` while `e2e.test` keeps its instrumentation, so those jobs stay green with an uninstrumented kubelet under test.

Adding `kubelet` to the override restores it, but only for the jobs that actually build it from source, which is worth being precise about:

- `dra-presubmit` and `dra-canary` set `kind_node_source=.`, and the kind CI and presubmit jobs go through `e2e-k8s.sh`, which runs `kind build node-image` against the checkout. kind forwards `os.Environ()` into the Kubernetes build and has `cmd/kubelet` among its targets, so the override reaches it.
- `dra-ci` points `kind_node_source` at a `dl.k8s.io` tarball and downloads `e2e.test`, so its `KUBE_RACE` and `KUBE_CGO_OVERRIDES` have nothing to act on. That is pre-existing and unrelated to #135870, but it does mean adding a name there would change nothing.
- Version-skew jobs copy a downloaded older kubelet onto the node after the build, so a build-time override does not affect what runs.

Happy to send the source-built part to kubernetes/test-infra so it can land alongside #135870 rather than after it.

/sig node
/sig testing
/kind cleanup

title: scheduler: pods blocked by namespaceSelector podAffinity are not requeued on matching pod add or namespace label change
body:
### What happened?

A pod whose only scheduling blocker is a required podAffinity term with a namespaceSelector stays Pending with no new scheduling attempt after a cluster change that makes it schedulable:

- an assigned pod matching the term labelSelector appears in a namespace whose labels match the namespaceSelector (assigned pod add), or
- labels are added to a namespace so that an existing assigned pod now matches the namespaceSelector.

The pod is only retried by the periodic unschedulable pods sweep (`--pod-max-in-unschedulable-pods-duration`, default 5m, deprecated), and it schedules successfully on the first attempt after the sweep.

A control with the same affinity term but without namespaceSelector (matching a pod in the same namespace) is requeued and scheduled within about 10s of the matching pod being added.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should be requeued when an assigned pod that satisfies the affinity term, including namespaceSelector evaluation, is added, consistent with the behavior for terms without namespaceSelector.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create namespaces ns-a and ns-c. ns-a has no labels initially.
2. Run pod worker in ns-a with labels app=worker.
3. Run pod scout in ns-c with this affinity:

```yaml
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: worker
        namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            team: one
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```

scout stays Pending with FailedScheduling, for example `0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod affinity rules`.

4. Label the namespace: `kubectl label ns ns-a team=one`.

Expected: scout is requeued and scheduled on the worker node. Actual: no new scheduling attempt within 60s. Reproduced twice; the scheduler log shows no requeue after the namespace update.

Alternative trigger (assigned pod add): with ns-a labeled team=one from the start, create scout before worker. scout stays Pending. Then create worker. The assigned pod add event arrives (visible in the scheduler log), but scout is not requeued within 60s. Reproduced twice.

Deleting scout and recreating it schedules immediately, which shows the world is schedulable and only the event-driven retry is missing. In a longer observation the stuck pod was scheduled by the periodic sweep about 5m08s after it was parked, on the first attempt after the flush.

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause (kubernetes/kubernetes master as of 2026-09-08, by code inspection):

- InterPodAffinity registers queueing hints only for `AssignedPod`, `TargetPod` and `Node` events. No `Namespace` event is registered, so a namespace label change cannot wake the pod.
- In `isSchedulableAfterAssignedPodChange`, the queued pod terms are matched with `podMatchesAllAffinityTerms` / `podMatchesAnyAffinityTerms` without unrolling `namespaceSelector` into `term.Namespaces`. The unrolling (`mergeAffinityTermNamespacesIfNotEmpty`) is done in the Filter and Scoring paths only. With no explicit namespaces in the term, `term.Namespaces` is empty and the `namespaceSelector` is evaluated against nil namespace labels, so the namespace half of `AffinityTerm.Matches` never succeeds and the hint returns `QueueSkip`. `podMatchesAllAffinityTerms` documents the assumption that the `NamespaceSelector` was already merged into the `Namespaces` set.
- The delete branch uses the same unmerged anti-affinity matching, so anti-affinity terms with `namespaceSelector` are likely affected for delete events as well (by code inspection, not reproduced here).

Related issues and PRs in the same family of InterPodAffinity event-driven requeue gaps: #141354 (open; pod deletion with self-affinity, plain labelSelector, different branch and term shape), #130784 (multiple required terms), #139161 (merged PR; queue hint fix for anti-affinities).

We are preparing a fix for the pod add path: unroll `namespaceSelector` before hint matching, reusing `mergeAffinityTermNamespacesIfNotEmpty`, with unit tests (the queueing hint tests currently have no `namespaceSelector` coverage), and will open a PR against master. Waking pods on namespace label changes additionally needs a `Namespace` cluster event class, which the scheduler framework does not provide today; happy to discuss whether that scope belongs in this change or a separate one. If it helps, we can also add coverage for the #141354 deletion scenario to the same test matrix.

This issue was prepared with the assistance of generative AI. All findings were verified with manual experiments on a local cluster.

title: protocol: HTTP2 validation not enforced for scheme: HTTPS / non-empty host, field silently dropped instead of rejected (KEP-5999)
body:
### What happened?

While doing manual Beta-readiness testing for [KEP-5999 (HTTP/2 cleartext container probes)](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/5999-h2c-container-probes) / #139429, I found that the two documented validation rules for HTTPGetAction.Protocol: HTTP2 are not actually enforced:

protocol: HTTP2 combined with scheme: HTTPS should be rejected.
protocol: HTTP2 combined with a non-empty host should be rejected.
Instead of rejecting the pod, the apiserver admits it and silently drops the protocol field, leaving scheme/host as submitted. This produces a pod running an ordinary HTTP/1.1 (or HTTPS) probe with no indication to the user that their protocol: HTTP2 setting was discarded , no validation error, no warning, no event.

### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl apply should fail with a validation error, per the behavior described in the KEP:

protocol: HTTP2 requires scheme: HTTP (the default). Setting protocol: HTTP2 with scheme: HTTPS is rejected during validation.

When protocol: HTTP2 is set, host must be empty... This is rejected during validation with a descriptive error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1.Start a cluster with the H2CContainerProbe feature gate enabled on kube-apiserver.
2.Create a Pod whose container has a livenessProbe.httpGet with port: 80, host: 1.2.3.4, and protocol: HTTP2 set together.
3.Observe that kubectl apply succeeds and the Pod is created, instead of being rejected by validation.
4.Get the created Pod's YAML and inspect spec.containers[0].livenessProbe.httpGet, note that protocol is absent, while host: 1.2.3.4 is present, showing the field was silently dropped rather than the request being rejected.
5.Repeat steps 2-4 with scheme: HTTPS in place of host: 1.2.3.4 , same outcome: protocol is silently dropped instead of the Pod being rejected.

title: clean up the feature WindowsHostNetwork.
body:
### What would you like to be added?

PR  #130250  ("Withdraw alpha support for HostNetwork containers on Windows", merged for 1.33) removed the actual implementation code — Windows pods can no longer use  hostNetwork: true  — as part of formally withdrawing KEP-3503. That's why  kep.yaml  shows  status: withdrawn ,  stage: alpha , and only  milestone.alpha: v1.26  (no beta/stable — hence "NEVER LOCKED", which is actually expected for a withdrawn KEP).

What was missed

The PR only marked the gate  Deprecated , it never finished the cleanup:

// pkg/features/kube_features.go
WindowsHostNetwork featuregate.Feature = "WindowsHostNetwork"
...
WindowsHostNetwork: {
    {Version: "1.26", Default: false, PreRelease: Alpha},
    {Version: "1.33", Default: false, PreRelease: Deprecated},
},

And there's a literal maintainer FIXME admitting it's unfinished, in  pkg/features/kube_features_test.go :

func TestEnsureAlphaGatesAreNotSwitchedOnByDefault(t *testing.T) {
    checkAlphaGates := func(feature featuregate.Feature, spec featuregate.FeatureSpec) {
        // FIXME(dims): remove this check when WindowsHostNetwork is fixed up or removed
        // entirely. Please do NOT add more entries here.
        if feature == "WindowsHostNetwork" {
            return
        }
        ...

This is a special-cased test bypass — normally the test enforces "alpha gates must be off by default," but  WindowsHostNetwork  needed an exemption, meaning something about its spec is non-standard for a normal alpha gate (going straight Alpha→Deprecated without ever reaching Beta/GA trips the usual assumptions the test suite makes). Nobody has gone back to remove the gate and delete this workaround.

There's also dead test code still referencing it in  pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox_test.go :

featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate, features.WindowsHostNetwork, false)

— toggling a gate that no longer guards any real code path.

What's needed to actually finish this

1. Delete the  WindowsHostNetwork  constant + its  VersionedSpecs  entry from  pkg/features/kube_features.go 
2. Delete the  FIXME(dims)  special-case block in  kube_features_test.go  (the test will then pass normally since the offending gate is gone)
3. Delete the dead  SetFeatureGateDuringTest(...WindowsHostNetwork...)  line in  kuberuntime_sandbox_test.go 
4.  test/compatibility_lifecycle/reference/feature_list.md  /  versioned_feature_list.yaml  are auto-generated — they'll update once the source is cleaned up

### Why is this needed?

clean up

title: DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate overlong rolling-update service socket paths
body:
### What happened?

On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name.

With normal defaults:

```text
plugin directory:
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name>

rolling service socket:
dra-<Pod UID>.sock
```

With a normal 36-byte Pod UID:

```text
full endpoint length = 71 + len(driverName)
```

A valid 37-byte driver name:

```text
abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io
```

produces exactly a 108-byte endpoint under the affected implementation. Kubernetes requires AF_UNIX pathname-based endpoints to remain shorter than 108 bytes. A valid 63-byte driver name produces a 134-byte old-style endpoint.

### What did you expect to happen?

Valid DRA drivers using `RollingUpdate` with the normal automatic/default directory and socket naming should receive an AF_UNIX-compatible endpoint. Rolling instances must remain distinguishable.

This expectation does not extend to arbitrary custom `PluginDataDirectoryPath` values.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use:

```go
DriverName("abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io")
RollingUpdate("11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555")
// no PluginDataDirectoryPath override
// no PluginSocket override
```

An injected `PluginListener` can observe the real automatically generated endpoint without relying on the local macOS Unix-socket behavior.

The affected implementation produces:

```text
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/abcdef.dra-example-driver.sigs.k8s.io/dra-11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555.sock
```

and its length is exactly 108 bytes. The valid 36-byte control driver produces 107 bytes.

### Anything else we need to know?

### Root cause

Rolling-update service socket naming includes the complete Pod UID. The default containing directory independently contains the complete driver name. The service socket did not check the combined full-path budget or fall back to a shorter basename.

### Relationship to existing work

- #139166 / #139623 addressed the rolling **registration socket** under `plugins_registry`.
- #139623 explicitly left `dra-<uid>.sock` service sockets unchanged.
- #141815 corrected the registration fallback's exact-108 boundary.
- #140837 added kubelet-side endpoint and driver validation but does not prevent this helper from generating an invalid automatic service endpoint.

### Affected scope

Reproduced on Kubernetes master at `3af569e862d19a046cdfd63cda837f9bb29da6fa`. Older releases were not verified.

No production incident was observed.

title: Namespace-scoped `RoleBinding` can grant write permissions on the namespace itself
body:
### What happened?

In a multi-tenant cluster where individual tenants get full control of a specific namespace, e.g. via binding to a `Role` like `cluster-admin` using a rule with all-wildcard matches, tenants may also edit and delete that namespace. This is in spite of namespaces themselves being a cluster-scoped resource.

In a fresh cluster created via `kubeadm`, a `RoleBinding` for the tenant to a `Role`/`ClusterRole` that allows creating `RoleBindings` (e.g. the default `admin` `ClusterRole`) is sufficient as the user can escalate their privileges by binding to any `ClusterRole` that grants write permissions on namespaces.

### What did you expect to happen?

A namespace-scoped `RoleBinding`-granted permission should not allow editing and deleting a cluster-scoped namespace resource.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a fresh cluster, e.g. created via kind, run the following set of commands:
```bash
kubectl create namespace tenant
kubectl create rolebinding namespace-admin --namespace=tenant --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=tenant
kubectl --as tenant label namespaces tenant tenant-change=true # can edit/patch
kubectl get namespaces tenant -o yaml # confirm label is there
kubectl --as tenant delete namespaces tenant # can delete
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This was brought up before in #134929 framed around service accounts, but the issue applies universally. It was rejected due to being intended behavior, an assessment I disagree with.

Namespaces *are* cluster-scoped resources and it's very unintuitive and unexpected that a namespace-scoped `RoleBinding` grants permissions on such a resource. Clusters without additional validating policies are in a less-secure state by default with this behavior. Further privilege escalation e.g. by adjusting pod security standards via namespace labels is possible in this way.

As a cluster admin, I expect that I can control things on a namespace level via the `Namespace` object without tenants interfering with this *in any scenario*.

As far as I can tell, this behavior is also not documented anywhere, at least I couldn't find anything on the [RBAC documentation page](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/rbac) where I'd expect this kind of behavior to be called out in a warning.

title: unit-master-golang-tip red: two upstream net/http bugs, not kubernetes bugs
body:
TestGrid: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-code-organization#unit-master-golang-tip&width=20

`ci-kubernetes-unit-golang-tip` has been red since 2026-09-10. Two upstream net/http bugs, both from Go tip commit e51216de8e (CL 829984, the fix for golang/go#81404):

- golang/go#81510: readLoop reads `Response.ContentLength` after `Body.Close` returns. `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/proxy TestRejectForwardingRedirectsOption` fails under `-race`, because `UpgradeAwareHandler` closes the backend body and then replaces `*response` in `ModifyResponse`.
- golang/go#81511: `Body.Close` after a failed Read now returns the Read error again. `k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/filters TestPerRequestWith*` fail with `tls: bad record MAC` from `Close()`, and `pkg/server TestRequestTimeoutBehavior` fails intermittently with `unexpected EOF`. The Go authors added a test for the new behavior in the same CL, so this one may end up as a documented change rather than a fix.

Not kubernetes bugs: both reproduce with no kubernetes code (programs in the golang issues), and go1.27.1, go1.26.1 and the commit before e51216de8e are all clean. The other red on this job, the go1.27 vet check for `%d` with a pointer, is #142076. Sibling for the kind job: #141992.

Tracking here so the red canary has an explanation. Closes when both golang issues are resolved, or when this job's toolchain moves past the fixes. If 81511 becomes intended behavior, the three apiserver tests need to stop asserting `Close() == nil`.
