title: kube-apiserver built with Go 1.27 returns 431 for impersonated or front-proxy users with about 500 groups
body:
### What happened?

We're reporting this ahead of v1.38 because it only appears when several conditions combine, and it's easy to miss until someone with a large group membership hits it.

Go 1.27 added `http.Server.MaxHeaderValueCount` with a default of 500 ([golang/go#79936](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79936)). Repeated header lines are counted individually. kube-apiserver does not set this field, and the identity headers it accepts carry one group per header line:

- `Impersonate-Group` (user impersonation)
- `X-Remote-Group` (request-header authentication, used by authenticating proxies)

As a result, kube-apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1) returns `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` for requests that impersonate, or are proxied on behalf of, a user with about 500 groups. For the curl request below, 495 groups produce 431 over HTTP/2 but 200 over HTTP/1.1, and 500 groups produce 431 over both; the exact threshold depends on the other request headers. v1.37.1 (go1.26.8) accepts the same requests, tested up to 1,000 groups.

The rejection happens in `net/http` before Kubernetes request handlers run. In our run with Metadata-level auditing and default log verbosity, the rejected requests had no audit record and no related kube-apiserver log message.

Go 1.27 has no `GODEBUG` override for this limit; one was proposed and declined ([golang/go#80020](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/80020)). Accepting the same repeated headers on a Go 1.27 server requires setting `MaxHeaderValueCount`.

Who is affected, as far as we can tell: only requests whose groups are carried in headers (impersonation, request-header authentication, and requests kube-apiserver proxies to aggregated API servers), for users with roughly 500 or more groups, on servers built with Go 1.27. Users with fewer groups are unaffected. Groups taken from client certificates, OIDC or webhook token authentication are not sent to kube-apiserver as headers, although aggregated API servers still receive them that way. We hit this with an enterprise directory in which some users belong to more than 1,000 groups.

### What did you expect to happen?

Requests for users with several hundred to over a thousand groups keep working through impersonation and request-header authentication, as they do with Go 1.26 builds, or the limit becomes explicit and documented rather than an implicit `net/http` default.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start etcd (listening on `127.0.0.1:2379`) and kube-apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.1 with a static token in `system:masters`, then wait until `/readyz` returns 200:

   ```sh
   openssl genrsa -out sa.key 2048 && openssl rsa -in sa.key -pubout -out sa.pub
   echo 'admintoken,admin,admin-uid,"system:masters"' > tokens.csv
   kube-apiserver --etcd-servers=http://127.0.0.1:2379 --bind-address=127.0.0.1 --secure-port=6443 \
     --cert-dir=./serving --token-auth-file=tokens.csv --authorization-mode=RBAC \
     --service-account-issuer=https://kubernetes.default.svc --service-account-key-file=sa.pub \
     --service-account-signing-key-file=sa.key --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/16
   ```

2. Impersonate a user with 495 groups:

   ```sh
   {
     echo 'header = "Authorization: Bearer admintoken"'
     echo 'header = "Impersonate-User: alice"'
     echo 'header = "Impersonate-Group: system:masters"'
     for g in $(seq 2 495); do echo "header = \"Impersonate-Group: group-$g\""; done
   } > impersonate.cfg
   curl -sk --http2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version} %{http_code}\n' -K impersonate.cfg \
     https://127.0.0.1:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default
   ```

   This prints `2 431` (curl must support HTTP/2; check `curl -V`). With 490 groups, or with kube-apiserver v1.37.1, it prints `2 200`.

We also tested request-header authentication separately: `--requestheader-client-ca-file`, `--requestheader-allowed-names`, `--requestheader-username-headers=X-Remote-User` and `--requestheader-group-headers=X-Remote-Group`, with `X-Remote-User` and repeated `X-Remote-Group` headers sent using a client certificate signed by that CA. It gave the same results as impersonation.

Results (`GET /api/v1/namespaces/default`, the group count includes `system:masters`):

| Groups | v1.37.1 (go1.26.8), HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 | v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1), HTTP/2 | v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1), HTTP/1.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 480 | 200 | 200 | 200 |
| 490 | 200 | 200 | 200 |
| 495 | 200 | 431 | 200 |
| 500 | 200 | 431 | 431 |
| 1000 | 200 | 431 | 431 |

Impersonation and request-header authentication gave identical results in every case. Other request headers count toward the same limit, which is why the threshold is slightly below 500 groups.

### Anything else we need to know?

- `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/secure_serving.go` sets `MaxHeaderBytes` (1 MiB) but not `MaxHeaderValueCount`. Under Go 1.27, `golang.org/x/net/http2.ConfigureServer` (v0.59.0) hands HTTP/2 to the `net/http` server, so the limit applies to both protocols.
- kube-aggregator forwards the user's groups to aggregated API servers as separate `X-Remote-Group` headers ([round_trippers.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/039223d3e2a1c6f5b1422c95fb396ff8c31d2619/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/round_trippers.go#L125-L142)). An aggregated API server built with Go 1.27 that keeps the default limit may therefore reject such requests. We measured this internally with a KubeVirt virt-api build using Go 1.27; the reproduction above exercises kube-apiserver only.
- Release branches 1.34 to 1.37 currently build with Go 1.26. A future Go 1.27 update on those branches would bring this behaviour with it.
- Authenticating proxies can forward hundreds of directory groups for a user; requests in that range are affected as shown above.
- Clients cannot reduce the header count by comma-joining groups: that format is not supported for `X-Remote-Group` or `Impersonate-Group` (#82468, #94683). #82468 also discusses a single structured user-info header, which would avoid the per-group header count entirely.
- A possible direction: an explicit, bounded and, if appropriate, configurable `MaxHeaderValueCount` in `k8s.io/apiserver` secure serving that supports the intended group sizes while keeping protection against floods of small headers, tested over both HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. We're happy to help with a fix once there's agreement on the approach.

/sig api-machinery
/sig auth

title: taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds records nanoseconds scaled by 1e9, not seconds
body:
### What happened?

`deletePodHandler` in `pkg/controller/tainteviction/taint_eviction.go` records the pod deletion latency as `float64(time.Since(fireAt) * time.Second)`. `time.Since` already returns nanoseconds, so the multiplication scales the value by another 1e9.

`taint_eviction_controller_pod_deletion_duration_seconds` is documented as "Latency, in seconds" with buckets from 0.005 to 240. Any latency below about 9.2s is recorded as a huge positive number and lands in the `+Inf` bucket. Above about 9.2s the multiplication overflows int64 and wraps around, so the recorded value is arbitrary. For example 10s is recorded as -8446744073709551616 and counts in the lowest bucket, while 20s is recorded as 1553255926290448384. `_sum` is meaningless in all cases.

### What did you expect to happen?

The metric records the latency in seconds, the same way `DeviceTaintEvictionController` does in `pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device_taint_eviction.go` with `podDeletionLatency.Seconds()`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Call `deletePodHandler` with a `fireAt` 10s in the past and read the histogram. The regression test in #141742 does this. Before the fix it records -8.44e+18, after the fix about 10.

### Anything else we need to know?

Introduced in ccda2d6fd413d02b9df2dd76ca643dfb42d62aaf (KEP-3902, which split TaintEvictionController out of NodeLifecycleController) and first released in v1.29.0. The metric is ALPHA.

Open PRs with the fix: #141742, and #141311 which was opened earlier. #141568 also includes it as part of a larger change.

/sig scheduling
/kind bug

v1.29.0 and later, including master. Found by reading the code, not on a running cluster.

title: Workqueue exponential backoff overflow
body:
### What happened?

The exponential workqueue rate limiter can return a negative delay when its calculated backoff is exactly `2^63` nanoseconds.

The overflow check in `TypedItemExponentialFailureRateLimiter.When` uses `backoff > math.MaxInt64`. Because `backoff` is a float64, the comparison converts `math.MaxInt64` to float64, which rounds up to `2^63`. Equality passes the check even though that value cannot fit in a `time.Duration`.

On linux/amd64, the conversion returns `math.MinInt64`. `AddRateLimited` passes this to `AddAfter`, where a non-positive duration causes an immediate retry instead of the configured maximum delay.

### What did you expect to happen?

Return the configured maximum delay when the calculated backoff cannot fit in a positive `time.Duration`.

### How can we reproduce it?

```go
limiter := workqueue.NewTypedItemExponentialFailureRateLimiter[string](time.Nanosecond, time.Second)
for i := 0; i < 63; i++ {
    limiter.When("item")
}
fmt.Println(limiter.When("item"))
// Got on linux/amd64: -2562047h47m16.854775808s
// Want: 1s
```

This needs no elapsed time or cluster. The calls advance the per-item failure counter directly. A power-of-two base delay reaches the same boundary at different retry counts.

### Anything else we need to know?

The earlier overflow guard from #31396 handles values above the boundary but misses equality. Changing the comparison to `>=` catches the boundary before the conversion.

A regression matrix using `math/big.Int` as the expected-value oracle reproduces the failure on current master. It covers all 63 positive power-of-two base delays, ordinary millisecond delays, the duration boundary, four maximum delays, and 65 successive retries.

### Kubernetes version

Reproduced from source at master commit `99a4ea72fe6`, with Go 1.27.1.

### OS version

Linux/amd64 (WSL).

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

title: Strategic merge patch list ordering repeatedly scans the order list
FileKeyRef ignores optional when the env file is missing, and reports an empty value as a missing key
body:
### What happened?

`FileKeyRef` ignores `optional` when the referenced env file does not exist, and it reports a key that is present with an empty value as missing. In both cases the container is left in `CreateContainerConfigError` and never starts.

Both follow from `ParseEnv` (`pkg/kubelet/util/env/env_util.go`) returning only `(string, error)`. The caller in `makeEnvironmentVariables` (`pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go`) therefore uses an empty return value as its not-found sentinel, and it returns on the open error before it looks at `optional`:

```go
runtimeVal, err = envutil.ParseEnv(envFilePath, key)
if err != nil {
	logger.Error(err, "Failed to parse env file", "pod", klog.KObj(pod))
	return result, fmt.Errorf("couldn't parse env file")
}

// If the key was not found, and it's not optional, return an error
if runtimeVal == "" {
	if optional {
		continue
	}
	return result, fmt.Errorf("environment variable key %q not found in file %q", key, envFilePath)
}
```

The `ConfigMapKeyRef` branch a few lines above handles the same two cases correctly, using the `ok` value from the map lookup.

### What did you expect to happen?

Both behaviours are specified, and the implementation does the opposite of the spec in each case.

For a missing file, the API doc on `FileKeySelector.Optional` says:

> Specify whether the file or its key must be defined. If the file or key does not exist, then the env var is not published.

KEP-3721's Failure and Fallback Strategy table says the same, row 4:

> Either the filepath or key specified in `FileKeySelector` field does not exist but `optional` field is set to true | Pod created | Container starts and env vars are not populated.

That wording traces back to review on the KEP, where @thockin asked ["If the file or key does not exist, then the env var is not published?"](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4524#discussion_r1631787996).

For an empty value, @thockin [asked](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4524#discussion_r1765785866) "What if the key is found but has no value?" and @AnishShah [answered](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4524#discussion_r1766063094):

> The pod will start with key and empty value.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Both reproduce on a stock kind cluster with no feature gates set, since `EnvFiles` has been beta and on by default since 1.35. I checked v1.36.1 and v1.37.0 and the behaviour is identical on both.

Case 1, missing file with `optional: true`. The `emptyDir` is never populated, so the file does not exist:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: filekeyref-missing-file
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo started; env | grep MY_VAR || echo 'MY_VAR unset'"]
    env:
    - name: MY_VAR
      valueFrom:
        fileKeyRef:
          volumeName: config
          path: missing.env
          key: MY_VAR
          optional: true
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: config
    emptyDir: {}
```

Expected the container to start with `MY_VAR` unset. Actual:

```
NAME                      READY   STATUS                       RESTARTS   AGE
filekeyref-missing-file   0/1     CreateContainerConfigError   0          20s

.status.containerStatuses[0].state
{"waiting":{"message":"couldn't parse env file","reason":"CreateContainerConfigError"}}

Warning  Failed  Error: couldn't parse env file
```

Case 2, a key present with an empty value:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: filekeyref-empty-value
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  initContainers:
  - name: setup
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "printf \"EMPTY=''\\n\" > /data/config.env"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config
      mountPath: /data
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo \"EMPTY=[$EMPTY]\""]
    env:
    - name: EMPTY
      valueFrom:
        fileKeyRef:
          volumeName: config
          path: config.env
          key: EMPTY
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: config
    emptyDir: {}
```

Expected the container to start and print `EMPTY=[]`. Actual:

```
NAME                     READY   STATUS                       RESTARTS   AGE
filekeyref-empty-value   0/1     CreateContainerConfigError   0          25s

.status.containerStatuses[0].state
{"waiting":{"message":"environment variable key \"EMPTY\" not found in file
 \"/var/lib/kubelet/pods/.../volumes/kubernetes.io~empty-dir/config/config.env\"",
 "reason":"CreateContainerConfigError"}}
```

The key is in the file. Reading it directly from the node gives exactly what the init container wrote:

```
# od -c of config.env on the node
0000000    E   M   P   T   Y   =   '   '  \n
```

### Anything else we need to know?

The missing-file path has never been covered by a test at any level. `test/e2e/common/node/file_key.go` has a test named `FileKeyRef, optional missing file or key`, described as covering the case where "either the filepath or key specified in FileKeySelector field does not exist but the optional field is set to true". Its init container writes `config.env` and both `fileKeyRef` entries point at that existing file, so only the missing key is exercised.

Validation does not prevent this. `validateFileKeyRefVolumes` in `pkg/apis/core/validation` only checks that the named volume exists in the pod spec and is an `emptyDir`. It cannot check for the file, which is written at runtime by an init container, so an absent file is a legitimate state.

`EnvFiles` is set to go GA and lock to default in 1.38, so it would be good to bring the behaviour in line with the spec before that.

I have a fix and will open a PR referencing this issue.

/kind bug

title: kube-apiserver: watch termination can bypass shutdown rate limiting
body:
### What happened?

With `--shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period` > 0, the apiserver is supposed to rate limit the termination of active watches during graceful shutdown (#114925). Active watches can instead return before the rate limiter is installed, and those watches are closed without any pacing.

The cause is a race in `k8s.io/apiserver`'s graceful shutdown:

- Each watch calls [Done()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/waitgroup/ratelimited_waitgroup.go#L70-L87) on a wait group when it ends. That call only blocks on the rate limiter if [Wait()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/waitgroup/ratelimited_waitgroup.go#L95-L108) has already installed it. Any Done that runs earlier returns immediately, unpaced.
- Watch handlers and the drain coordinator wait on the same signal. Each watch handler watches [ShuttingDown()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/lifecycle_signals.go#L153-L155) which is the NotAcceptingNewRequest signal. It [returns as soon as that fires](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L299-L307).
- The drain coordinator listens for the same signal. It only calls `Wait()` after waking on [the same NotAcceptingNewRequest](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.1/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver.go#L676-L706). Nothing orders the coordinator against the watches.

Because these goroutines wake on the same signal, multiple watch handlers can reach `Done()` before the drain coordinator installs the limiter. One symptom is that `activeWatchesBefore` in the `[graceful-termination] active watch request(s) have drained` log is well below the number of watches that were open when shutdown began.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `--shutdown-watch-termination-grace-period` > 0, shutdown-triggered watch termination should use the configured rate limiting. The limiter should be initialized before active watch handlers are signaled to return, so scheduling between the watch handlers and the drain goroutine cannot bypass that pacing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The following unit test in k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server reproduces the missing ordering using the existing generic-apiserver test helpers. It does the following:

1. Start a `GenericAPIServer` with `ShutdownWatchTerminationGracePeriod > 0` (`newGenericAPIServer(t, ..., true)`).
2. Register a watch handler that blocks on `ServerShutdownSignalFrom(ctx).ShuttingDown()`. After the channel closes, probe `WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(1)` and balance any successful call with `Add(-1)`. A successful `Add(1)` demonstrates that the handler observed shutdown before the wait group entered waiting mode.
3. Open 200 watches, then cancel the server context.

On master (`99a4ea72fe6`), the test failed in 50 of 50 runs (`-count=50`):

```
--- FAIL: TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering (1.19s)
    genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go:637: 1 of 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode
--- FAIL: TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering (0.73s)
    genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go:637: 87 of 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode
...
```

Across the 50 runs, between 1 and 197 of the 200 watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode. This demonstrates the missing ordering.

<details>
<summary>Test (applies to master as is)</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
index 24d918ebf97..9f532990262 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/genericapiserver_graceful_termination_test.go
@@ -564,6 +564,80 @@ func TestGracefulTerminationWithKeepListeningDuringGracefulTerminationEnabled(t
 	}
 }
 
+// This test checks that the watch wait group has entered waiting mode
+// before active watch handlers observe the shutdown signal.
+func TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering(t *testing.T) {
+	s := newGenericAPIServer(t, &fakeAudit{}, true)
+	client := newClient(false)
+	doer := setupDoer(t, s.SecureServingInfo)
+
+	// the more watches, the more likely one of them wins the race
+	const n = 200
+	startedWG := sync.WaitGroup{}
+	startedWG.Add(n)
+	var lock sync.Mutex
+	var shutdownBeforeWait int
+	s.Handler.NonGoRestfulMux.Handle("/apis/watches.group/v1/namespaces/foo/bar", http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) {
+		signals := apirequest.ServerShutdownSignalFrom(req.Context())
+		startedWG.Done()
+		if signals == nil {
+			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError)
+			return
+		}
+		<-signals.ShuttingDown()
+
+		// After observing shutdown, a positive Add should be rejected.
+		// Success means the watch wait group has not yet entered waiting mode.
+		if err := s.WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(1); err == nil {
+			s.WatchRequestWaitGroup.Add(-1)
+			lock.Lock()
+			shutdownBeforeWait++
+			lock.Unlock()
+		}
+		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
+	}))
+
+	_, ctx := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
+	stopCtx, stop := context.WithCancelCause(ctx)
+	defer stop(errors.New("test has completed"))
+	runCompletedCh := make(chan struct{})
+	go func() {
+		defer close(runCompletedCh)
+		if err := s.PrepareRun().RunWithContext(stopCtx); err != nil {
+			t.Errorf("unexpected error from RunWithContext: %v", err)
+		}
+	}()
+	waitForAPIServerStarted(t, doer)
+
+	resultCh := make(chan result, n)
+	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
+		go func() {
+			resultCh <- doer.Do(client, func(httptrace.GotConnInfo) {}, "/apis/watches.group/v1/namespaces/foo/bar?watch=true", 0)
+		}()
+	}
+	startedCh := make(chan struct{})
+	go func() {
+		defer close(startedCh)
+		startedWG.Wait()
+	}()
+	waitForeverUntil(t, startedCh, "in-flight watch requests did not reach the server")
+
+	stop(errors.New("shutting down"))
+	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
+		resultGot := <-resultCh
+		if err := assertResponseStatusCode(resultGot, http.StatusOK); err != nil {
+			t.Errorf("%s", err.Error())
+		}
+	}
+	waitForeverUntil(t, runCompletedCh, "the apiserver Run method did not return")
+
+	lock.Lock()
+	defer lock.Unlock()
+	if shutdownBeforeWait != 0 {
+		t.Errorf("%d of %d watch handlers observed shutdown before the watch wait group entered waiting mode", shutdownBeforeWait, n)
+	}
+}
+
 func TestMuxAndDiscoveryComplete(t *testing.T) {
 	// setup
 	testSignal1 := make(chan struct{})
```

Run with `go test ./staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server -run '^TestGracefulTerminationWatchShutdownOrdering$' -count=50`.

</details>

Introduced by #114925 (v1.27). The code is unchanged on master.

title: Service creation cannot handle 100 QPS on 5,000-node clusters
body:
Service creation cannot sustain 100 QPS on a 5,000-node cluster, whereas other resources in the scale test (such as ConfigMaps and Secrets) handle 100 QPS without issues.

When we switched Service creation in the 5,000-node load test from sequential execution (~15.6 QPS) to 100 QPS, effective throughput dropped to ~5.5 Services/s and `POST services` requests timed out after 34s.

Looking at the ClusterIP allocation path, there appears to be lock contention serializing Service creation:
- Dynamic ClusterIP allocation holds a mutex across the entire allocation call, including the synchronous request that writes the `IPAddress` object to etcd.
- While that lock is held, updating the allocated and available IP gauges after each create or delete lists all existing `IPAddress` objects from the informer cache twice and parses every IP string to check subnet containment.

References:
- [5,000-node scale test run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/142740/pull-kubernetes-gce-master-scale-performance-5000/2107481865647558656)
- [ClusterIP allocation lock](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/cidrallocator.go#L347-L371)
- [IPAddress creation and metric update](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/ipallocator.go#L142-L169)

/cc @aojea @serathius
/sig network
/sig scalability

title: kubectl config set panics on users.<name>.exec and users.<name>.auth-provider
body:
### What happened?

```console
$ kubectl config set users.foo.exec x --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
panic: unrecognized type: <nil>
```

Same with `users.<name>.auth-provider`. Exit code 2.

/sig cli


### What did you expect to happen?

An error instead of a panic.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```sh
# /tmp/kc doesn't need to exist
kubectl config set users.foo.exec x --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
kubectl config set users.foo.auth-provider x --kubeconfig /tmp/kc
```


### Anything else we need to know?

`modifyConfig` in `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/config/set.go` has no case for pointer fields and falls through to the `panic` at the end. `kubectl config unset` on these paths doesn't panic.

Similar to #142588 (fix in #142589), but a different code path.

title: PodGroup protection controller: inverted error check requeues successful keys forever and drops failed ones
body:
### What happened?

`processNextWorkItem` in `pkg/controller/scheduling/podgroupprotection/podgroup_protection_controller.go` has its error check inverted:

```go
err := processFunc(ctx, key)
if err != nil {
	queue.Forget(key)
	return true
}

queue.AddRateLimited(key)
utilruntime.HandleError(fmt.Errorf("%v %v failed with: %w", kind, key, err))
```

As a result:

1. **Successful syncs are requeued forever.** Every key processed without error is put back with `AddRateLimited` and logged at error level as `PodGroup <ns>/<name> failed with: %!w(<nil>)`. Because a missing object also returns `nil`, keys for PodGroups/CompositePodGroups that were already deleted keep cycling indefinitely (backoff caps at 1000s), and the rate limiter's per-item failure map grows with every PodGroup the controller has seen. `handlePodChange` enqueues the PodGroup whenever one of its pods reaches a terminal phase, so this hits every PodGroup with a completed pod, not only ones being deleted.

2. **Failed syncs are never retried.** If removing the finalizer fails (for example a 409 Conflict on the `Update`), the key is `Forget`-ed and dropped. A PodGroup or CompositePodGroup that is being deleted and has no remaining pods/children produces no further events, so it stays in `Terminating` until the next informer resync.


### What did you expect to happen?

Keys that sync successfully are forgotten; keys that fail are requeued with rate limiting, as in the standard controller pattern (and as before #141021).


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unit-level reproduction against current master:

```go
q := workqueue.NewTypedRateLimitingQueue(workqueue.DefaultTypedControllerRateLimiter[string]())
q.Add("ns/pg")
processNextWorkItem(ctx, "PodGroup", q, func(context.Context, string) error { return nil })
// q.NumRequeues("ns/pg") == 1, and logs: "PodGroup ns/pg failed with: %!w(<nil>)"

q.Add("ns/pg2")
processNextWorkItem(ctx, "PodGroup", q, func(context.Context, string) error { return errors.New("conflict") })
// q.NumRequeues("ns/pg2") == 0 -> never retried
```

In a cluster: run kube-controller-manager with `--feature-gates=GenericWorkload=true`, create a PodGroup with a pod that completes, and watch the controller-manager repeatedly log `failed with: %!w(<nil>)` for that PodGroup.


### Anything else we need to know?

This regressed in #141021 (commit 86760556650) when `processNextWorkItem` was generalised to serve both the PodGroup and CompositePodGroup queues. The original implementation from #137641 used `if err == nil { Forget; return }`.

It is in v1.38.0-alpha.2 but not in any stable release yet.

The existing unit tests call `processPodGroup` / `processCompositePodGroup` directly and never exercise `processNextWorkItem`, which is why this was not caught. I'd like to send a fix that restores the check and adds a table test for `processNextWorkItem` covering both paths.

```console
v1.38.0-alpha.2 (master @ 6029cad6874)
```

title: WorkloadWithJob: Jobs with names of 58+ characters never start because the PodGroupTemplate name exceeds 63 bytes
body:
### What happened?

With `WorkloadWithJob` enabled, a Job whose name is 58+ characters never starts pods. The Job controller names the PodGroupTemplate `<job-name>-pgt-0` ([job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/controller/job/job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521)), and `spec.podGroupTemplates[].name` is a DNS label limited to 63 bytes ([types.go#L218](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L218)). Workload creation is rejected and the Job requeues forever:

```
Workload.scheduling.k8s.io "<job>-65657c449d" is invalid: spec.podGroupTemplates[0].name: Invalid value: "<job>-pgt-0": must be no more than 63 bytes
```

The Workload/PodGroup object names are already truncated and hashed ([names.go#L34-L50](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/scheduling/schedulingv1/workloadbuilder/names.go#L34-L50)), but the template name is not.

### What did you expect to happen?

Any valid Job name (up to 63 characters) gets a valid Workload and PodGroup, and the Job runs.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable `GenericWorkload` and `WorkloadWithJob`, enable `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`, then:

```sh
kubectl create job $(printf 'a%.0s' {1..58}) --image=busybox -- true
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=FailedWorkloadCreate
```

A 57-character name works; 58 and 63 fail.

### Anything else we need to know?

The template name is local to the Workload, so it doesn't need to embed the Job name at all. A fixed or bounded name (e.g. `pgt-0`, or a truncated prefix plus a hash) would avoid the limit. Existing Workloads reference the current name, so a change has to keep finding templates that already exist.

### Kubernetes version

master @ 0887d3330e9

title: PodGroup rejects system priority classes: spec.priority is capped at HighestUserDefinablePriority
body:
### What happened?

A PodGroup that references a built-in system PriorityClass is always rejected. Priority admission resolves `spec.priority` from the class ([admission.go#L203-L222](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L203-L222)), and the v1beta1 `PodGroupSpec.Priority` field caps it at `HighestUserDefinablePriority` ([types.go#L704](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L704)). `system-cluster-critical` (2000000000) and `system-node-critical` (2000001000) are both above that cap:

```
PodGroup.scheduling.k8s.io "..." is invalid: spec.priority: Invalid value: 2000000000: must be less than or equal to 1000000000
```

With `WorkloadWithJob` enabled, any Job using a system priority class is stuck: the Workload is created, PodGroup creation fails, and no pods are ever created. The controller also emits no event when PodGroup creation fails ([job_scheduling_manager.go#L620-L623](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/controller/job/job_scheduling_manager.go#L620-L623)), so the error shows up only in the kube-controller-manager log.

### What did you expect to happen?

PodGroups (and Jobs) can use the system priority classes, just as Pods can. The user-defined cap should still apply to non-system classes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Enable `GenericWorkload` and `WorkloadWithJob`, enable `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`, then:

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: pg
spec:
  priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical
  schedulingPolicy:
    basic: {}
```

The same request with a user-defined PriorityClass of value 1000000000 succeeds.

### Anything else we need to know?

The same `+k8s:maximum` tag is also on `PodGroupTemplate.Priority` ([L287](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L287)) and `CompositePodGroupTemplate.Priority` ([L358](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L358)), and on the matching v1alpha3 fields. Clamping the value in the controller won't work, because admission rejects a priority that doesn't match the class ([admission.go#L217-L219](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L217-L219)). The likely fix is to relax the API cap to match `PriorityClass` validation ([validation.go#L48-L55](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/apis/scheduling/validation/validation.go#L48-L55)) and also add a `FailedPodGroupCreate` event.

### Kubernetes version

title: Swap e2e "Basic functionality" LimitedSwap tests can't fail
body:
### What happened?

While looking into #138226 I noticed the LimitedSwap QoS tests in `test/e2e_node/swap_test.go` don't actually test anything. There are two bugs:

1. `getSwapTestPod` builds `resources` for the requested QoS class but never puts them on the pod. It's just returned `getSleepingPod(...)` since 2230ed7dc6a, so every entry runs a BestEffort pod. You can see it in both swap CI jobs, where Burstable and Guaranteed log:
   `Calculating swap for burstable pods: ... containerMemoryRequest: 0, swapAllocation: 0`
   (e.g. [ubuntu run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-swap-conformance-ubuntu-serial/2108165536956289024) and [crio run](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-node-crio-swap-serial/2108202027736633344))

2. `expectLimitedSwap` checks the limit with `gomega.Or(>= expected-4Ki, <= expected+4Ki)`, which matches any number. I checked it with expected = 128Mi and it accepts 0 and 1TiB.

### What did you expect to happen?

Each entry should run a pod of the QoS class it names, and the swap limit check should use `And`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Grep any swap serial job's build log for "Calculating swap for burstable pods": the request is always 0. For the matcher:
```go
m := gomega.Or(gomega.BeNumerically(">=", 128<<20-4096), gomega.BeNumerically("<=", 128<<20+4096))
ok, _ := m.Match(0) // true
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Fixing both will make the Guaranteed and "request equals limit" entries fail as written. `calcSwapForBurstablePod` expects a non-zero limit for them, but the kubelet correctly gives them no swap, so the expected value has to be 0 unless the pod is Burstable with a memory request that differs from its limit. The NodeConformance entries use `getSwapTestPod` too.

TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrentWithRelease

file: pkg/registry/core/service/ipallocator/cidrallocator_test.go


### Since when has it been flaking?

Since d8d5b004c2bd9cecaa82c7077c87f60691157675 (PR #142758, merged 2026-10-06)
"ipallocator: use RWMutex for ServiceCIDR map and thread-safe rand"


### Testgrid link

https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/140855/pull-kubernetes-unit-windows-master/2108320062355017728

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The test panics with "channel full" raised from `RaceFreeFakeWatcher.Add` (staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/watch.go:253).

The fake clientset's `ObjectTracker` hands out watchers backed by a fixed 100-event channel (`watch.DefaultChanSize`) and delivers events with a non-blocking send that panics when the channel is full.

`TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrentWithRelease` runs 50 goroutines x 10 rounds of allocate+release, producing ~1000 watch events. On a busy/slow CI machine (Windows presubmits are especially prone) the informer reflector does not consume events fast enough, the 100-event channel overflows, and the whole
test binary panics.

This is a test-infrastructure flake, not a production bug: the production `MetaAllocator` code is fine; the fake watch plumbing in the test harness cannot absorb the event volume the test generates under CPU contention. Reproduced locally with `GOMAXPROCS=2` (and even `GOMAXPROCS=1`).

### Anything else we need to know?

`TestCIDRAllocateNextConcurrent` (same file, same harness) is exposed to the same failure mode.

title: resourceclaim controller: deleted claims stay visible in the MutationCache for up to 1h
body:
The controller's claim MutationCache (`pkg/controller/resourceclaim/controller.go:356`) uses `IncludeAdds: true` with a 1h TTL, but the claim informer handlers never call `OnAddOrUpdate`/`OnDelete`. After a generated claim is deleted and the informer observes it, `claimExists` and `findPodResourceClaim` still return it from the mutation cache, so the controller does not recreate it until the entry expires.

Reproduced at 4dfdf5067a2 with a unit test (mutation, API delete, wait for informer, `claimExists` returns true); wiring the informer events the way #140063 did for the ResourceSlice controller fixes it. `claimExists` came with #140227 and is in v1.37.

title: Expose per-resource storage write revision metric for watch cache and informer lag
body:
[WatchCacheLag](https://perf-dash.k8s.io/#/?jobname=gce-5000Nodes&metriccategoryname=GenericMeasurements&metricname=WatchCacheLag) and InformerCacheLag compare `apiserver_watch_cache_resource_version` against the global `etcd_debugging_mvcc_current_revision`.

When a resource has no writes while other resources mutate, its watch cache RV stays at the last write until an etcd bookmark arrives. Because etcd bookmarks are infrequent, P99 lag is inflated idle phases (see graph below for services. The flat 0s at beginning and end are the only time services are changed, and sawtooth happens during times without writes.)

![Watch cache delay sawtooth during idle resource phases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jefftree/kubernetes/issue-assets/watch_cache_lag_services.png)

We should record the last written storage revision per resource (e.g. `apiserver_storage_resource_version{group, resource}`) on successful writes in [etcd3/store.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go) and compare `apiserver_watch_cache_resource_version` against that metric instead of the global etcd revision.

title: kube-scheduler waits indefinitely when GenericWorkload is enabled but its API is disabled
body:
## What happened?

Enabling `GenericWorkload=true` on the control-plane components without enabling `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1` on kube-apiserver leaves kube-scheduler running but unready. Scheduling is blocked for ordinary Pods, even when no Workloads or PodGroups have been created.

The API server starts successfully and passes `/readyz`. Scheduling API discovery only advertises `scheduling.k8s.io/v1`, and `/apis/scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1/podgroups` returns 404.

The scheduler repeatedly logs:

```text
"Failed to watch" err="failed to list *v1beta1.PodGroup: the server could not find the requested resource"
```

Its `/readyz?verbose` endpoint returns HTTP 500:

```text
[+]leaderElection ok
[+]shutdown ok
[-]sched-handler-sync failed: reason withheld
readyz check failed
```

In an isolated single-node kind cluster, kube-apiserver and kube-controller-manager were `1/1 Running`, but kube-scheduler was `0/1 Running`. CoreDNS, kindnet, kube-proxy, and local-path-provisioner remained Pending with no assigned node. kind timed out waiting for the node to become Ready.

Kube-controller-manager also repeatedly logged the missing-PodGroup API error, although the manager process itself passed readiness.

## What did you expect to happen?

Most rebases we never have to coordinate the merge of changes for kubeapiserver with the feature gate.
This seems to be a potential issue for upgrades.

## Discussion Questions

Should we handle the API not being enabled gracefully and fall back even if feature gate is enabled?

## How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use a Kubernetes build whose GenericWorkload scheduler consumes PodGroups through `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1`.

Create `generic-workload.yaml`:

```yaml
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
featureGates:
  GenericWorkload: true
nodes:
- role: control-plane
```

Build a kind node image from the Kubernetes source revision to test, then create an isolated cluster:

```sh
kind build node-image --type source --image kindest/node:generic-workload-test .
kind create cluster \
  --name generic-workload-repro \
  --image kindest/node:generic-workload-test \
  --config generic-workload.yaml \
  --kubeconfig ./generic-workload.kubeconfig \
  --retain --wait 60s
export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/generic-workload.kubeconfig"
```

## Anything else we need to know?

### Control cases and workaround

| GenericWorkload | Scheduling v1beta1 API served | Scheduler result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enabled | No | HTTP 500 readiness; ordinary Pods remain unscheduled |
| Enabled | Yes | HTTP 200 readiness; waiting Pods are scheduled |
| Disabled | No | HTTP 200 readiness |

All three combinations were checked in the isolated cluster. Adding only this kube-apiserver flag allowed the existing scheduler to finish startup and acquire its leader lease without restarting the scheduler:

```text
--runtime-config=scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1=true
```

For a new kind cluster, add this top-level setting alongside `featureGates`:

```yaml
runtimeConfig:
  scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1: "true"
```

### Source analysis

- `pkg/controlplane/instance.go` disables `scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1` by default.
- `pkg/registry/scheduling/rest/storage_scheduling.go` requires both API-resource enablement and the feature gate before installing PodGroup storage.
- `pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go` registers the v1beta1 PodGroup informer whenever `GenericWorkload` is enabled, without checking API availability.
- `cmd/kube-scheduler/app/server.go` waits for informer cache synchronization before completing startup and entering scheduling. Repeated 404s prevent the PodGroup informer from synchronizing; there is no configuration-specific timeout or diagnostic.
- The PodGroup protection controller and resource claim controller also wait for PodGroup cache synchronization when this feature is enabled.

## AI assistance disclosure

AI assistance was used to reproduce the behavior in an isolated cluster, analyze the relevant Kubernetes source paths, and draft this issue.

title: kube-scheduler: (Composite)PodGroup update event handlers don't distinguish a real update from a coalesced delete+create
body:
### What happened?

An informer can deliver a delete of a PodGroup (PG) / CompositePodGroup (CPG) followed by a create of an object with the same namespace/name as a single `UpdateFunc(old, new)` call. This happens whenever both operations fall into a watch gap and the reflector relists (`DeltaFIFO.Replace`): the handler sees an update whose old and new have different UIDs, and the scheduler never observes the intermediate deletion. Because the two objects are unrelated, anything that is only immutable within one object's lifetime can differ between them: `creationTimestamp`, `parentCompositePodGroupName`, `priority`, etc.

`Scheduler.updatePodGroup` and `Scheduler.updateCompositePodGroup` methods don't distinguish that case from a real in-place update. They unconditionally call `Cache.UpdateGenericPodGroup`, `SchedulingQueue.UpdateGenericPodGroup` and `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue` with an Update event, and every one of those callees is written under the assumption that only mutable fields changed.

### What did you expect to happen?

The update handlers should recognise `oldObj.UID != newObj.UID` and process the event as a delete of the old object followed by an add of the new one. Everything downstream of the update path can then keep assuming it is looking at the same object with only mutable fields changed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Call `sched.updatePodGroup(oldPG, newPG)` where `newPG` has a different UID, a later `creationTimestamp` and a different `parentCompositePodGroupName`, then inspect the cache hierarchy, the `workloadForest` and the root QueuedPodGroupInfo in the queue.

### Anything else we need to know?

Sketch of a prospective fix:

```go
func (sched *Scheduler) updatePodGroup(oldObj, newObj any) {
	...
	if oldPG.UID != newPG.UID {
		// The informer coalesced a delete and a re-create of a PodGroup with the same
		// name into one update. Replay it as such, so that the cache, the workload
		// forest and the queued hierarchy never see "immutable" fields change in place.
		sched.deletePodGroup(oldPG)
		sched.addPodGroup(newPG)
		return
	}
	if oldPG.ResourceVersion == newPG.ResourceVersion {
		return
	}
	...
}
```

and the analogous one in `updateCompositePodGroup`. Note that the `EventHandlingLatency` observation in that branch should probably be attributed to the Delete/Add labels rather than Update.

### Kubernetes version

`master` @ 137705d1d2709dbe645e26a5541827eec8c174f7. Affects every release with the `PodGroup` / `CompositePodGroup` event handlers.

The one exception (cpu-manager [2106490733216141312](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager/2106490733216141312)) was a truncated CNI tarball during setup, which looks unrelated.

Possible fixes:

1. Move these jobs to a zone or region with n2d capacity. This needs a change to the test-infra job config.
2. Make `test/e2e_node/remote/gce/gce_runner.go` retry in other zones of the same region when it gets `ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED`.

The runner also tries to delete an instance with an empty name after a failed create (`Deleting instance ""` → `could not parse resource []`). It's harmless, but it clutters the log.

body:
### Which jobs are failing?

- ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-e2e-containerd-ec2
- ci-containerd-node-arm64-e2e-serial-ec2

### Which tests are failing?

Essentially every test that starts a pod on the Amazon Linux 2023 (arm64) node. For example:

In the NodeConformance job, the AL2023 node gets about 206 failures (all timeouts) before the 4h test timeout kills the run. The Ubuntu 26.04 node in the same jobs passes all tests.

### Since when has it been failing?

- ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-e2e-containerd-ec2:
  - last pass: 2026-10-09 17:23 UTC ([2108609096054738944](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-e2e-containerd-ec2/2108609096054738944))

- ci-containerd-node-arm64-e2e-serial-ec2:

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-kubernetes-node-arm64-e2e-containerd-ec2 , https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-containerd#ci-containerd-node-arm64-e2e-serial-ec2

### Reason for failure (if possible)

The runc binary in the arm64 containerd-main tarball no longer runs on AL2023, so every pod sandbox on that node fails to start.

Kubelet events:

```
Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to start sandbox "...": failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed: unable to retrieve OCI runtime error (open /run/containerd/io.containerd.runtime.v2.task/k8s.io/<id>/log.json: no such file or directory): /home/containerd/usr/local/sbin/runc did not terminate successfully: exit status 1
```

The containerd shim log has the real error:

```
/home/containerd/usr/local/sbin/runc: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.38' not found (required by /home/containerd/usr/local/sbin/runc)
```

AL2023 ships glibc 2.34. Inspecting `gs://k8s-staging-cri-tools/containerd/main/containerd-cni-2.4.0-92-g92f321c8d.linux-arm64.tar.gz`:

- `usr/local/sbin/runc` is dynamically linked (libc, libseccomp) and requires `__isoc23_strtol@GLIBC_2.38`.
- `.comment` says `GCC: (Debian 14.2.0-19) 14.2.0`, i.e. Debian trixie.
- The amd64 tarball's runc only requires `GLIBC_2.34`, so amd64 jobs are unaffected for now.

Timeline:

1. kubernetes/test-infra#37979 ("bump kubekins-e2e to debian trixie") merged 2026-10-09 10:11 UTC.
2. Autobump kubernetes/test-infra@ba8872e06f (15:06 UTC) moved `ci-containerd-arm64-build` to `kubekins-e2e:v20261009-d7b232c8fe-master`.
3. The 18:00 UTC `ci-containerd-arm64-build` run rebuilt the tarball in that image. The first failing e2e runs follow it.

The tarball is republished under the same filename on every build, even when the containerd commit hasn't changed. So passing and failing runs both report containerd `2.4.0-84-g3ea5bdbfb`, but the binaries differ.

Ruled out:

- The AMI (`ami-0ae8605ed708e3c3e`) is the same in passing and failing runs.
- The kubelet range `ef06af9b9d0..031bf130d6f` contains no relevant changes.

### Anything else we need to know?

Possible fixes:

1. Short term: pin `ci-containerd-arm64-build` (in `config/jobs/containerd/containerd/containerd-periodic-jobs.yaml`) to the last bookworm-based kubekins image (`v20261006-705822de48-master`) until a proper fix lands.
2. Longer term: build runc statically, or against an older glibc, in containerd's `test/build.sh`, so the test tarball doesn't depend on the builder image's glibc. The amd64 build will hit the same problem when its base moves to trixie.

title: CRI-sourced CPU and PSI _seconds_total counters lose sub-second precision vs cAdvisor
body: ## What happened? When container/pod metrics are sourced from the CRI (`ListPodSandboxMetrics`, e.g. with the `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature), the fractional `*_seconds_total` counters only ever advance in **whole-second** increments. Two families are affected: the CPU time counters (`container_cpu_*_seconds_total`) and the PSI pressure-stall counters (`container_pressure_*_seconds_total`). Sub-second time is lost in both. Because the counter only moves in integer steps, `rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[1m])` returns values quantized to multiples of `1/60` (`0, 0.0167, 0.0333, 0.0667, ...`), producing stair-step / square-wave graphs instead of a smooth signal. (With an `N`-second rate window the step is `1/N`; a 1m window gives `1/60 ≈ 0.0167`.) It is most visible on low-CPU containers, where the quantization dominates the signal. Credits to @nemric for finding the issue and sharing the following data from their cluster: with cAdvisor with cri-o ### Root cause The CRI `Metric` message carries its value as a `UInt64Value` (uint64): ```proto message Metric { ... UInt64Value value = 5; } ``` kubelet's CRI metrics collector emits that value **verbatim** as the Prometheus sample, with no per-metric unit conversion (`pkg/kubelet/metrics/collectors/cri_metrics.go`): ```go pm, err := metrics.NewConstMetric(desc, typ, float64(m.GetValue().Value), m.LabelValues...) ``` A `_seconds_total` counter expressed as a `uint64` **cannot represent fractional seconds**. A producer converting the cgroup counter to seconds must therefore use integer division and truncate: CPU usage as `ns / 1e9`, PSI stall time as `µs / 1e6`. Either way the fraction is gone before it ever reaches kubelet. By contrast, cAdvisor carries the *same* cgroup nanosecond counter as a `float64` and keeps full precision: ```go // cadvisor metrics/prometheus.go value: float64(s.Cpu.Usage.Total) / float64(time.Second) ``` So switching the metric source from cAdvisor to CRI silently **regresses** CPU-metric precision, even though both read the identical kernel counter. ## What did you expect to happen? CRI-sourced `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` to carry sub-second precision like cAdvisor, so `rate()` produces a smooth, accurate signal. ## How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. A node whose container metrics are provided via CRI (e.g. CRI-O) and consumed by kubelet (CRI-sourced container metrics). 2. Query, over a window with some low-CPU containers: ```promql sum(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{image!="", container!=""}[1m])) by (container, id) ``` 3. Observe series locked to multiples of `1/60` (≈0.0167) rather than continuous values. Note: this is **not** a data-volume problem; more samples or a longer window cannot recover it. A longer window only shrinks the quantization step to `1/window`; the counter itself only ever has integer-second values, so there is nothing to interpolate. ## Anything else we need to know? **Affected metrics** (all fractional `_seconds_total` counters routed through CRI `ListPodSandboxMetrics`): CPU time (cgroup nanoseconds truncated to integer seconds): - `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` - `container_cpu_user_seconds_total` - `container_cpu_system_seconds_total` - `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total` PSI pressure-stall time (cgroup microseconds truncated to integer seconds): - `container_pressure_cpu_stalled_seconds_total` - `container_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total` - `container_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total` - `container_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total` - `container_pressure_io_stalled_seconds_total` - `container_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total` The PSI counters are hit **harder**: pressure-stall times are frequently well under a second, so truncation flattens many of them to a constant `0` rather than merely stair-stepping. (The same limitation applies to any CRI metric whose natural unit is fractional.) **Proposed fix (additive and backward-compatible).** Add a `double` carrier to the CRI `Metric` message: ```proto // DoubleValue is the wrapper of double. message DoubleValue { double value = 1; } message Metric { ... UInt64Value value = 5; // kept for backward compatibility DoubleValue double_value = 6; // NEW: carries fractional metric values } ``` - **Producers** set `double_value` for fractional metrics and continue populating `value` (truncated/rounded) so older kubelets keep working. - **Consumer** (kubelet) prefers `double_value` when present, else falls back to `value`: ```go val := float64(m.GetValue().GetValue()) if dv := m.GetDoubleValue(); dv != nil { val = dv.GetValue() } pm, err := metrics.NewConstMetric(desc, typ, val, m.LabelValues...) ``` - No change needed in cAdvisor (it is already correct and the reference behavior). **Version-skew handling:** the new field is additive, so new-producer/old-kubelet and old-producer/new-kubelet both degrade gracefully to the existing integer `value`. Using `DoubleValue` as a message wrapper (like `UInt64Value`) gives a nil-vs-set presence check, avoiding ambiguity between "unset" and "a real 0.0". ## Kubernetes version ``` latest ``` ## Cloud provider / Environment - Container runtime: CRI-O `latest` /sig node /kind bug

title: StatefulSet maxUnavailable counts unavailable pods below partition and can block partitioned rolling updates
body:
### What happened?

With `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` enabled, a partitioned rolling update can stall when an unavailable pod sits **below** `partition`, even though that pod is intentionally held on the old revision and is outside the update range.

Example:
- `replicas: 5`
- `podManagementPolicy: Parallel`
- `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 2`
- `updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable: 1`
- pods `2..4` healthy on the old revision (should be eligible to update)
- pod `1` unavailable (NotReady / crashloop)

Observed: the controller does not delete/update pods `2..4`. The unavailable pod below the partition appears to consume the entire `maxUnavailable` budget, so the canary/update range never progresses.

This matches current unit coverage, e.g. in `TestStatefulSetControlRollingUpdateWithMaxUnavailableAndUnavailableStalePod`:
- `Parallel/5 replicas partition=2: unavailable pod below partition (#1) consumes budget, no update`

Related prior fix for unavailable pods **on the old revision in the update path**: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/137409. That fix does not address unavailable pods **outside** the partition range blocking updates **inside** it.

### What did you expect to happen?

For a partitioned update, unavailable pods with ordinal `< partition` should not prevent progress on ordinals `>= partition`.

Proposed rule to confirm:
- Count unavailable pods toward `maxUnavailable` only for ordinals in the update range (`>= partition`), **or** otherwise ensure a partitioned Parallel update can still make progress when unavailability is only below the partition.

`partition` exists specifically to hold lower ordinals unchanged during canary/phased rollouts; counting those held pods against the update budget makes canary + `maxUnavailable` brittle.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a StatefulSet with 5 replicas, `podManagementPolicy: Parallel`, RollingUpdate with `partition: 2`, `maxUnavailable: 1`.
2. Make pod ordinal `1` NotReady (or otherwise unavailable).
3. Change the pod template to trigger a new revision.
4. Observe that pods `2..4` are not updated while pod `1` remains unavailable.

Alternatively, the existing unit test case above already encodes this behavior against `updateStatefulSetAfterInvariantEstablished` in `pkg/controller/statefulset`.

Happy to add/adjust a focused unit test alongside a fix if this semantics change is accepted.

### Anything else we need to know?

**API / docs tension**

Current API godoc for `RollingUpdateStatefulSetStrategy.MaxUnavailable` says the count applies to all pods in `0 .. Replicas-1`. So today’s behavior is consistent with that wording and with existing tests.

**Why still filing**

KEP-961’s update loop is centered on the range from `Replicas-1` down to `partition`. For canary use, counting pods below `partition` against the burst budget is surprising and can silently stall the update.

**Explicit ask for sig-apps / STS reviewers**

1. Should `maxUnavailable` accounting for Parallel rolling updates be scoped to ordinals `>= partition`?
2. Should OrderedReady keep today’s stricter whole-set counting for compatibility?

I can work on the fix + tests once the intended semantics are confirmed.

title: Disruption controller: consider enqueueing all affected PDBs on pod events (label changes + overlaps)
body:
### What happened?

Opening this for sig-apps consideration around which PodDisruptionBudget(s) the disruption controller enqueues from pod events.

Today, pod add/update/delete go through `getPdbForPod`, which returns a **single** PDB from the pod’s **current** labels. That has two related consequences:

**1) Pod label changes do not wake the previously matching PDB**

`updatePod` ignores the old pod object and only looks up PDBs for the new labels. If a pod moves from selector A → selector B, PDB-A is not enqueued from that update and its status can stay stale until resync or another event.

**2) When multiple PDBs match one pod, only one is enqueued**

This looks intentional: `getPdbForPod` warns (`MultiplePodDisruptionBudgets` / “Chose … arbitrarily”) and returns `pdbs[0]`. Overlaps are not forbidden; only one matching PDB is woken on the pod event, so siblings can stay stale until resync. That choice is not a documented stable order (e.g. by name).

Not proposing to ban overlapping selectors — only asking whether “pick one for enqueue” is still the right tradeoff next to the label-change gap.

### What did you expect to happen?

For discussion:

1. On pod update, should we enqueue PDBs matching **old** and **new** labels?
2. On overlaps, should we enqueue **all** matching PDBs (keep the Warning)?
3. Or is today’s single-PDB / current-labels-only enqueue still preferred?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**Label change:** PDB-A selects `app=a`; relabel a pod to `app=b`. PDB-A is not reconciled from that update.

**Overlaps:** two PDBs match the same pod; on pod add/update/delete only one is enqueued (Warning may fire).

### Anything else we need to know?

Related: `pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go` (`updatePod`, `getPdbForPod`).

Happy to help implement or add tests if sig-apps wants this direction; until then treating this as a behavior discussion rather than a clear regression.

title: mount-utils: kernel octal escapes (\040, \011, \134) are not decoded, so GetMountRefs returns paths that do not exist
body:
### What happened

`staging/src/k8s.io/mount-utils` reads `/proc/mounts` without decoding the kernel's octal escapes
(`\040` space, `\011` tab, `\134` backslash). A mount on `/mnt/a b` is listed as `/mnt/a\040b`;
`GetMountRefs` then looks for the literal path `/mnt/a\040b`, which does not exist.

Proven on a privileged Linux bind mount:

* `GetMountRefs("/mnt/a b")` returned the escaped path and nothing for the real path;
* when a decoy directory literally named `/mnt/a\040b` exists, the lookup matches the decoy.

Relevant code: `mount_helper_unix.go:115,137,146`, `mount_linux.go:741,748-749`.

### Impact

Hardening rather than a pod-facing security issue: pod-provided paths come from DNS labels, UIDs
and hashes, so a pod cannot create a path with a space. A node-level actor or a PV `local.path`
would be needed.

### Proposed fix

Decode the escapes when parsing the mount table — the dependency tree already has a correct
implementation (`moby/sys/mountinfo`), which this package already uses elsewhere.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-storage-bugs

title: StorageVersionMigration: a failed migration removes old versions from the CRD's status.storedVersions
body:
### What happened?

When a StorageVersionMigration (SVM) for a custom resource **fails**, the migration runner in kube-controller-manager still rewrites the CRD's `status.storedVersions` to contain only the current storage version. That's the same thing it does after a successful migration, even though some objects are still stored in the old version.

`storedVersions` is the guard that stops a version from being removed from `spec.versions` while objects may still be stored in it. KEP-4192 says the field is trimmed once the migration is **Completed**, and then "users (or management tools such as operators) are at liberty to proceed with removal of the old API versions from the CRD, if they wish, without any risk of data loss." After a failed migration the old version can be removed too. Once it's removed, the objects that were never migrated can't be decoded, and **LIST of the whole resource fails**.

The cause is in `finishCRDMigration` in `pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator/migrationrunner.go`. `cleanupCRD` calls it for both succeeded and failed SVMs. The `storedVersions` update is gated only on the CRD generation being unchanged (`canUpdateStoredVersions`), not on `success`:

```go
var canUpdateStoredVersions bool
if migratingCond != nil && migratingCond.ObservedGeneration == crd.Generation {
	canUpdateStoredVersions = true
}
...
if canUpdateStoredVersions {
	// Wipe out all stored versions that we have migrated off of ...
	applyConfig.Status.WithStoredVersions(<storage version>)
}
```

The unit test case "Migration failed: CRD condition updated" in `migrationrunner_test.go` currently expects `storedVersions: ["v2"]` after a failed migration.

A migration fails with objects left unmigrated whenever the migrator's no-op patch of an object gets a non-retriable error. The message is `N/M not yet migrated. migration encountered unhandled error: ...`. One example is an admission policy or webhook that rejects updates to some objects.

End-to-end result against a real kube-apiserver, etcd and kube-controller-manager (integration test, see below):

```
SVM failed: 1/2 not yet migrated. migration encountered unhandled error: testcrds.stable.example.com "cr2" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'freeze-cr2' with binding 'freeze-cr2' denied request: cr2 is frozen
CRD StorageMigrating condition: reason=MigrationFailed message="The migration has failed"
CRD status.storedVersions after FAILED migration: [v2]
cr2 still stored at v1 in etcd: true
removing v1 from spec.versions: err=<nil>
GET cr2 at v2 after removing v1: err=Internal error occurred: StorageError: corrupt object, Code: 7, Key: /stable.example.com/testcrds/default/cr2, ResourceVersion: 0, AdditionalErrorMsg: object not decodable revision=218: request to convert CR from an invalid group/version: stable.example.com/v1
LIST at v2 after removing v1: err=storage is (re)initializing: failed to list <unspecified>: failed to read one or more testcrds.stable.example.com from the storage: StorageError: corrupt object, ... request to convert CR from an invalid group/version: stable.example.com/v1
```


### What did you expect to happen?

After a failed migration, `status.storedVersions` keeps every version that may still be stored, so removing `v1` from the CRD is rejected. Only a successful migration should trim it, as KEP-4192 describes.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a 1.37 cluster (StorageVersionMigrator is GA and enabled by default):

1. Create a CRD `testcrds.stable.example.com` with a single version `v1` (served, storage), and create two objects `cr1` and `cr2`.
2. Create a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and binding (`validationActions: [Deny]`) that rejects `UPDATE` of `testcrds` when `object.metadata.name == 'cr2'` (expression `object.metadata.name != 'cr2'`).
3. Add `v2` to the CRD and make it the storage version (`v1` stays served). `status.storedVersions` is now `["v1", "v2"]`.
4. Create a StorageVersionMigration for `{group: stable.example.com, resource: testcrds}`.
5. The SVM ends with `Failed=True` ("1/2 not yet migrated"), yet the CRD's `status.storedVersions` becomes `["v2"]` and `cr2` is still stored as `v1` in etcd.
6. Removing `v1` from `spec.versions` is now accepted. Afterwards, `GET cr2` and `LIST testcrds` fail with `corrupt object ... request to convert CR from an invalid group/version: stable.example.com/v1`.

I reproduced this with an integration test in `test/integration/storageversionmigrator` that does exactly these steps (PR to follow).


### Anything else we need to know?

Fix (PR to follow): only update `storedVersions` when the migration succeeded, and correct the unit test expectation. Fixing it doesn't restore `storedVersions` on clusters where a failed migration already trimmed it.

title: client-go connrotation: nil dial function panics despite documented default
body:
### What happened?

`connrotation.NewDialerWithTracker` documents that a nil `DialFunc` uses a default network dialer. Instead it stores nil in `Dialer.dial`. `DialContext` calls that nil function and panics before attempting any connection. `NewDialer(nil)` has the same behavior because it delegates to `NewDialerWithTracker(nil, nil)`.

On current master (`4e7c871bf42b2bcb26f6bbe48618cb4c3ffde264`), a standalone `go run` of the reproducer below prints `panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`. No cluster or network service is needed to trigger it.

### What did you expect to happen?

A nil custom dial function should use the documented default dialer and return an ordinary connection error (or a connection on a reachable address), without panicking. A caller-supplied dial function must keep its existing behavior.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import "k8s.io/client-go/util/connrotation"

func main() {
    _, _ = connrotation.NewDialer(nil).Dial("tcp", "127.0.0.1:1")
}
```

Run from the Kubernetes repository with `go run repro.go`. The panic occurs at `connrotation.go` in `DialContext` when it invokes `d.dial`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Relevant SIG: API Machinery. The constructor comment explicitly promises a default dialer when `dial` is nil, so this is an implementation error rather than a proposed API change. I found no matching issue or active PR for the nil-dialer path.

title: kubelet deletes a rotated container log even when writing its compressed copy failed
body:
### What happened?

When the kubelet compresses a rotated container log (`containerLogManager.compressLog` in `pkg/kubelet/logs/container_log_manager.go`), it ignores the errors from closing the gzip writer and the output file:

```go
if _, err := io.Copy(w, r); err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("failed to compress %q to %q: %w", log, tmpLog, err)
}
// The archive needs to be closed before renaming, otherwise an error will occur on Windows.
w.Close()
f.Close()
compressedLog := log + compressSuffix
if err := c.osInterface.Rename(tmpLog, compressedLog); err != nil { ... }
// Remove old log file.
r.Close()
if err := c.osInterface.Remove(log); err != nil { ... }
```

`gzip.Writer.Close` writes the remaining compressed data and the gzip trailer. If that write fails, for example with `ENOSPC` on a node whose log filesystem is full (when rotation is busiest), `compressLog` still renames the incomplete archive into place, **deletes the original log**, and returns success. The log content is lost and the `.gz` left behind is corrupt.

Reproduced by limiting the file size (`RLIMIT_FSIZE`) so the gzip header fits but the compressed data written by `Close` doesn't:

```
compressLog returned: <nil>
original log still present: false
compressed log size: 16 bytes (original 2250 bytes)
decompressing the .gz: 5 bytes, err=unexpected EOF
```

### What did you expect to happen?

If the compressed copy can't be written completely, `compressLog` returns an error, removes the temporary file and keeps the original rotated log, so it can be compressed again later.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unit test in `pkg/kubelet/logs` (Linux):

```go
log := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "0.log.20260101-000000")
os.WriteFile(log, []byte(strings.Repeat("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z stdout F log line\n", 50)), 0640)

var lim syscall.Rlimit
syscall.Getrlimit(syscall.RLIMIT_FSIZE, &lim)
orig := lim
lim.Cur = 16 // the gzip header fits, the data flushed by Close doesn't
syscall.Setrlimit(syscall.RLIMIT_FSIZE, &lim)
err := (&containerLogManager{osInterface: container.RealOS{}}).compressLog(log)
syscall.Setrlimit(syscall.RLIMIT_FSIZE, &orig)
// err == nil, the original log is gone, and log+".gz" is a truncated 16-byte gzip file
```

On a node, the same happens when the filesystem holding `/var/log/pods` runs out of space while the kubelet compresses a rotated log.

### Anything else we need to know?

Fix: check the errors from `w.Close()` and `f.Close()` before renaming the archive and removing the original. I'll send a PR with a regression test.

#81132 / #139700 are about making `rotateLatestLog` atomic. This is a separate problem in `compressLog`.

/area kubelet

title: [scheduler] Topology placement misses conflicts when a domain value is empty
body:
### What kind of issue is this?

/kind bug
/sig scheduling

### What happened?

The topology-aware workload scheduling plugin can fail to detect conflicting topology domains among already-scheduled Pods when one domain has an empty label value.

In `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/topologyaware/topology_placement.go`, `getScheduledPodsTopologyDomain` initializes `topologyDomain` to an empty string and uses `topologyDomain != ""` to determine whether a domain has already been recorded.

However, Kubernetes permits empty label values. If the first scheduled Pod is on a node with `topology=""` and the next is on a node with `topology="d1"`, the conflict check is skipped for the second Pod. The function returns `"d1"` instead of an error.

This can allow the scheduler to continue placement generation even though the already-scheduled Pods violate the PodGroup's single-topology-domain constraint.

### What did you expect to happen?

The plugin should detect conflicting topology domain values, including conflicts involving an empty string, and return an error.

### How can we reproduce it?

Add a case to `TestGeneratePlacements` in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/topologyaware/topology_placement_test.go` with:

- A PodGroup whose topology constraint key is `topology`.
- An already-scheduled Pod on `node2`, where `topology=""`.
- Another already-scheduled Pod on `node3`, where `topology="d1"`.
- An expected status of `fwk.Error`.

Run:

`go test ./pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/topologyaware -run '^TestGeneratePlacements$' -count=1`

I reproduced the failure locally in both test variants, with CompositePodGroup disabled and enabled. Both reported `expected status Error, got <nil>`.

### Additional context

The likely cause is using the empty string as both a valid domain value and an uninitialized sentinel. Tracking whether a domain has been seen separately from its value would avoid this ambiguity.

title: [Bug] PodGroup preemptionPolicy rejects when PriorityClass: Never
body:
### What happened?

When creating a `PodGroup` that references a `PriorityClass` with `preemptionPolicy: Never` it gets rejected by priority admission if the `PodGroup` doesn't set its own `spec.preemptionPolicy`.

API defaulting sets the omitted field to `PreemptLowerPriority` before admission runs. Priority admission then derives `Never` from the referenced `PriorityClass` and rejects the mismatch. Even though the user did not give any conflicting value.

`Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "pg-set-preemption-policy.yaml": podgroups.scheduling.k8s.io "test-pg" is forbidden: the string value of PreemptionPolicy (PreemptLowerPriority) must not be provided in pod group spec; priority admission controller computed Never from the given PriorityClass name`
Original discussion: https://github.com/kuberay-project/kuberay/pull/5266#discussion_r4070093850 CC: @machichima @marosset 

### What did you expect to happen?

When  `spec.preemptionPolicy`  is not set, priority admission should populate it from the referenced `PriorityClass`. For this example, the `PodGroup` should be admitted with  `preemptionPolicy: Never`.
Explicitly set fields that conflict with the PriorityClass should still continue to be rejected.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

•  `GenericWorkload=true`
•  `PodGroupPreemptionPolicy=true` 
•  `scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha3`  enabled
• The Priority admission plugin enabled

Create the `PriorityClass`:
```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: podgroup-no-preemption
value: 1000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: Never
```
Create a PodGroup, and do not set `spec.preemptionPolicy`:
```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: PodGroup
metadata:
  name: preemption-policy-repro
  namespace: default
spec:
  priorityClassName: podgroup-no-preemption
  schedulingPolicy:
    gang:
      minCount: 1
```
Creation is rejected with the error above. Explicitly adding `spec.preemptionPolicy: Never `avoids the error.

### Anything else we need to know?

Looking into it:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/scheduling/v1alpha3/defaults.go#L31-L38: `SetDefaults_PodGroup` defaults nil to be `PreemptLowerPriority` when the feature gate is enabled
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L224-L237
Priority admission derives the policy from PriorityClass and rejects a non-nil

This also exists for CompositePodGroup

title: audit: truncate backend marks events sent to other audit backends as truncated
body:
### What happened?

The truncate audit backend makes a shallow copy of an oversized event, removes the request and response objects from the copy, and adds the `audit.k8s.io/truncated: "true"` annotation. The copy shares its `Annotations` map with the original event, so the original gets the annotation too (`truncate()` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/audit/truncate/truncate.go`).

The original is the event the other audit backends receive, and the apiserver reuses it for the later stages of the same request. With `--audit-log-truncate-enabled` and an audit webhook, every event the log backend truncates reaches the webhook complete, request object included, but annotated as truncated. Later stages of that request are annotated as truncated in all backends.

### What did you expect to happen?

Only the truncated copy has the annotation. The original event and what the other backends receive are unchanged.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In package `truncate`, send an oversized event through `audit.Union(truncate(fake), fake)`:

```go
event := &auditinternal.Event{
	Level:         auditinternal.LevelRequest,
	RequestObject: &runtime.Unknown{Raw: []byte("\"" + strings.Repeat("A", int(defaultConfig.MaxEventSize)) + "\"")},
	Annotations:   map[string]string{"authorization.k8s.io/decision": "allow"},
}
var truncated, other *auditinternal.Event
b := audit.Union(
	NewBackend(&fake.Backend{OnRequest: func(ev []*auditinternal.Event) { truncated = ev[0] }}, defaultConfig, auditv1.SchemeGroupVersion),
	&fake.Backend{OnRequest: func(ev []*auditinternal.Event) { other = ev[0] }},
)
b.ProcessEvents(event)
```

`truncated` has the annotation and no request object, as expected. `other` and `event` also have the annotation, while still holding the request object.

### Anything else we need to know?

The annotation write has been shared with the original since the backend was added in 2018. I'll send a PR that clones the annotations before adding it, with a regression test.
